d-f-malan: Daniël François Malan was born on 22 May 1874 in Riebeek-West in the Cape Colony, the fifth of nine children of a wealthy farmer and clergyman of the same name and of Ana Magdalena du Toit. The family descended from a French Huguenot refugee, Jacques Malan from Provence, who reached the Cape before 1689. He took a degree in music and science at Victoria College, Stellenbosch, and trained for the ministry of the Dutch Reformed Church at the Stellenbosch seminary, also gaining a master's degree in philosophy. In 1900 he left for the University of Utrecht, where he obtained a doctorate in divinity in 1905.

Ordained after his return, Malan served as assistant minister in Heidelberg, Transvaal, then in Montagu from 1906 to 1912 and in Graaff-Reinet until 1915. He fought for the acceptance of Afrikaans and was a founding member of the Afrikaanse Taal- en Kultuurvereniging in 1930. In 1915 he gave up the ministry to edit a new Cape newspaper, De Burger, later Die Burger, which he used as a springboard into politics; he also became the Cape leader of the National Party.

Elected to Parliament for Calvinia in 1918, he was Minister of the Interior, Education and Public Health under J. B. M. Hertzog from 1924 to 1933. When Hertzog's party fused with Jan Smuts's South African Party in 1934, Malan and 19 other members formed the Purified National Party, which he led in opposition for 14 years. He opposed South African participation in the World War II, and after the split in the United Party in 1939 the defectors joined his party, strengthening his position.

Malan defeated Smuts and the United Party in the 1948 general election and served as the fourth prime minister of South Africa until 1954. The National Party implemented apartheid, the system of racial segregation laws, and its foundations were firmly laid during his six and a half years in office.

Under the Privy Council Appeals Act of 1950, South Africans lost the right of appeal to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in London. On 24 February 1953 he was granted dictatorial powers to oppose black and Indian anti-apartheid movements. He resigned in 1954, aged 80, hoping that Nicolaas Havenga would succeed him, but J. G. Strijdom defeated Havenga. Malan died at his home, Môrewag, in Stellenbosch on 7 February 1959.
da-lat: Da Lat stands 1,500 metres above sea level on the Langbian Plateau, in the southern part of the Central Highlands of Vietnam. Its subtropical highland climate contrasts with the tropical lowlands elsewhere in southern Vietnam. The average temperature is 14 to 23 °C, mist covers the valleys almost all year, and the town is nicknamed the City of Eternal Spring. The name Đà Lạt derives from the language of the local ethnic group Lạt and means the stream or water of the Lạt.

In the 1890s explorers in the area, among them the bacteriologist Alexandre Yersin, asked the French governor-general Paul Doumer to create a resort centre in the highlands, then part of the French colony of Cochinchina, and he agreed. Étienne Tardif, a member of the road-building expedition of 1898-99, proposed the present site. The first hotel was built in 1907, and Ernest Hébrard carried out the urban planning, with a health complex, golf course, parks and schools but no industry. Europeans came to escape the heat of the coast, and boarding schools taught children from the whole of Indochina. In the 1920s and 1930s there were ideas of making it a summer or administrative capital of French Indochina, a project Governor-General Jean Decoux supported.

After the French withdrawal Da Lat remained a resort in South Vietnam, and the South Vietnamese National Military Academy took over the former French academy there in 1954. The city was little affected by the Vietnam War, apart from a battle between 31 January and 11 February 1968, during the Tet Offensive.

French colonial influence marks the architecture. Da Lat Railway Station, built in 1938 in Art Deco style, was recognised as a national historical monument in 2001, and the Lycée Yersin opened in 1927. The third of three mansions linked with the last emperor, Bao Dai, was built in 1933-1938 as his residence and is now a museum. The surrounding highlands supply vegetables, tea, coffee and flowers to the rest of Vietnam.
da-nang: Da Nang is surrounded by mountains to the west and the South China Sea to the east, and the Han River divides the central city. It borders Huế to the north across the Hải Vân Pass, and lies 764 km south of Hanoi and 964 km north of Ho Chi Minh City. Most of its names refer to its position at the mouth of the Hàn River: it was known as Cửa Hàn, Hàn River Estuary, in the Đại Việt period and as Tourane or Turon under the French. Some take Da Nang to be an adaptation of the Cham word da nak, 'opening of a large river'; other Champa researchers propose daknan, 'the large water', or a Raglai word meaning 'river source'.

The city's origins go back to the kingdom of Champa, established in 192 CE, whose sphere at its peak stretched from Huế to Vũng Tàu. Indrapura, at the village of Dong Duong about 50 km from Da Nang, was the Cham capital from about 875 to about 1000. The Cham city of Singhapura, identified with a site at Trà Kiệu, and the valley of Mỹ Sơn also lay in the region.

The Portuguese explorer António de Faria anchored at Da Nang in 1535, and through his influence Portuguese ships began calling more often at Hội An. French and Spanish traders and missionaries landed at Hội An in the 17th and 18th centuries. An American, John White, arrived on 18 June 1819 in the brig Franklin of Salem, Massachusetts, and was told that the country was recovering from devastating wars and that the little produced was already allocated.

In 1847 French vessels sent by Admiral Cécille bombarded the city, ostensibly over the persecution of Roman Catholic missionaries. In August 1858 French troops under Admiral Charles Rigault de Genouilly, on the orders of Napoleon III, landed at Đà Nẵng in the punitive Cochinchina Campaign. During the Vietnam War the air base on the site of the present airport was used by South Vietnamese and United States air forces, and it became one of the busiest in the world, averaging 2,595 aircraft operations a day. The Marble Mountain Air Facility was built there in 1965.

Da Nang is one of Vietnam's centrally governed cities. Before 1997 it was part of Quang Nam–Da Nang province; on 1 January 1997 it was separated from Quảng Nam province as a centrally governed municipality. A reorganisation that took effect on 1 July 2025 formed a new Da Nang by reabsorbing Quảng Nam. Its port, National Route 1 and the North–South Railway make it a transport hub.
dabhol: Dabhol, also written Dabul, is a small seaport town in the Ratnagiri district of Maharashtra. It lies on the northern and southern sides of the Vashishti River, which also flows by the town of Chiplun. Under the Bahmani dynasty the port was known as Mustafabad and later as Hamjabad before it took its present name. From the 14th to the 16th century it was the principal port of the southern Konkan, trading with ports of the Mediterranean Sea, the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf.

The Russian traveller Afanasy Nikitin, who visited India from 1468 to 1474, found Dabhol a large town and extensive seaport, to which horses from Mysore, Arabia and Khorasan were brought for sale, and which had links with all the major ports from India to Ethiopia. In the 15th and 16th centuries it was an opulent Muslim trading centre, first under the Bahmani sultans and later under those of Bijapur. It was the port with the most convenient access to the Bahmani capital at Bidar, and its fortunes rose with that dynasty; at its height it was arguably the most important port between Chaul and Goa.

That prominence made it a target. In December 1508 a Portuguese expeditionary force under Francisco de Almeida bombarded, sacked and razed the town in the Battle of Dabul, a prelude to the Battle of Diu, though the fort was not taken. The Portuguese tried several more times over the following decades to destroy it; at the last recorded attack, in 1571, the governor was Khwaja Ali Shirazi, and 150 men were killed at Dabhol.

The break-up of the Bahmani state into smaller Deccan sultanates hastened the port's decline. As new capitals were built its position was no longer so favourable, and during the 16th century much commerce moved south to the rising port of Rajapur. Shivaji conquered Dabhol around 1660 and annexed it to the new Maratha kingdom. It passed to Sambhaji, who gave it to Khando Ballal Chitnis as a reward for saving him from drowning in a river in Goa.

The Dabhol vatan is still claimed by descendants of the Chitnis family of Satara, although some descendants of the Shirke family argue that it should be theirs. On the southern side of the town, between the villages of Veldur and Ranavi, stands the Dabhol LNG power plant, which was set up by the company Enron.
dachau-concentration-camp: The camp stood on the grounds of an abandoned gunpowder and munitions factory northeast of the medieval town of Dachau, about 16 kilometres northwest of Munich. After the takeover of Bavaria on 9 March 1933, Heinrich Himmler, then Chief of Police in Munich, toured the site to see whether it could hold prisoners in protective custody. It opened on 22 March 1933 with about 200 prisoners, and Himmler announced it as the first concentration camp for political prisoners, able to hold 5,000 people. It remained in operation until April 1945, nearly all of the twelve years of the Nazi regime.

At first the camp held communists, Social Democrats and other opponents of the Nazi Party. Its purpose widened to forced labour and then to the imprisonment of Jews, Romani, Germans and Austrians whom the party regarded as criminals, and finally of foreign nationals from occupied countries. Clergy imprisoned for opposing the regime, mainly Catholic, were also held there. The camp trained guards of the SS-Totenkopfverbände and served as a model for other camps. Its iron gate bore the motto Arbeit macht frei, and forced labour soon became a method of torture and murder.

Over 4,000 Soviet prisoners of war were shot at the SS range at Hebertshausen from 25 November 1941. Hundreds of prisoners suffered and died in medical experiments, among them hypothermia experiments under Sigmund Rascher in which nearly 100 died. From 1944 the camp system grew to include nearly one hundred sub-camps near armaments factories. In April 1945 Himmler forbade handing the camp to the Allies. American forces liberated the main camp on 29 April 1945, and about 10,000 of the roughly 30,000 prisoners were then sick.

After the war the site held SS men awaiting trial, then from 1948 ethnic Germans expelled from eastern Europe, and for a time a United States military base. It closed in 1960. Former prisoners joined to erect a memorial on the site, whose display was reworked in 2003 and follows the path of new arrivals. Two barracks have been rebuilt, the other thirty are marked by low cement curbs filled with pebbles, and visitors may see the crematorium ovens. The memorial site is open to the public.
dacia: Dacia was the land of the Dacians, with its core in Transylvania and stretching to the Danube in the south, the Black Sea in the east and the Tisza in the west, with the Carpathian Mountains in the middle. Its extent varied by period. The Greek writers Herodotus and Thucydides first mention the Getae, a related people of the lower Danube. Ptolemy lists 43 towns in Dacia, 33 of them arguably of Dacian origin; most had the suffix dava, meaning a settlement or village, as in Sucidava and Setidava.

Dacian kings are recorded from the 2nd century BCE, among them Rubobostes, who defeated the Celts in what is now Transylvania, and Oroles. Burebista, a contemporary of Julius Caesar, ruled the Getae and Dacians from 82 to 44 BCE, reorganised the army, conquered the Bastarnae and the Boii, and moved the capital from Argedava to Sarmizegetusa Regia. His kingdom reached its widest extent under him; after he was murdered in 44 BCE it split into four, later five, parts. Stability returned under Duras and later Decebalus, who ruled the Dacians from 87 CE.

A Dacian raid into Moesia in 85 CE began a series of wars with Rome. Cornelius Fuscus was defeated and killed in 87, the Romans won at Tapae in 88, and Domitian made terms by which Decebalus became a client king of Rome. Trajan resumed the conflict in 101 to 102 and again in 105 to 106, aiming, according to the account, to end a treaty seen as humiliating and to take the Dacian gold mines and the treasure of Decebalus.

The Romans razed Sarmizegetusa, and Decebalus took his own life to avoid capture. Trajan marked the victory with the Column of Trajan in Rome. The Romans founded a new capital, Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa, about 40 km away.

Much land remained outside Roman authority, and groups of 'Free Dacians' persisted. Under Aurelian the army and Roman citizens left the province between 271 and 275, and it was reorganised south of the Danube as Dacia Aureliana. Later peoples held the region in turn: the Goths and Carpi, the Huns from 376, the Gepids and then the Avars. Many Dacians within the empire were Romanised, which scholars link to the origin of the Romanians.
dacians: The Dacians spoke the Dacian language, which has a debated relationship to Thracian, and were somewhat influenced by the neighbouring Scythians and by the Celtic invaders of the 4th century BCE. Greek writers called them Getae, and Roman writers Daci or Getae; modern historians often use the name Geto-Dacians. They left no records of their own, so their origins are traced through material culture. From roughly 500 BCE they developed a distinct civilization able to support large centralised kingdoms by the 1st century BCE and the 1st century CE.

According to Herodotus, the Getae were the first people Darius subdued before reaching the Danube. Greek and Roman chroniclers record that the Getae under Dromihete captured the Macedonian general Lysimachus in the 3rd century BCE and released him after a debate in their assembly. Dacian polities were confederacies, united only periodically under kings such as Burebista and Decebalus. Burebista, king from about 70 to 44 BCE, united a large territory, and Julius Caesar contemplated a campaign against him; his state lasted only until his death.

Dacia then became a Roman province, from 106 to 271 or 275 CE, with a new capital at Ulpia Traiana Sarmizegetusa, 40 kilometres from Sarmizegetusa Regia, which the Romans razed. Only about half of Dacia was included. The Carpi, often called Free Dacians, remained outside it.

Dacian society was divided into the aristocracy, the tarabostes, who alone could cover their heads with a felt hat, and the common people, the comati. They farmed, kept bees and livestock, grew vines, made pottery and worked metal, including the gold and silver mines of Transylvania. Their fortified cities used the murus dacicus, a double-skinned stone wall with rubble fill and tie beams. Their characteristic weapon was the falx, a single-edged scythe-like blade that forced the Roman army to adapt its equipment.
dada: Dada developed in the context of the First World War, its aftermath and the Futurist movement. Its principles were first collected in Hugo Ball's Dada Manifesto of 1916, and Ball is seen as the founder. Most art historians trace its origin to the Cabaret Voltaire in Zürich, co-founded by the poet and cabaret singer Emmy Hennings and Ball, and named after Voltaire, whose novel Candide mocked the dogmas of his day. Opening night was attended by Ball, Hennings, Tristan Tzara, Jean Arp and Marcel Janco. There is no single agreed origin for the name: one story says that Richard Huelsenbeck pushed a paper knife into a dictionary and landed on the French word dada, meaning hobby horse.

Participants framed their activity as a protest against war, nationalism and cultural conformity, and used nonsense, chance and ridicule to negate prevailing aesthetic values. Dadaists worked in sound poetry, collage and photomontage, found objects and assemblage. They invented the chance collage, made by dropping torn scraps of paper on a larger sheet and pasting them where they landed. Tzara's manifesto of 1920 proposed writing poems from words cut out of a newspaper and drawn at random. Ball invented sound poetry. In New York and Paris, Marcel Duchamp's readymades became emblematic of its anti-art stance.

The movement spread to Berlin, Paris, New York and other centres, each with its own emphasis: performance and poetry in Zürich, politically charged photomontage in Berlin, and object-based experiments in New York. In Cologne, Max Ernst, Johannes Baargeld and Arp held an exhibition in 1920 in a pub, which the police closed on grounds of obscenity until the charges were dropped. By 1924 in Paris Dada was melding into Surrealism. It influenced pop art, Fluxus, the Situationist International and avant-garde composers such as John Cage, and some theorists argue that it was the beginning of postmodern art.
dadabhai-naoroji: Naoroji was born in Navsari into a Gujarati-speaking Parsi Zoroastrian family and was educated at the Elphinstone Institute School. As an ordained priest he founded the Rahnumai Mazdayasan Sabha on 1 August 1851 to restore the Zoroastrian religion to its original purity and simplicity, and in 1854 he founded the Gujarati fortnightly Rast Goftar to clarify Zoroastrian concepts and promote Parsi social reforms.

In 1855 he became Professor of Mathematics and Natural Philosophy at Elphinstone College in Bombay, the first Indian to hold such a post. He then went to London as a partner in Cama & Co, resigned within three years on ethical grounds, and in 1859 established his own cotton trading company.

In 1865 Naoroji launched the London Indian Society, and in 1867 he helped to found the East India Association, a predecessor of the Indian National Congress, to put the Indian point of view before the British public. In 1874 he served as Diwan of Baroda under the Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III, and he sat on the Legislative Council of Bombay from 1885 to 1888. He was elected President of the Indian National Congress in 1886 and again in 1893 and 1906, when he was a staunch moderate whose standing prevented a split between moderates and extremists.
In 1892 he was elected as a Liberal for Finsbury Central, the first British Indian MP. He took his oath on his copy of the Khordeh Avesta rather than the Bible, and lost his seat in 1895.

In 1888 the Prime Minister, Lord Salisbury, said that a British constituency was unlikely to elect a black man, and the remark was understood to refer to Naoroji. It was criticised by the Queen and by Liberals. Naoroji was a member of the Royal Commission on Indian Expenditure, created in 1896 largely because of his work on the drain of wealth.

Naoroji argued that British rule caused a transfer of wealth from India to Britain. He named six factors in this external drain, among them foreign government, the Home Charges paid for Britain's administration and Indian army, the cost of empire building, and highly paid foreign personnel who spent or took their money abroad. His Poverty and Un-British Rule in India of 1901 estimated a drain of 200 to 300 million pounds not returned to India.

He presented himself as a subject of the Empire and urged equal employment for qualified Indians so that revenue would stay in India. The book influenced Mahatma Gandhi, who wrote to him in 1894 that Indians looked up to him as children to a father. Naoroji died in Bombay on 30 June 1917 aged 91, and is often called the Grand Old Man of Indian Nationalism.
daedalus: The name Daidalos seems to be attested in Linear B, the writing system of Mycenaean Greek, in the form da-da-re-jo-de, possibly referring to a sanctuary. A craftsman named Daedalus is first mentioned in roughly 1400 BCE on the Knossian Linear B tablets, and Homer later names him as the maker of a dancing floor for Ariadne, referring to mythology his audience already knew. His parentage was a later addition, with various authors giving different fathers and mothers. The Athenians rewrote the Cretan-born Daedalus as an Athenian, a grandson of the ancient king Erechtheus who fled to Crete only after killing his nephew.

Daedalus is widely praised as an inventor, artist and architect, though classical sources disagree on which inventions are his. Pliny's Natural History credits him with carpentry, including the axe, the saw and glue, and he is said to have first made masts and sails for the navy of King Minos. Pausanias attributed to him numerous archaic wooden cult figures. Plato, in the Meno, uses his moving statues as a metaphor for true understanding, which must be shackled in place if it is not to wander off. Daedalic sculpture takes its name from him.

In the myths he built a hollow wooden cow so that Pasiphaë, the wife of King Minos, could mate with a bull sent by Poseidon; she bore the Minotaur, which Minos imprisoned in the Labyrinth Daedalus built. When Minos imprisoned him, Ovid says, he made wings of feathers, thread and beeswax. His son Icarus disobeyed his warning, flew too close to the Sun and fell into the sea.

According to the tradition, Daedalus was jealous of his nephew, called Perdix, Talos or Calos, who invented the saw and the compasses, and tried to murder him by throwing him from the Acropolis. Athena saved the boy and turned him into a partridge, and Daedalus fled to Crete. He later reached Camicus in Sicily and the protection of King Cocalus.

Accounts of his death differ: a snake bite at Telmessos, a small island in the Nile where he was worshipped, or a water snake in Lycia. These anecdotes are literary and late. Modern interpreters, among them Edith Hamilton, read him as an example of practical intelligence guided by restraint, set against the recklessness of Icarus.
dag-hammarskjold: Dag Hjalmar Agne Carl Hammarskjöld was born in Jönköping on 29 July 1905 into a noble family. He was the fourth and youngest son of Hjalmar Hammarskjöld, Prime Minister of Sweden from 1914 to 1917, and Agnes Hammarskjöld, and he spent most of his childhood in Uppsala, in Uppsala Castle. He studied at Katedralskolan and at Uppsala University, where by January 1930 he held a Licentiate of Philosophy and a Master of Laws. He received a doctorate from Stockholm University for a thesis on the spread of the business cycle.

From 1930 to 1934 he was secretary of a governmental committee on unemployment, and in 1936 he became secretary at the Riksbank, Sweden's central bank, chairing its General Council from 1941 to 1948. He was state secretary in the Ministry of Finance from 1936 to 1945, Swedish delegate to the Organization for European Economic Cooperation, cabinet secretary at the Ministry of Foreign Affairs from 1949 to 1951 and minister without portfolio from 1951 to 1953. He took part in the Paris conference that established the Marshall Plan, and although he served in a Social Democratic cabinet he never joined a party. He was elected to the Swedish Academy on 20 December 1954.

After Trygve Lie announced his resignation as Secretary-General of the United Nations on 10 November 1952, months of negotiation between the Western powers and the Soviet Union failed to agree on a successor. French representative Henri Hoppenot proposed Hammarskjöld on 30 March 1953. The powers hoped for an administrator who would avoid politics, and the Soviet representative Valerian Zorin found him harmless. Hammarskjöld took office in April 1953, aged 47. He visited every department, gave up the private elevator for general use and spearheaded a meditation room at the headquarters. In 1955 he visited China to negotiate the release of 11 captured US pilots, in 1956 the United Nations Emergency Force was established, and he intervened in the Suez Crisis.

On 18 September 1961 Hammarskjöld was flying to negotiate a cease-fire between United Nations forces in the Congo and Katangese troops under Moise Tshombe. His Douglas DC-6 crashed near Ndola in Northern Rhodesia, and all 15 others on board also died. A 1962 Rhodesian inquiry blamed pilot error, while a later UN investigation could not determine the cause. His death set off a succession crisis, since there was no line of succession and the Security Council had to vote on a successor.

He was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize posthumously, the only person so honoured. John F. Kennedy praised him as a statesman of the century, while in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the wider Global South his legacy is controversial, because of his performance in the Congo Crisis.
dagestan: Dagestan lies in the North Caucasus along the western shore of the Caspian Sea, with about 405 kilometres of coastline. Most of it is mountainous, with the Greater Caucasus covering the south, where the highest point is the peak of Bazardüzü, on the border with Azerbaijan. The name means land of the mountains, from the Turkic word dağ, mountain, and the Persian suffix -stan, land. Because the terrain impedes travel and communication, the region is unusually diverse, with more than 30 local languages, most of them of the Nakh-Daghestanian family.

In the first centuries CE Caucasian Albania, which covered what is now Azerbaijan and southern Dagestan, became subordinate to the Parthian Empire and then a province of the Sasanian Empire. By the 6th century the Sasanian rulers had built a strong citadel at Derbent, known as the Caspian Gates. After the Arab conquest of 643 the people of the Derbent region became the first in what is now Russian territory to adopt Islam, and it spread from the towns into the highlands. The Mongols conquered Derbent between 1236 and 1239, and the Timurids followed.

In the early 16th century the Safavids reconsolidated Persian rule, which lasted intermittently until the early 19th century. In the 16th and 17th centuries legal traditions were codified, and mountain communities called djamaats won considerable autonomy. The Ottoman Empire held Dagestan between 1578 and 1606.Persia ceded southern Dagestan to Russia in the Treaty of Gulistan of 1813, and the Treaty of Turkmenchay of 1828 consolidated Russian control.

Heavy taxation, expropriation of estates and the building of fortresses, among them Makhachkala, provoked the highlanders to rise under the Imamate of Dagestan, led by Ghazi Mohammed, Hamzat Bek and Shamil, who led it from 1834 to 1859. The Caucasian War lasted until 1864. After the Bolshevik Revolution and years of fighting, the Dagestan Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic was proclaimed on 20 January 1921.

Dagestan is a republic of Russia with its capital and largest city at Makhachkala, and its main towns include Derbent. It has over 3.1 million inhabitants, and Russian is the lingua franca although 14 languages are official. Most of its people are Sunni Muslims of the Shafii school, while the Caspian coast around Derbent has a Shia population. Its Sufi traditions go back to the 14th century, and Derbent, with its Sasanian citadel, remains its oldest city.
dagobert-i: Dagobert was the eldest son of Chlothar II and Haldetrude and the grandson of Fredegund. Chlothar had reigned alone over all the Franks since 613 and made his son king of Austrasia, almost certainly to bind the Austrasian nobility to the ruling Franks.

As a child Dagobert lived under the care of Arnulf of Metz and Pepin of Landen, forebears of the Carolingian dynasty. Chlothar at first excluded Alsace, the Vosges and the Ardennes from the grant, but the Austrasian nobility forced him to concede them. Dagobert then created a new duchy in the south-west of Austrasia, the later Duchy of Alsace, to guard against Burgundian or Alemannic ambitions, and made his courtier Gundoin its first duke.

On his father's death in 629 Dagobert inherited Neustria and Burgundy. His half-brother Charibert claimed Neustria, but Brodulf, who petitioned on Charibert's behalf, was assassinated by Dagobert, who became sole king of the Franks and later gave Aquitaine to Charibert as a consolation. In 629 he concluded a treaty with the Byzantine emperor Heraclius that entailed the compulsory baptism of Jews throughout his kingdom. He protected the markets at Duurstede and Utrecht, raided Spain, and helped Sisenand to the Visigothic throne, receiving a golden dish of some 500 pounds. When Charibert and his son Chilperic were assassinated in 632, Burgundy and Aquitaine were firmly under his rule.

In 631 he led an army against Samo, ruler of the Slavic Wends, after Wends had robbed and killed Frankish merchants. His Austrasian forces were defeated at Wogastisburg, though his Alemannic and Lombard allies repelled the Wends. In 632 the Austrasian nobles rose under the mayor of the palace, Pepin of Landen, and in 634 Dagobert appeased them by making his three-year-old son Sigebert III king there. He made Paris his capital and built the Saint-Denis Basilica.

Dagobert died in 639, aged thirty-six, and was the first Frankish king buried at Saint-Denis, which set a precedent for later French rulers. Most historians consider him the last of the great Merovingian kings. After his death Pepin of Landen recovered his position at Metz.

The historian Patrick Geary called the combined rule of Dagobert and Chlothar the apogee of Merovingian royal power, and the pattern of division and assassination continued until Pepin the Short deposed the last Merovingian in 751. A biography, the Gesta Dagoberti, written in the 830s, is mostly unreliable. The nursery rhyme Le bon roi Dagobert, probably of the 18th century, has no historical accuracy.
dahod: Dahod stands on the banks of the Dudhimati River in the state of Gujarat. It lies 214 kilometres from Ahmedabad and 159 kilometres from Vadodara. Tradition says the city took its name from the saint Dadhichi, who had an ashram on the river bank. The alternative name Dohad is said to mean "two boundaries", because the borders of Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh are close by.

Dahod is best known as the birthplace of the sixth Mughal emperor, Aurangzeb, son of the fifth emperor, Shah Jahan. He was born there in 1618, during the reign of Jahangir. Aurangzeb is said to have ordered his ministers to favour the town because it was his birthplace. The freedom fighter Tatya Tope is known to have escaped to Dahod and is believed to have spent his last days in the region.

The British built the railway colony, known as the Parel area, which still follows its original architecture. A locomotive workshop of the Western Railway stands beside it, and its workers have drawn many people from other states to the town. Dahod was later separated from Panchmahal District and became the headquarters of a district of its own.

At the 2011 census Dahod had a population of 130,503. It is a medical centre for eastern Gujarat and for the neighbouring parts of Rajasthan and Madhya Pradesh, and it has a growing engineering sector, including a plant planned by Siemens India for building and maintaining freight locomotives. The Najmi Masjeed, inaugurated in 2002, is one of the largest mosques of the Dawoodi Bohra community. Dahod station lies on the New Delhi to Mumbai main line.
dahomey-amazons: Tradition says that King Houegbadja, who ruled from 1645 to 1685, began the group that became the Mino as a corps of elephant hunters called the gbeto. Another tradition holds that the gbeto were older and that he only organised them, and a third that they offered their own service to the king. Queen Hangbe, who ruled from 1716 to 1718, is said to have set up a female bodyguard, and European merchants recorded such women. Some sources dispute this and even question whether Hangbe existed.

Dahomey's men suffered heavy losses in its wars with neighbouring states, and the kingdom owed Oyo a yearly tribute of male slaves. The shortage of men probably led the kings to recruit women. According to tradition, King Agaja used the women against the Kingdom of Whydah in 1727.

Under King Ghezo, who ruled from 1818 to 1858, Dahomey became increasingly militaristic, and he raised the army's budget and gave it a formal structure. The women called themselves ahosi, "king's wives", or Mino, "our mothers"; Europeans named them Amazons. Recruits included foreign captives and free Dahomean women, some enrolled from the age of eight. Members could not have children or live as married women, though they were legally married to the king. Their status was semi-sacred and tied to the Fon belief in Vodun.

By the middle of the nineteenth century visitors reported between 1,000 and 6,000 women, about a third of the army. They served as huntresses, riflewomen, reapers, archers and gunners, each regiment with its own uniforms, weapons and commanders. The Mino also sat in the Grand Council, where most of them favoured peace with the Egba of Abeokuta.

The Mino fought chiefly against African neighbours, and their victims were killed or enslaved. Captives taken to the United States on the Clotilda said that the Dahomey Amazons had taken part in their enslavement. Against Abeokuta they suffered a crushing defeat with many casualties.

In 1890 King Béhanzin began fighting French forces in the First Franco-Dahomean War. At Cotonou, Dahomean troops, many of them Mino, charged the French lines and were decisively crushed. At Adegon on 6 October 1892, in the second war, the French met the bulk of the Mino corps with a bayonet charge; Dahomey lost 86 regulars and 417 Mino, the French six soldiers. The troops were disbanded when Dahomey became a French protectorate in 1894. A woman named Nawi, thought to have been the last survivor, died in November 1979.
dahshur: Dahshur is an ancient Egyptian pyramid complex and necropolis on the Western Desert plateau, at the edge of the cultivated plain. Together with the pyramid complexes at Saqqara, Abusir and Giza to its north it forms the pyramid fields of the ancient capital city of Memphis. It is listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site and shares its name with the nearby village of Manshiyyat Dahshur.

The pyramids of Dahshur gave the Egyptians the experience needed to move from step-sided to smooth-sided pyramids, and so to build the Great Pyramid of Giza. The first was the Bent Pyramid of King Sneferu, the first attempt at a smooth-sided pyramid. It proved unsuccessful because of miscalculations about the weight placed on the soft ground of sand, gravel and clay, which tended to subside, and its angle changed, which gave it its name. Sneferu then ordered the Red Pyramid, named for its red limestone, a fully built, free-standing, smooth-sided pyramid 104 metres high with an angle of 43 degrees. It is believed to be his resting place.

Kings of the Middle Kingdom also built at the site. The White Pyramid of Amenemhat II of the 12th Dynasty was filled with sand and limestone; the weather eroded the sand, and the limestone was taken for other pyramids, so it collapsed. Senusret III built a pyramid with galleries and tombs underneath for two princesses, Sit-Hathor and Merit. The Black Pyramid of Amenemhat III is badly eroded, but remains the most imposing monument after Sneferu's two pyramids, and its polished granite capstone is in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo. Several pyramids of the 13th Dynasty followed, of which only that of Ameny Qemau has been excavated.

Undisturbed tombs of royal women found near the pyramid of Senusret III held a large amount of lapidary work and jewellery, judged to show the highest stage of metalworking in Egypt in that period. Two treasures of the king's daughters came from a gallery tomb beside the pyramid. Extensive cemeteries of officials of the Old Kingdom and Middle Kingdom have been found around the pyramids. The Bent Pyramid and the Red Pyramid are among the oldest, largest and best preserved pyramids in Egypt.
dail-eireann: The name means Assembly of Ireland, a dáil being a meeting, tryst or encounter of any kind. The first legislature in Ireland was the Parliament of Ireland, which sat from 1297 to 1800 and was abolished by the Act of Union of 1800; members elected for Ireland then sat in the House of Commons of the United Kingdom until 1922.

In the United Kingdom general election of 1918 Sinn Féin contested the Irish seats on a pledge to establish a constituent assembly as the supreme national authority. It won 73 of the 105 Irish seats, and its members refused to recognise the United Kingdom parliament and convened instead as Dáil Éireann, the unicameral legislature of a unilaterally declared Irish Republic and the first Irish parliament since 1801.

The first meeting took place in the Mansion House in Dublin on 21 January 1919, attended by 27 members. One of its first acts was to ratify a provisional constitution. The body was prohibited in the following September and forced underground, meeting in several locations. Neither the First nor the Second Dáil was recognised by the British government, and internationally the Dáil of the Irish Republic was recognised only by the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic. In 1921 the United Kingdom government set up a Parliament of Southern Ireland, which nationalists rejected and boycotted.

On 6 December 1922, after the Anglo-Irish Treaty of 1921, the Dáil became the lower house of the bicameral Oireachtas of the new Irish Free State. The first Dáil under its constitution was styled the 3rd Dáil, and every one since has met in Leinster House. On 29 December 1937 the Constitution of Ireland replaced the Free State, and the first Dáil to meet under it was the Ninth Dáil. The present Dáil derives from the 1937 constitution, but a continuity from the First Dáil of 1919 is considered to exist.

The Dáil is the lower house and principal chamber of the Oireachtas, which also includes the president and the Seanad Éireann. Its members, known as Teachtaí Dála or TDs, are directly elected by proportional representation using the single transferable vote, and the constitution sets their number between one per 20,000 and one per 30,000 of the population. A Dáil may not continue for longer than five years. It is the dominant branch of the Oireachtas: it nominates the Taoiseach for appointment by the president and approves the budget.

The chairperson, the Ceann Comhairle, is chosen from among the TDs but must observe strict impartiality and votes only in the event of a tie. Debate is generally in English, though TDs may switch between Irish and English. When a vote is taken, the question is first put in Irish, and members answer Tá or Níl.
daimyo: The title is written with dai, meaning large, and myō, which stands for myōden, private land. The first to hold it were the shugo daimyō, who arose from among the shugo during the Muromachi period, approximately 1336 to 1573. They held military and police powers and economic power within a province, and the largest ruled several provinces. The Ashikaga shogunate required them to live in Kyoto, so they appointed relatives or retainers, called shugodai, to represent them in their home provinces.

During the Ōnin War, in which shugo-daimyō fought each other, provincial uprisings took place and the deputies living in the provinces strengthened their position. At the end of the fifteenth century those shugo-daimyō who had controlled their deputies stayed in power, and the others were replaced by a new class, the sengoku-daimyō, who rose from the ranks of the shugodai and the jizamurai. These were de facto independent lords whose samurai and peasants were loyal to them rather than to the shogun, in other words warlords.

After the Battle of Sekigahara in 1600 Shōgun Tokugawa Ieyasu reorganised the daimyo and their territories into han, assessed by rice production, and only those heading a han of 10,000 koku or more counted as daimyo. He divided them by their relation to the Tokugawa: the shinpan, who were related to it, the fudai, who had been vassals or allies, and the tozama, who had not allied with it before Sekigahara. Only fudai could hold posts in the shogunate, whereas tozama in general could not.

Daimyo often hired samurai to guard their land and paid them in land or food, since relatively few could afford to pay in money. Under the Tokugawa they had to keep residences in Edo as well as in their fiefs and to spend alternate years in each, a practice called sankin-kōtai. The Tokugawa at first regarded the tozama as potentially rebellious, but such control policies led to peaceful relations for most of the Edo period.

In 1869, the year after the Meiji Restoration, the daimyo and the kuge formed a new aristocracy, the kazoku. The han were abolished in 1871 and replaced by prefectures, and the daimyo and their samurai were pensioned off. Many daimyo were at first appointed governors but were soon called to Tokyo, which cut off any independent base for rebellion.
dakovo: Đakovo is a town in Slavonia in Croatia, 37 km south-west of Osijek and 34 km south-east of Našice, at an elevation of 111 m, and it is the centre of the fertile Đakovo region. The name comes from the Greek diákos, in Slavic form đak, 'pupil'; it is uncertain whether it came directly from Greek, from Hungarian diák or from the local Slavic form. In Roman antiquity the settlement of Certissia stood on the same spot until it disappeared in the Migration Period.

The settlement is first mentioned in 1239, when Béla IV of Hungary granted it to the Diocese of Bosnia, and the bishop moved his seat there in 1246. A predecessor of the present St Peter's Cathedral was built in 1355. In 1374 the place is recorded as Dyacou, and on 25 July 1386 Croatian rebels captured Queen Mary of Hungary and her mother Elizabeth near it. Ottoman rule began after the Battle of Gorjani in 1537 and lasted nearly 150 years, during which Đakovo, then called Yakova, was the centre of a kaza in the Sanjak of Pojega.

In 1805 a herd of Lipizzan horses was evacuated to Đakovo when Napoleon invaded Austria and Hungary, and part of it stayed. In 1910 the population of 6,304 comprised 4,894 Croatians, 890 Germans, 249 Hungarians and 164 Serbs. Around then the town was a district capital in Virovitica County in the Kingdom of Croatia-Slavonia. From 1 December 1941 until 7 July 1942 the Ustaše operated the Đakovo internment camp, mostly for Jewish, Roma and Serb women and children.

Đakovo has 19,491 inhabitants in the town itself, and its economy rests on farming, livestock, leather and wool processing, wood processing and food production. The Cathedral basilica of St Peter, built in 1866–1882 under Josip Juraj Strossmayer, then Catholic bishop of Đakovo and Srijem, is the most important sacral building in Slavonia. A park of the 19th century near the bishop's palace is a protected horticultural monument. The folklore festival Đakovački vezovi is held every year at the beginning of July, with traditional costumes, dances and a horse and wedding wagon show, and white Lipizzaner horses from the breeding centre at Ivandvor, active since 1506, can be seen on the racecourse. The region is also known for its Slavonian cooking and wines.
dakshinapatha: The name joins two Sanskrit words, dakshina, south, and patha, road. The later Vedic texts divide the Indian subcontinent into three parts: Aryavarta in the north, Madhya Desha in the centre and Dakshinapatha in the south. The Aitareya Brahmana, of the first half of the first millennium BCE, names peoples of the south of Vindhyan and north Deccan origin, among them the Satvants, Vidarbha, Andhra, Nishadas and Kuntis. The grammarian Panini, about 500 BCE, mentions the Asmaka Kingdom in connection with the south and with Kalinga.

The term has carried three meanings. It can denote the ancient south of the subcontinent below Uttarapatha, usually the Deccan and sometimes Tamilakam and Ceylon as well. It can mean the great southern highway, running from Magadha to Pratishthana. It has also been used for a kingdom on the Godavari River. The Junagarh rock inscription of 150 CE, set up by an Indo-Scythian king, records that he twice defeated Satakarni, the lord of Dakshinapatha, in fair fight and did not destroy him because of the nearness of their connection.

The southern road was one of two great highways that have linked the parts of the subcontinent since the Iron Age. The other, the Uttarapatha or great northern road, ran from Taxila through the Punjab to the Yamuna and followed that river south to Mathura; from there a route went on to Ujjain in Malwa and to Broach on the western coast. According to the writer Sanjeev Sanyal, the course of the northern road has stayed roughly the same since before the Mauryas, while the southern road appears to have drifted.

The route of Rama into exile in the epic may reflect an early version of it. By the time of the Buddha it started at Varanasi and ran through Vidisha in central India to Pratishthana, now Paithan, and it probably extended to the Chola, Chera and Pandya kingdoms of the far south. By the Mauryan period there would have been a branch from Ujjain to the ports of Gujarat, which made Ujjain a major city by the Gupta era. The modern highway that roughly corresponds to it runs much further east than the old road but still meets the northern road at Varanasi.
dal-riata: The name Dál Riata comes from Old Irish and means the portion of Riata. Bede wrote that the kingdom was named after its founder, a man called Reuda, while the 11th-century Duan Albanach says that the three sons of Erc, Fergus Mór, Loarn and Óengus, conquered Scotland. Tradition has seen Gaelic in Scotland as the result of migration or takeover from Ireland. The archaeologist Ewan Campbell argues that there is no archaeological or place-name evidence for either. He suggests that Argyll and Antrim formed a maritime province united by the sea, and that the medieval accounts were dynastic propaganda. His theory has been challenged.

The kingdom reached its largest extent under Áedán mac Gabráin, who died about 608. In 575 Columba negotiated an alliance with the Cenél Conaill at the Convention of Druim Cett. Áedán campaigned as far as Orkney but was defeated by Æthelfrith of Bernicia at Degsastan about 603. Under Domnall Brecc the kingdom suffered defeat at the Battle of Magh Rath in 637, and Domnall was killed in 642; Dál Riata then became tributary to Northumbria.

In the 730s the Pictish king Óengus mac Fergusa conquered Dál Riata, and Alex Woolf concludes that he effectively destroyed it, though some scholars see a revival under Áed Find, who died in 778. Viking raids began in 795. Tradition attributes a merger of the Dál Riatan and Pictish crowns to Cináed mac Ailpín, who became king of the Picts about 843, and the two peoples formed the Kingdom of Alba.

In Argyll there were four main kindreds: the Cenél nGabráin in Kintyre, the Cenél nÓengusa on Islay and Jura, the Cenél Loairn in Lorne and the later Cenél Comgaill in Cowal and Bute. Dunadd was the most important royal site; excavation found weapons, quern-stones, jewellery moulds, and glassware and wine amphorae from Gaul.

Most people lived by subsistence farming, with oats and barley as the main crops, and herding was especially important. Travel by sea was the easiest way to move any distance, and houses were grouped into twenties, each group providing 28 oarsmen for the war fleet. The monastery of Iona played a key role in spreading Christianity in northern Britain and in insular art.
dalai-lama: Dalai Lama is part of the full title Holiness Knowing Everything Vajradhara Dalai Lama, which Altan Khan gave to Sonam Gyatso, the leader of the Gelug school, in 1578 at Yanghua Monastery. Dalai combines the Mongolic word for ocean with the Tibetan bla-ma, master. Sonam Gyatso had just given teachings to the Khan, and the title was extended to the whole tulku lineage, so he became the 3rd Dalai Lama, while the first two were awarded it after their deaths. The 1st, Gendun Drup (1391 to 1474), was a disciple of Tsongkhapa and abbot of Drepung, and the 2nd established the method of finding later incarnations through visions at the oracle lake, Lhamo Lhatso.

The 4th Dalai Lama, Yonten Gyatso (1589 to 1617), was a Mongol, a great-grandson of Altan Khan, and his connection led the Mongols to support the Gelug zealously. The Gelug were the newest school and lacked an established network of Tibetan clan patronage, so they relied more on foreign patrons. After his death the Tsangpa rulers of Central Tibet forbade a search for his incarnation, but in 1618 the child was secretly identified and later recognised as the 5th Dalai Lama, Lobsang Gyatso.

From 1642 to 1951 the Dalai Lama led the secular government of Tibet, directly or through regents, in the government known as the Ganden Phodrang, which governed the Tibetan Plateau with varying degrees of autonomy. The Qing dynasty established control over Tibet in 1720, and Chinese authorities have asserted the right to oversee the selection of spiritual leaders since the 18th century, a practice formalised in 1793. The 6th Dalai Lama, Tsangyang Gyatso, gave up his monk's robes in 1702 and chose a layman's life.

Since the time of the 5th Dalai Lama in the 17th century the Dalai Lama has been a symbol of the unification of the state of Tibet. His religious authority goes beyond the Gelug tradition and represents Buddhist values not tied to a single school. The extent and nature of the Dalai Lama's secular and religious power remains contested. One interpretation is the mchod yon, usually translated as priest and patron relationship, an alliance between Tibetan Buddhist leaders and secular rulers such as the Mongols, Manchus and Chinese authorities. Critics, including Sam van Schaik, hold that the theory oversimplifies the situation, and historians such as Melvyn Goldstein have called Tibet a vassal state or tributary.
dali-kingdom: Nanzhao was overthrown in 902, and three short-lived dynasties ruled its successor kingdoms in quick succession: Great Changhe, Great Tianxing and Great Yining. In 934 Duan Siping, an official in the Tonghai Area Command, organised a coalition of Nanzhao sympathisers and overthrew the Yang regime, and in 937 he seized power and established himself at Dali. The Duan clan professed Han ancestry, and Yuan records say they came from Wuwei in Gansu, which neither Song nor Dali sources confirm. The kingdom took its name from Dali, which means marble in Chinese.

Relations with the Song dynasty were cordial, though Dali was essentially independent. The founder of the Song, Taizu, declared the Dadu River the border and refused further claims, so as to avoid the costly wars the Tang had fought against Nanzhao. Dali established tribute relations in 982, but Song officials allowed it to offer tribute at court only three times. Its horses were prized as military assets. In 1094 the former prime minister Gao Shengtai forced King Duan Zhengming to give up the throne and renamed the realm the Dazhong Kingdom; when he died in 1096 the Duan family regained it, but the Gao clan stayed in power at court and later fought among themselves.

Möngke Khan sent envoys demanding surrender, and the king of Dali had them killed. Möngke put his brother Kublai in charge of the invasion. Kublai's army crossed the Jinsha River at night and routed the Dali army, and in late 1253 three Mongol columns converged on the city of Dali. King Duan Xingzhi fled to Shanchan and it took two more years of fighting to capture both cities. In 1256 he surrendered, and the Duan family continued to govern Yunnan as vassals of the Mongols under the title Maharaja. The Ming conquered Yunnan in 1382.

The administration of Dali has been characterised as a mandala state similar to Southeast Asian kingdoms, with some Chinese influence. The Duan rulers gave Sinitic-style appointments and hereditary fiefs to clans such as the Gao, Yang and Dong, and allied with the leaders of peripheral peoples. The kings styled themselves Buddha-kings, and ten of the 22 kings retired to become monks. The ruling elite wrote in Chinese script, supplemented by Bai characters, so most sources are in Classical Chinese. Most Bai people trace their ancestry to Nanzhao and Dali, though the records of those kingdoms do not mention them.
dalian: Dalian is a prefecture-level, sub-provincial port city in Liaoning province, on the southern tip of the Liaodong peninsula. It is the southernmost city in Liaoning and in Northeast China as a whole, and shares maritime boundaries with cities across Liaodong Bay and the Bohai Strait and with North Korea across the Korea Bay. Its climate is humid continental, with warm, wet summers under the East Asian monsoon and cold, dry winters. The municipal area consists of Dalian proper and Lüshunkou, formerly the city of Lüshun, known in Western and Russian sources as Port Arthur, about 40 kilometres away.

The Qin and Han empires annexed the Dalian peninsula from a Korean state, and in the Sixteen Kingdoms era the Korean state of Goguryeo controlled the region. In the 1880s the Qing government built bridges and heavily fortified the peninsula. Mining camps on the northern coast of Dalian Bay grew into the small town of Qingniwa, from which modern Dalian originated. The British briefly occupied Qingniwa in the Second Opium War in 1858 and returned it in 1860. Japan overcame the Chinese defences in the First Sino-Japanese War, and in the Treaty of Shimonoseki of 17 April 1895 China ceded the Liaodong Peninsula, Taiwan and Penghu.

The Russian Empire coerced a lease of the area from the Qing dynasty in 1898 and built a commercial town called Dalny, a name meaning far-away. After the Russo-Japanese War of 1904-1905 Japan occupied the area as the Kwantung Leased Territory and renamed the city Dairen, the Japanese reading of the Chinese name of Dalian Bay. Shipbuilding and locomotive works were already located in the city before and during the Second Sino-Japanese War. Many farmers and fishers from Shandong settled in the area during the Chuang Guandong migration, and the Dalian dialect, a Jiaoliao Mandarin speech, has a few loanwords from Japanese and Russian.

After Japan's surrender, the Soviet Manchurian offensive took the city on 22 August 1945. Unlike many cities of the northeast, it never reverted to Nationalist authority. The Soviets and the Chinese Communists cooperated to develop its industry and port, which had been relatively undamaged in the war, and in 1945 the first Communist mayor of the Lüda Administrative Office was appointed.

Dalian is Liaoning's second largest city after the provincial capital Shenyang, with 7,450,785 inhabitants at the 2020 census. It is a shipping, financial and logistics centre of East Asia. Zhongshan Square, laid out by the Russians, is surrounded by classical buildings that the Japanese built in the first half of the 20th century. Dalian University of Technology and Dalian Maritime University, founded in 1909, are among its universities.
dalit: The Sanskrit word dalit is rendered as broken or scattered; the same people were also called Harijans. They were excluded from the fourfold varna of the caste hierarchy in Hinduism. Their status was tied to hereditary occupations that caste Hindus considered polluting or debased, such as working with leather, disposing of dead animals, manual scavenging and sanitation work. The economist and reformer B. R. Ambedkar said that untouchability entered Indian society around 400 CE, through the struggle for supremacy between Buddhism and Brahmanism. Several scholars have drawn parallels with the Burakumin of Japan and the Baekjeong of Korea.

Gopal Baba Walangkar (c. 1840–1900) is generally considered the pioneer of the Dalit movement, and Ambedkar himself held him to be its progenitor. Harichand Thakur (c. 1812–1878) led the Matua organisation among the Namasudra community in the Bengal Presidency, and Jyotirao Phule (1827–1890) worked to improve conditions for Dalits; his Gulamgiri of 1873 is regarded as a seminal moment in Dalit literature. In the nineteenth century the Brahmo Samaj, Arya Samaj and Ramakrishna Mission took part in the cause.

The Laxminarayan Temple in Wardha was the first upper-caste temple to welcome Dalits openly, in 1928, and the last King of Travancore issued a Temple Entry Proclamation in 1936. After independence in 1947 Article 17 of the Constitution outlawed untouchability. The Untouchability (Offences) Act of 1955 was amended in the same year into the Protection of Civil Rights Act, and when neither proved effective the Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe (Prevention of Atrocities) Act of 1989 followed.

Most Dalits in India are Hindu, with significant populations following Buddhism, Sikhism, Christianity and Islam. In 1956 Ambedkar launched the Dalit Buddhist movement, and about half a million Dalits joined him in rejecting Hinduism. Mass conversions to Christianity involved groups such as the Chuhras of Punjab, the Chamars of North India, the Vankars of Gujarat and the Pulayas of Kerala. Among Sikhs the two Dalit castes of Punjab are the Mazhabis and the Ramdasias.

The 2011 census counted Scheduled Caste communities at 16.6 per cent of India's population. A study found more than 900 Dalit sub-castes, with divisions between them. Dalit literature has formed an identity across languages including Marathi, Bangla, Hindi, Kannada, Punjabi, Tamil and Odia; its earliest identifiable writers include Madara Chennaiah, an 11th-century cobbler-saint, and Dohara Kakkaiah. Dalit communities also settled in the Caribbean, where about a third of the immigrants arriving in 1883 are estimated to have been Dalits, and later in Britain and the United States.
dalmatia: Dalmatia is a narrow belt of land on the eastern shore of the Adriatic Sea, stretching from the island of Rab in the north to the Bay of Kotor in the south. The Dalmatian Hinterland ranges in width from about 50 kilometres in the north to a few kilometres in the south and is mostly covered by the rugged Dinaric Alps. Seventy-nine islands and about 500 islets run parallel to the coast, the largest being Brač, Pag and Hvar. The coast has a Mediterranean climate, and olives and grapes grow there. The name comes from the Dalmatae, an Illyrian tribe that lived in the area in the 1st millennium BCE.

The area was part of an Illyrian kingdom between the 4th century BCE and the Illyrian Wars, when the Roman Republic established a protectorate south of the river Neretva. The province of Illyricum was formally established around 32-27 BCE. In 9 CE the Dalmatians rose in the last of a series of revolts, together with the Pannonians; after it was crushed, Illyricum was split in 10 CE into Pannonia and Dalmatia. Urban centres were almost completely romanised, while in the countryside the Illyrians kept their language, gods and tribal organisation.

From the middle of the 6th century Slavic migrations pushed the Romance-speaking population to the coast and islands. By 619 the Slavs and Avars had ruined the capital Salona, which allowed settlement in the nearby palace of Diocletian, and the Croats and other Slavs founded their own territories. The Kingdom of Croatia was founded in 925. The Republic of Venice held parts of Dalmatia from 1000 to 1358 and from 1420 to 1797, while the Republic of Ragusa existed from 1358 to 1808. Most of the hinterland fell to the Ottoman Empire in the early 16th century, and Venice later reconquered it.

At the Congress of Vienna in 1815 Dalmatia was granted to the Emperor of Austria as the Kingdom of Dalmatia. In 1848 Croatian demands for union with Croatia, supported above all by Dubrovnik, were blocked by the March Constitution. Until 1909 Italian and Croatian were both official languages; by 1910 all but one of the 82 urban communities had a Slav majority. After the First World War Dalmatia became part of the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs.

Dalmatia is a historical region only and has no formal status in Croatian law, so its extent rests largely on the borders of the Austrian kingdom. It roughly corresponds to the four southernmost Croatian counties, with seats at Zadar, Šibenik, Split and Dubrovnik. Split is the largest city, followed by Zadar, Šibenik and Dubrovnik. The major rivers are the Zrmanja, Krka, Cetina and Neretva.
damascus: Damascus stands in south-western Syria on a plateau 680 metres above sea level, about 80 kilometres inland from the Mediterranean and sheltered by the Anti-Lebanon Mountains, which block rain from the sea. The Barada River, fed by mountain streams of melting snow, supplies the city with water, and the Ghouta, an irrigated belt of farmland, has produced vegetables, cereals and fruit since ancient times. The site lay at a crossroads of the north–south route linking Egypt with Asia Minor and the east–west desert route linking Lebanon with the Euphrates valley.

The name first appears as tjmsqw in a list of places of the Egyptian king Thutmose III, in the 15th century BCE, and as Dimašqa in the Amarna letters; its origin is uncertain. Greek myths gave three explanations of the Greek form Damaskós, among them a founder named Damaskos, a son of Hermes.

Radiocarbon dating at Tell Ramad, on the outskirts, suggests occupation possibly from around 6300 BCE, and settlement in the wider Barada basin goes back to 9000 BCE, though no large settlement stood within the city's later walls until the second millennium BCE. The Amarna letters of about 1350 BCE name Biryawaza as its ruler. Around 1260 BCE the region was a battleground between the Hittites and the Egyptians, and under a treaty between Hattusili III and Ramesses II control of the Damascus area passed to Egypt in 1259 BCE. After the Sea Peoples arrived around 1200 BCE, Damascus emerged as an influential centre, and from the 11th to the 7th century BCE it was the hub of an Aramaic kingdom.

Damascus was the capital of the Umayyad Caliphate from 661 to 750. When the Abbasid dynasty won, the seat of Islamic power moved to Baghdad and the city's importance declined. It regained significance in the Ayyubid, Mamluk and Ottoman periods.

Damascus is the capital of Syria and the seat of its central government, with a metropolitan area that includes Douma, Harasta, Darayya and Jaramana. The Ancient City of Damascus was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1979 and holds over 125 cultural heritage sites from the Hellenistic, Roman, Byzantine, Islamic and Ottoman periods; the best known of its more than 200 mosques is the Umayyad Mosque. Damascus University is the oldest and largest university in Syria.
damghan: Damghan lies 342 km east of Tehran on the high road to Mashhad, at an elevation of 1,250 m, and serves as capital of Damghan County and its Central District. The historical town was called Qumis, after a province of the same name stretching from Sabzevar to Garmsar, and up to the first century CE Damghan was the capital of that province. The name is derived from deh, village, and moghan, Magi, a name given by Zoroastrians. Tradition ascribes the founding of the town to Hooshang, the great-grandson of Keyumars and founder of the Pishdadi dynasty. Its climate is cold semi-arid. The city is known for pistachios and for paper almonds with very thin shells.

Excavation at Tepe Hissar, in the village of Heydarabad southeast of the city, shows that the area was inhabited in the Chalcolithic period, in the fifth millennium BCE, with metal production in its earliest layers. Its layers belong to several periods, including the Median, Achaemenid, Seleucid, Parthian and Sasanian, and it reached its peak in the Seleucid and Parthian periods. Ernst Herzfeld and Erich Schmidt were the first archaeologists to explore it. After the conquest of Persia by Alexander the Great, the nearby city of Hecatompylos, meaning hundred gates, was the main population centre.

Damghan was half destroyed in the earthquake of 856 and was an important city in the Middle Ages, though few remains of that time survive. It was capital of the province of Qumis until it was destroyed by the Afghan Hotak dynasty in 1723. Fath-Ali Shah Qajar was born in a citadel in the western part of the city in 1772, and later Qajar rulers built palaces at the spring of Cheshmeh-Ali, 30 km to the north.

Damghan is known for its monuments. The Tarikhaneh Mosque was built over a Sasanian fire temple and is one of the oldest mosques in Iran, with massive columns, wood carvings and two minarets of the 11th century. Many Seljuk buildings survive, including the Gunbad-i Chihil Dukhtaran mausoleum, built in AH 466 (1087 CE) and 14.8 m high, the shrine of Imamzade Ja'far and the tomb of Pir-i Alamdar. North of the city stand the Ismaili fortresses of Gerdkuh, said to have been used by Hassan Sabah and conquered by the Ilkhanate under Hulagu Khan, and Mehrnegar on Mansourkuh. Sections of the old walls, some from the Sasanian era, remain.
dammam: Dammam is the seat and largest city of the Eastern Province of Saudi Arabia, an industrial port on the Persian Gulf coast. It forms the core of Greater Dammam, which includes the neighbouring governorates of Khobar and Qatif. The climate is hot desert, with extremely hot summers, sparse rainfall mostly in winter, and dust storms called shamals that generally come from the north in summer. Water comes from desalination plants, and large stretches of the shallow Gulf have been reclaimed.

The area that became Dammam was settled by the Dawasir tribe around 1923 with the permission of King Ibn Saud, and it was originally a fishing hamlet. In 1866 the United Kingdom attacked the fort at Dammam, then held by the Second Saudi state, and was repelled. After the unification of Saudi Arabia Dammam was made capital of the newly formed Eastern Province.

An oil concession agreement was signed in Jeddah in spring 1933 between the government of King Abdulaziz and the Standard Oil Company of California. Drilling of the first well began on 30 April 1935, and Dammam No. 1 was abandoned in January 1936 after poor results. Most of the next wells disappointed. Work on Dammam No. 7 began on 7 December 1936, and by 4 March 1938 it was producing a promising amount of oil. The well, later called the Prosperity Well, showed that the kingdom held very large reserves of hydrocarbons.

In 1950 Dammam had 22,000 inhabitants, and by 2000 759,000. The area was planned from the start on modern principles, with residential and commercial districts separated and broad, straight roads. Dhahran International Airport opened in 1961, and in 1999 commercial flights moved to the larger King Fahd International Airport. King Abdulaziz Port, founded in the late 1940s, is the largest port on the Persian Gulf, and the King Fahd Causeway, 28 kilometres long, links the region to Bahrain. Saudi Aramco dominates the oil sector, with its headquarters in nearby Dhahran, and industrial cities were built to encourage other industries.
danelaw: The Danelaw approximately covered Yorkshire, the central and eastern Midlands and the East of England. The name is first recorded in the early 11th century as Dena lage, and only then was it used for a geographic area. Five fortified towns became particularly important: Leicester, Nottingham, Derby, Stamford and Lincoln. Known as the Five Boroughs, they broadly delineate the area now called the East Midlands. Borough derives from the Old English burh, a fortified enclosure containing several households.

The term can also describe the legal arrangements made in the treaties between Alfred the Great, king of Wessex, and the Danish warlord Guthrum after Guthrum's defeat at the Battle of Edington in 878. They allowed the Danes to govern themselves in exchange for loyalty to the English crown and set equivalences for matters such as the wergild payable in reparation. The wapentake, the standard land division in the Danelaw, was effectively interchangeable with the hundred.

The Great Heathen Army landed in East Anglia in 865 under a combined leadership that included Halfdan Ragnarsson and Ivar the Boneless. In 867 it captured Northumbria and its capital York. Mercia fell in a campaign lasting until 874, after which Guthrum led the army. Only Wessex still resisted. After Edington, Alfred demanded as a term of surrender that Guthrum be baptised, and Alfred acted as his godfather.

In the 910s Edward the Elder and his sister Æthelflæd, the Lady of the Mercians, conquered Danish territories in the Midlands and East Anglia, and some Danish jarls who submitted were allowed to keep their lands. Viking rule ended in Northumbria when Eric Bloodaxe was driven out in 954. Cnut the Great later ruled a unified English kingdom from 1016 to 1035 as part of his North Sea Empire. The Danelaw still appeared in legislation in the early 12th century, in the Leges Henrici Primi, as one of the laws into which England was divided.

Scandinavian settlement can still be seen in the North of England and the East Midlands, above all in place-names with Old Norse endings such as -by, meaning village, and -thorp, meaning hamlet. Contact between Old East Norse and Old English brought many Norse words into English, including law itself, sky, window, and the pronouns they, them and their. Four of the five boroughs became county towns, of Leicestershire, Lincolnshire, Nottinghamshire and Derbyshire; Stamford did not.
danes: Denmark has been inhabited since ancient times by Germanic peoples including the Angles, Cimbri, Jutes, Herules and Teutones. The first mention of Danes within Denmark is on the Jelling Rune Stone, which records the conversion of the Danes to Christianity by Harald Bluetooth in the 10th century. Between about 960 and the early 980s Harald established a kingdom stretching from Jutland to Scania.

Danish Viking expansion brought Norway and England into the Danish North Sea Empire, though England broke away after the death of Canute the Great in 1035. The Danish realm later spread along the southern Baltic coast. In the 14th century King Olaf II acquired Norway, with Iceland and the Faroe Islands, and his mother Margrethe I united Norway, Sweden and Denmark in the Kalmar Union.

Sweden won its independence in 1523, which ended the union and created Denmark–Norway. The kingdom grew wealthy in the 16th century from tolls on traffic through the Øresund, since it controlled both shores. In 1524 Hans Mikkelsen and Christiern Pedersen translated the New Testament into Danish, which became an immediate best-seller. Denmark–Norway colonised Greenland in the 17th century. After a failed war with the Swedish Empire, the Treaty of Roskilde of 1658 removed the Scandinavian Peninsula areas from Danish control and set the borders between Denmark, Norway and Sweden that exist today. The people of Scania came to be fully integrated as Swedes.

Defeat in the Napoleonic Wars cost Denmark Norway and territory in what is now northern Germany. That loss, the Danish Golden Age that followed and the liberal and national movements of the 1830s helped form a Danish national identity. After the revolutions of 1848 Denmark became a constitutional monarchy on 5 June 1849, when Frederick VII accepted a constitution that separated powers and gave the vote to all adult men.

Danishness, the basis of modern Danish identity, stresses the connection of the people to the territory, the thousand-year-old monarchy and the 19th-century national romantic idea of the people. It has not been tied to a racial or biological heritage. N. F. S. Grundtvig named the Danish language and attachment to Denmark as its defining marks, and Danish identity was built on peasant culture and Lutheran theology. About fifty thousand Danish-identifying German citizens live in Southern Schleswig, and Danish emigrants settled notably in the United States, Canada, Argentina and Peru.
danevirke: The Danevirke consists of several walls, trenches and the Schlei Barrier. The walls stretch for 30 kilometres, from Hedeby on the Baltic coast in the east to the marshlands in the west of the peninsula, and stand between 3.6 and 6 metres high. Excavations of 1969 to 1975 used tree-ring dating to show that the main structure was built in three phases between 737 and 968, at about the same time as Offa's Dyke on the border of Wales and England. Later carbon dating showed that some parts are older still.

Written sources say that King Godfred began work in 808, fearing an invasion by the Franks, who had conquered Frisia and Old Saxony. Legend credits Queen Thyra, wife of Gorm the Old, with ordering the wall built, and most of the work in the tenth century is attributed to Harald Bluetooth.

The early ramparts were of soil, followed by a timber palisade built in 737, later wrapped in a stone wall. The Danevirke was strengthened in the early twelfth century, when the moats were deepened and the ramparts raised. King Valdemar the Great then built the brick wall known as Valdemarsmuren, a wall of stone in mortar about 7 metres high on a granite base. It was the last true reinforcement. Danish kings used the structure as a gathering point for expeditions, including raids on the Slavs of the southern Baltic. It lost its purpose from the fourteenth century, because of the cost of manning it and the development of siege engines.

In the nineteenth century the Danevirke became a symbol of Denmark in its struggle with Germany over Schleswig. It was strengthened with cannon emplacements and entrenchments in 1850 and 1861. In the Second Schleswig War of 1864 no battle took place at it: General de Meza withdrew his army to Dybbøl after the frozen Schlei and marshes made a flanking attack possible, a decision that shocked Danish opinion and cost him his command.

The site has stayed in German possession since 1864. After the Allied invasion of Normandy in the Second World War, the Wehrmacht considered turning the wall into an anti-tank trench, and the Danish archaeologist Søren Telling persuaded Heinrich Himmler to forbid it. The Danevirke and the nearby Viking town of Hedeby were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2018.
dang-district: The Dang district lies in the south-eastern part of the state of Gujarat in India, with its administrative headquarters at Ahwa. It has an area of 1,764 square kilometres. The meaning of its name is uncertain: in common speech dang means a hilly village, and it can also mean bamboo. The name is also tied to the Dandakaranya of the Ramayana, and tradition says that Rama passed through the area on his way to Nashik during his exile. In ancient Indian scriptures it is known as Danda Aranyaka, the bamboo forest.

Before Independence the five tribal kings of Dang fought several wars with the East India Company. According to the history of the Dangs, the largest was at Lashkaria Amba, where the kings of all five states joined to defend the region and the British were beaten and agreed to a compromise. By the treaty signed in 1842 the Company was allowed to use the forests and their natural products, in return for about 3,000 silver coins paid to the five kings. Historically there were 14 Dang states, and the five kingdoms that remained are Daher-Amala, Linga, Gadhvi, Vasurna and Pimpri.

The five kings still receive a yearly political pension under the agreement of 1842, which continued after the privy purses of the princely states were ended in 1970 because the agreement was between the monarchy of Dang and the Government of India, not the Crown. At Holi they gather in Ahwa for a royal ceremony, in decorated buggies with bands and tribal dancers, to receive it. 65 percent of them belonged to scheduled tribes. 53 percent. Part of the Purna Wildlife Sanctuary lies in the district, and Saputara is a hill station.
dangun: In the legend, Tan'gun's grandfather was Hwanin, the Lord of Heaven. Hwanin's son Hwanung yearned to live on the earth among the valleys and mountains, and with 3,000 followers he descended onto Taebaeksan, now believed to be Paektu Mountain, where he founded Sinsi, the City of God. With his ministers of clouds, rain and wind he instituted laws and moral codes and taught humans the arts, medicine and agriculture. A tiger and a bear prayed to become human. Hwanung gave them twenty cloves of garlic and a bundle of mugwort and told them to eat only this and stay out of the sunlight for 100 days. The tiger left after about twenty days, but the bear persevered and became a woman, Ungnyeo.

Ungnyeo made offerings to Hwanung but had no husband, and she prayed beneath a divine birch tree for a child. Hwanung took her as his wife, and she bore a son, Tan'gun Wang'gŏm. He ascended the throne, built the walled city of Asadal near Pyongyang, though its location is disputed, and called his kingdom Joseon, now called Gojoseon to distinguish it from the later Joseon kingdom. The bear and the tiger are said to represent two tribes that sought the favour of the heavenly prince.
His reign is usually reckoned from 2333 BCE, following the Tongguk t'onggam of 1485, and sources place it in the reign of the Chinese emperor Yao, though they differ on the year.

The earliest recorded version of the legend is in the 13th-century Samguk yusa, which cites the lost Gogi and China's Book of Wei, though the surviving Book of Wei holds nothing about Tan'gun. Similar versions appear in the Jewang Un-gi of Yi Seunghyu and in early Joseon records.

Tan'gun drew attention in the late Goryeo dynasty, when Koreans fought the Mongol Yuan dynasty, and the Joseon dynasty built shrines to him. At the end of the 19th century he became a figure of resistance to imperialism, and he was central to nationalism and the independence movement under Japanese rule. Until 1961 the official South Korean era, the Dangi, counted years from 2333 BCE. National Foundation Day on 3 October was begun as a religious anniversary by Daejongism, which worships him, as do the followers of Cheondoism.
daniel-defoe: Daniel Foe was probably born in the parish of St Giles Cripplegate, London, and his birth date is uncertain, with sources offering dates from 1659 to 1662. The summer or early autumn of 1660 is considered the most likely. He later added the aristocratic-sounding De to his name. His father, James Foe, was a prosperous tallow chandler of probable Flemish descent. His parents were Presbyterian dissenters, and around the age of 14 he was sent to Charles Morton's dissenting academy at Newington Green.

Defoe entered business as a general merchant, dealing in hosiery, woollen goods and wine, and he was rarely out of debt. On 1 January 1684 he married Mary Tuffley, and the marriage lasted 47 years and produced eight children. In 1685 he joined the Monmouth Rebellion but gained a pardon, and after William III was crowned in 1689 he became one of the king's close allies and a secret agent. In 1692 he was arrested for debts of £700 and declared bankruptcy.

His first notable publication was An Essay Upon Projects, a series of proposals for social and economic improvement, in 1697. His poem The True-Born Englishman of 1701 defended William against xenophobic attacks. While imprisoned in a case of seditious libel he wrote to William Paterson, and Robert Harley, the leading minister, accepted his services and released him in 1703. Defoe then published the weekly Review, which was the main mouthpiece of the government in promoting the Act of Union of 1707. By September 1706 Harley had ordered him to Edinburgh as a secret agent.

As many as 545 titles have been attributed to Defoe. He used at least 198 pen names, and since most of his works were published anonymously, scholars have had difficulty crediting them all.
