Moll Flanders and Roxana were published anonymously for over fifty years, until Francis Noble named him on their title pages in 1774 and 1775.

Robinson Crusoe, published in 1719 when he was in his late fifties, tells of a man shipwrecked on a desert island for twenty-eight years. Crusoe's struggles with faith run through the narrative. The book had run through four editions before the end of 1719, and its imitations gave rise to a genre called the Robinsonade. Defoe died on 24 April 1731, probably while in hiding from his creditors, and was buried at Bunhill Fields.
daniel-oconnell: Daniel O'Connell was born at Carhan House, near Cahersiveen, County Kerry, to the O'Connells of Derrynane, a wealthy Roman Catholic family that, under the Penal Laws, had retained its land only through Protestant trustees. His parents were Morgan O'Connell and Catherine O'Mullane. He grew up at Derrynane House in the household of his childless uncle Maurice O'Connell, who made him his heir presumptive. After legal studies in London, including a pupillage at Lincoln's Inn, he returned to Ireland in 1795.

In 1802 he married his third cousin Mary O'Connell, in defiance of his uncle, who thought he should have sought an heiress. They had four daughters and four sons, and each of the sons later sat in Parliament. O'Connell's principles drew on the Enlightenment and on William Godwin's Enquiry Concerning Political Justice; for a period Thomas Paine's The Age of Reason made him a deist, but by 1809 he had returned to the Church.

In 1823 O'Connell established the Catholic Association. For a Catholic rent of a penny a month, typically paid through the local priest, it drew the labouring poor into a national movement. It mounted monster rallies of over 100,000 people and emboldened enfranchised tenants to vote for pro-emancipation candidates in defiance of their landlords. His enemies derided him as the King of Beggars. Disavowing revolutionary violence, he held that no political change was worth the shedding of a single drop of human blood.

Emancipation passed in 1829, but the Parliamentary Elections (Ireland) Act of the same year raised the county franchise threshold five-fold to ten pounds and cut the Irish electorate from 216,000 voters to 37,000. At Westminster O'Connell championed reform causes and was known internationally as an abolitionist. He relaunched the Repeal Association in April 1840, and on 15 August 1843 he gathered a crowd at the Hill of Tara estimated by The Times at close to one million.

In 1845 O'Connell condemned the proposed non-denominational Queen's Colleges, which dismayed the Young Irelanders grouped around The Nation. Weakened by this split and by criticism of his political compromises, he made a pilgrimage to Rome and died in Genoa in May 1847, aged 71. In accord with his wishes, his heart was buried in Rome and the rest of his body in Glasnevin Cemetery in Dublin. The Repeal Association was dissolved in June 1848.

Honoré de Balzac called him an incarnation of a people. In the German states he became a folk hero among Catholics, and his Catholic Association served as a model for the Katholischer Verein Deutschland. Dublin's Sackville Street was renamed O'Connell Street in 1922.
daniel-webster: Webster was born on 18 January 1782 in Salisbury, New Hampshire, in what is now the city of Franklin. His father, Ebenezer Webster, was a farmer and local official who had served in the French and Indian War and the American Revolutionary War. Webster was the second-youngest of eight siblings and was close to his older brother Ezekiel. After admission to the bar he practised at Boscawen, and after his father's death in 1806 he handed the practice to Ezekiel and moved to Portsmouth, where he handled over 1,700 cases in a decade.

Elected to the House of Representatives in 1813, Webster criticised the War of 1812 and opposed conscription, wartime taxes and a new embargo. He then moved to Boston and became a leading attorney before the Supreme Court, winning Dartmouth College v. Woodward, McCulloch v. Maryland and Gibbons v. Ogden. Back in the House from 1823, he chaired the Judiciary Committee under Speaker Henry Clay. In 1827 the Massachusetts legislature elected him to the Senate, where he worked with Clay to build the National Republican Party.

After Andrew Jackson defeated John Quincy Adams in 1828, Webster led the opposition to Jackson's domestic policies. His Second Reply to Hayne of 1830 answered the theory of nullification of John C. Calhoun. He supported Jackson against the nullification crisis but broke with him over the Second Bank of the United States, joined in forming the Whig Party and ran unsuccessfully for president in 1836.

Webster became secretary of state under William Henry Harrison in 1841. He negotiated the Webster–Ashburton Treaty, which settled border disputes with Britain. Returning to the Senate in 1845, he led the Cotton Whigs, who stressed good relations with the South over anti-slavery policy. He had called slavery a great moral, social and political evil in 1837 but did not think Congress should interfere with it in the states. As Millard Fillmore's secretary of state from 1850 he helped pass the Compromise of 1850, which included a new fugitive slave law and was unpopular in much of the North.

Webster suffered from cirrhosis of the liver. He died at his Marshfield estate in Massachusetts on 24 October 1852, aged 70, his last words being 'I still live', and was buried in Winslow Cemetery. Historians have offered mixed opinions on his moral qualities and his ability as a national leader. Stephen Vincent Benét made him the main character of the story The Devil and Daniel Webster.
danishmendids: The dynasty was founded by Danishmend Gazi, whose name or title is Persian for 'wise man'. Information about him is scarce and was mostly written long after his death, and the sources about his origins are steeped in later tradition. The Byzantine historian Niketas Choniates gives him Arsacid descent, while the Armenian historians Matthew of Edessa and Vardan Areveltsi call him Armenian. Other accounts make him a nephew of the Great Seljuk sultan Malik-Shah I or a maternal uncle of Suleiman ibn Qutulmish, first ruler of the Sultanate of Rum. The Danishmendnâme, a 14th-century epic romance, calls him a native of Malatya.

The Danishmends established themselves in Anatolia after the Battle of Manzikert in 1071, and Danishmend Gazi used the Seljuk dynastic struggles that followed the death of Suleyman I of Rum in 1086 to found a dynasty in central Anatolia, probably first at Amasia. The state centred on Sivas, Tokat and Niksar, reached for a time as far west as Ankara and Kastamonu, and took Malatya in 1103. In 1100 Gazi's son Emir Gazi captured Bohemond I of Antioch, who stayed a prisoner until 1103, and a Seljuk-Danishmend alliance defeated the Crusade of 1101. In 1116 the Danishmends helped Mesud I become Seljuk sultan, and in 1130 Emir Gazi killed Bohemond II of Antioch in battle.

From 1134 the rulers held the title Melik, granted by the Abbasid caliph al-Mustarshid. When Melik Mehmed Gazi died in 1142 his lands were divided between his brothers Yaghibasan, who ruled from Sivas, and Ayn el-Devle, who ruled from Malatya. The Seljuk sultan Kilij Arslan II attacked Yaghibasan in 1155, and after Nur ad-Din of Mosul, whom Yaghibasan had asked for help, died in 1174 the Sivas lands were incorporated into the Seljuk sultanate. The occupation of Malatya in 1178 ended Danishmend rule, and the remaining Danishmends entered Seljuk service.

Danishmend Gazi is the central figure of the Danishmendnâme, in which he is confused with an 8th-century Arab warrior, Sidi Battal Gazi. Danishmend rulers entered Turkish folk literature as Melik Gazi, and shrines called tombs of Melik Gazi at Niksar, Bünyan, Kırşehir and elsewhere may belong to different rulers. Melikgazi is also a district of Kayseri, which Melik Mehmed Gazi is considered to have first built as a Turkish city. The Danishmendid coinage was bilingual, with Greek inscriptions, and showed a figure slaying a dragon, thought to represent St. George.
dante-alighieri: Dante was born in Florence, probably around May 1265, a date deduced from allusions in the Divine Comedy. His father, Alighiero di Bellincione, was a businessman and moneylender, and his mother Bella, probably of the noble Abati family, died before he was ten. Dante claimed descent from the ancient Romans, but the earliest relative he could name was his great-great-grandfather Cacciaguida degli Elisei. His family was loyal to the Guelphs, who supported the papacy, against the Ghibellines, who supported the Holy Roman Empire.

Dante fought with the Florentine Guelphs at the Battle of Campaldino on 11 June 1289 and joined the Guild of Physicians and Apothecaries around 1295, which allowed him to hold public office. After the Guelphs defeated the Ghibellines they split into the White Guelphs, Dante's party, led by Vieri dei Cerchi, and the Black Guelphs, led by Corso Donati. The Whites wanted more freedom from Rome. In 1301 a delegation including Dante went to persuade Pope Boniface VIII not to send Charles of Valois to Florence, but the Pope kept Dante in Rome.

On 1 November 1301 Charles of Valois entered Florence with the Black Guelphs, who destroyed much of the city. In March 1302 Dante was condemned to exile for two years and a large fine, accused of corruption during his two months as prior in 1300. He did not pay and was condemned to perpetual exile, with the threat of being burned at the stake if he returned. He was a guest of Moroello Malaspina in Lunigiana in 1306–07, and in 1318 Guido II da Polenta invited him to Ravenna.

Dante died in Ravenna on 14 September 1321, aged about 56, of quartan malaria contracted while returning from a diplomatic mission to Venice. He was buried at the Church of San Pier Maggiore, later the Basilica di San Francesco. In 1329 Cardinal Bertrand du Pouget classified his Monarchia as heretical and sought to have his bones burned, but allies interceded. Florence built a tomb for him in Santa Croce in 1829, which has stayed empty, and in 2008 its city council rescinded his sentence.

Most of his work was composed after his exile. La Vita Nuova, the story of his love for Beatrice Portinari in poems and prose, is the only major work that predates it. The Divine Comedy describes a journey through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise, guided first by Virgil and then by Beatrice. He wrote it in Tuscan rather than Latin, and his use of the Florentine dialect helped establish standardised Italian. His De vulgari eloquentia was one of the first scholarly defences of the vernacular. Giovanni Boccaccio wrote the first formal biography.
danube: The Danube is the second-longest river in Europe after the Volga. It rises in the Black Forest of Germany, where the Brigach and the Breg meet at Donaueschingen, and flows southeast through four capital cities, Vienna, Bratislava, Budapest and Belgrade, before emptying into the Black Sea through the Danube Delta in Romania and Ukraine. Its drainage basin covers 817,000 square kilometres. Since ancient times it has been a traditional trade route.

The ancient Greeks called it the Istros, from a root possibly related to words for swift. Its Thraco-Phrygian name was Matoas, the bringer of luck, and the modern languages of the basin use names derived from the Latin Danubius. Geologically it is much older than the Rhine: before the last ice age the waters from the Alps now feeding the Rhine were carried east by the Urdonau, or original Danube.

The Danube basin was the site of some of the earliest human cultures, among them the Linear Pottery cultures and, from the sixth to third millennium BCE, the Vinča culture. The Vučedol culture of the third millennium BCE is known for its ceramics. Darius the Great of Persia crossed the river in the late 6th century BCE to subdue the Scythians, and in 336 BCE Alexander the Great advanced from Macedonia as far as the Danube and defeated the Triballian king Syrmus. The river was long a frontier of the Roman Empire. The Paris Conferences of 1856 and 1921 established an international regime to safeguard free navigation, and the Danube Commission was set up by seven riparian countries in 1948.

The Danube passes through or borders ten countries. Since the Rhine-Main-Danube Canal was completed in 1992 it has been part of a waterway of about 3,500 kilometres from Rotterdam on the North Sea to Sulina on the Black Sea. It supplies drinking water to about 20 million people and is an important source of hydropower. The Danube Delta is the largest river delta in the European Union and a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991. Johann Strauss's waltz The Blue Danube made the river's name known worldwide.
daodejing: The text is traditionally ascribed to Laozi, whose historical existence is debated; his name means Old Master. The first biographical reference to him is in the Records of the Grand Historian by Sima Qian. Tradition makes him an older contemporary of Confucius, but no scholarship in the West follows an early dating of the whole text, and most modern scholars hold it to be a compilation. Sayings attributed to Laozi were probably written down from the second half of the 5th century BCE and reached a relatively stable form in the late Warring States period, around the middle of the 3rd century BCE.

Manuscript finds have changed the debate. The Guodian bamboo slips of about 300 BCE are shorter than the received text and lack its last fifteen chapters. Two nearly complete silk copies were found in 1973 in a tomb at Mawangdui dated to 168 BCE, and they put the Te Ching half before the Tao Ching.

The received text has about 5,162 to 5,450 Chinese characters in 81 brief chapters, in two parts: the Daojing, chapters 1 to 37, and the Dejing, chapters 38 to 81. The Heshang Gong version divided it into 81 chapters; earlier versions are reported with 64, 68 or 72. The style is laconic and poetic, combining short declarative statements with deliberate contradictions, and it names no particular persons, times or places.

The text describes the Dao as the source and ideal of all existence, unseen but not transcendent, immensely powerful yet humble. It aims to lead its students back to a natural state in harmony with the Dao, and it treats language and conventional wisdom as biased and artificial. A central concept is wu wei, literally non-action.

The three main transmitted editions are named after the commentaries of Yan Zun, Heshang Gong and Wang Bi. From the early Tang dynasty it was mainly transmitted with the last two, and in 719 Wang Bi's was declared authoritative, though Heshang Gong's remained dominant into the Song dynasty.

It is foundational to Taoism alongside the Zhuangzi and has been profoundly influential in Chinese culture, art and medicine. Its terms were reinterpreted by Legalist thinkers, Confucians and above all by Chinese Buddhism. First translated into French in the early 19th century, it is one of the most translated texts in world literature.
dar-es-salaam: Dar es Salaam lies at 6°48' S, 39°17' E, on a natural harbour on the Swahili coast of East Africa, with sandy beaches in places. The climate is tropical savanna, hot and humid for much of the year, with about 1,150 millimetres of rain annually and two rainy seasons, the long rains in April and May and the short rains in November and December. The city is co-extensive with the Dar es Salaam Region, which has five districts: Kinondoni, Ilala, Ubungo, Temeke and Kigamboni.

In the 19th century Mzizima, Swahili for 'healthy town', was a coastal fishing village on the edge of the Indian Ocean trade routes. In 1865 or 1866 Sultan Majid bin Said of Zanzibar began building a new city close to it and named it Dar es Salaam, commonly translated from Arabic as 'abode of peace'. The town declined after Majid's death in 1870.

It revived in 1887, when the German East Africa Company established a station there. Its growth then followed its role as the administrative and commercial centre of German East Africa, and industrial expansion after the building of the Central Railway Line in the early 1900s. It continued as the main administrative and commercial centre of Tanganyika and then of Tanzania. In 1974 a decision was made to move the capital to Dodoma, a move officially completed in 1996.
In 1949 the town became a municipality, with nominated town councillors who elected a mayor, according to the historian John Iliffe. The city's first radio station began operating in the early 1950s.

Dar es Salaam is the largest city and financial centre of Tanzania, with a population of more than 7 million. About 70 per cent of its people are Muslim, and it has many churches, mosques and Hindu temples. The Port of Dar es Salaam handles about 90 per cent of the country's cargo, and the Central Line runs west from the city to Kigoma. The TAZARA railway, built in the late 1960s and early 1970s, links it to Zambia.

The Tingatinga painting style originates in the city. It has the National Museum, which shows bones of Paranthropus boisei found by Louis Leakey at Olduvai, and the University of Dar es Salaam, the oldest public university in Tanzania.
dara-shikoh: Muhammad Dara Shikoh was born at Ajmer on 20 March 1615, the first son and third child of Prince Khurram, the later Shah Jahan, and Mumtaz Mahal. He studied the Quran, history, Persian poetry and calligraphy, and beside his native Persian learned Hindi, Arabic and later Sanskrit. He and his elder sister Jahanara Begum were their father's favourite children.

On 1 February 1633 he married his half-cousin Nadira Banu Begum at Agra, and he contracted no other marriage. In the same year he was appointed heir apparent, which Shah Jahan formally confirmed on 10 September 1642 with the title Shahzada-e-Buland Iqbal, Prince of High Fortune. He was made governor of Allahabad in 1645 and of Gujarat in 1648.

Dara followed the Qadiri Sufi saint Mian Mir of Lahore, to whom Mullah Shah Badakhshi introduced him, and the mystic Sarmad Kashani, and he formed a friendship with the seventh Sikh Guru, Guru Har Rai. The treatise known as Majma-ul-Bahrain was written in Persian in 1654–55. His Persian version of fifty Upanishads, completed in 1657 and often called Sirr-i-Akbar, proposes in its introduction that the hidden book named in the Quran is the Upanishads. Annemarie Schimmel notes that he remained committed to the fundamentals of Islam and repeatedly called himself a Hanafi Qadiri.

He was a patron of painting, music and dancing, tastes that Aurangzeb frowned upon. The album of paintings and calligraphy that bears his name was presented to his wife in 1641–42; after her death the inscriptions linking it to him were deliberately erased.

After Samugarh he retreated by Delhi, Lahore, Multan and Thatta to Kathiawar, where Shah Nawaz Khan, governor of Gujarat, helped him raise a new army. After the rout at Deorai on 11 March 1659 he sought refuge in Sindh with the Afghan chieftain Malik Jeevan, whose life he had saved more than once, but Malik Jeevan seized him and informed Aurangzeb, whose army took him on 10 June 1659.

In Delhi he was paraded through the streets in chains on an elephant. A convocation of nobles and clergy called by Aurangzeb declared him a threat to the public peace and an apostate from Islam, and he was killed in front of his son on the night of 30 August 1659. He was buried in an unidentified grave in Humayun's tomb. In 2020 Sanjeev Kumar Singh, a municipal engineer, identified one of three unmarked cenotaphs beneath the dome as his, relying on the Alamgirnama; several historians and archaeologists have accepted the identification.
darial-pass: The Darial Gorge is a gorge of the River Terek on the border between Russia and Georgia, at the east base of Mount Kazbek and south of present-day Vladikavkaz. It is about 13 kilometres long, and its steep granite walls reach 1,800 metres in places. The Georgian Military Road runs through it.

The pass was historically one of only two crossings of the Caucasus range, the other being the Derbent Pass, and it has been fortified since at least 150 BCE. Writers of late antiquity imagined it as a boundary between the known world and the unknown land of the barbarians. It is the main border crossing between Georgia and Russia.

The name comes from the Persian Dar-i Alān, meaning Gate of the Alans, who held the lands north of the pass in the first centuries CE. The Romans and Persians both fortified it, and the fortification was known variously as the Iberian Gates or the Caucasian Gates. Classical writers often mistakenly called it the Caspian Gates. Strabo calls it Porta Caucasica and Porta Cumana, Ptolemy calls it Fortes Sarmatica, and the Georgian annals call it Darialani. Josephus wrote that Alexander the Great built iron gates at an unspecified pass that some Latin and Greek authors identified with Darial.

The Sassanid Empire took the pass in 252–253 when it conquered and annexed Iberia. In 628 control passed to the Western Turkic Kaganate under a treaty between Tong Yabgu Kagan and Iberia, which also established free trade, and in 644 to the Rashidun Caliphate. It was later held by the Kingdom of Georgia and was a point of contention between the Ilkhanate and the Golden Horde. Kabardians occupied it in 1597, and it was captured by the Russian Empire in the period of its annexation of the Kingdom of Georgia, 1801–1830. It remained a strategic Russian outpost until the dissolution of the Soviet Union.
darius-i: Darius was the eldest of five sons of Hystaspes, who according to the Behistun Inscription was satrap of Bactria in 522 BCE. His mother's identity is uncertain: one modern historian thought she was a woman named Rhodogune, while others, citing recently found texts from Persepolis, name her as Irdabama, a landowner descended from a family of local Elamite rulers. Herodotus says that before seizing power Darius served as a spearman in the Egyptian campaign of Cambyses II, and the Behistun Inscription makes Hystaspes a second cousin of Cyrus, though that may have been invented to legitimate Darius's accession.

The oldest records say that Cambyses II lost his mind, had his brother Bardiya murdered and died of an infected leg wound. Darius and six nobles then went to Sikayauvati and killed a usurper, Gaumata, who had taken the throne by pretending to be Bardiya. Darius ruled from 522 BCE. After his coronation at Pasargadae he found support for Bardiya strong, and revolts broke out in Elam, Babylonia, Persis, Media, Parthia, Assyria and Egypt. He suppressed each in turn, taking his armies through the empire. The Babylonian revolt, led by Nebuchadnezzar III, was the most notable.

In 516 BCE he marched into Central Asia, and he conquered the lands around the Indus in 515 BCE. He appointed Scylax of Caryanda to explore the Indian Ocean from the mouth of the Indus to Suez. In 513 BCE he crossed the Bosphorus on a bridge of boats and the Danube to invade European Scythia, where the Scythians evaded his army, laid waste the country and blocked wells. He conquered Thrace and the northern Aegean, and Macedonia submitted as a vassal. At its territorial peak the empire stretched from parts of the Balkans in the west to the Indus Valley in the east.

Darius divided the empire into provinces, each governed by a satrap, organised a uniform monetary system, made Aramaic a co-official language beside Old Persian, improved roads and introduced standard weights and measures. He built at Susa, Pasargadae, Persepolis, Babylon and in Egypt. A trilingual inscription in Elamite, Old Persian and Babylonian, carved on a cliff at Mount Behistun, records his conquests and begins with his ancestry; he repeatedly claims to be rightful king by the grace of Ahura Mazda. It later became a key source for the Old Persian language and for the decipherment of cuneiform. Greek historians know him for a punitive expedition against Athens and Eretria after the Ionian Revolt.
darius-ii: Darius II, called Ochus before he took a royal name, came to the throne on the death of Artaxerxes I after a struggle among that king's sons. Babylonian records of the Murashu archive show the transition but name no rival, while Greek and Latin historians, chiefly Ctesias of Cnidus, describe it. Darius received his royal name and recognition from supporters in Babylon, while his half-brothers Xerxes II and Sogdianus claimed authority elsewhere.

After 45 days Sogdianus had Xerxes assassinated. Darius gathered support from figures such as Arbarius, Sogdianus's former cavalry commander, Arsames, satrap of Egypt, and the Paphlagonian eunuch Artoxares. He and his wife and half-sister Parysatis arranged negotiations, and Sogdianus was seized when he came and executed in a pit of hot ashes. Greek sources often call Darius Nothos, the Bastard. He seems to have depended heavily on Parysatis.

Revolts followed. His full brother Arsites, satrap of Syria, rebelled for unclear reasons with Artyphius, son of the earlier rebel Megabyzus. Their army defeated a royal force twice and lost a third battle; the Greek mercenaries were bribed to surrender, and both leaders were executed with hot ashes. Pissuthnes, satrap of Lydia, also revolted.

Darius sent Tissaphernes, who persuaded the Greek mercenaries to change sides, and Pissuthnes was sent to Persia to be executed. Tissaphernes became satrap of Lydia. In Armenia the satrap Terituchmes, who had married Darius's daughter Amestris, plotted to murder her, and an Armenian noble, Udiastes, killed him in battle. Xenophon and Diodorus Siculus mention further minor revolts among the Medes, Cadusians, Pisidians, Arabs and Egyptians.

Darius did not meddle in Greek affairs while Athenian power was intact, and he confirmed peace with Athens through an envoy, Epilycus, either by a new agreement or by renewing the Peace of Callias. Pissuthnes's son Amorges held out at Iasus with mercenaries paid by Athens. After the Athenian disaster at Syracuse, the king ordered Tissaphernes and the satrap Pharnabazus II to collect overdue tribute from the Greek towns and to make war. Tissaphernes allied with Sparta, and with the Spartan navy the Persians took Iasus from Amorges in 412 BCE. In 408 BCE Darius sent his son Cyrus to Asia Minor to prosecute the war with more energy.

Darius died in the nineteenth year of his reign and was followed by his son Artaxerxes II. Parysatis bore him Artaxerxes II and Cyrus the Younger, among others, and seven further children died in childhood.
darius-iii: Darius was born about 380 BCE as a distant member of the Achaemenid dynasty. He was the son of a certain Arsames and the grandson of Ostanes, whose father Darius II had ruled from 424 to 405 BCE. Before his accession he bore the name Artashata. He first appears in the 350s BCE in the Cadusian expedition of Artaxerxes III, when he distinguished himself by killing a warrior in single combat. The king rewarded him with the satrapy of Armenia.

Artaxerxes III died in September 338 BCE, poisoned by the court eunuch Bagoas, who put the king's youngest son Arses on the throne and later poisoned him too. In 336 BCE Bagoas installed Darius. By one legend Bagoas tried to poison Darius as well and was forced to drink the poisoned cup himself.

The last century of Achaemenid rule is poorly documented, and Darius is known almost entirely from Greek historians, who portray his career as the opposite of Alexander's success. In the spring of 334 BCE Alexander the Great invaded Asia Minor and defeated the Persians at the Granicus, a battle Darius did not attend. At Issus, in the next major battle, his army had a large numerical advantage but was outflanked after its left collapsed, and Darius left the field. Alexander captured the royal baggage train, including Darius's family. Alexander refused to release them unless acknowledged as ruler of Asia.

At Gaugamela in 331 BCE Darius had troops properly organised, the support of several satraps and level ground for his scythed chariots. He fled before the battle was decided, and the Persian losses meant he could never again raise an imperial army. Alexander took Babylon, Susa and Persepolis, and Darius reportedly offered him all territory west of the Euphrates in exchange for peace several times, without success.

Darius withdrew from Ecbatana towards Bactria. The satrap Bessus and Nabarzanes, who controlled access to the king, bound Darius and put him in an ox-cart. According to Curtius, when Alexander approached, Bessus and two others wounded the king with javelins and left him to die. Ancient sources say Alexander sent the body to Persepolis for a royal burial. The tomb has not been found. Alexander married Darius's daughter Stateira at Susa in 324 BCE.

Modern historians read Alexander's funeral for Darius as a political act that presented him as a successor and avenger rather than a foreign conqueror. Some historians regard Darius as cowardly and inefficient, since the whole empire fell under him. Bessus took the name Artaxerxes V, was captured by Alexander, tortured and executed.
darlowo: Darłowo is a seaside town on the Slovincian Coast of north-western Poland, south of the Baltic Sea, in Sławno County. By the 11th century a fortress named Dirlow existed where the River Wieprza enters the Baltic, and from it a district belonging to the castellany of Sławno was administered. A town was later founded in the district, though not at the fortress itself. The original medieval outline of the Old Town, with its main square in the middle, has been preserved.

The town was probably founded in 1270 by Vitslav II of the Danish Principality of Rügen, and is first mentioned in a document of 5 February 1271. It was granted Lübeck law on 21 May 1312 under the Brandenburg margraves, passed to the Duchy of Pomerania in 1347, and began building its castle in 1352. It became a full member of the Hanseatic League in 1412 and had a trade fleet larger than those of the surrounding towns, trading with Lübeck and sending ships as far as Normandy and Spain.

Eric of Pomerania, later king of Norway, Denmark and Sweden, was born in the town in 1382. After losing his thrones he returned to his birthplace and expanded his duchy, modernising and extending the castle between 1449 and 1459. He was buried in St Mary's Church after his death in 1459. From 1569 to 1622 Darłowo was capital of a small duchy of its own. After the Thirty Years' War, Brandenburg took Farther Pomerania with Rügenwalde into its province, and the town entered a period of economic stagnation.

In 1871 the town became part of the German Empire, and a railway reached it in 1878. In 1935 a German Army firing range for heavy guns was built nearby. After the Second World War the Potsdam Conference assigned the town to Poland, its German population was expelled, and it was repopulated in 1946-47 with Poles and Lemkos. The Gothic castle, on a plan resembling a square with a tower 24 metres high, now serves as a museum, and the Old Town and its beaches draw holidaymakers.
darmstadt: Darmstadt lies in the southern part of the Rhine-Main area, in the Upper Rhine Plain, a rift about 350 km long that runs between Frankfurt in the north and Mannheim in the south. Its southeastern boroughs sit in the spurs of the Odenwald, a low mountain range between the Main and Neckar rivers. The city has around 160,000 inhabitants.

The name first appears towards the end of the 11th century as Darmundestat. In 1330 the Holy Roman Emperor Ludwig the Bavarian chartered it as a city, when it belonged to the counts of Katzenelnbogen, who made it a secondary residence and built a small castle on the site of the present, much larger palace. Its theatre, the Staatstheater, dates back to 1711, and many landmarks of the Grand Duchy of Hesse were designed by Georg Moller, the court master builder. During the 19th century the population grew from a little over 10,000 to 72,000, and a polytechnical school founded in 1877 became the Technical University, which in 1882 was the first university in the world to set up a chair in electrical engineering.

In early 1933, soon after the Nazis took power, Darmstadt was the first city in Germany to force Jewish shops to close, for one day. In 1942 more than 3,000 Jews from the city were gathered in the Liebigschule and later deported to concentration camps, where most eventually died. United States forces entered the city on 25 March 1945.

Darmstadt holds the official title City of Science. It is the seat of the European Space Agency's European Space Operations Centre, of EUMETSAT, and of Merck, the world's oldest pharmaceutical company. At the GSI Centre for Heavy Ion Research several elements were synthesised, and darmstadtium, number 110, was named after the city in 2003. The Mathildenhöhe, home of the Darmstadt artists' colony and a major centre of the Jugendstil movement, was recognised as a World Heritage Site in 2021, together with the Russian Chapel built for Tsar Nicholas II, whose wife Alexandra was born in the city.
daroca: According to some writers, the earliest Celtiberian village on the site was called Darek. The Romans named it Agiria and built a strong castle to defend the Laminium road, which ran through it and linked Zaragoza with Valencia. The Arabs called it Calat-Darawca, from 862, and held it for 400 years until Alfonso the Battler conquered it in 1120. In the 12th century Ramon Berenguer IV gave it the laws and privileges that made it capital of the Community of Daroca, which had great social and military influence in the Middle Ages.

Daroca had a vote in the courts and hosted assemblies under Peter II in 1196 and Peter IV in 1338, when peace with Castile was arranged. It resisted a siege in a war against Peter of Castile and became a city on 26 April 1366.

The town was governed by a council whose principal members were the justice, judge, jurors, almutazaf and scribes. Offices lasted a year and appointments were made on 1 January. Christians, Jews and Muslims enjoyed the same laws and privileges, though each group was organised separately, and agriculture and livestock were the main occupations. After the death of Charles II, Daroca backed the Austrian claimant Charles III against Philip, duke of Anjou, and was occupied and sacked in the War of the Spanish Succession. This ended almost six centuries of municipal autonomy, as a royal magistrate replaced the justice.

Daroca is a city and municipality in the province of Zaragoza, in Aragon, in the basin of Calatayud and the valley of the Jiloca river, south of the city of Zaragoza. It is the centre of a judicial district. More than 4 kilometres of medieval walls survive, with gates including the Puerta Baja, the Puerta Alta and the Portal de Valencia. Its churches include San Miguel, San Juan and Santo Domingo, and the Basilica of Santa María de los Sagrados Corporales is associated with a Eucharistic miracle dated to 1239. The Fountain of the twenty pipes is also among its sights. Agriculture, especially vine and vegetable growing, has been in decline, and local effort is directed at commerce and tourism.
dartmoor: Dartmoor is an upland area in southern Devon. The granite that forms it dates from the Carboniferous period and was intruded as a pluton, probably about 309 million years ago. It is the largest area of granite in Britain, though most of it lies under peat. The landscape consists of moorland capped by exposed granite hilltops known as tors, each a mass of granite left standing where deep chemical weathering removed the surrounding, more heavily jointed rock.

The highest point is High Willhays at 621 m. Much more rain falls here than in the surrounding lowlands, and in places the peat holds dangerous bogs. The moor takes its name from the River Dart, which begins as the East Dart and West Dart and joins at Dartmeet. Many of Devon's rivers rise here and have traditionally powered tin mining and quarrying.

Most prehistoric remains date to the late Neolithic and early Bronze Age, and Dartmoor holds the largest concentration of Bronze Age remains in the United Kingdom. The climate was then warmer and much of the moorland was wooded. Settlers cleared the forest, mainly by fire, and established the first farming communities, and these practices greatly expanded the upland moors and contributed to the acidification of the soil and the build-up of peat.

Bronze Age fields divided by reaves cover over 10,000 hectares of the lower moors. About 5,000 hut circles survive, the remnants of Bronze Age houses, with good examples at Grimspound, and the moor has many standing stones, stone circles, kistvaens and cairns. The Upper Erme stone row, at 3,300 m, is the longest on Dartmoor.

From around 1000 BCE the climate grew wetter and cooler over a thousand years, and much of the high moor was largely abandoned. Settlers moved back in the early medieval period when the weather warmed, building houses of granite in the style known as the Dartmoor longhouse. The earliest surviving farms, known as the Ancient Tenements, mostly date from the 14th century or earlier.

Dartmoor has been protected as a National Park since 1951 and covers 954 km2. Over half of it is private land, the Forest of Dartmoor being owned by the Duke of Cornwall, and about 37 per cent is common land. Since the Dartmoor Commons Act 1985 much of it has been designated access land. Parts of the northern moor have been used for military training since the Napoleonic Wars. The moor is also a Special Area of Conservation for its blanket bogs, heaths and oak woods.
darwin-northern-territory: Darwin lies on the western shoreline of the Northern Territory, where the Beagle Gulf opens into the Timor Sea. The central business district occupies a low bluff overlooking Darwin Harbour. The Stuart Highway begins in the city and runs south through Tennant Creek and Alice Springs to Port Augusta in South Australia. The climate is tropical, with a wet season that usually arrives in late November or early December.

The Larrakia people are the traditional custodians of the area, which they call Garramilla, 'white stone', after its rock and sea cliffs. They had trading routes with Southeast Asia and imported goods from as far as South and Western Australia. Dutch ships visited the northern coast in the 1600s. On 9 September 1839 HMS Beagle sailed into the harbour, and John Clements Wickham named it Port Darwin in honour of Charles Darwin, who had sailed on the ship's earlier voyage.

The settlement became the town of Palmerston in 1869. South Australia administered the Northern Territory until its transfer to the Commonwealth in 1911, when the town was renamed Darwin. On 10 December 1919 Captain Ross Smith landed there in a Vickers Vimy and won a prize of 10,000 pounds for the first flight from London to Australia in under 30 days. Darwin has been almost entirely rebuilt four times, after cyclones in 1897 and 1937, Japanese air raids in the Second World War and Cyclone Tracy.

Cyclone Tracy struck on 25 December 1974, killed 71 people and destroyed over 70% of the city's buildings. Some 30,000 of the 46,000 inhabitants were evacuated in the largest airlift in Australian history. The Darwin Reconstruction Commission, led by Clem Jones, rebuilt the city in the late 1970s.

Darwin is the capital and largest city of the Northern Territory and had 139,902 inhabitants at the 2021 census, nearly 63% of the territory's population. Few historic buildings survive; the Administrator's Office of 1883 was rebuilt after 1974. Charles Darwin University is the main provider of higher education, and the Alice Springs to Darwin railway, completed in 2003, links the city with Adelaide.
das-kapital: Karl Marx began intensive economic studies in the 1840s and, after the revolutions of 1848 and his exile, resumed systematic research in London in 1850. The writing of Capital then stretched over several decades. The work engages three traditions: classical political economy, including Adam Smith and David Ricardo, German idealist philosophy, especially Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, and French socialist thought. Marx said his aim was to lay bare the economic law of motion of modern society, looking for the historical laws of capitalism's origins, development and decline. He delivered the manuscript of Volume I to the Hamburg publisher Otto Meissner in April 1867, and it appeared in September.

Volume I treats the process of production. It begins with the commodity, which has a use-value and an exchange-value, and argues that value is congealed abstract labour, measured by socially necessary labour time. Surplus value comes from the labourer working longer than is needed to reproduce the value of their labour power; Marx distinguishes absolute surplus value, gained by lengthening the working day, from relative surplus value, gained by cheapening wage goods.

Volume II, published by Friedrich Engels in 1885, examines the circulation of capital. Volume III, published by Engels in 1894, considers capitalist production as a whole, including how surplus value divides into profit, interest and rent, and the tendency of the rate of profit to fall. Running through the work are commodity fetishism, in which relations between people appear as relations between things, and the accumulation of capital, which Marx argues creates a reserve army of unemployed labour.

The first volume was received quietly in Germany. Engels sent hostile pseudonymous reviews to newspapers to draw attention, and the first edition of 1,000 copies took four years to sell out. In the late 19th and early 20th centuries the book, often in simplified form, became a foundational text of workers' movements and socialist parties. George Bernard Shaw studied it in 1883 and called it a revelation. It has also shaped sociology, political science and philosophy, and Marxian economics grew from it. Its labour theory of value, its predictions about capitalism and its association with 20th-century communist states have been criticised.
date-masamune: Date Masamune was born Bontenmaru, later Tojiro, the eldest son of Date Terumune, probably at Yonezawa Castle. He led his first campaign at 14 in 1581, helping his father against the Soma clan, and in 1584, aged 17, succeeded Terumune, who retired. A childhood smallpox left him blind in his right eye, and accounts differ on how the eye was lost altogether: one says he plucked it out himself, another that his retainer Katakura Kojuro removed it. He was known for his crescent-moon helmet, and his army for black armour and golden headgear.

After the Date retainer Ouchi Sadatsuna defected to the Ashina clan, Masamune campaigned against the Ashina and the allies of Sadatsuna, even kin. In 1585 Nihonmatsu Yoshitsugu offered to surrender; when Masamune demanded most of his territory, Yoshitsugu seized Terumune at Miyamori Castle, and Terumune and Yoshitsugu both died as the party fled. Masamune took revenge at the Battle of Hitotoribashi in January 1586, attacked Nihonmatsu again in 1588, and by the end of 1589 held southern Mutsu Province.

In 1590 he delayed joining Toyotomi Hideyoshi's campaign against Odawara. Expecting execution, he appeared in his finest clothes, and Hideyoshi spared him, saying he could be of some use, but reduced his lands. His men served in the Imjin War of 1592-1598. After Hideyoshi's death in 1598 Masamune supported Tokugawa Ieyasu, fought on the eastern side in the Sekigahara campaign of 1600 and received the Sendai Domain. Promised a million koku, it produced only 640,000. In 1604 he moved there with 52,000 vassals and their families, and fought in the Osaka campaigns of 1614 and 1615.

Ieyasu and Hidetada regarded him with caution, but he gained the trust of Iemitsu, who liked to hear the stories of warlords of the Warring States period. He died in 1636, aged 68, of esophageal cancer and peritonitis, and the shogunate approved his eldest legitimate son, Date Tadamune, as heir.

Masamune sheltered Christian missionaries, released the missionary Sotelo from Ieyasu's custody, and funded the embassy of Hasekura Tsunenaga to Rome, sailing in the ship San Juan Bautista built with European techniques. At least five members stayed in Spain, and about 600 descendants carry the surname Japon. Once Ieyasu outlawed Christianity, Masamune obeyed and let Christians be persecuted in his domain. The nickname One-Eyed Dragon is first found in a poem by Rai San'yo in 1830, and no record shows him wearing an eyepatch; his portrait shows both eyes open, as his will directed.
datong: Datong lies in the Datong Basin of northern Shanxi, at an elevation of 1,040 metres, bordering Inner Mongolia to the north and west and Hebei to the east. It is the northernmost city of Shanxi and about 250 kilometres west of Beijing. Mountains surround the urban area on three sides, with passes only to the east and southwest. Its climate is continental and dry, with long, cold winters and very warm summers. The area was a frontier between agricultural China and the nomads of the Great Steppe, and was known for its trade in horses.

The area lay near the state of Dai, which the Zhao clan of Jin conquered in 457 BCE. Under the Qin it was Pingcheng County, part of the commandery of Yanmen. The Han founded a site within present-day Datong in 200 BCE, after their victory over the Xiongnu at the Battle of Baideng. Near a pass to Inner Mongolia along the Great Wall, Pingcheng prospered as a stop for camel caravans moving from China into Mongolia, and it was sacked at the end of the Eastern Han.

Pingcheng was the capital of the Xianbei-founded Northern Wei dynasty from 398 to 494, and the Yungang Grottoes were carved in the later part of that period, between 460 and 494. Under the Tang it was the seat of the prefecture of Yunzhou, and the first Guandi temple was built. It was renamed Datong in 1048 and was the Xijing, the Western Capital, of the Jurchen Jin dynasty before the Mongols sacked it.

Under the Ming, Datong was an important military stronghold against the Mongols to the north, and many of its notable structures, among them the Drum Tower and the Nine-Dragon Wall, date from that time. It was sacked again at the end of the Ming in 1649 and rebuilt by 1652. In the Second Sino-Japanese War the Japanese included the region in the puppet state of Mengjiang, and it returned to Shanxi after the war. In 1982, with part of its city walls still standing, it was listed among China's national historical and cultural cities.

Datong is a prefecture-level city of about three million people. Coal mining has long been its dominant industry, and a locomotive works opened in 1954 made almost all of the QJ class of steam locomotive, built as late as 1988. The Yungang Grottoes, 16 kilometres west of the city, hold over 50,000 carved images of Buddhas and bodhisattvas, most about 1,500 years old, and are a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Hanging Temple, built into a cliff face near Mount Heng, dates to the Northern Wei.
daugavpils: The town's history began in 1273, when the Livonian Order under Ernst von Ratzeburg built Dünaburg Castle on the site of a Lithuanian settlement, Naujinis, about 18 km from the present city. Lithuania ruled the area between 1281 and 1313. In 1577 Ivan the Terrible captured and destroyed the castle, and in the same year Stephen Báthory built a new castle and town 20 km downriver. It received Magdeburg town rights in 1582. In 1621 Dyneburg became the capital of the Inflanty Voivodeship of the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth. Russian troops held it, as Borisoglebov, from 1656 to 1667, until the Treaty of Andrusovo returned it to the Commonwealth. After the First Partition of Poland in 1772 it passed to the Russian Empire.

Under Russian rule the fortress was built between 1810 and 1878, and the city was connected to the Saint Petersburg-Warsaw railway in 1860. It was called Dvinsk from 1893 to 1920. A large Jewish community lived there from the 1780s onwards, and the census of 1897 counted 32,400 Jews among 69,700 inhabitants. Two prominent rabbis lived in the city: Joseph Rosen, the Rogatchover Gaon, and Meir Simcha of Dvinsk. The painter Mark Rothko was born there in 1903. The newly independent Latvian state renamed the city Daugavpils in 1920, after fighting there from 1919 to 1920 among Latvians, Poles and Soviet troops.

Soviet rule lasted from 1940 to 1941 and again from 1944 to 1991, with German occupation between 1941 and 1944. After the German invasion of 26 June 1941 the Germans and Latvian collaborators carried out mass executions of Jews, and the survivors were forced into a ghetto. Only about 100 survivors remained of a community of 16,000 when the town was liberated in 1944.

Daugavpils is a state city in southeastern Latvia on the Daugava River, the second largest in the country after Riga, which lies some 230 kilometres to the northwest. Its parts north of the river belong to the historical region of Latgale and those to the south to Selonia. It is a major railway junction and industrial centre. The population has long been multicultural: the 1935 census counted Latvians, Jews, Poles, Russians and Belarusians, and since the Second World War the city has had an overwhelmingly Russian-speaking population. Church Hill holds Lutheran, Catholic, Orthodox and Old Believer churches side by side, and the fortress houses the Mark Rothko Art Centre.
dauphin-of-france: The word dauphin is French for dolphin. Count Guigues IV of Albon, who died in 1142, ruled in Viennois within the Kingdom of Burgundy, under the suzerainty of the Holy Roman Empire. He bore a dolphin on his coat of arms and was nicknamed le Dauphin, and in time the nickname became a title. From about 1285 the counts of Albon used the title Dauphin de Viennois officially, and their domains came to be known as the Dauphiné.

In 1343 Humbert II of Viennois, who had no heirs, began negotiations with King Philippe VI of France over the future of the Dauphiné. By 1349 he decided to give up his rule, and the final agreement named the king's grandson Charles as his successor, on condition that the Dauphiné remain a separate polity and not be absorbed into the French realm. In the summer of 1349 Charles became the first Dauphin de Viennois of the House of Valois. In 1350 his father ascended the French throne as John II, and for the first time the same person was both heir to the throne and Dauphin.

Originally the Dauphin ruled the Dauphiné personally. It was legally part of the Empire, whose emperors had stipulated that it must never be united with France. Because Dauphins were often minors or occupied elsewhere, the Dauphiné suffered from anarchy in the 14th and 15th centuries. Louis, the son of Charles VII, defied his father by staying in the province longer than the king allowed, and married Charlotte of Savoy against his wishes. Charles VII's soldiers drove him out in 1456. After he succeeded as Louis XI in 1461, he united the Dauphiné with France under royal control.

From then on the title was held by the next heir in the direct line, automatically at birth, at the parent's accession or at the previous Dauphin's death, whereas the British title Prince of Wales is in the monarch's gift. A Dauphin combined the arms of the Dauphiné with the French fleurs-de-lis. The sons and grandsons of a Dauphin ranked above their cousins.

The Constitution of 1791 abolished the title, and the heir was restyled Prince Royal. It was revived on the accession of Charles X in 1824, when his son Louis-Antoine, Duke of Angoulême, became Dauphin, and it fell into disuse after the removal of the Bourbons in 1830.
david: The First Book of Samuel and the First Book of Chronicles identify David as the son of Jesse of Bethlehem, the youngest of eight sons. He had at least two sisters, Zeruiah, whose sons all served in his army, and Abigail. The Bible does not name his mother, though the Talmud calls her Nitzevet, and the Book of Ruth makes him the great-grandson of Ruth the Moabite and Boaz. In the biblical narrative God, angered by the disobedience of King Saul, sends the prophet Samuel to anoint the shepherd David as king in his place. David then enters Saul's service as an armour-bearer and plays the lyre to soothe the king.

According to the Book of Samuel, David becomes a hero by killing the Philistine Goliath and then falls out with Saul and goes into hiding. After the deaths of Saul and Jonathan he becomes king first of Judah and eventually of all Israel. He conquers Jerusalem, makes it his capital and brings the Ark there. After committing adultery with Bathsheba and arranging the death of her husband Uriah, he survives the rebellion of his son Absalom. Denied permission to build the temple because of his bloodshed, he dies at 70 and names Solomon, his son with Bathsheba, as successor. Almost half the Psalms are headed as his, but the headings are late additions.

In the last two centuries BCE the son of David became an apocalyptic and heavenly figure who would deliver Israel, the background for early Christian ideas of the Messiah, and the Gospel of Matthew and the Gospel of Luke describe Jesus as descended from him. In the Quran he is a prophet and king who killed Goliath and was given the Psalms.

The only sources directly attesting David's life are biblical. Some scholars believe the Books of Samuel were substantially composed in the time of Josiah at the end of the 7th century BCE. The Tel Dan stele, found in 1993 and erected by Hazael of Damascus, contains a phrase most scholars read as House of David, taken as evidence that outsiders saw a Judahite dynasty descended from a founder named David. Richard Nelson holds that David was certainly historical but was more like a chief than a king.
david-alfaro-siqueiros: David Alfaro Siqueiros was born José de Jesús Alfaro Siqueiros, the second of three children. His mother died when he was four, and he was raised largely by his paternal grandparents. In 1911, at fifteen, he took part in a student strike at the Academy of San Carlos, and at eighteen he joined Venustiano Carranza's Constitutional Army against President Victoriano Huerta, an experience that exposed him to the lives of the working and rural poor. In 1919 he went to Europe, where he absorbed cubism in Paris, met Diego Rivera and studied Renaissance fresco painters in Italy.

In 1922 he returned to Mexico City to paint murals under José Vasconcelos, alongside Rivera and José Clemente Orozco, and in 1923 he helped found the Syndicate of Revolutionary Mexican Painters, Sculptors and Engravers. In Los Angeles in 1932 he led a team using airbrushes, spray guns and projectors. His América Tropical, depicting American imperialism in Latin America, was whitewashed by 1938. On 24 May 1940 he led an attack on Leon Trotsky's house in Coyoacán. Trotsky was unhurt, but his 14-year-old grandson was shot and survived, and the bodyguard Robert Sheldon Harte was found executed.

Siqueiros went into hiding, was arrested in Jalisco and held at Lecumberri prison, but never stood trial and left to paint a mural in Chile. In 1952 he made The People to the University, the University to the People in Mexico City, and in 1960 he was arrested after criticising President Adolfo López Mateos, remaining in prison until the spring of 1964.

His last major work, the Polyforum Siqueiros, was completed in 1971 and combines architecture, mural painting and polychromed sculpture. He believed that art should be public, educational and ideological, and he painted the struggle of working people, stressing the angles of the body and the strength of hands. He died in Cuernavaca on 6 January 1974 and was interred in the Rotunda of Illustrious Persons. A few days earlier he had donated his house in Polanco to the Mexican state.
david-ben-gurion: David Grün was born on 16 October 1886 in Płońsk, in Congress Poland, then part of the Russian Empire. His father, Avigdor Grün, was a court scribe and unofficial legal adviser who co-founded a Zionist group, Beni Zion, after the publication of Theodor Herzl's Der Judenstaat in 1896. His mother died in 1897. His formal education ended after his bar mitzvah, and at fourteen he and two friends formed a youth club, Ezra, which promoted Hebrew studies and emigration to the Holy Land.

He landed at Jaffa on 7 September 1906 and worked as a day labourer at Petah Tikva, where he caught malaria. He adopted the name Ben-Gurion in 1909. Deported to Egypt by the Ottoman authorities in March 1915, he travelled to the United States, where a speaking tour to raise a Jewish pioneer force produced few recruits.

In 1919 Ben-Gurion led the centrist faction of the Labor Zionist movement in forming Ahdut HaAvoda. He helped found the Histadrut, the Zionist labour federation, in 1920 and was its general secretary from 1921 to 1935. After the British White Paper of 1939 limited Jewish immigration to Palestine, he changed his policy towards the British and began preparing the Yishuv for war, while also urging support for the British war effort. He became executive head of the World Zionist Organization in 1946.

On 14 May 1948, the last day of the British Mandate, he proclaimed the State of Israel and was the first to sign its Declaration of Independence. During the 1948 war he ordered the militias merged into the Israel Defense Forces; in the Altalena Affair he had the Irgun's arms ship shelled, and sixteen Irgun fighters and three soldiers died. The war involved the expulsion and flight of most of the Palestinian Arab population, and historians disagree about his part in it. Benny Morris holds that he created an atmosphere of transfer without written orders.

Elected prime minister after the election of 14 February 1949, he held office until 1963 except for 1954 and 1955, when Moshe Sharett led the government. He oversaw the airlift of Jews from Arab countries, the National Water Carrier and settlement of the Negev, and he backed Israel's invasion of the Sinai in the Suez Crisis of 1956. He also pursued a reparations agreement with West Germany.

Ben-Gurion retired from politics in 1970 and lived in a modest hut at the kibbutz of Sde Boker, writing an eleven-volume history of Israel's early years. He suffered a cerebral haemorrhage on 18 November 1973 and died on 1 December. He is buried beside his wife Paula at Midreshet Ben-Gurion. Israel's main airport and Ben-Gurion University of the Negev bear his name, and his hut is now a visitors' centre.
david-friedrich-strauss: Strauss was born in Ludwigsburg, near Stuttgart, on 27 January 1808. At twelve he was sent to the evangelical seminary at Blaubeuren, where his masters Friedrich Heinrich Kern and Ferdinand Christian Baur taught their pupils to appreciate the ancient classics and the principles of textual criticism, which could be applied to sacred texts as to classical ones. In 1825 he entered the Tübinger Stift. He later taught Latin, history and Hebrew at Maulbronn and Blaubeuren, and in October 1831 went to Berlin to study under Schleiermacher and Hegel, though Hegel died just as he arrived. In the autumn of 1833 he resigned a Tübingen post to finish his book on Jesus.

Das Leben Jesu, kritisch bearbeitet appeared in 1835 and 1836, when he was 27, and was a sensation. Without denying that Jesus existed, Strauss argued that the miracles of the New Testament were mythical additions with little basis in fact. By myth he meant not mere falsity but the imaginative expression of religious truth. He held that the early church developed the stories to present Jesus as the Messiah of Jewish prophecy. This was a third way between rationalism, which explained miracles as misread natural events, and the supernaturalist view that the accounts were entirely accurate.

The book brought fierce controversy. When Strauss was elected to a chair of theology at the University of Zurich, the storm was so great that the authorities pensioned him before he began, and effigies of him were burnt at the Shrove Tuesday festival. He gave the pension of 1000 Swiss francs a year to the poor. In 1840 and 1841 he published Christliche Glaubenslehre, which argued that the history of Christian doctrines was the history of their disintegration. He then left theology for over twenty years and wrote biographies. His last work, Der alte und der neue Glaube (1872), caused almost as great a sensation, since friends saw in it a one-sided view of Christianity and a turn from spiritual philosophy to materialism.

Strauss died in Ludwigsburg on 8 February 1874. George Eliot translated his Life of Jesus into English in 1846. Albert Schweitzer wrote in The Quest of the Historical Jesus that research fell into two periods, before and after David Strauss. Marcus Borg has suggested that the details of Strauss's argument have not had a lasting impact, but that his basic claims, that many gospel narratives are mythical in character and that myth is not the same as falsehood, have become part of mainstream scholarship.
david-hume: David Hume was born David Home on 7 May 1711 in a tenement on the north side of Edinburgh's Lawnmarket, the second of two sons. His father Joseph, an advocate of Ninewells, died just after David's second birthday, and his mother Catherine raised the family on her own. By the age of 25 he had no income and no learned profession, and he worked as a merchant's assistant before travelling to La Flèche in Anjou, where he had frequent discussions with the Jesuits of the college there and probably used its library.

Hume published A Treatise of Human Nature in 1739 and 1740, aiming to introduce the experimental method of reasoning into the study of human nature. By his own account it fell dead-born from the press. His main teaching was that the mind consists of perceptions, divided into impressions and fainter ideas, and that every idea is copied from some impression. He argued that reasoning from past experience to the future cannot be justified, because it presupposes that nature is uniform, which cannot itself be shown. Belief in causes therefore rests on custom and habit. He held that the self is only a bundle of perceptions, that morals rest on sentiment, not reason, and that free will is compatible with causal determinism.

He was chiefly known in his lifetime as a historian and essayist. From 1754 to 1762 he published the six-volume History of England, which runs from the invasion of Julius Caesar to the Revolution in 1688 and widened its subject beyond kings, parliaments and armies to literature and science.

From 1763 to 1765 Hume was attached to Lord Hertford in Paris, serving as secretary to the British embassy and in 1765 as chargé d'affaires. In January 1766 he took Jean-Jacques Rousseau to England, where the two quarrelled, and Hume published an account of the dispute. He died of an abdominal cancer in Edinburgh on 25 August 1776. James Boswell saw him a few weeks earlier, and Hume told him that he thought the idea of life after death a most unreasonable fancy. He asked for a simple Roman tomb, which stands on Calton Hill. Immanuel Kant credited Hume with waking him from his dogmatic slumber, and his influence runs through utilitarianism, logical positivism and cognitive science.
david-ii-of-scotland: David was born on 5 March 1324 at Dunfermline Abbey, one of twin sons of Robert the Bruce and Elizabeth de Burgh. His mother died in 1327. Under the Treaty of Edinburgh-Northampton he was married on 17 July 1328, aged four, to the seven-year-old Joan, daughter of Edward II of England and Isabella of France. Robert the Bruce died on 7 June 1329, and David became king at the age of five. He and Joan were crowned at Scone Abbey on 24 November 1331, and he was the first Scottish monarch to be anointed at his coronation.

During his minority the kingdom was governed by guardians, several of whom fell in battle, among them Donald, Earl of Mar, at Dupplin Moor in August 1332 and Archibald Douglas at Halidon Hill in July 1333. After Dupplin, Edward Balliol, a protégé of Edward III of England, was crowned by the English, and the Second War of Scottish Independence began. After the English victory at Halidon Hill, David and Joan were sent to France, reaching Boulogne on 14 May 1334. He returned to Scotland on 2 June 1341, landing at Inverbervie, and took government into his own hands at the age of 17.

In 1346, under the Auld Alliance, David invaded England to draw Edward III away from France. His army was defeated at the Battle of Neville's Cross on 17 October 1346, and he was wounded by two arrows to the face and taken prisoner. He remained in captivity in England for eleven years. By the Treaty of Berwick of 3 October 1357 the Scots agreed to pay 100,000 marks at 10,000 marks a year. When the instalment of 1363 could not be raised, David offered to bequeath the throne to Edward III or one of his sons, and in 1364 the Scottish parliament rejected a proposal to make Lionel of Antwerp the next king. From 1364 David governed actively and dealt firmly with defiant nobles.

Queen Joan died on 7 September 1362. David married Margaret Drummond in about February 1364 and tried to divorce her in 1370 because she had borne no children; Pope Urban V reversed the divorce. David died unexpectedly of natural causes at Edinburgh Castle on 22 February 1371, aged 46, and was buried before the high altar of Holyrood Abbey. As the last male of the House of Bruce, he was succeeded by his nephew Robert II. Despite long periods in exile and captivity, he had ensured the survival of his kingdom and left the monarchy in a strong position.
david-iv-of-georgia: David IV was the only son of King George II of Georgia and Queen Helen, born in Kutaisi. He grew up in a time of war and devastation caused by the Seljuks. Opposition to George II led to a transfer of power to the young David, who came to the throne at sixteen. He inherited a kingdom much reduced from its early eleventh-century extent, now consisting largely of Abkhazia and Kartli. Since 1080, when the emir Ahmed captured Kutaisi, Georgia had accepted Seljuk suzerainty and paid annual tribute, yet seasonal raids continued.

David reorganised an army whose morale had been shattered, forming small detachments of minor nobles and peasants from royal estates and developing a strategy of surprise attacks on Muslim encampments. He stopped the Seljuk incursions and then launched counterattacks. The duke Liparit V of Kldekari conspired against him in 1093 and was imprisoned; after a second conspiracy he was exiled to Constantinople. David then campaigned against Kvirike IV of Kakheti-Hereti and captured the fortress of Zedazeni in 1101 or 1103.

Around 1103 to 1105 he convened the Council of Ruisi-Urbnisi, which addressed corruption in the Church. From 1110 he fought the Turks, and on 14 February he destroyed Turkish forces at Botora. At the Battle of Didgori in August 1121 he defeated the Seljuks, with a Latin battalion of 200 to 1,000 men among his forces, and went on to take the Emirate of Tbilisi.

David died in Tbilisi on 24 January 1125, after a reign of thirty-four years, having named his eldest son Demetrius as successor. At his request he was buried at the main entrance of Gelati Monastery, so that all who came to its academy would step on his tomb. Around 1120 he composed Hymns of Repentance, a sequence of eight free-verse psalms. The epithet the Builder first appears in a charter of 1452. Georgian historiography regards his reign as the beginning of the Golden Age of the Kingdom of Georgia.
david-livingstone: David Livingstone was born on 19 March 1813 in the mill town of Blantyre, Scotland, the second of seven children of Neil Livingstone and Agnes Hunter. At the age of 10 he began work in a cotton mill, where he and his brother John worked 14-hour days tying broken threads. At 21 he was excited by a pamphlet setting out Gützlaff's call for missionaries to China, who should be trained as medical doctors. He joined Anderson's University in Glasgow in 1836 to study medicine and chemistry, paying his way by working at the mill from Easter to October.

Livingstone left London on 17 November 1840 for the Cape of Good Hope. To improve his Tswana and find sites for mission stations, he journeyed far north of Kolobeng with William Cotton Oswell, and in 1849 they crossed the Kalahari Desert and reached Lake Ngami. In August 1851 they reached the Zambezi. In 1852 he travelled to Linyanti, where the Kololo chief Sekeletu gave him authority to investigate trade routes to the coast. They reached the Portuguese city of Luanda in May 1854, after great difficulties and Livingstone's near death from fever. He returned to Britain in December 1856, and his Missionary Travels of 1857 was a bestselling travelogue.

In 1858 he agreed to lead a second Zambezi expedition. The river proved impassable past the Cahora Bassa rapids, which he had failed to explore earlier. From January 1866 he sought the source of the Nile from Zanzibar, believing it lay farther south than Lake Albert or Lake Victoria. He was wrong about the Nile, but he identified for European science Lake Ngami, Lake Malawi, Lake Bangweulu and Victoria Falls.

Livingstone lost contact with the outside world for six years and was ill for most of his last four. He died on 1 May 1873 at Chief Chitambo's village at Chipundu, southeast of Lake Bangweulu, from malaria and internal bleeding caused by dysentery. His attendants Chuma and Susi buried his heart under a tree near the spot. By the late 1860s his reputation had suffered from the failure of his missions and of the Zambezi expedition, but it was restored by Henry Morton Stanley and by the loyalty of his servants. The Universities' Mission to Central Africa was founded at his request in 1860. He is recorded as having converted only one African, the Kwena chief Sechele.
david-lloyd-george: David Lloyd George was born on 17 January 1863 in Chorlton-on-Medlock, Manchester, to Welsh parents, Elizabeth Lloyd and William George. His father died of pneumonia in June 1864, and his mother took the children to her native Llanystumdwy in Carnarvonshire, where they lived with her brother Richard Lloyd, a shoemaker, lay minister and strong Liberal, who became a towering influence on his nephew. He qualified as a solicitor in 1884 and set up his own practice in 1885.

He won the by-election for Caernarfon Boroughs on 10 April 1890, narrowly, and held the seat until 1945. As a radical Liberal he supported Welsh devolution, the disestablishment of the Church in Wales and land reform. His fierce opposition to the Second Boer War brought him national fame, though he insisted that the British Empire should rest on freedom rather than racial arrogance.

Lloyd George became President of the Board of Trade in 1905 and Chancellor of the Exchequer in 1908. His 1909 People's Budget imposed a 20 per cent tax on the unearned increase in land values, higher death duties and income tax, and a Supertax on incomes over £3,000, to pay for welfare programmes and battleships. He also helped to secure the disestablishment of the Anglican Church in Wales, in force from 1920.

As Minister of Munitions from 1915 he took arms production from the generals and made it an industrial department. He became Secretary of State for War in June 1916 and prime minister in December 1916, the first Welshman in the post, replacing Asquith. He created a smaller war cabinet and, against U-boat food shortages, introduced the convoy system and rationing.

After the war he negotiated independence for the Irish Free State in 1921. In 1922 he was embroiled in a scandal over the sale of honours, and the Carlton Club meeting decided that the Conservatives should end the coalition, and he resigned. He led the Liberal Party from 1926 to 1931, and in May 1940 his speech in the Norway Debate helped undermine Chamberlain as prime minister.

Lloyd George died of cancer on 26 March 1945, aged 82, and was buried four days later beside the river Dwyfor at Llanystumdwy, under a boulder with no inscription. The Lloyd George Museum nearby, designed by Clough Williams-Ellis, opened in 1963. Scholars have praised his welfare reforms and his leadership to victory in the First World War, and criticised his presidential style and his scandals.
david-ricardo: David Ricardo was born in London on 18 April 1772, the third surviving of the 17 children of the stockbroker Abraham Israel Ricardo. The family were Sephardic Jews of Portuguese origin who had recently moved from the Dutch Republic. He began working with his father at 14. At 21 he eloped with a Quaker, Priscilla Anne Wilkinson, and converted to Unitarianism against his father's wishes, and his father disowned him.

He made his fortune financing government borrowing. A popular story that he profited from the Battle of Waterloo is not supported: he was already very rich, and in June 1815 he sold his government stock before the result was known in London. He later bought Gatcombe Park in Gloucestershire.

Ricardo wrote his first economics article at 37 and published The High Price of Bullion in 1810. His Principles of Political Economy and Taxation (1817) concluded that land rent grows as population increases. He tried to repair what he saw as problems in Adam Smith's labour theory of value, holding that with three factors of production, land, labour and capital, no single one could determine value alone. In his theory of profit, rising real wages lower real profits.

Against mercantilism, which treated trade as a way to gain gold or silver, he argued that industry specialisation and free trade always produce positive results, even when one country is more efficient in every product. The term comparative advantage was introduced later by John Stuart Mill and his contemporaries. In 1821 Ricardo also wrote that machinery was often injurious to the labouring class.

In 1818 Ricardo bought a seat in Parliament for £4,000 as part of a loan, and as member for Portarlington voted for free trade, parliamentary reform and criminal law reform. He opposed the Corn Laws, which he thought raised rents and directed profits to landlords. He died on 11 September 1823, aged 51, of an ear infection that spread to the brain.

Early socialists such as Thomas Hodgskin drew radical conclusions from his value theory, Henry George drew on his concept of rent, and Piero Sraffa edited his works. Parliament repealed the Corn Laws in 1846.
davos: Davos lies on the Landwasser river in the Rhaetian Alps, between the Plessur and Albula Ranges. The municipality covers nearly the whole valley of the Landwasser and its side valleys, an area of 284 square kilometres. Its centre is two adjacent villages, Davos Dorf and Davos Platz, 1,560 metres above sea level, just below the Wolfgang Pass, which carries a road and a Rhaetian Railway line towards Klosters and the Prättigau. The name is first recorded in the 13th century as Tavaus and may derive from a word for a ravine.

Rhaeto-Romans settled the area in the High Middle Ages. Davos is first mentioned in 1213. From about 1280 the barons of Vaz allowed German-speaking Walser colonists to settle and gave them extensive self-administration rights; an agreement of 1289 freed the people of Davos from personal taxes. Davos became the largest Walser settlement area in eastern Switzerland, and natives still speak a dialect atypical for Grisons. After the last baron of Vaz died in 1338, Davos passed to the Count of Toggenburg, and later to the Counts of Montfort, who sold it to Duke Sigmund of Tyrol in 1466.

In 1436 the League of the Ten Jurisdictions was founded in Davos. An agreement of 1438 confirmed its rights, and in 1450 the League allied with the League of God's House. Davos made a treaty with the Grey League in 1471 and refused to follow Austrian orders, and a compromise placed it under the House of Matsch, with Austria keeping a right to repurchase it.

From the middle of the 19th century Davos became a health resort. Doctors, among them Alexander Spengler, judged the microclimate of the high valley excellent for lung disease patients. Robert Louis Stevenson wintered there in 1880, and a Davos sanatorium inspired the Berghof in Thomas Mann's novel The Magic Mountain. The painter Ernst Ludwig Kirchner lived there from 1917. The sanatoria attracted many German patients, and during the Second World War Davos was a centre of Nazi activity in Switzerland. It was also a centre of speed skating and later a ski resort.

Davos has a permanent population of 10,832 (2020), most of whom speak German. It is a tourist community and regional centre with one of Switzerland's largest ski resorts. HC Davos hosts the Spengler Cup, an international ice hockey tournament first held in 1923. Since 1971 the town has hosted the annual meeting of the World Economic Forum. Seven of its sites are listed as Swiss heritage sites of national significance, among them the Kirchner Museum.
dawda-jawara: Dawda Kairaba Jawara was born on 16 May 1924 at Barajally in the central river region of The Gambia, the son of Almammi Jawara, a well-to-do trader from an aristocratic family, and Mamma Fatty. As a child he attended local Arabic schools to memorise the Quran. He was later educated at the Methodist Boys' School in Banjul and at Achimota College in the Gold Coast, and trained as a veterinary surgeon at Glasgow, Liverpool and Edinburgh.

He returned in 1953 as a veterinary officer. Travelling the country to vaccinate cattle, he made contacts among cattle owners, district chiefs and village heads, who later formed the bulk of his early political support. Adults in the colony area around Bathurst had the vote, but those in the protectorate did not. In 1959 the People's Progressive Society changed its name to challenge the urban-based parties, and Jawara became secretary of the party and was elected to the House of Representatives in 1960.

After the elections of 1962 Jawara became prime minister, self-government followed in 1963 and independence came on 18 February 1965, with Elizabeth II remaining head of state. In 1970 The Gambia became a republic and he was elected its first president. On 29 July 1981 an attempted coup led by Kukoi Samba Sanyang was defeated with the help of Senegalese troops, whom Jawara had asked for aid; several hundred people were killed. In December 1981 treaties in Dakar created the Senegambian Confederation, with Abdou Diouf as president and Jawara as vice-president; it collapsed in 1989.

In 1985 his government began the Economic Recovery Program, an adjustment programme drawn up with economists from the Harvard Institute for International Development and the International Monetary Fund. In December 1991 he announced that he would not seek re-election in 1992, but after the announcement was met with panic he agreed to stand again and won 56% of the vote.

On 22 July 1994 soldiers led by Lieutenant Yahya Jammeh took the capital. Jawara was taken to Senegal by an American warship and lived in exile until 2002, and the new ruling council dissolved the constitution. He returned as an elder statesman but was forbidden to take part in politics, and he died on 27 August 2019. His portrait appeared on Gambian dalasi banknotes and coins from 1971 to 1994. He was knighted in the 1966 New Year Honours and was the last living Gambian to have received a knighthood under the monarchy.
dayak-people: Dayak is a loose term for more than 200 Austronesian ethnic groups native to Borneo, found chiefly in the central and southern interior, often in highlands or near rivers.
