Each has its own dialect, customs, laws and territory. The name is commonly thought to come from a Bruneian and Melanau word for interior people, related to a Kenyah word for upstream. Dutch and German writers used it for any non-Muslim native of Borneo, so the difference between Dayak and non-Dayak natives could be understood as a religious one. James Brooke wished to use it only for the Land Dayaks, or Bidayuh, and the Sea Dayaks, or Iban.

In the early 1900s educated people from these groups, such as Hausman Baboe, adopted the name as a unifying term in Kalimantan. In 1954 Tjilik Riwut sorted the groups into 18 tribes and 403 sub-tribes.

Dayak languages belong to several subgroups of the Malayo-Polynesian family, including Land Dayak, Malayic and Barito, and about 170 languages and dialects are spoken on the island. Historically most Dayaks were swidden cultivators who supplemented their living with forest produce, fishing, hunting and occasional wage labour. In the traditional longhouse, sometimes more than 200 metres long, households had separate apartments and shared areas for cooking, ceremonies and blacksmithing. The people living in it were governed by its customs.

Many groups regard tattoos as sacred and as marks of origin, rank or rites of passage. Beads, including heirloom beads called pesaka, were used in rituals and passed down in families. The short mandau, a machete with an upward protrusion on the handle, could be drawn very quickly, which mattered in headhunting. The indigenous religion of the Dayak, called Kaharingan in Indonesia, is a form of animism in which shamans guide the souls of the dead and heal the sick by retrieving souls.

The Dayaks were once feared for the practice of headhunting, called ngayau. In 1894 the Tumbang Anoi Agreement, a meeting of Dayak groups from all over Kalimantan at Damang Batu, ended the tradition by agreement, since it was held to cause conflict between groups. Headhunting resurfaced in the mid-1940s, when the Allied powers encouraged it against the Japanese occupation, and again in the late 1960s and around the turn of the century in violence involving ethnic Chinese and Madurese settlers.

Since the 19th century many Dayaks have converted to Christianity, brought by missionaries of the Rheinische Missionsgesellschaft and later the Basler Mission, and some groups, such as the Bakumpai, to Islam. Dayak soldiers served with the Sarawak Rangers, whose successor is the present-day Royal Ranger Regiment.
dayton-agreement: The basic elements of the settlement had been proposed in international talks as early as 1992, but the negotiations that led to Dayton followed the failure of earlier peace efforts and the Croatian military Operation Storm of August 1995, together with a government offensive against the Republika Srpska conducted alongside NATO's Operation Deliberate Force. In September and October 1995 the Contact Group, above all the United States and Russia, pressed the leaders of the three sides to attend negotiations. A US team led first by Anthony Lake and then by Richard Holbrooke carried out five rounds of shuttle diplomacy from August to October, and the parties adopted principles for a settlement on 8 and 26 September.

The conference was held from 1 to 21 November 1995. The main regional participants were Slobodan Milošević, president of Serbia, whom the Bosnian Serbs had empowered to speak for them, Franjo Tuđman, president of Croatia, and Alija Izetbegović, president of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was led by US Secretary of State Warren Christopher and Holbrooke, with Carl Bildt for the EU and Igor Ivanov for Russia as co-chairmen. The secure site was chosen to take the parties out of their comfort zone, to keep them from negotiating through the media and to house over 800 staff. The agreement was initialled on 21 November and signed ceremonially in Paris on 14 December 1995, with witnesses including Bill Clinton, Jacques Chirac, John Major and Helmut Kohl.

The agreement made Bosnia and Herzegovina a single sovereign state composed of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina and the Republika Srpska, a complete state and not a confederation. It retained a central government with a rotating state presidency, a central bank and a constitutional court. The constitution is Annex 4, and a boundary line between the two entities was drawn. Before it, Bosnian Serbs controlled about 46% of the territory, Bosniaks 28% and Bosnian Croats 25%; afterwards the Serb share was 49%, the Bosniak 30% and the Croat 21%. The NATO-led IFOR, deployed on 20 December 1995, handled military implementation, the Office of the High Representative civil implementation, and the Organization for Security and Co-operation in Europe the first elections in 1996.

Scholars differ on the settlement. Charles-Philippe David calls it the most impressive example of conflict resolution, and it has been praised for establishing lasting peace. Critics, including Patrice McMahon and Jon Western, argue that a decentralised system undermined the authority of the state, and others point to its complex government, its dependence on international actors and its division of Bosnia into three constituent nations and two entities by ethnic identity.
de-administrando-imperio: Constantine VII, born in 905, became co-emperor in 908 but was too young to rule, and Romanos I Lekapenos took over the imperial government after being crowned co-emperor in December 920. Constantine ruled personally from January 945 until his death in November 959. A scholar-emperor, he gathered a circle of educated men who wrote three unfinished books, De Administrando Imperio, De Ceremoniis and On the Themes, and a biography of his grandfather Basil I.

De Administrando Imperio had at least one anonymous collaborator. Its date is debated: chapters 29 and 45 give dates corresponding to 948/949 and 951/952, while other scholars place its compilation after 952 and before his death. The author never gave it a title; it opens with a salutation to his son.

The work joins two earlier treatises, one on the peoples neighbouring the empire and one on its provinces, to which Constantine added his own instructions for his son Romanos II. According to its preface it has four parts: a key to foreign policy towards the northerners and Scythians, the diplomacy to pursue with them, a survey of the surrounding nations and a summary of recent imperial administration. Chapters 1 to 8 and 10 to 12 explain policy towards the Pechenegs and Turks.

Chapters 12 to 40 hold traditional accounts, mixed with legends, of how the Saracens, Lombards, Venetians, Serbs, Croats, Magyars and Pechenegs came to occupy their lands. Chapters 43 to 46 deal with the north-east, Armenia and Georgia, and chapters 49 to 52 give instructions on taxing new provinces and on civil and naval administration. Its geographic and historical information is often confused and filled with legends, but is in essence reliable. The Greek is plain, since the emperor said he avoided lofty Atticisms.

Four copies survive. Johannes Meursius published the first edition in 1611 and gave it the Latin title by which it is known. Anselmo Banduri produced another in 1711, and Immanuel Bekker one in 1840. The first modern edition, by Gyula Moravcsik, with an English translation by R. J. H. Jenkins, appeared in Budapest in 1949, with commentaries following in 1962. Because it was written as a manual for his successor, it is regarded as one of the most important sources for Byzantium and its neighbours.
de-beers: The name De Beers comes from two Afrikaner brothers, Diederik Arnoldus de Beer and Johannes Nicolaas de Beer, who owned a farm named Vooruitzicht in the Boshof District of the Orange Free State. After diamonds were found on their land they were forced by the increasing demands of the British government to sell it on 31 July 1871 to the merchant Alfred Johnson Ebden for £6,600.

The farm became the site of the Big Hole and the De Beers mine. Cecil Rhodes got his start by renting water pumps to miners during the diamond rush that began in 1869, and invested the profits in buying up the claims of small mining operators. The Rothschild family financed his expansion. De Beers Consolidated Mines was formed in 1888 by merging the companies of Rhodes and the diamond magnate Barney Barnato.

In 1889 Rhodes agreed with the London-based Diamond Syndicate that it would buy a fixed quantity of diamonds at an agreed price, which regulated output and kept prices up; supply was cut during the slump of 1891 to 1892. During the Second Boer War Kimberley was besieged, and Rhodes placed the company's resources at the defenders' disposal, with its workshops making shells, an armoured train and a gun named Long Cecil. When Rhodes died in 1902 De Beers controlled 90 per cent of world diamond production.

The Premier Mine near Pretoria, registered in 1902, yielded the Cullinan Diamond in 1905. Its owner refused to join the cartel and sold through the dealers Bernard and Ernest Oppenheimer, but production was soon absorbed into De Beers. Ernest Oppenheimer joined the board in 1926 and became chairman in 1929, and he consolidated the company's monopoly until his death in 1957.

His son Harry Oppenheimer expanded it into several countries. De Beers kept prices high by buying rivals' stones, stockpiling and limiting supply. Its share of rough diamonds fell from as high as 90 per cent in the 1980s as producers in Canada and Australia sold outside its channel, and in 2011 Anglo American bought the Oppenheimers' 40 per cent stake.

De Beers advertised diamonds as a symbol of love and commitment. In 1947 the copywriter Frances Gerety coined the slogan A Diamond is Forever for the agency N. W. Ayer & Son, and in 2000 Advertising Age named it the best advertising slogan of the 20th century. Mining takes place in Botswana, Namibia, South Africa and Canada, in Botswana and Namibia through joint ventures with the governments. The company has been criticised for profiting under apartheid, though Harry Oppenheimer opposed that system, and for price fixing and monopoly behaviour.
de-revolutionibus-orbium-coelestium: Copernicus first outlined his system in a short, anonymous manuscript, the Commentariolus, which he circulated among friends; a physician's library list of 1514 describes a manuscript that matches it. By the 1530s a substantial part of the main work was complete, but he hesitated to publish until Cardinal Nikolaus von Schönberg urged him to in 1536. In 1539 the young mathematician Georg Joachim Rheticus came to Frauenburg to study with him, and his Narratio Prima of 1540 summarised the theory and was well received. Under Rheticus's pressure Copernicus gave the book to Bishop Tiedemann Giese, to be printed by Johannes Petreius at Nuremberg.

The book follows the layout of Ptolemy's Almagest, which it updated and replaced. Book I gives the general vision: the heavens and the Earth are spherical, the celestial bodies move in regular circles, and the Earth rotates on its axis and circles the Sun. Book II covers spherical astronomy and a catalogue of the fixed stars, Book III the precession of the equinoxes and the Sun, Book IV the Moon, Book V the positions of the five planets, and Book VI their deviation in latitude from the ecliptic.

Copernicus placed the motionless Sun at the centre, with Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn around it and the Moon circling the Earth. Holding that celestial motions must be uniform and circular, he still needed epicycles. Only after Kepler proposed ellipses in 1609 were deferents and epicycles abolished. An unsigned preface, added by the Lutheran preacher Andreas Osiander, who supervised the printing, presented the theory as a calculus consistent with observation, not a claim of literal truth. Rheticus was furious, and Giese urged the Nuremberg council to issue a correction, which it did not. Johannes Kepler later demonstrated that Osiander wrote it.

Demand was low at first: an initial print run of 400 did not sell out, and the book was technical. Owen Gingerich's census of surviving copies showed, against Arthur Koestler's claim that it was a book nobody read, that nearly all leading astronomers owned and read it, though they mostly ignored the cosmology and used the new planetary models. Erasmus Reinhold's Prutenic Tables of 1551, based on Copernicus's methods, were used in the calendar reform of 1582.

Martin Luther was quoted in 1539 rejecting the idea, and Philipp Melanchthon wrote against it in 1549. On 5 March 1616 the Sacred Congregation of the Index suspended the book until corrected. It was withdrawn, not banned, and nine sentences that stated the heliocentric system as certain were to be changed. After corrections were approved in 1620, reading was permitted, but only to qualified scholars. The book left the Index in 1758.
de-stalinization: Joseph Stalin died on 5 March 1953. The collective leadership that followed him, made up of Georgi Malenkov as premier, Lavrentiy Beria as head of the Ministry of the Interior and Nikita Khrushchev as First Secretary of the Party, began the reforms that came to be called de-Stalinization. The term itself gained currency after the dissolution of the Soviet Union and was not used in Khrushchev's time, when the effort was described as overcoming the cult of personality. Denouncing Stalin was dangerous, since he had been placed on a pedestal at home and among communists abroad.

The first phase has been called silent de-Stalinization. Beria began the release of Gulag prisoners before he was arrested on 26 June 1953 and executed on 23 December. The revision of Stalin's policies was done in secret and often without explanation, with unpublicised rehabilitations of figures such as Marshal Mikhail Tukhachevsky.

About 90,000 prisoners returned from the camps in 1954 and 1955 alone, which made secrecy hard to keep. In December 1955 Khrushchev proposed a commission to investigate Stalin's activities. It found that of 1,920,635 people arrested for anti-Soviet activities, 688,503 were executed.

De-Stalinization became official on 25 February 1956, when Khrushchev addressed a closed session of the 20th Party Congress in the speech On the Cult of Personality and Its Consequences. He set out some of Stalin's crimes, condemned his treatment of the Old Bolsheviks and denounced his dictatorial rule. Some historians hold that Khrushchev meant to free officials from fear of repression, others that he meant to put the blame on Stalin and spare the Party. At the 22nd Congress in 1961, Stalin's body was moved on 31 October from Lenin's Mausoleum to the Kremlin Wall Necropolis, and on 11 November Stalingrad was renamed Volgograd.

Stalin's name was taken off cities, buildings and the state anthem, and hundreds of his monuments were removed across the USSR and the Eastern bloc. A resolution of 25 October 1956 called the Gulag labour system inexpedient, and it was closed by an order of 25 January 1960. Former prisoners often met hostility on their return.

The speech was central to the Khrushchev Thaw, and China under Mao Zedong and Albania under Enver Hoxha cited it as a cause of the Sino-Soviet split and condemned Khrushchev as a revisionist. In North Korea an attempt to remove Kim Il Sung in August 1956 failed. Historians regard the start of the process as a turning point. It stalled under Brezhnev and accelerated under Mikhail Gorbachev, and Polly Jones and Anne Applebaum have both described it as fragile.
dead-sea: The Dead Sea is an endorheic lake with no outlet streams, and its main tributary is the Jordan River. It lies in the Jordan Rift Valley, formed by the Dead Sea Transform, a fault along the boundary between the African Plate and the Arabian Plate. In the late Pliocene and early Pleistocene the valley was repeatedly flooded from the Mediterranean, forming the Sedom Lagoon, which deposited rock salt up to 2.3 km thick. As the climate became more arid, Lake Lisan shrank and grew saltier, leaving the Dead Sea as its last remainder.

Historical English names include the Salt Sea, the Lake of Sodom, from the biblical account of its destruction, and Lake Asphaltites, from Greek and Latin. The Hebrew Bible records dwelling in caves near the sea before the Israelites came to Canaan and extensively in the time of King David. Greek and Jewish writers report that the Nabateans held a monopoly over the sea. The sixth-century Madaba Map indicates that trade across it was prevalent in the Byzantine period, and Greek Orthodox monks settled in the remote region, where Mar Saba is still a place of pilgrimage.

The Jewish village of Ein Gedi, inhabited continuously since the 5th century BCE, was destroyed by fire in the 7th century. From the seventh century the area declined and its population fell. Sugarcane was grown near the shores from the Crusader period and reached its peak under the Mamluks. Christopher Costigan explored the Jordan and the Dead Sea by boat in 1835, followed by Thomas Howard Molyneux in 1847, William Francis Lynch in 1848 and John MacGregor in 1869.

The Dead Sea lies between Jordan to the east and the West Bank and Israel to the west, and its shore is the lowest land-based elevation on Earth. It is about 304 m deep and, with a salinity of 34.2% measured in 2011, among the saltiest bodies of water, so that macroscopic life cannot live in it. Its surface area fell from 1,050 km2 in 1930 to 605 km2. Asphalt for Egyptian mummification and, in modern times, potash have been taken from it, and the area is also a health resort.
dead-sea-scrolls: The first scrolls were found between November 1946 and February 1947 by Bedouin shepherds, among them Muhammed edh-Dhib, who fell into a cave near what is now the Qumran site and found seven scrolls in jars. They included the Isaiah Scroll, the Habakkuk Commentary and the Community Rule. They passed through several hands, among them the cobbler and antiques dealer Khalil Eskander Shahin, known as Kando, and Metropolitan Athanasius Yeshue Samuel.

Scholars did not find the original cave for two years. It was rediscovered on 28 January 1949 by a Belgian United Nations observer and an Arab Legion officer, and in November 1951 Roland de Vaux began a full excavation of Qumran. Further caves followed, among them the third, with the Copper Scroll, on 14 March 1952. In the fourth cave the fragments were torn into up to 15,000 pieces, which scholars assembled in a room called the scrollery.

About 40 per cent of the identified texts are copies of books of the Hebrew scriptures, about 30 per cent are Second Temple texts that were not canonised, such as the Book of Enoch, the Book of Jubilees and the Wisdom of Sirach, and the remaining 30 per cent are sectarian writings not known before, such as the Community Rule, the War Scroll and the Pesher on Habakkuk. Parts of all but one of the books of the Hebrew Bible are present; the Book of Esther is missing.

Before the discovery the oldest Hebrew manuscripts of the Bible were Masoretic texts of the 10th century CE, such as the Aleppo Codex. The biblical manuscripts among the scrolls go back to the 2nd century BCE, and they showed both the stability of the Masoretic tradition and substantial textual variation before the text was standardised about 100 CE.

Who wrote the scrolls is debated. The Qumran-Essene hypothesis of Roland de Vaux and Józef Milik, almost universally held until the 1990s, holds that the Essenes, or another sectarian group living at Khirbet Qumran, composed them and hid them in the caves during the Jewish Revolt between 66 and 68 CE. Others argue that they came from libraries in Jerusalem and were hidden by people fleeing the Romans in 70 CE. Palaeography dates fragments from 225 BCE to 50 CE according to Cross and Avigad, and radiocarbon tests support a date in the last two centuries BCE and the first century CE. Most of the scrolls are held in the Shrine of the Book at the Israel Museum in Jerusalem, completed in April 1965.
dean-barrow: Dean Oliver Barrow was born on 2 March 1951 in Belize City, then in British Honduras, where he grew up. He attended St. Michael's College in Belize, took a law degree at the University of the West Indies at Cave Hill in Barbados in 1973 and a Certificate of Legal Education at the Norman Manley Law School in Jamaica in 1975, and later studied at the University of Miami.

He entered the legal profession in 1974, working with his maternal uncle Dean Lindo, and became a partner in Lindo's firm in 1977. He later founded his own firm, Barrow and Williams, with Rodwell Williams. Among its more controversial clients were Lord Ashcroft and his associated businesses, including Belize Bank and Belize Telemedia Limited.

Barrow entered electoral politics in December 1983, winning a seat on the Belize City council as one of a slate of nine. In 1984 he stood for the newly created Queen's Square constituency, defeated Ralph Fonseca of the People's United Party and joined the first cabinet of Manuel Esquivel as attorney-general and minister of foreign affairs. He held his seat in 1989, when his party lost power, and became deputy leader in 1990 after the death of Curl Thompson. Back in government in 1993, he added the ministry of national security to his former posts; his detractors called him Minister of Everything.

In the heavy defeat of 1998 he was one of only three party candidates to win, and he replaced the defeated Esquivel as party leader and Leader of the Opposition. The general election of 7 February 2008 gave his party 25 of 31 seats, and he was sworn in the next day as the country's first black prime minister, serving also as minister of finance. He won a reduced majority in 2012 and a third consecutive victory in November 2015, which he said would be his last election as leader.

Citing his health, he at first intended to step down by the end of 2019, but on 18 November 2018 his cabinet urged him to stay until the general election of 2020, and he agreed. He did not contest Queen's Square in that election and endorsed his sister, Denise Barrow, to succeed him. He has returned to private practice as head of litigation at Barrow and Williams. His eldest son, Moses Michael Levi Barrow, a former rapper under the name Shyne, was elected to the House of Representatives in 2020 and later became leader of the party and of the opposition.
debrecen: Debrecen is first documented in 1235 as Debrezun. It became more important when small villages nearby were deserted during the Mongol invasion, and it grew rapidly after the middle of the 13th century. In 1361 Louis I of Hungary granted its citizens the right to choose the town's judge and council. During the Ottoman period it had no castle or city walls and survived through the diplomatic skill of its leaders. It came under Ottoman control as a sanjak between 1558 and 1693, and in 1693 Leopold I, Holy Roman Emperor, raised it to free royal town status.

The Reformation took root in the 16th century, first Lutheranism and then Calvin's teachings. From 1551 the Calvinist government forbade Catholics from moving to the town, and a synod in 1567 adopted the Second Helvetic Confession. The town earned the names the Calvinist Rome and the Geneva of Hungary, and its Reformed College, founded in 1538, was a predecessor of today's University of Debrecen.

In 1849 the Hungarian revolutionary government fled to Debrecen from Pest-Buda. In April, Lajos Kossuth proclaimed the dethronement of the Habsburgs and the independence of Hungary at the Great Church, and Russian forces allied to the Habsburgs defeated the Hungarian army near the town in the last battle of the war of independence.

German forces entered the city on 20 March 1944. A ghetto was ordered on 28 April, and in June the Jews of Debrecen were deported to a nearby brickyard; most were later deported to Auschwitz, arriving on 3 July. Soviet troops captured the city on 20 October 1944, and 70 percent of its buildings were damaged in the fighting.

Debrecen is Hungary's second-largest city, after Budapest, on the Great Hungarian Plain 220 km east of the capital, and the seat of Hajdú-Bihar County. The University of Debrecen, formed in 2000 from three earlier universities, is the largest in Hungary. The Reformed Great Church can accommodate about 5,000 people, and the park of the Nagyerdő lies in the city.
deccan-plateau: The Deccan Plateau extends over about 422,000 square kilometres in the western, central and southern regions of India, forming the bulk of the Deccan Peninsula. It stretches from the Satpura and Vindhya ranges in the north to the northern fringes of the Nilgiri Hills in the south and is bounded by the Eastern and Western Ghats. It covers most of Maharashtra, Telangana, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh excluding their coastal regions. The terrain is rocky, with an average elevation of about 600 metres, and the plateau is subdivided into the Maharashtra, Karnataka and Telangana plateaus.

The Western Ghats block rain-bearing winds, so the plateau is drier than the coast and has a semi-arid climate. Rivers such as the Godavari, Krishna and Kaveri flow eastwards to the Bay of Bengal. In the north-west the Deccan Traps are layers of basalt more than 2 kilometres thick, laid down by lava flows at the end of the Cretaceous period about 66 million years ago. The word Deccan comes from the Sanskrit dakṣiṇa, meaning south.

Ash mounds associated with Neolithic cultures date back to 8000 BCE, and iron technology spread through the region towards 1000 BCE. Since at least the 1st century BCE the region has been connected to the Silk Road and to trade with the Mediterranean and East Asia. Dynasties such as the Satavahanas, Pallavas, Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas, Hoysalas, Kakatiyas and Cholas ruled parts of it between the 6th century BCE and the 14th century CE.

In the Late Middle Ages the Vijayanagara Empire held most of the southern part of the plateau, while the upper part was ruled by the Bahmani kingdom and its successors, the Deccan sultanates. The Maratha Empire, founded by Shivaji, briefly captured the region in the early 18th century. After the defeat of Mysore in the late 18th century and the Vellore Mutiny of 1806 the British East India Company consolidated its power, and the British took direct control in 1857. After independence in 1947 states were reorganised on linguistic lines in the 1950s, and Telangana was created in 2014.

The plateau is one of the oldest and most stable land formations of the subcontinent and is rich in iron ore, coal and mica, and has yielded precious and semi-precious stones. Major cities on it include Bengaluru and Hyderabad. Historians have used the name Deccan differently over time, and Stewart Gordon called it a relational term for the area beyond the southern border of a northern kingdom.
deccan-sultanates: The Deccan sultanates is a historians' term for five Persianate Muslim kingdoms on the Deccan Plateau between the Krishna River and the Vindhya Range: Ahmadnagar, Berar, Bidar, Bijapur and Golconda. They emerged as the Bahmani Sultanate disintegrated. Ahmadnagar was the first to declare independence, in 1490, followed by Bijapur and Berar in the same year, Bidar around 1492 and Golconda in 1512. Their founders were of varied origins: Ahmadnagar's dynasty descended from Malik Hasan Bahri, a Marathi Muslim of Brahmin origin, Berar's founder was a Kannadiga Muslim of Brahmin origin, Bidar's a Georgian slave, and Golconda's a slave of Iranian Turkmen origin. All based their legitimacy on succeeding the Bahmani Sultanate and kept using Bahmani coinage.

The sultanates were generally rivals, and factions divided their courts between Deccani Muslims and foreign-born nobles. In Ahmadnagar, a coup under Jamal Khan led to massacres of foreign nobles in 1588-1591 and the flight of Persian nobles to Bijapur, among them the historian Firishta. In 1565 four of the five allied to defeat the Vijayanagara Empire at the Battle of Talikota, after which the city of Vijayanagara was destroyed and Bijapur took the Raichur Doab. Ahmadnagar conquered Berar in 1574, and Bijapur annexed Bidar in 1619.

The Mughal Empire then absorbed them. Berar was taken from Ahmadnagar in 1596, and Chand Bibi repulsed a Mughal attack the same year. After her death in July 1600 the Mughals took Ahmadnagar, but Malik Ambar defied them and set up Murtaza Shah II at Paranda. Shahaji, with Bijapur's help, put an infant Nizam Shahi scion on the throne, but Aurangzeb annexed the sultanate in 1636 after defeating him. In Bijapur the Marathas revolted under Shivaji and seized much of the realm. Aurangzeb's campaign of 1686-87 conquered Bijapur and Golconda, ending the last of the sultanates.

The courts fostered Dakhani, a language that grew by borrowing from Arabic, Persian, Marathi, Kannada and Telugu, and was later called Dakhani Urdu. Deccani miniature painting flourished at Ahmadnagar, Bijapur and Golconda. Architecture of the period includes the Charminar and the Gol Gumbaz, and a number of the sultanates' monuments are on a tentative list for UNESCO World Heritage nomination. The Nizam Shahi, Adil Shahi and Qutb Shahi rulers are noted for religious tolerance; under Ahmad Shah I, Ahmad Shah I's record keeper Dalapati wrote the encyclopaedic Nrisimha Prasada, naming his overlord Nizamsaha.
decebalus: Nothing is known of the youth or background of Decebalus. After the death of the Great King Burebista, Dacia split into four and then five smaller kingdoms, and Decebalus seems to have risen at the court of King Duras, who claimed authority over all Dacian land. A Dacian pot inscribed Decebalus per Scorilo has led to the suggestion that he was the son of a Scorilo, though one scholar, Lucian Boia, calls this idea originally a scholarly joke. In 85 and 86 the Dacian army raided and attacked the Roman province of Moesia under a leader the Roman sources call Diurpaneus, whom recent writers take to be most likely Decebalus himself.

The Dacians killed Oppius Sabinus, governor of Moesia, and Emperor Domitian came to deal with the problem himself, then returned to Rome and left Cornelius Fuscus in command. Fuscus advanced into Dacia, and two Roman legions, among them the V Alaudae, were ambushed and defeated at the pass of Tapae. Fuscus was killed, and Decebalus was crowned after the ageing Duras abdicated. A Roman army defeated the Dacians near Tapae in 88, but Domitian was facing revolts on the Rhine and defeats at the hands of the Marcomanni and the Iazyges. He made peace, agreeing to annual payments of eight million sesterces, and Decebalus's brother Diegis went to Rome to receive a diadem. Decebalus used engineers supplied by Domitian to strengthen his fortifications.

Trajan came to power in 98, and in 101 crossed the Danube. Decebalus was defeated at the Second Battle of Tapae and again at Adamclisi, and by early 102 he accepted terms that cost him territory and his fortresses, though he kept his throne. He then rearmed, annexed land from the Iazyges and in 105 attacked the Roman positions. Trajan demanded his surrender, which he refused, and the Romans took and destroyed the capital Sarmizegetusa in 106.

Decebalus escaped with his family and continued a guerrilla war in the Carpathian mountains. Cornered by Roman detachments, he killed himself by cutting his throat rather than be taken to Rome, as Trajan's Column shows. A cavalry scout, Tiberius Claudius Maximus, reached him, and Decebalus's head and right hand were taken to Trajan. Part of Dacia was absorbed into the Empire. The Greek historian Dio Cassius described him as shrewd in the understanding and waging of war, expert in ambushes and a worthy antagonist of the Romans. From the 19th century he became a national hero of Romania, honoured as a symbol of resistance, often paired with Trajan on banknotes and in the imagery of rulers.
decembrists: Many Russian officers were encouraged by the early liberal reforms of Tsar Alexander I, which Count Mikhail Speransky advanced until his exile in 1812. The tsar later turned back to restraint and conservatism, after unrest he believed came from liberalisation. Officers who had served in the Napoleonic Wars, and had seen the suffering of peasant soldiers, were drawn to reform. They formed secret societies, among them the Union of Salvation and the Union of Prosperity, and later the Northern Society in the capital and the Southern Society in Ukraine. Pavel Pestel recorded that the nobility, who were to petition the emperor to free the serfs, could not be persuaded.

Alexander I died on 1 December 1825 (19 November Old Style). His brother Konstantin had privately renounced the throne two years earlier, but this was not generally known, and the guards swore allegiance to him. When Nicholas stepped forward, the Northern Society tried to persuade regiments not to swear to him, and elected Prince Sergei Trubetskoy interim ruler. On 26 December (14 December Old Style) about 3,000 men under their officers assembled in Senate Square and refused the oath to Nicholas I, proclaiming loyalty to Konstantin. Trubetskoy deserted, and Prince Eugene Obolensky was appointed in his place.

For hours the rebels stood against some 9,000 loyal troops, while a crowd of onlookers fraternised with them without joining. Count Mikhail Miloradovich, sent by Nicholas to parley, was shot dead by Pyotr Kakhovsky. A squad of grenadiers entered the Winter Palace but failed to seize it, and the revolt was put down. In the south the police had arrested Pestel the day before. Sergey Muravyov-Apostol raised the Chernigov Regiment on 10 January 1826 (29 December Old Style), and the rising was defeated within five days.

At the trial members of the Northern and Southern Societies and the United Slavs were judged, and five leaders were sentenced to hang. Many others were sent to prison or exiled to Siberia, and the first convicts left for the mines of Nerchinsk on 25 July 1826. Enlisted soldiers received harsher treatment: 178 were sentenced to run the gauntlet and about four thousand were sent to the Caucasus. Autocracy lasted almost a century more, although Nicholas I turned his attention to the empire's internal problems and set Speransky to codify the laws.

Historians describe the revolt as the beginning of a revolutionary movement and the first open breach between the government and the reformist nobility. Alexander Herzen put the profiles of the executed on the cover of his periodical Polar Star, and Alexander Pushkin addressed poems to Decembrist friends. Leo Tolstoy began a novel about the movement that grew into War and Peace.
decimus-junius-brutus-albinus: Decimus Brutus was probably the son of the senator Decimus Junius Brutus and his notorious wife Sempronia, a participant in the conspiracy of Catilina in 63 BCE. His father, grandfather and great-grandfather had all been consuls. He was adopted by a patrician named Postumius Albinus, and some ancient sources and his own coins call him Albinus, but he seems not to have changed his name, and his contemporaries used his birth name.

Caesar said on several occasions that he loved him like a son, and named him an heir in the second degree in his will and guardian of any child he might have. He is often confused with his distant cousin Marcus Junius Brutus.

He served in Caesar's army in the Gallic Wars and in 56 BCE commanded the fleet against the Veneti. In the Battle of Morbihan he destroyed their ships by attacking their sails with sickle-like hooks fixed on long poles, leaving them helpless for Roman boarding parties. He also served against Vercingetorix in 52 BCE. In the civil war he sided with Caesar and was again entrusted with fleet operations: left in charge of the naval blockade of Massilia, he built a fleet from scratch within thirty days, defeated the Massilian fleet twice and, with Gaius Trebonius, secured the city's surrender.

In 44 BCE Caesar made him Praetor Peregrinus and designated him governor of Cisalpine Gaul for the next year. He helped persuade Marcus Brutus to join the conspiracy against Caesar. On the Ides of March he persuaded Caesar to attend the Senate, escorted him there and kept Mark Antony away; according to Nicolaus of Damascus he struck Caesar through the thigh.

Antony opposed Decimus's claim to Cisalpine Gaul, and when the Senate ordered him to give up the province he refused. In 43 BCE he occupied Mutina, and Antony blockaded him. The consuls Aulus Hirtius and Gaius Pansa marched to relieve the siege with Octavian, and Antony was defeated at the battles of Forum Gallorum on 14 April and at Mutina on 21 April.

Octavian coldly told Decimus he had come to oppose Antony, not to help Caesar's murderers, and many of Decimus's soldiers deserted to him. He fled across the Alps, was left exposed when Plancus switched sides and was executed in mid-September by Camelus, a Gallic chief loyal to Antony. Several of his letters survive in Cicero's correspondence.
declaration-of-the-rights-of-man-and-of-: The ideas of the Declaration came largely from the Enlightenment: individualism, Jean-Jacques Rousseau's social contract and the Baron de Montesquieu's separation of powers. The United States Declaration of Independence of 1776 was an influence too. Marquis de Lafayette prepared the principal early drafts with Thomas Jefferson, then American diplomat in France. Presented to the legislative committee on 11 July 1789, his draft was rejected by pragmatists such as Jean Joseph Mounier, who feared raising expectations that could not be met. The final text owes most to Emmanuel Joseph Sieyès, with Honoré Mirabeau a central figure in editing it, and it was published on 26 August 1789 as a statement of principle.

A preamble calls the rights natural, unalienable and sacred. Article II names them as liberty, property, security and resistance to oppression. Article I declares that men are born and remain free and equal in rights. Article III places sovereignty in the Nation, in contrast to the divine right of kings, and Article VI calls law the expression of the general will, with all citizens equally admissible to public office according to their capacity.

Other articles forbid arbitrary arrest, require that penalties be established by law before the offence, presume innocence, protect opinions, including religious ones, as long as they do not trouble public order, and declare the free communication of thoughts one of the most precious rights. Taxes are to be consented to by citizens or their representatives.

The rights were granted only to men, and the 1791 Constitution distinguished active citizens, French men of at least 25 who paid taxes equal to three days' work and were not servants, from passive citizens. About 4.3 million of some 29 million people held the vote. In September 1791 Olympe de Gouges answered with her Declaration of the Rights of Woman and of the Female Citizen. The Declaration did not abolish slavery in the French colonies, but it inspired the uprisings in Saint-Domingue that became the Haitian Revolution.

It was attached as a preamble to the Constitution of 1791 and is included at the start of the constitutions of the Fourth Republic (1946) and Fifth Republic (1958), where it is valid as constitutional law. In 2003 UNESCO added the first printed version to its Memory of the World International Register.
decolonisation: Decolonisation is the ending of colonialism, the process by which imperial nations establish and dominate foreign territories, often overseas. The meanings of the term are disputed. According to David Strang it is achieved through sovereign statehood with recognition by the international community or through full incorporation into an existing sovereign state. The United Nations holds that the core requirement is the right to self-determination, which can be exercised with or without independence.

As a movement for independence from the metropoles, decolonisation began in 1775 with the American Revolution. In the two hundred years after 1783, 165 colonies gained independence from Western imperial powers. Explanations differ: some stress rising education, some economic shifts, some the inspiration of earlier revolutions and some the rising cost of empire.

The first colonies to declare independence were the thirteen North American colonies of Britain, which formed the United States in 1776. The Haitian Revolution, a revolt of 1789 and a slave uprising of 1791 in the French colony of Saint-Domingue, led to independence from France in 1804. The Napoleonic Wars cut the links between Spain and its American colonies and began their decolonisation, and Brazil became independent from Portugal in 1822.

After the First World War the German, Austro-Hungarian, Ottoman and Russian empires broke up, and former German and Ottoman territories were governed as League of Nations mandates, among them Syria and Lebanon under France. Nationalism in the French colonies strengthened between the wars, producing Abd el-Krim's Rif War of 1921 to 1925 in Morocco. Lebanon declared independence in 1943 and Syria in 1945.

After 1945 a wave of decolonisation came first in Asia, then in the Middle East, and in the 1960s in sub-Saharan Africa. It was often not carefully planned but a response to politics in the colony, politics at home and international pressure. The British Empire usually held a constitutional conference in London before independence. The last wave followed the Cold War, with the collapse of the Soviet Union, the independence of Palau and the handovers of Hong Kong and Macau.

New states had to build governments, laws, armies and schools, to create loyalty to the state through flags, anthems and official histories, and to develop currencies, banks and taxation. In settler colonial states such as New Zealand, Australia, Canada and the United States, settlers stayed, and Indigenous peoples continue to make demands for decolonisation and self-determination.
David Strang writes that the loss of their empires turned France and Britain into second-rate powers. John Kenneth Galbraith argues that decolonisation after the Second World War had economic causes.
deeg: Deeg lies in the Deeg district of eastern Rajasthan, about 32 km from the city of Bharatpur, at an average elevation of 174 m. Its nearness to Agra gave it a part in the politics of the region. Deeg Fort is square in plan and stands on slightly raised ground; its walls of rubble and mud are strengthened by twelve towers, the largest of which, the Lakha-Burj, is at the north-west corner. The towers carried cannon. A wide, shallow moat surrounds the fort, crossed by a bridge on the northern side that leads to the only gate.

After acquiring the throne, the Jat ruler Maharaja Badan Singh chose Deeg as his stronghold and capital and began the building of a palace there, so that Deeg became the first capital of the Jats of Bharatpur. The town was almost constantly under threat of Mughal invasion, and his son Maharaja Suraj Mal ordered a fortress built to protect the palace. In 1804 both the Battle of Deeg and the Siege of Deeg set the British East India Company against Bharatpur's Jat rulers and their Maratha allies.

The palace complex served the Jat Maharajas as a summer retreat. It consists of several palaces called Bhawans set among charbaghs and water gardens, among them the Gopal Bhawan, the Kishan Bhawan, the Nand Bhawan, the Keshav Bhawan, the Hardev Bhawan, the Suraj Bhawan and the twin pavilions of Sawan and Bhadon.

The palace was in use until the early 1970s and now holds a museum. Its 900 fountains are run twice a year, at the Braj Holi festival in February or March and at a festival in September, and a fair named after Maharaja Jawahar Singh is held each year around September. Inside the fort a partly ruined palace, or haveli, of red sandstone is the principal building; parts of it were rebuilt in the 20th century. The 2011 Indian census counted 44,999 inhabitants.
deioces: Deioces was the founder and first king of the Median Kingdom, a polity on the Iranian plateau. Herodotus writes his name as Dēiokēs, Assyrian texts give it as Da-a-a-uk-ku, and it derives from an Iranian form meaning the land. Friedrich von Spiegel took it to mean the resident and headman of a village. The date of his reign is disputed. Herodotus says he ruled for 53 years and was the first Median king to win independence from Assyria, but his report is a mixture of Greek and Oriental legends and is not historically reliable.

Assyrian sources show the Medes of this period under many local lords and not a single king, and Igor Diakonoff believes that Deioces was one of these small lords, to whom the history of his successors lent fame. Herodotus's Deioces is sometimes associated with Daiukku, an Assyrian provincial governor whom Sargon II captured and exiled to Syria in 715 BCE, but the association is highly unlikely, since those events lay around Lake Urmia.

According to Herodotus, the Medes lived in small villages with independent rulers when Deioces set out to make himself king. He enforced justice in his own village and gained a reputation as a neutral judge, and people from other villages came to him. He then announced that the work was too troublesome and resigned. Theft and chaos increased, and the Medes gathered and chose him as king. He established a guard of spearmen and built a new capital, Ecbatana, whose name means the gathering place and which is believed to be Hamadan today, although Henry Rawlinson looked for it near Lake Urmia.

Herodotus describes the royal complex as seven concentric walls, each higher than the one outside it, painted white, black, red, blue, a lower red, copper and gold, with the palace and treasure within the last. Deioces stayed in his palace and dealt with the outside only through messengers, and it was forbidden to laugh or spit in his presence. He also created the King's Eyes and Ears, a body of people assigned to spy for the king, which existed in the Achaemenid period. His son Phraortes succeeded him. Some Iranologists identify Deioces with Hushang of the Shahnameh.
deir-el-bahari: Deir el-Bahari, also called Dayr al-Bahri, is a complex of mortuary temples and tombs on the west bank of the Nile, opposite Luxor, and part of the Theban Necropolis. Its Arabic name means the Northern Monastery, and its Coptic name refers to the monastery of Apa Phoibammon. Hathor was a prominent goddess there, and the cliffs were sacred to her before pharaonic construction. Amun, supreme god of Thebes, Osiris and Anubis were also honoured in its temples and chapels.

Its history begins with the 11th Dynasty king Mentuhotep II, who built a funerary temple on several levels in the great bay to commemorate the reunification of Egypt after the First Intermediate Period. Its terraced plan, with a royal tomb built into the platform, pioneered the cliffside temple style. The shrines and tombs of royal wives and daughters, who served as priestesses of Hathor, stood along the west wall of the terrace.

Centuries later the 18th Dynasty queen Hatshepsut had her temple, Djeser-Djeseru, built beside it, designed by her steward and architect Senenmut. It rises in colonnaded terraces to 30 metres, and its reliefs recite the divine birth of the queen and an expedition to the Land of Punt. Some of her statues were destroyed in a posthumous condemnation of her, and others were rededicated to Thutmose III. He added a smaller temple above hers, Djeser-Akhet. In the Ptolemaic and Roman periods Hatshepsut's temple became a cult centre for the deified Imhotep and Amenhotep, son of Hapu.

In the Third Intermediate Period the site became a burial ground for priests. A tomb in a recess of the cliffs, known as TT320 or DB320, held a cache of forty royal mummies moved from the Valley of the Kings by priests of the 21st Dynasty, most likely to prevent looting. They included Ahmose I, Thutmose III, Seti I and Ramesses II. It was found in 1881. A second cache of 153 priests' mummies came to light in 1891 at Bab el-Gasus.

Édouard Naville excavated for the Egypt Exploration Fund from 1893 to 1906, and Herbert Winlock led the Metropolitan Museum of Art's expeditions from 1911 to 1931. Polish missions have undertaken major conservation work since the 1960s and rediscovered the temple of Thutmose III. The site belongs to the UNESCO World Heritage listing Ancient Thebes with its Necropolis.
deir-el-medina: The village lies in a small natural amphitheatre on the west bank of the Nile, within walking distance of the Valley of the Kings to the north and the Valley of the Queens to the west. It may have been built apart from the wider population to preserve the secrecy of the work in the tombs. Its first datable remains belong to the reign of Thutmose I, and it took its final shape in the Ramesside period.

Houses averaged 70 square metres, with mudbrick walls on stone foundations, painted white outside, and four to five rooms, high windows and niches for statues and small altars. The hill of Gurnet Murai cut off the north breeze and any view of the river valley, so the village is not thought to have been a pleasant place.

The population was mixed, Egyptians, Nubians and Asiatics, and was divided into left and right gangs, each with a foreman. The workmen were salaried state employees paid in rations at up to three times the rate of agricultural labourers. They worked eight days and then had two days off, and in the reign of Merneptah more than a third of the year was time off. A large proportion of the community, including women, could at least read. The villagers had their own court, consulted oracles carried on litters and kept 16 to 18 chapels, honouring Amenhotep I and his mother Queen Ahmose-Nefertari as patrons over many generations.

In about the 25th year of Ramesses III the labourers, exasperated by delayed supplies, threw down their tools and wrote to the vizier complaining of missing wheat rations: eighteen days of the month had passed without them. The authorities addressed the complaint and they returned to work the next day, but several strikes followed, and further complaints are recorded under Ramesses IX and Ramesses X. After the reign of Ramses IV conditions grew unsettled, with unreliable grain supplies and gangs of tomb robbers, and the village was abandoned because of tomb robbery, Libyan raids and civil war.

Ernesto Schiaparelli first excavated the site seriously between 1905 and 1909, finding many ostraca. A French team directed by Bernard Bruyère excavated the village, dump and cemetery between 1922 and 1951, and Jaroslav Černý studied the texts for almost 50 years until his death in 1970; the peak above the village was renamed Mont Cernabru for them. About 5,000 ostraca came from a well near the village, and thousands of papyri and ostraca still await publication. In the Christian era the temple of Hathor became a monastery of Saint Isidorus, which gave the site its Arabic name. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
dejima: Dejima, meaning exit island, measured about 120 metres by 75 and was linked to the mainland by a small bridge, guarded on both sides, with a gate on the Dutch side. It held houses for about twenty Dutchmen, warehouses and quarters for Japanese officials. The shogun Iemitsu ordered its construction in 1634 to lodge the Portuguese traders in Nagasaki and prevent the spread of their religion, one of many edicts he issued between 1633 and 1639 to limit contact with other countries. The island was created in 1636 by cutting a canal through a small peninsula. Twenty-five local Japanese families owned the land and received an annual rent from the Dutch.

Portuguese traders had developed Nagasaki from 1570 with the daimyo Omura Sumitada. After a rising of mostly Christian people in the Shimabara-Amakusa region, the Tokugawa government expelled the Portuguese in 1639. The Dutch East India Company, which had run a post at Hirado since 1609, was moved to Dejima in 1641, after officials used the Christian-era dates on its new warehouses as a pretext to demolish them. From then only Chinese and Dutch ships could come to Japan, and only to Nagasaki.

The Dutch were closely watched by officials, gatekeepers, night watchmen and about 150 interpreters, all paid by the company. Ships were inspected, religious books and weapons confiscated, and no religious services were allowed. Engelbert Kaempfer compared the island to a prison. Ships were allowed in numbers that fell from an average of seven a year in 1641-1671 to two a year from 1715. After the company's bankruptcy in 1795 the Dutch government took over, and during the Napoleonic Wars Dejima was for a time the only place where the Dutch flag still flew. The chief Dutch officer, the Opperhoofd, was replaced every year and travelled to Edo to pay homage to the shogun, yearly until 1790 and every fourth year afterwards.

The Dutch brought silk, cotton, sugar, books and scientific instruments and bought copper, silver, camphor, porcelain, lacquerware and rice. Staff of the post sold more than 10,000 foreign books to the Japanese between the late 18th and early 19th centuries, a basis of rangaku, Dutch learning. Physicians such as Kaempfer, Carl Peter Thunberg and Philipp Franz von Siebold were sometimes called to high-ranking Japanese patients. Billiards, chocolate, coffee and cabbage are among things introduced through the island.

After the Dutch negotiated their own treaty in 1858 Dejima ceased to be the exclusive trading post, and land reclamation later merged it into Nagasaki. It was designated a national historic site in 1922, and restoration began in 1996, with plans to rebuild 25 buildings in their early 19th-century state.
delaware-river: The river has two branches that rise in the Catskill Mountains of New York. They merge at Hancock, New York, and the river then flows south along the borders of New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and Delaware. It crosses the Kittatinny ridge at the Delaware Water Gap, between nearly vertical walls of sandstone, quartzite and conglomerate. At Trenton it crosses the Atlantic Seaboard Fall Line and becomes tidal, and below it widens into Delaware Bay, past Philadelphia, Camden and Wilmington. It is the longest free-flowing river in the Eastern United States.

Before the arrival of Europeans the river was the homeland of the Lenape, who called it Lënapei Sipu, the Lenape river. In 1609 a Dutch East India Company expedition led by the English navigator Henry Hudson visited it. In 1638 Swedish settlers under Peter Menuet founded New Sweden on the river, with Fort Christina near modern Wilmington as a trading post; the Dutch asserted dominance in 1655. Both powers called it the South River, to tell it from the North River, now the Hudson. After the English took New Netherland in 1664 it was renamed for Thomas West, 3rd Baron De La Warr, the first royal governor of Virginia.

George Washington crossed the river with the Continental Army on the night of 25–26 December 1776, and the surprise attack on the Hessian troops at Trenton the next morning succeeded. In the Philadelphia Campaign the British needed control of the river to supply their fleet, and the Battle of Red Bank and the Siege of Fort Mifflin were fought along its shores.

The river is the backbone of the Philadelphia metropolitan area. It supplies drinking water to about 17 million people, including half of New York City through the Delaware Aqueduct. In 1931 the United States Supreme Court allowed New York to draw water from its tributaries, subject to the laws of Congress, after New Jersey brought suit. The Delaware Water Gap National Recreation Area came about after a plan to dam the river at Tocks Island failed. Since 1941 the main shipping channel has been kept at a depth of 40 feet.
delft: Delft lies between Rotterdam to the southeast and The Hague to the northwest. The city came into being beside a canal, the Delf, whose name comes from the Dutch word delven, to dig. Where this canal crossed the creek wall of the silted-up river Gantel, a count established his manor, probably around 1075. In 1389 the Delfshavensche Schie canal was dug through to the river Maas, where the port of Delfshaven was built, connecting the town to the sea.

In 1400 Delft had about 6,500 inhabitants, the third largest city of the county of Holland. A great fire destroyed a large part of the city in 1536. William of Orange took up residence in 1572 in the former Saint-Agatha convent, later called the Prinsenhof, as leader of the Dutch resistance to Spanish rule, and a Spanish attack was repelled in October 1573. After the Act of Abjuration of 1581 the city became the de facto capital of the Dutch Republic, as seat of the stadtholder. William was buried in the Nieuwe Kerk because the family's traditional burial place at Breda was in Spanish hands, which began a tradition for the House of Orange.

In the 17th century an office of the Dutch East India Company, opened in 1602, and the making of Delftware, styled on imported Chinese porcelain, brought a new heyday. Painters of the Delft School, among them Pieter de Hoogh, Carel Fabritius and Gerard Houckgeest, are known for domestic scenes and church interiors. On 12 October 1654 a store of about 30 tonnes of gunpowder in a former convent exploded after its keeper opened it to check a sample. The blast levelled the central part of the city and was heard on the island of Texel, some 110 km away. Most accounts give more than 100 dead, and Fabritius was among them.

Delft is a city and municipality in the province of South Holland. The Oude Kerk, built between 1246 and 1350, holds the graves of Vermeer and Leeuwenhoek, and the Nieuwe Kerk, built between 1381 and 1496, holds the royal vault. The Oostpoort, built around 1400, is the only remaining gate of the old walls. Delft University of Technology was founded in 1842 as an academy for civil engineering.
delhi: Delhi lies in North India, spread chiefly to the west of the Yamuna river and bordered by the state of Haryana on the north, west and south and by Uttar Pradesh on the east. Two prominent features of its geography are the Yamuna flood plains and the Delhi Ridge. The Yamuna, a sacred river in Hinduism, is the only major river flowing through Delhi, and its floodplains are fertile but prone to flooding. The Delhi Ridge, which rises from the Aravalli Range to the south, reaches a height of 318 metres.

There are several legends about the origin of the name. One derives it from Dhillu or Dilu, a king who built a city here in 50 BCE. Another says the Tomaras used the Prakrit word dhili, loose, because the Iron pillar of Delhi had a weak foundation.

Seven cities have traditionally been associated with the region. The earliest, Indraprastha, is described in the Sanskrit epic Mahabharata as a city on a knoll on the banks of the Yamuna. The topography of Purana Qila matches this description, but excavations have yielded only painted grey pottery of the eleventh century BCE and no signs of a built environment or fortifications. The earliest architectural relics date from the Maurya period, about 300 BCE. The Tomara Rajput King Anang Pal built Lal Kot in 1052 CE, and the Chauhan Rajputs under Vigraharaja IV conquered it in the mid-12th century.

From the early 13th century until the mid-19th century Delhi was the capital of two major empires, the Delhi Sultanate and the Mughal Empire. It was a notable centre of the Indian Rebellion of 1857. In 1911 New Delhi, a southern region within Delhi, became the capital of the British Indian Empire. During the Partition of India in 1947 Delhi was transformed from a Mughal city to a Punjabi one, losing two-thirds of its Muslim residents, in part under pressure from arriving Hindu and Sikh refugees from western Punjab.

Delhi, officially the National Capital Territory of Delhi, is a union territory of India that contains New Delhi, the capital of the Republic of India since 1950. It became a union territory on 1 November 1956. The Qutub Minar, Humayun's Tomb and the Red Fort, all from the Sultanate and Mughal periods, are its three UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Delhi was an early centre of Sufism and Qawwali music, and its Khariboli dialect was part of the development that produced Urdu literature and later Modern Standard Hindi.
delhi-sultanate: The sultanate was established in 1206 in the former Ghurid territories in India. Its foundation was laid by the Ghurid conqueror Muhammad Ghori, who defeated a Rajput confederacy led by the Ajmer ruler Prithviraj Chauhan near Tarain in 1192. It began as one of several principalities held by Muhammad Ghori's Turkic slave-generals, who divided the Ghurid lands among themselves.

The rise of the sultanate belonged to a wider movement of Turkic nomads from the Central Asian steppes into Muslim lands. Muslim rulers enslaved Turks and raised many of them as army slaves, called Mamluks, and some became rulers. Qutb ud-Din Aibak, a former slave of Muhammad Ghori, was the first sultan of Delhi.

The history is usually divided into five periods: Mamluk (1206 to 1290), Khalji (1290 to 1320), Tughlaq (1320 to 1414), Sayyid (1414 to 1451) and Lodi (1451 to 1526). Under the Khalji and Tughlaq dynasties conquests continued deep into southern India, and the sultanate reached its largest extent under the Tughlaq Muhammad bin Tughluq, when it held most of the subcontinent. Razia Sultana reigned from 1236 to 1240. The sultanate repelled attacks by the Mongols of the Chagatai Khanate.

Timur's devastating raid on Delhi in 1398 changed northern India. Rival Hindu powers such as the Vijayanagara Empire and the Kingdom of Mewar re-emerged, and the Bengal and Bahmani sultanates asserted independence. In 1526 Babur, a Timurid ruler, invaded northern India and conquered the sultanate, which the Mughal Empire succeeded.

Chroniclers such as Ziauddin Barani called the state the Empire of Delhi, and Ibn Battuta called it Hind and Sind. Its early elite consisted largely of first-generation immigrants from Iran and Central Asia. The sultans generally accepted Hindu officials and vassals in the administration, and non-Muslim subjects paid the jizya as dhimmis. Alauddin Khalji replaced private markets with government-run markets and imposed strict price controls.

The campaigns brought destruction. The historian Richard Eaton tabulated 37 instances of Hindu temples desecrated or destroyed between 1234 and 1518, and notes that sultans also ordered temples protected or repaired. Sources record the sack of cities in Gujarat and large killings, among them 30,000 at Chittor under Alauddin Khalji and 180,000 in Odisha under Firuz Shah Tughlaq.
The Hindustani language began to emerge in this period, and Amir Khusrau wrote in a form of it he called Hindavi. Mosques and tombs under high domes and arches introduced Central Asian styles.
delian-league: After the Greek victories at Plataea and Mycale in 479 BCE, the allied fleet besieged Sestos and then captured Byzantion in 478 BCE, but the behaviour of the Spartan general Pausanias alienated many allies and he was recalled. Sparta was then eager to end its part in the war. Its king Leotychidas had proposed moving all the Greeks of Asia Minor to Europe, but the Athenian commander Xanthippus rejected this, saying the Athenians would protect the Ionians, who had been their colonists.

A congress on the island of Delos then founded a new alliance. According to Thucydides its official aim was to 'avenge the wrongs they suffered by ravaging the territory of the king'. Members swore to have the same friends and enemies and dropped iron ingots into the sea to symbolise the permanence of the alliance.

Members could provide ships or pay a tax into the common treasury, and most chose to pay. The Athenian politician Aristides was occupied with fixing the tax of new members. Under Cimon the League expelled the remaining Persian forces from the Aegean, and Cimon forced Karystos in Euboea to join and conquered Skyros. Athens treated attempts to leave harshly. Naxos was defeated in about 471 BCE, and Thasos, which seceded in 465 BCE after Athens founded Amphipolis near its mines, surrendered after more than two years of siege, lost its walls, ships and mines and had to pay tribute.

Thucydides saw this as the point where the alliance became a hegemony. In 454 BCE Pericles moved the treasury to Athens, allegedly to keep it safe from Persia; Plutarch records that his rivals saw it as using the money for building projects such as the Parthenon.

In 460 BCE Athens sent a large fleet to support a revolt in Egypt against Persia, and the expedition was destroyed; Isocrates puts the loss at some 20,000 men and modern estimates at 50,000 men and 250 ships. Cimon died during the blockade of Citium on Cyprus. Some writers report a peace with Persia, the Peace of Callias, in 450 BCE, while others think it a later invention.

Athens began to plant kleruchiai, quasi-colonies serving as garrisons, and officials supervised the tribute. After an unsuccessful revolt, Mytilene on Lesbos lost the land of the whole island to Athenian settlers, and Melos was conquered and its men put to death. By 431 BCE the League's threat to Spartan hegemony and Athens's heavy administration led to the Peloponnesian War.

The Spartans, aided by the Persians and by Athenian internal strife, defeated the Athenian empire after 27 years of war, and the League was dissolved in 404 BCE under Lysander. Athens founded the Second Athenian League in 377 BCE against Spartan and then Theban power but never recovered its former strength.
delos: Delos lies near Mykonos, close to the centre of the Cyclades, and covers only 3.43 square kilometres. Stone huts found on the island show that it has been inhabited since the third millennium BCE. The island had been a holy sanctuary for a millennium before Olympian mythology made it the birthplace of Apollo and Artemis.

Between 900 BCE and 100 CE Delos was a major cult centre, where Dionysus and Leto, mother of the twins Apollo and Artemis, were also revered. Athens carried out purifications of the island. In the 6th century BCE the tyrant Pisistratus ordered all graves in sight of the temple dug up. In the sixth year of the Peloponnesian War, on the instruction of the Delphic Oracle, the whole island was cleared of the dead, and a decree forbade burial or birth there. After the Persian Wars the Delian League, founded in 478 BCE, met in the temple, and its treasury stayed there until Pericles removed it to Athens in 454 BCE.

In the Hellenistic period a Phoenician colony traded widely, and inscriptions show a Samaritan community and a Jewish presence. In 167 or 166 BCE, after the Roman victory in the Third Macedonian War, the Roman Republic ceded Delos to the Athenians, who expelled most of the original inhabitants. Strabo writes that the Romans made it a free port, partly to damage the trade of Rhodes. Traders bought tens of thousands of slaves there, captured by Cilician pirates or in the wars that followed the break-up of the Seleucid Empire, and Delos held the largest slave market of the region.

After Corinth was destroyed in 146 BCE Delos took over part of its role as a trading centre. Attacks by the forces of Mithridates VI of Pontus in 88 and 69 BCE greatly reduced its prosperity and population, and before the end of the first century BCE Puteoli replaced it as the main focus of Italian trade with the east. The island was eventually abandoned around the eighth century CE.

Excavations on the island are among the most extensive in the Mediterranean. The remains include the Doric Temple of the Delians dedicated to Apollo, the Terrace of the Lions given by the people of Naxos shortly before 600 BCE, of which seven lions remain, and houses with floor mosaics such as the House of Dionysus. UNESCO inscribed Delos on the World Heritage List in 1990.
demeter: In Greek tradition Demeter is the second child of the Titans Rhea and Cronus and the sister of Hestia, Hera, Hades, Poseidon and Zeus. Hesiod's Theogony, from about 700 BCE, tells how, like her siblings except Zeus, she was swallowed as a newborn by her father and freed when Zeus made Cronus disgorge his children. In the earliest conceptions she is the goddess of grain and threshing, and her functions were extended to the earth in general, so that she was often identified with Gaia. Her religious tradition rests on ancient agrarian cults that predated the Olympian pantheon.

Demeter presided over crops, grains and food, but also over sacred law and the cycle of life and death. Her cult titles include Sito, she of the grain, and Thesmophoros, giver of customs. In the Homeric Hymn to Demeter, Hades abducted her daughter Persephone with the permission of Zeus. Demeter searched for nine days until the sun god Helios told her what had happened. In her grief the seasons halted and living things began to die. Zeus sent Hermes to bring Persephone back, but Hades had made her eat pomegranate seeds, which bound her to the Underworld for part of every year.

Her search took her to Eleusis, where King Celeus took her in as an old woman and she nursed his sons Demophon and Triptolemus. When she tried to make Demophon immortal in the hearth's flames, his mother Metanira cried out, and Demeter abandoned the attempt. She and Persephone then taught Triptolemus the secrets of agriculture.

Her two major festivals were sacred mysteries. The Thesmophoria, held on 11 to 13 October, was open to women only, and the Eleusinian Mysteries to initiates of any gender or social class; the Eleusinian Mysteries promised the initiated a happy afterlife. Major cults are known at Eleusis, Megara, Corinth, Delos, Pergamon, Akragas and Enna. Around 205 BCE her worship merged with that of the Roman goddess Ceres, with a Greek-inspired rite brought from southern Italy by Greek priestesses who were granted Roman citizenship. In art Demeter is shown with flowers, fruit and grain, sometimes with Persephone, and Marcus Manilius assigned her the constellation Virgo.
demetrius-i-of-macedon: Demetrius was the son of Antigonus I Monophthalmus, founder of the Antigonid dynasty, and his wife Stratonice. He served with his father in the Second War of the Diadochi. At the Battle of Paraitakene he commanded the cavalry on the right flank, and his success there prevented the battle from being a complete loss. After the Battle of Gabiene he was one of the few who implored his father to spare the captured Eumenes.

At twenty-one he was left to defend Syria against Ptolemy I and was defeated at the Battle of Gaza, though he partly repaired the loss at the Battle of Myus. In 310 BCE he was soundly defeated when he tried to expel Seleucus I Nicator from Babylon, and as a result of this war Antigonus lost almost two thirds of his empire, as all the eastern satrapies fell to Seleucus.

In 307 BCE Demetrius sailed to Athens with 250 ships, expelled the garrison placed there under Demetrius of Phalerum and took Munychia. The Athenians worshipped him as a tutelary deity under the title Soter, Saviour. In 306 BCE he destroyed the naval power of Ptolemaic Egypt at the Battle of Salamis and conquered Cyprus. Antigonus then took the title king and gave it to his son as well.

His siege of Rhodes in 305 BCE failed, but his siege engines earned him the name Poliorcetes. They included a battering ram 55 metres long needing a thousand men to work it and a wheeled tower called Helepolis, 38 metres tall. The Rhodians afterwards used the abandoned bronze to build the Colossus of Rhodes. Antigonus and Demetrius were defeated at the Battle of Ipsus in Phrygia in 301 BCE by a coalition of Seleucus, Cassander and Lysimachus. Antigonus was killed.

In 294 BCE Demetrius took Athens after a long blockade and established himself on the throne of Macedon by murdering Alexander V, the son of Cassander. He took Thebes in 291 BCE after a rebellion by the Boeotians. His rule was continually threatened by Pyrrhus of Epirus, and in 288 BCE the combined forces of Pyrrhus, Ptolemy I and Lysimachus, helped by discontented subjects, obliged him to leave Macedon.

He then attacked provinces of Lysimachus in Asia, but famine and pestilence destroyed most of his army. Abandoned by his troops, he surrendered to Seleucus and died in confinement in 283 BCE after three years. His son Antigonus II Gonatas received his remains, which were buried at Corinth with a splendid funeral. Demetrius's descendants held the Macedonian throne until the Romans conquered Macedon in 168 BCE. Plutarch wrote a biography of him, paired with Mark Antony.
demetrius-ii-nicator: Demetrius II was a son of Demetrius I Soter. While he was a young boy, his father fought Alexander Balas for the Seleucid throne and lost; his father, mother and older brother were all killed. The boy fled to Crete, where guardians raised him. In 147 BCE, while Balas was occupied with a revolt in Cilicia, Demetrius returned to Syria with a force of Cretan mercenaries led by a man called Lasthenes.

In 145 BCE Ptolemy VI Philometor of Egypt marched into Syria in support of Balas but switched sides, sealing the alliance by marrying his daughter Cleopatra Thea to Demetrius. Ptolemy and Demetrius defeated Balas at the Battle of the Oenoparus river; Balas fled to Arabia and was killed, and Ptolemy died of his wounds three days later. Demetrius then cut his soldiers' wages and debased the coinage, and punished Antioch severely, so that Cretan mercenaries slaughtered citizens who resisted.

The Antiochenes rose and besieged him in his palace until Jewish troops restored his control, burning much of the city. The general Diodotus proclaimed Balas's infant son king as Antiochus VI Dionysus, and many soldiers defected to him. Demetrius lost Apamea and Antioch and held out in Seleucia Pieria. Mithridates I of Parthia had taken advantage of the division to seize Mesopotamia, and in 139 or 138 BCE Demetrius marched east to recover it.

He was at first successful but was defeated in the Iranian mountains and taken prisoner in July or August 138 BCE. Mithridates kept him in Hyrcania, married him to a Parthian princess named Rhodogune and, when Demetrius twice tried to escape, humiliated him on the second occasion with a gift of golden dice. In Syria his younger brother Antiochus VII Sidetes took the throne and married Cleopatra Thea. In 130 BCE Phraates II released Demetrius, hoping to start a civil war between the brothers, and Demetrius regained his throne.

The Seleucid kingdom was by now a shadow of its former self, and Cleopatra Thea detested her returned husband. Around 128 BCE Demetrius led an expedition into Egypt to support Queen Cleopatra II against her brother Ptolemy VIII; ancient sources condemned it as foolish. At Pelusium his own troops mutinied, and Ptolemy VIII sent Alexander II Zabinas to fight him. In 126 BCE Demetrius was defeated in a battle at Damascus.

He fled to Ptolemais, but Cleopatra Thea closed its gates against him, and he was captured and killed on a ship near Tyre, having been denied temple asylum. Alexander II succeeded him, while his widow ruled at Ptolemais in co-regency with two of their sons. Pietro Metastasio's libretto Demetrio, first set by Antonio Caldara in 1731, drew on his story.
demetrius-of-phalerum: Demetrius was born in Phalerum, an ancient port of Athens, around 350 BCE, the son of Phanostratus, a man without rank or property, and the brother of the anti-Macedonian orator Himeraeus. He was educated in the school of Theophrastus together with the poet Menander, and perhaps also studied under Aristotle. He began his public career about 325 BCE, at the time of the disputes concerning Harpalus, and soon gained a reputation for public speaking. He belonged to the pro-oligarchic party of Phocion and acted in that statesman's spirit.

After the death of Phocion in 317 BCE, Cassander, King of Macedon, placed Demetrius at the head of the administration of Athens, an office he held for ten years. He instituted extensive legal reforms, among them a sumptuary law restricting funerary luxury, which is known from a mention in Cicero and is visible in the cemeteries of Athens that archaeologists have recorded. He also had the Homeric and other poems recited on the stage by rhapsodists, as a less costly amusement than tragedy. Lower-class Athenians and pro-democratic factions resented the limits he set on the democratic franchise and saw him as a pro-Macedonian puppet.

Tradition says the Athenians erected 360 statues to him, though Stephen V. Tracy argues that this story is not historical. In 307 BCE Demetrius Poliorcetes, an enemy of Cassander, captured Athens, and Demetrius fled. His enemies had him condemned to death, and all his statues but one were demolished. He went first to Thebes and, after Cassander's death in 297 BCE, to the court of Ptolemy I Soter at Alexandria, where he lived on the best terms with the king and devoted himself mainly to literary work.

Under Ptolemy II Philadelphus, Demetrius fell into disfavour, apparently for supporting the wrong candidate, and was sent into exile in Upper Egypt, where he is said to have died of a snake bite. His writings on history, politics, philosophy and poetry, including a collection of Aesopic fables, have all been lost, and the treatise On Style that bears his name may be by a later writer. According to Strabo, he inspired the creation of the Mouseion, the home of the Library of Alexandria, modelled on Aristotle's school. The Letter of Aristeas says he organised the library under Ptolemy I, though other sources credit Ptolemy II.
demir-kapija: The place was known in Classical times as Stenae, from the Greek word for gorge. On Mount Ramniste, at the foot of the town, stand the ruins of a fortress from the Paeonian era, about 3,000 years old, one of only three known Paeonian structures in Macedonia. The fortress is also said to date from the era of the Macedonian dynasty, around 450 BCE, as a lookout over troop movements to the north.

In the Middle Ages the town was a Slav settlement called Prosek, and in the thirteenth century it was the seat of Dobromir Hriz, with Strez as its well-known commander. The present name comes from the Ottoman Turkish Demir Kapi, meaning iron gate. Remains from the Paeonian, Ancient Macedonian, Roman, Byzantine, early Christian, Ottoman and Samuil periods have been found.

Demir Kapija is a small town and the seat of Demir Kapija Municipality. The Vardar flows through a gorge near it, and a cave called Bela Voda is 955 metres long. The road through the gate leads to the Valandovo and Gevgelija valley, and the town has a railway station on the line from Niš in Serbia to Thessaloniki in Greece.

The gorge is recognised as an Important Bird Area of 10,500 hectares, home to rock partridges and Egyptian vultures among others, and is a national monument of nature. King Aleksandar Karadjordjevic had a summer home and winery built here, and wine is still produced in the area under the Agropin name.
democratic-party-of-albania: The party was founded on 12 December 1990 as an anti-communist movement. Avdyl Matoshi, Azem Hajdari, Sali Berisha and Gramoz Pashko took a major part in its founding. Most of its followers were dissidents who had been persecuted under the communist regime of Enver Hoxha. In the elections of 1991, the first since 1923 to allow more than one party, the ruling Labour Party had the greater advantage, including influence over the media, and the opposition could not reach the countryside. The Democratic Party promised membership of the European Community, strong ties with the United States and a free-market economy. It came second.
