The party won the parliamentary elections of 22 March 1992. Sali Berisha became the second President of Albania, an office that then held executive powers, and Aleksandër Meksi became prime minister. In 1997 the collapse of pyramid investment schemes led to civil unrest, especially in the south, and many investors blamed the government. The Socialist Party, the reformed successor of the Labour Party, won the elections of 29 June 1997. On 12 September 1998 Azem Hajdari was assassinated, and Berisha accused the Socialist government of the killing.

The party lost the elections of 24 June 2001 and alleged irregularities; observers reported irregularities too, though not how far they affected the result. In 2005 it won 56 of the 140 seats, and with its allies held 79, so that Berisha became prime minister. Albania joined NATO in 2009. The party and its alliance won the elections of 28 June 2009. After defeat in 2013 Berisha resigned as leader, and on 23 July 2013 Lulzim Basha won the first leadership vote of all members.

The party is regarded as centre-right, with conservative and conservative-liberal views, and it supports NATO and Albania's accession to the European Union. Its headquarters stand in Tirana, about 50 metres from the parliament. After a third defeat in 2021 the party split between supporters of Basha and of Berisha. On 11 December 2021 Berisha's faction held a national council that voted to remove Basha, who did not recognise the result. In 2024 the Court of Appeal upheld a ruling that recognised the decisions of that council.
democratic-progressive-party: The party's roots lay in the Tangwai movement, which formed in opposition to the Kuomintang's one-party rule during martial law. It was founded as an alternative, but still illegal, party on 28 September 1986 by eighteen organizing members at the Grand Hotel Taipei, with 132 people joining in attendance. Its members contested the 1986 election as nonpartisan candidates, since competing parties remained illegal until the following year. The early members drew heavily on family members and defence lawyers of political prisoners and on intellectuals and artists who had spent time abroad, all committed to democracy and to freedom of speech, press, assembly and association.

At its founding the party held three factions: the Kang group, led by Kang Ning-hsiang, the New Tide faction, led by Wu Nai-ren and Chiou I-jen, and the Progress Faction, led by Lin Cheng-chieh, who opposed independence. In 1991 the party charter came to advocate a new constitution and a Republic of Taiwan by referendum, and many pro-unification members left. In 1999 a party congress resolved that Taiwan was already an independent country under the name Republic of China, and that constitutional changes should be approved by referendum. The pressure the party put on the Kuomintang is credited with the political reforms of the 1990s, notably the direct election of the president and of all members of the National Assembly and Legislative Yuan.

The party won the presidency with Chen Shui-bian in March 2000, with a plurality, ending 91 years of Kuomintang rule in the Republic of China. In 2002 it became the first party other than the Kuomintang to reach a plurality in the Legislative Yuan, though an opposition coalition kept control of the chamber. Chen was narrowly re-elected in 2004. After the party lost the 2008 elections, Tsai Ing-wen became its leader, the first woman to lead a major party in Taiwan. On 16 January 2016 she won the presidency and the party gained a majority of 68 of 113 seats in the Legislative Yuan, its first. Lai Ching-te won the presidency in January 2024.

The National Party Congress selects, for two-year terms, the 30 members of the Central Executive Committee and the 11 members of the Central Review Committee, and the Central Executive Committee chooses the 10 members of the Central Standing Committee. For many years the party officially recognised factions among its members, including the New Tide, Formosa, Justice Alliance and Welfare State Alliance factions, which often reflected the time at which members had entered the party. In 2006 it ended that recognition. The party is a longtime member of Liberal International, and its platform includes democracy, human rights, social welfare and a distinct Taiwanese identity.
democratic-republic-of-the-congo: The Democratic Republic of the Congo covers 2,345,408 km2, the second-largest country in Africa after Algeria, and straddles the Equator, with one-third of its land to the north and two-thirds to the south. The Congo Basin occupies nearly the whole country and holds the Congo rainforest, the second-largest in the world after the Amazon, crossed by the Congo River and tributaries such as the Kasai, Sangha, Ubangi and Aruwimi.

Plateaus merge into savannas in the south and southwest, and the Rwenzori Mountains lie in the far east. The name is taken from the Congo River, which early European sailors named in the 16th century after the Kingdom of Kongo. Mobutu Sese Seko renamed the country Zaire in October 1971.

People lived in the area as early as 90,000 years ago, and the expansion of Bantu peoples brought major change in the first millennium BCE. Organised states emerged, among them early federated states around Pool Malebo, the Kingdom of Kongo, which ruled near the mouth of the Congo River from the 14th to the 19th century, and the Luba and Lunda Empires, which ruled between the 15th and 19th centuries.

King Leopold II of Belgium ruled the Congo Free State as his personal possession until 1908, using forced labour and concessionary companies to extract rubber, and violence, disease and exploitation caused catastrophic population loss. The 1904 Casement Report and diplomatic pressure led to its annexation as the Belgian Congo in 1908. Belgian rule continued direct control, racial segregation and forced labour. The Congolese National Movement under Patrice Lumumba won the elections of May 1960, and Lumumba became prime minister on 24 June 1960.

After the assassination of Lumumba and a series of secessionist movements, Mobutu seized power in 1965 and imposed a personalist dictatorship. His overthrow in 1997 ended the First Congo War, and the Second Congo War of 1998–2003 caused an estimated several million deaths and the assassination of President Laurent-Désiré Kabila.
The country has a population of about 116 million, with French as the official language, Lingala the most widely spoken of over 200 indigenous languages, and over 250 ethnic groups.
democratic-republican-party: The party, known at the time as the Republican Party, originated in Congress to oppose the nationalist and economically interventionist policies of Alexander Hamilton, Secretary of the Treasury under President George Washington. Washington had won the first presidential election of 1788 to 1789 unanimously, at a time when no formal national parties existed. The Republicans and the opposing Federalist Party each became more cohesive during Washington's second term, partly through the debate over the Jay Treaty. Members generally called themselves Republicans and feared that the Federalists, whom they denounced as supporters of monarchy and aristocracy, threatened the principles of republicanism.

Jefferson lost the 1796 presidential election to the Federalist John Adams. The Alien and Sedition Acts, passed under Adams, restricted speech critical of the government, and numerous journalists aligned with the Republicans were prosecuted under the Sedition Act, sparking a backlash. Jefferson and Madison drafted the Kentucky and Virginia Resolutions in response. After the elections of 1800 the transfer of power was peaceful. Jefferson's administration eliminated the whiskey excise, shrank the army and navy, repealed the Alien and Sedition Acts, reduced the national debt and completed the Louisiana Purchase. Madison, who followed him in 1809, led the country through the War of 1812.

After the war Madison and his allies established the Second Bank of the United States and adopted protective tariffs, a move away from the party's earlier emphasis on states' rights and a strict reading of the Constitution. The Federalists collapsed after 1815, beginning the Era of Good Feelings under James Monroe, who tried to end party conflict. The party was strongest in the South and on the western frontier and weakest in New England. It built networks of newspapers in major cities, and its techniques later became standard American practice.

Without an effective opposition the party divided, factions having already formed among moderates, radicals and the Old Republicans, who accused later administrations of betraying republican principles. After the 1824 presidential election it split into rival groups. The coalition built by Andrew Jackson and Martin Van Buren became the Democratic Party. The supporters of John Quincy Adams and Henry Clay formed the National Republican Party, which later became part of the Whig Party. Because the party was diverse and changing, both major parties could claim to stand for Jeffersonian principles. Slavery divided it from the start, though in 1807 Congress outlawed the international slave trade with Jefferson's support.
democritus: Many anecdotes about Democritus survive, but modern scholars doubt their accuracy. According to Aristotle he was born in Abdera on the coast of Thrace, though some called him a Milesian. Apollodorus put his birth in 460 BCE, and Democritus called himself forty years younger than Anaxagoras. His father, Hegesistratus, was said to be wealthy enough to have received Xerxes on his march through Abdera.

Democritus spent his inheritance on travel. He is said to have crossed much of Asia, and he wrote on Babylon and Meroe. Diodorus Siculus states that he lived in Egypt for five years. He also bought the works of Greek philosophers, and Leucippus, founder of atomism, is said to have influenced him most. Nearly eighty treatises are attributed to him, but none of his original work survives, and much of what is known comes from Aristotle.

Early sources credit Leucippus with creating atomism, while later sources credit only Democritus, so their separate contributions are hard to tell apart. Democritus held that the universe was originally nothing but tiny atoms moving in chaos until collisions joined them into larger units. Atoms are too small for the senses, infinite in number and kind, and always moving in the void. Ordinary objects are complexes of atoms, and sensory qualities exist only by convention. The only true realities, he said, are atoms and the void.

In ethics he made peace of mind the aim of action, to be reached through moderation and freedom from fear and passion. His moral advice survives mostly as maxims. In mathematics, Archimedes reports that Democritus had already asserted that a cone is one-third of a cylinder with the same base.

Ancient accounts say that he lived to a very great age, some claiming over a hundred years. He seems to have died in poverty, though his fellow citizens esteemed him and honoured him with money and bronze statues. He was known in antiquity as the laughing philosopher for his emphasis on cheerfulness. His atomic picture partly resembles the 19th-century understanding of atoms, which led some to regard him as more of a scientist than other Greek philosophers.
demosthenes: Demosthenes was born in 384 BCE, the son of a wealthy sword-maker, also named Demosthenes, of the deme of Paeania. His rival Aeschines claimed his mother Kleoboule was Scythian by blood, an allegation some modern scholars dispute. He was orphaned at seven, and his guardians Aphobus, Demophon and Therippides mishandled his inheritance. He began to learn rhetoric because he wished to take them to court and, being of delicate physique, could not take the usual gymnastic education. Plutarch says he overcame a stammering pronunciation by speaking with pebbles in his mouth and practised before a large mirror. At twenty he delivered his first judicial speeches, successfully claiming what remained of his inheritance.

He then made his living as a logographer, writing speeches for use in private suits, and as an advocate, and he stopped advocacy once he entered politics. He first spoke publicly on politics in 354 BCE. In 357 BCE he was among the first volunteer trierarchs, and in 348 BCE he paid for a theatrical production as a choregos. Between 355 and 351 BCE he wrote prosecutions such as Against Androtion and Against Leptines, which show his principles on foreign policy: the importance of the navy, of alliances and of national honour.

Most of his major orations opposed Philip II of Macedon, who had seized Amphipolis and Pydna in 357 BCE. In 352 BCE he called Philip the worst enemy of Athens, and in 351 BCE, in the First Philippic, he told the Athenians that if anything happened to Philip they would soon raise up a second one. After Chaeronea Philip made peace with Athens on lenient terms, and Demosthenes was chosen to deliver the Funeral Oration. When Philip was assassinated in 336 BCE, Demosthenes rejoiced and played a leading part in the uprising of Athens against the new king, Alexander the Great. Alexander moved swiftly to Thebes, which submitted, and when the Athenians begged mercy he admonished them but imposed no punishment.

After his efforts against Macedon failed, the revolt met a harsh reaction. Antipater sent men to track him down, and Demosthenes killed himself to avoid arrest by Archias of Thurii. He was among the Athenian politicians who published their speeches, which survived in Athens and in the Library of Alexandria. Sixty-one orations attributed to him survive, though some are pseudonymous. The Alexandrian Canon listed him among the ten great Attic orators, and Cicero praised him as the perfect orator.
demotic-egyptian-script: Demotic derives from northern forms of hieratic used in the Nile Delta. Egyptians called it document writing, and the 2nd-century scholar Clement of Alexandria called it letter-writing. Early Demotic developed in Lower Egypt during the later part of the Twenty-fifth Dynasty and is found especially on steles from the Serapeum of Saqqara. It is generally dated between 650 and 400 BCE, since most of its texts belong to the Twenty-sixth Dynasty and to the following Achaemenid rule. After the reunification of Egypt under Psamtik I, Demotic replaced Abnormal Hieratic in Upper Egypt, and under Amasis II it became the official administrative and legal script. It is written and read from right to left.

At first Demotic served only administrative, legal and commercial texts, while hieroglyphs and hieratic were kept for religious texts and literature. Middle Demotic, from about 400 to 30 BCE, was the script of the Ptolemaic Kingdom, and from the 4th century BCE it rose in status, as its growing use for literary and religious texts shows. By the end of the 3rd century BCE Koine Greek was the administrative language, and Demotic contracts lost most of their legal force unless they carried a note in Greek of being registered with the authorities. Alphabetic or uniliteral signs make up between a third and a half of all signs in a given text, and foreign words are written almost entirely with them.

Under Roman rule Demotic was used less and less in public life, though literary texts in Late Demotic survive, especially from the 1st and 2nd centuries CE. Greek did not replace Egyptian as the language of everyday speech, but Demotic was afterwards used only for a few ostraca, subscriptions to Greek texts, mummy labels and graffiti. The last dated example is a graffito on the walls of the temple of Isis at Philae, dated 12 December 452, which reads simply Petise, son of Petosiris.

The Rosetta Stone, discovered in 1799, is inscribed with a proclamation in three scripts: hieroglyphs, Demotic and Greek. It has 32 lines of Demotic, the middle script. The Demotic was deciphered before the hieroglyphs, beginning with the efforts of Antoine Isaac Silvestre de Sacy. Early Western scholars, notably Thomas Young, called it Enchorial Egyptian.
denarius: The word denarius comes from the Latin deni, meaning containing ten, because the coin was originally worth 10 asses. A predecessor was first struck in 269 or 268 BCE, a Greek-styled silver coin of didrachm weight made in Neapolis and other Greek cities in southern Italy, inscribed as struck for Rome. The first distinctively Roman silver coin appeared around 226 BCE; modern numismatists call these coins quadrigati, after the four-horse chariot on the reverse. Rome overhauled its coinage shortly before 211 BCE and introduced the denarius alongside a short-lived denomination, the victoriatus. It contained an average of 4.5 grams of silver, one seventy-second of a Roman pound.

The denarius was the standard Roman silver coin from about 211 BCE to the reign of Gordian III (238-244 CE), when it was gradually replaced by the antoninianus, and it formed the backbone of Roman currency throughout the Republic and the early Empire. About 141 BCE it was re-tariffed at 16 asses, reflecting the decreasing weight of the as. One gold aureus equalled 25 silver denarii.

Slow debasement began towards the end of the Republic. Under Augustus its weight fell to 3.9 grams, and under Nero it was reduced to 3.4 grams. After Nero it held about 3.24 grams, and in the late 3rd century later emperors reduced it to 3 grams. Its silver content fell from a purity above 90% in the 1st century CE to under 60% by 200 and to 5% by 300, and by the reign of Gallienus the antoninianus was a copper coin with a thin silver wash. The denarius was last issued, in bronze, under Aurelian between 270 and 275 and in the first years of Diocletian.

A legionary of the Republic earned 112.5 denarii a year, which Julius Caesar doubled to 225, while a common soldier or unskilled labourer of the late Republic and early Empire was paid one denarius a day. The New Testament gospels refer to the denarius as a day's wage for a common labourer, and the coin held up in the Render unto Caesar passage is commonly thought to be a denarius with the head of Tiberius.

Its name outlived the coin. It survives in the Arabic dinar, in the denier of France, in the Italian denaro, Spanish dinero, Portuguese dinheiro and Slovene denar, all meaning money, and in the d for penny in the pounds, shillings and pence used in the United Kingdom until 1971.
denbighshire: Denbighshire borders the Irish Sea to the north, Flintshire to the east, Wrexham to the south-east, Powys to the south, and Gwynedd and Conwy to the west. Its geography is defined by the broad valley of the River Clwyd, surrounded by rolling hills on all sides except the north, where it reaches the coast. The lower valley, the Vale of Clwyd, is given over to crops, while cattle and sheep graze the uplands. The eastern edge follows the ridge of the Clwydian Range, with a high point at Moel Famau (555 metres), which with the upper Dee Valley forms an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty. The Denbigh Moors lie in the west.

The oldest known evidence of habitation in Wales comes from here. The Bontnewydd Palaeolithic site, near St Asaph, has remains of probable Neanderthals about 225,000 years old, with stone tools from the later Middle Pleistocene, and is one of the most significant in Britain. The county also holds several medieval castles, among them Castell Dinas Brân, Denbigh and Rhuddlan, as well as St Asaph Cathedral.

The present county was formed on 1 April 1996 under the Local Government (Wales) Act 1994, from parts of the county of Clwyd. It includes the district of Rhuddlan, formed in 1974 entirely from Flintshire, and most of the Glyndŵr district. Its borders therefore differ from those of the historic county of the same name, and parts of historic Denbighshire lie today in Conwy, Wrexham and Powys.

Denbighshire has an area of 840 square kilometres and a population of about 95,800. Rhyl is the largest town, and Ruthin is the administrative centre. Rhyl and Prestatyn form a single built-up area on the coast, and the other main towns are Denbigh, Ruthin and Rhuddlan; St Asaph is the only city. In the south the only towns are Corwen and Llangollen, where the Llangollen International Musical Eisteddfod takes place each July. The economy rests on agriculture and tourism, the latter beginning with the arrival of the coast railway in the middle of the 19th century, which opened the area to Merseyside and brought a boom in seaside guest houses.
deng-xiaoping: Deng Xiaoping was born on 22 August 1904 in Guang'an, Sichuan, into a landowning peasant family. His given name was Xiansheng, meaning ancient sage, a title of Confucius; his tutor objected and called him Xixian instead. In the 1920s he studied and worked in France as part of the Work–Study Movement, where he was introduced to Marxism–Leninism, and then studied in Moscow. He joined the Chinese Communist Party in 1924 and returned to China in late 1927. In Wuhan he began using the name Xiaoping and first met Mao Zedong.

From 1929 to 1931 Deng was the Central Committee's chief representative in Guangxi, where he helped lead the Baise and Longzhou Uprisings. The Seventh Red Army under his political leadership lost several bloody battles, and he left the army without authorization; he later called it one of the worst mistakes of his life. He was purged in 1933 but rehabilitated at the Zunyi Conference, and took part in the Long March. From January 1938 he was political commissar of the 129th Division of the Eighth Route Army under Liu Bocheng. He attended the proclamation of the People's Republic on 1 October 1949.

In 1952 he came to Beijing as Vice Premier. When Mao launched the Cultural Revolution in 1966, fearing that the economic policies of Deng and Liu Shaoqi could restore capitalism, Deng was forced from all his positions. After Mao's death on 9 September 1976 he was restored to office on 22 July 1977, repudiated the Cultural Revolution, restored the National College Entrance Examination and became China's paramount leader by 1978.

Deng's reform and opening up introduced market incentives, special economic zones and foreign investment, and moved China toward a socialist market economy. He negotiated the handover of Hong Kong and Macau and formulated the principle of one country, two systems. He also ordered the crackdown on the 1989 Tiananmen Square protests, which halted his political reforms and remains a subject of international condemnation. His southern tour in 1992 was crucial to the continuation of economic reform. Deng died on 19 February 1997.
denia: Dénia is a coastal city and municipality in the province of Alicante, Spain, on the Costa Blanca halfway between Alicante and Valencia. It is the capital and judicial seat of the comarca of Marina Alta and the closest Spanish mainland city to Ibiza. There is evidence of human habitation since prehistoric times, with significant Iberian ruins on the hillsides nearby.

In the 4th century BCE the town was a Greek colony of Massalia or Emporion. It allied itself with Rome in the Punic Wars and was absorbed into the Roman Empire as Dianium, after the goddess Diana; in the 1st century BCE Quintus Sertorius set up a Roman naval base there. After the Muslim conquest of Iberia and the dissolution of the Caliphate of Córdoba, Dénia became the capital of a taifa kingdom over part of the Valencian coast and Ibiza. Slavic Muslim slaves, the saqālibah, led by Mujahid ibn Yusuf ibn Ali, gained control of the province and extended the kingdom as far as Mallorca. It lost its independence in 1076, when Ahmad al-Muqtadir of Zaragoza captured it.

The Christians conquered the town in 1244, and it almost emptied after the exile of most of the Muslim population before the Valencian government repopulated it. It became a marquisate in 1487. Francisco Gómez de Sandoval y Rojas, Duke of Lerma, a favourite of Philip III of Spain, won many privileges for it, but the Expulsion of the Moriscos in 1609 made 25,000 people leave the marquisate and left its economy in a dismal state. From 1803 it became an increasingly important trading port.

Dénia is dominated by a large Moorish castle on a rocky crag, built in the 11th and 12th centuries and rebuilt in the early 19th century by the French, who occupied the city for four years during the Peninsular War. The castle holds the Palau del Governador and its museum, and the Museu Etnològic tells more of the city's history. A ferry service links it to Ibiza and the other Balearic Islands. The Fallas festival is held each year from 14 to 19 March.
denis-diderot: Denis Diderot was born in Langres, Champagne, the son of Didier Diderot, a cutler. He studied at a Jesuit college in Langres and received a Master of Arts from the University of Paris in 1732. He abandoned the idea of entering the clergy in 1735 and briefly studied law. When he decided to become a writer and translator his father disowned him, and he lived a bohemian existence for about ten years.

His first original work, the Philosophical Thoughts of 1746, argued for reconciling reason with feeling, and he was then a deist. The Indiscreet Jewels followed in 1748, and the Letter on the Blind of 1749 introduced him as an original thinker. On 23 July 1749 he was arrested and held at the fortress of Vincennes, where he annotated a copy of Paradise Lost with a toothpick for a pen. He moved gradually from deism towards materialism and atheism.

For the newsletter of his friend Friedrich Melchior Grimm he reported on the Paris art Salons from 1759 to 1771 and again in 1775 and 1781. In the theatre he wrote Le Fils naturel (1757) and Le Père de famille (1758) and in 1758 introduced the idea of the fourth wall. Jacques the Fatalist, Rameau's Nephew and D'Alembert's Dream were published only after his death.

The Encyclopédie, begun with Jean le Rond d'Alembert, was suspended by the courts in 1752 and banned by the Church in 1758 and the government in 1759. Diderot wrote about 7,000 articles and damaged his eyesight correcting proofs. In 1766 Catherine the Great bought his library of some 3,000 volumes for 15,000 livres and paid him a salary as its custodian. He reached Saint Petersburg on 9 October 1773 and stayed five months at her court.

Diderot died of pulmonary thrombosis in Paris on 31 July 1784 and was buried in the Église Saint-Roch. His library went to the National Library of Russia. Goethe called Rameau's Nephew the classical work of an outstanding man.
denis-of-portugal: Denis was born in Lisbon on 9 October 1261, the eldest son of Afonso III of Portugal and Beatrice of Castile, an illegitimate daughter of King Afonso X of Castile. The marriage, made around 1253, settled a dispute over the sovereignty of the Algarve, but Afonso was still married to Matilda II of Boulogne, who accused him of bigamy before Pope Alexander IV in 1255. The pope condemned Afonso III for adultery in 1258 and placed him under interdict, and Pope Urban IV legitimised Denis and his siblings in 1263. Denis married Elizabeth of Aragon, who was later canonised, and as heir he shared government with his father.

Denis came to the throne in 1279 and reigned for over 46 years. In 1284 he opened inquiries into the expropriation of royal property, to the church's detriment, and the next year he promulgated amortisation laws that prohibited the church and religious orders from buying land. He also persuaded Pope Nicholas IV in 1288 to separate the Order of Santiago in Portugal from the one in Castile, and in 1289 he signed the Concordat of Forty Articles with the pope. He went to war with Castile in 1295, and the Treaty of Alcañices two years later brought forty years of peace.

He created numerous towns and trade fairs, ordered many castles built, and set up the Bolsa de Comércio, approved on 10 May 1293, the first documented form of marine insurance in Europe. In 1308 he signed the first Portuguese commercial agreement with England, and in 1317 he hired the Genoese sailor Manuel Pessanha as hereditary admiral, effectively founding the Portuguese Navy. He also ordered the pine forest near Leiria planted to protect farmland from advancing coastal sands and to supply timber for ships.

The last years were troubled by rivalry between his legitimate heir Afonso and his illegitimate son Afonso Sanches, which led to civil war in 1322-1324. Queen Elizabeth acted as intermediary, and by legend rode out between the armies at Alvalade in 1323. Denis died at Santarém on 7 January 1325 and was buried at Odivelas.

He wrote lyric poetry in the troubadour tradition, and 137 songs attributed to him survive, including his love songs, the Cantigas de Amigo. Contemporary chronicles describe him as wise and able, though he is also described as sometimes cruel in family relations. The historian Duarte Nunes de Leão first called him father of his country in 1600.
denizli: Denizli lies in Aegean Turkey and is the seat of Denizli Province. It stands near the ruins of Laodicea on the Lycus, the ancient metropolis of Phrygia, and of Hierapolis, with the mineral-coated hillside hot springs of Pamukkale about 20 kilometres to the north. The ruins of Colossae lie near Honaz, about 16 kilometres to the west. The climate is Mediterranean, with hot, dry summers and mild to cool, rainy winters.

The word deniz means sea or large lake, though none lies nearby. The original Turkish name is said to have been Tonguzlu, from a word for wild boar, meaning a place where boars dwell. Sound changes turned it into denizlü and then Denizli, which avoided the association with the pig, considered offensive in Islam. Ibn Battuta recorded the city as Dun Ghuzluh, said to mean the town of the swine.

In antiquity an important Greek town called Attouda stood here, through the Greek and Roman eras and into the Byzantine period, near Hierapolis and Laodicea. Seljuk Turks conquered the city, and inhabitants of Laodicea were resettled here in the Seljuk period.

Ibn Battuta, who visited, noted seven mosques for Friday prayers, splendid gardens, perennial streams and gushing springs. He also noted that most of the artisans were Greek women, because many Greeks lived there subject to the Turks and paid the jizya and other taxes to the sultan. He added that he needed an escort of horsemen on the way, since the surrounding plain was infested by a band of brigands called al-Jarmiyān, a reference to the Germiyanids.

In the 17th century the Ottoman traveller Evliya Çelebi described a square fortress with four gates and some fifty armed watchmen, with the main city outside it in 44 districts and 3,600 houses, 57 mosques, seven madrasahs, six baths and 17 dervish lodges. He wrote that everyone lived in vineyards, so that upper classes and ordinary people did not avoid one another. The city lived in peace for centuries without direct involvement in wars. During the Turkish War of Independence the Greek Army reached Sarayköy, 20 kilometres to the north-west, but did not enter Denizli and was driven from the region by Mustafa Kemal Pasha.

The urban area of Denizli forms parts of the districts of Merkezefendi and Pamukkale and had a population of 691 783 in 2024. Textile production and export have driven its economic development in recent decades. Visitors come to Pamukkale and Hierapolis, which are World Heritage Sites, and to the thermal spas at Karahayıt. Laodicea, founded by the Seleucid king Antiochus II and named after his wife Laodice, was known for its woollen and cotton cloths; it later had one of the seven churches of Asia Minor.
denmark: Metropolitan Denmark occupies 42,957 square kilometres and consists of the northern part of the Jutland peninsula and an archipelago of 406 islands. It lies between the North Sea to the west and the Baltic Sea to the east, and shares a 68-kilometre border with Germany.

Zealand, the largest island, holds the capital, Copenhagen, and some larger islands are linked by bridges, among them a bridge-tunnel across the Øresund to Sweden. The Kingdom of Denmark also includes Greenland and the Faroe Islands, which govern themselves under their own parliaments.

The earliest archaeological finds date to the Eem interglacial period, and Denmark has been inhabited since around 12,500 BCE, with agriculture evident from 3900 BCE. The Nordic Bronze Age, from 1800 to 600 BCE, was marked by burial mounds that yielded lurs and the Sun Chariot.

The first tribal Danes came to the country in the Roman Iron Age, from the east Danish islands and Scania, and spoke an early form of North Germanic; earlier, most of Jutland had been settled by the Jutes. The Danevirke defences were built in phases from the 3rd century, and the scale of the work in 737 CE is attributed to the emergence of a Danish king. Ribe, the oldest town in Denmark, was founded about 700 CE.

The unified Kingdom of Denmark emerged in the eighth century as a maritime power in the struggle for control of the Baltic Sea. It formed the Kalmar Union with Norway and Sweden in 1397, and the union lasted until Sweden's secession in 1523. The remaining Denmark–Norway endured a series of wars in the 17th century that ended in territorial cessions to Sweden. The constitution of 5 June 1849 ended the absolute monarchy. In the Second Schleswig War Denmark lost Schleswig-Holstein, and North Schleswig became Danish again in 1920.

Denmark industrialised from the mid-19th century and became a major agricultural exporter, and social and labour market reforms of the early 20th century formed the basis of the present welfare state. It stayed neutral in the First World War. A German invasion in April 1940 violated its neutrality in the Second World War, a resistance movement emerged in 1943, and the country was liberated in May 1945. Denmark joined what is now the European Union in 1973 but negotiated opt-outs, among them keeping its own currency, the krone. It is a constitutional monarchy with a unicameral parliament, the Folketing, and a population of over 6 million in May 2025.
denpasar: Denpasar is a coastal city in the southern part of Bali, at an elevation of about 4 metres above sea level, and the Badung River divides it before flowing into the Gulf of Benoa. It is bordered by Badung Regency to the west and north, Gianyar Regency to the east, and the Indian Ocean and the Badung Strait to the south. The name comes from the Balinese words dén, north, and pasar, market, and points to the city's origin as a market town on the site of what is now Kumbasari Market.

The city was founded by I Gusti Ngurah Made Pemecutan, a descendant of the Puri Pemecutan of Badung. The name emerged when the Badung region was led by two sub-kingdoms, the Puri Pemecutan and the Puri Jambe Ksatrya. In the 18th and 19th centuries Denpasar was the capital of the Kingdom of Badung, and its earlier name was Badung. The royal palace was looted and razed during the Dutch intervention of 1906. A statue in the central square, Taman Puputan, commemorates the Puputan of 1906, in which as many as a thousand Balinese, including the king and his court, died in front of the invading Dutch troops rather than surrender.

Tuban Airfield, now part of Denpasar International Airport, opened in 1931 and was seized by Japanese forces in 1942. In 1958 Denpasar became the seat of government of the province of Bali. Act No. 1 of 1992, of 15 January 1992, established the City of Denpasar as independent of Badung Regency, and it was inaugurated on 27 February 1992.

Denpasar is the capital and largest city of the province of Bali and the main gateway to the island. Most of its people are Hindu, and the Balinese are the largest ethnic group. Pura Jagatnatha, built in 1953, is its most important Hindu temple, and Pura Maospahit dates from the 14th century and was heavily damaged by the 1917 earthquake. Puri Pemecutan, the former royal palace, was rebuilt in a modest style. The Bali Museum is built in the traditional Balinese style.
deodoro-da-fonseca: Manuel Deodoro da Fonseca was born on 5 August 1827 in Alagoas, the son of Lieutenant Colonel Manuel Mendes da Fonseca and Rosa Maria Paulina da Fonseca. In 1843, aged 16, he entered the Military School of Rio de Janeiro, following seven siblings into military service, and he completed his studies in 1847. Posted to Pernambuco, he took part in suppressing the Praieira revolt of 1848 to 1849 and was commended for bravery. He later served in the Uruguayan War and the Paraguayan War, and became a national figure.

In 1885 Fonseca became vice-president of the province of Rio Grande do Sul, and in 1886 its president. Involvement in the Military Question, the clashes between the armed forces and the imperial government, brought him back to Rio de Janeiro, where he took the lead of the army faction that supported the abolition of slavery. In 1888 he was appointed military commander of Mato Grosso and resigned the next year when the empire's last ministry, under the Viscount of Ouro Preto, was appointed. On 15 November 1889 he led the coup that deposed Pedro II and proclaimed the republic.

As head of the provisional government he ruled largely by decree. The first decree, of 16 November, made federalism the form of government; others legalised civil marriage, separated church and state and widened the electorate to literate males. After a revolt on 18 December, martial law was declared on 23 December, a military tribunal was created to judge civilians accused of subversion and discussion of politics in the press was in effect forbidden.

The finance minister Ruy Barbosa's financial reform began the speculative crisis known as the Encilhamento. A constituent assembly, elected on 15 September 1890, completed the constitution on 24 February 1891, modelled chiefly on that of the United States, and elected Fonseca president.

His government was marked by tension between his centralising tendencies and the federalism of civil society and part of the military. On 3 November 1891 he dissolved the National Congress. Facing the threat of the First Naval Revolt, he resigned on 23 November 1891, and Vice-President Floriano Peixoto succeeded him. He died in Rio de Janeiro on 23 August 1892 and was buried in the Caju Cemetery; in 1937 his remains were moved to a monument in Praça Paris.
departement: The earliest known suggestion of dividing France into departments comes from 1665, when Marc-René d'Argenson proposed areas that would serve only for the administration of bridges and highways. Before the Revolution the country was organised into provinces. The National Constituent Assembly decided in late 1789 to create a more uniform division, and a decree of 22 December 1789 provided for the end of the provincial governments. The modern department system, as all-purpose units of government, was decreed on 26 February 1790. The Abbé Sieyès was particularly identified with the project.

The boundaries were chosen to break up France's historical regions, in an attempt to erase cultural differences and build a more homogeneous nation. They were also set so that every settlement lay within a day's ride of its department's capital, a security measure to keep the whole territory under close control. Most departments took the name of a principal river or other physical feature, and even Paris was in the department of Seine. The provinces continued to exist administratively until 21 September 1791.

There were initially 83 departments, and by 1809 the gains of the Republic and of the First French Empire had raised the number to 130. After Napoleon's defeats the Congress of Vienna returned France to its pre-war size, and the number fell to 86. The acquisition of Nice and Savoy in 1860 brought the total to 89. After the Franco-Prussian War of 1871 Bas-Rhin and parts of other departments were ceded to the German Empire, and the part of Haut-Rhin that stayed French became the Territoire de Belfort, the 90th department in 1922. In 1946 French Guiana, Guadeloupe, Martinique and Réunion became overseas departments.

Each department's seat is a prefecture, generally a town roughly at its centre, chosen so that it could be reached on horseback from any town in the department within 24 hours. The departments are numbered in the alphabetical order of their names, with some alterations, and Seine-Saint-Denis is nicknamed 93. By 1793 the revolutionary government had turned the departments into transmission belts for policies enacted in Paris, a role they kept with few exceptions until the early 1960s. The system has inspired similar divisions in many countries, and the 1833 territorial division of Spain follows the French model. Algeria was divided into departments from 1848 until independence in 1962.
deportation: Deportation is the expulsion of a person or group by a state from its sovereign territory. Its definition varies with place, context and period. Some definitions require transfer beyond the state's borders, which distinguishes it from forcible transfer inside them. Collective expulsion, which compels non-nationals as a group to leave without a reasonable and objective examination of each case, is prohibited by several instruments of international law.

Expulsions are well recorded in antiquity, particularly in Mesopotamia. The kingdoms of Israel and Judah suffered several, among them deportations by the Neo-Assyrian Empire after the fall of Israel and during Sennacherib's campaign in the 8th century BCE. The Neo-Babylonian Empire deported much of the Judean population when it conquered Judah in 597 and 587 BCE. The Achaemenid Empire used deportation against rebellious peoples, with no ill-treatment recorded.

The Sasanians used it widely in their wars with the Romans. Romans defeated at the Battle of Edessa under Shapur I, including the emperor Valerian, were taken to Persis and other regions, and cities such as Bishapur and Gundeshapur were populated by prisoners of war, who were also given farmland. In the Middle Ages the Almoravid state deported Christians from Spain to Morocco in 1109, 1126, 1130 and 1138.

With the Age of Discovery, deporting individuals to overseas colonies became common. From 1717 Britain deported around 40,000 religious objectors and criminals to America until 1776, and then sent more than 160,000 convicts to the Australian colonies between 1787 and 1855. In Russia, the Grand Principality of Moscow developed internal exile, beginning with the transfers that followed its conquest of the Novgorod Republic in the 15th century, and the practice continued as katorga and later the Gulag.

Under Joseph Stalin in the 1930s and 1940s the Soviet Union carried out forced transfers of some 6 million people, with millions of deaths, and many historians have described them as ethnic cleansing, crimes against humanity or genocide. Nazi Germany deported Jews, Poles, Romani and homosexuals to concentration and extermination camps, and during the Holocaust the word deportation was a euphemism that frequently meant the victims were then killed.
der-blaue-reiter: The forerunner of the group was the Neue Künstlervereinigung München (New Artists' Association Munich), co-founded in 1909 on the initiative of Marianne von Werefkin, Alexej von Jawlensky, Adolf Erbslöh and the collector and aviation pioneer Oscar Wittenstein, with Kandinsky as its first chairman. Disputes with its conservative members grew as Kandinsky's painting became more abstract. In December 1911 the jury rejected his Composition V for the association's third exhibition. Kandinsky, Gabriele Münter, Franz Marc and others then formed a rival group and quickly organised a parallel show at the Thannhauser Gallery, in rooms next to the official exhibition.

The name is also the title of a painting by Kandinsky of 1903, but it is unclear whether that is its origin. Kandinsky wrote 20 years later that it came from Marc's enthusiasm for horses, his own love of riders and their shared love of blue, which for him was the colour of spirituality. The artists shared a desire to express spiritual truths. They valued the link between painting and music, the symbolic power of colour and a spontaneous, intuitive approach, and they were interested in medieval art, primitivism and the Cubist, Fauvist and Rayonist ideas of France, which moved them towards abstraction.

The First Exhibition of the Editorial Board of Der Blaue Reiter opened on 18 December 1911 at Heinrich Thannhauser's Moderne Galerie and showed 43 works by 14 artists. A second exhibition of black-and-white works followed from 12 February to 2 April 1912 at Hans Goltz's gallery.

The first show toured Cologne, Berlin, Bremen, Hagen, Frankfurt, Hamburg, Budapest, Oslo, Helsinki, Trondheim and Göteborg until July 1914. The almanac, edited by Kandinsky and Marc and paid for by Bernhard Koehler, appeared in 1912 in an edition of about 1,100 copies, with more than 140 reproductions and 14 major articles. Its pictures included folk art, children's drawings and works from Africa and the South Pacific, with thirteen by child artists but five by Van Gogh, Cézanne and Gauguin.

The group disbanded at the start of the First World War in 1914. Marc and August Macke were killed in combat, Kandinsky returned to Russia, and Werefkin and Jawlensky fled to Switzerland. Its end also ended Munich's role as a centre of the avant-garde. The Nazis denigrated the artists and confiscated, sold or destroyed so-called degenerate art, though the sales made the paintings widely known. In 1923 Kandinsky, Lyonel Feininger, Paul Klee and Jawlensky formed Die Blaue Vier (The Blue Four).
der-spiegel: The first issue of Der Spiegel appeared in Hanover on Saturday, 4 January 1947. The British occupation administration initiated and sponsored it, and it followed a magazine called Diese Woche (This Week), first published in November 1946. The founders were John Seymour Chaloner, a British army officer, and Rudolf Augstein, a former Wehrmacht radio operator. After disagreements with the British, the magazine was handed to Augstein as chief editor and renamed Der Spiegel, meaning The Mirror.

After 1950 the magazine was owned by Augstein and John Jahr. In 1969 Augstein bought out the publisher Gruner + Jahr for DM 42 million and became sole owner, and in 1974 he made employees with more than three years of service associates in management and profits. Since 1952 the magazine has had its own building in the old town of Hamburg. Circulation grew from 15,000 copies in 1947 to 437,000 in 1961, reached about 900,000 in the 1970s and passed one million after German reunification in 1990. Spiegel Online, launched on 25 October 1994, was the world's first online news magazine.

The magazine is known above all for investigative journalism. As early as 1950 the federal parliament opened an inquiry after its accusation that bribed members of parliament had promoted Bonn over Frankfurt as the seat of government. In 1962, after it published a report on the possible low state of readiness of the armed forces, the defence minister Franz Josef Strauss had it investigated. Police raided the editorial offices, and Augstein and other editors were arrested on charges of treason, as was the report's author, Conrad Ahlers, who was seized on holiday in Spain.

When the legal case collapsed, the scandal brought a major shake-up in Chancellor Konrad Adenauer's cabinet, and Strauss had to stand down. The affair was generally received as an attack on press freedom. Der Spiegel later played a leading part in revealing the Flick affair of the 1980s.
derbent: Derbent occupies a strip of land about three kilometres wide in the North Caucasus between the Caspian Sea and the Caucasus Mountains. It connects the Eurasian Steppe to the north with the Iranian Plateau to the south, and its rulers could control land traffic between the steppe and West Asia. The only other practicable crossing of the Caucasus ridge was the Darial Gorge. The name is derived from the Persian Darband, a gate in a barrier. In Arabic texts the city is Bab al-Abwab, the Gate of All Gates, and it is often identified with the Gates of Alexander.

The first intensive settlement dates from the 8th century BCE, and the site was intermittently controlled by Persian monarchs from the 6th century BCE. The Persian name came into use at the end of the 5th or beginning of the 6th century CE, when Kavad I of the Sasanian dynasty re-established the city. Walls 20 metres high with thirty towers are believed to belong to the time of his son Khosrow I, who also directed the building of the fortress. The city became a strong military outpost and harbour of the Sasanian Empire.

Arab Muslims captured Derbent in 643, made it an administrative centre and introduced Islam. Because it lay on the northern branch of the Silk Route, the Khazars contested it. In the 10th century it became the capital of an emirate, still flourishing at the Mongol invasion of 1239, and Timur's armies occupied it in the 14th century. The Shirvanshahs repeatedly tried to conquer it, and Ibrahim I of Shirvan took it in 1437. Under the Treaty of Gulistan of 1813, after the Russo-Persian War, Qajar Iran ceded Derbent and the rest of Dagestan to the Russian Empire.

Derbent is a city in Dagestan, Russia, and the southernmost city of the country. The citadel, ancient city and fortress were classified as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2003. The citadel, Narin-kala, encloses an area of 4.5 hectares, and the walls reaching down to the sea date from the Sasanian period. The city has long had a mixed population, with Persian-speaking, Azeri, Jewish, Armenian and Lezgin communities.
derby: Derby lies in a relatively low-lying area along the lower valley of the River Derwent, where the south-east foothills of the Pennines meet the lowlands and the valley of the River Trent to the south. It is a city and unitary authority area, administratively independent from Derbyshire County Council, and was the original county town of Derbyshire before that status was given to Matlock. County Hall on St Mary's Gate was built in 1660 to host the county's courts and meetings.

The Romans established the town of Derventio, considered to have been at Little Chester, the site of the old Roman fort. The town was later captured by the Anglo-Saxons and then by the Vikings, who made it Djúra-bý, one of the Five Boroughs of the Danelaw. Lady Æthelflæd of Mercia captured it in July 917, and it was annexed to the Kingdom of Mercia. During the Civil War of 1642 to 1646 it was garrisoned by Parliamentary troops under Sir John Gell, who was appointed Governor of Derby in 1643.

In 1717 John Lombe and George Sorocold built in Derby the first water-powered silk mill in Britain, after Lombe had reputedly stolen the secrets of silk-throwing from Piedmont in Italy. The Midland Railway had its headquarters in Derby, with its locomotive and carriage and wagon works, and the railways had a major influence on the town in the Victorian period. Rolls-Royce opened a car and aircraft factory there in 1907. Derby remained a major rail manufacturing centre, second only to Crewe and Wolverton. It has had a cathedral since 1927, but did not gain city status until 1977.

Derby contains the southern part of the Derwent Valley Mills World Heritage Site, and its Silk Mill houses the Museum of Making. Derby Arboretum, given to the town by Joseph Strutt in 1840, was the first planned urban public park in the country. The emblem of the city is the Derby Ram, the subject of a folk song. The painter Joseph Wright of Derby, the astronomer John Flamsteed and the physician Erasmus Darwin are among those born there.
derbyshire: Derbyshire is a ceremonial county of the East Midlands, bordered by Greater Manchester, West Yorkshire, South Yorkshire, Nottinghamshire, Leicestershire, Staffordshire and Cheshire. It covers 2,625 square kilometres, with uplands in the north and centre and lowlands to the south and east. The Peak District National Park covers most of the upland, and Kinder Scout, at 636 metres, is the highest point.

The main rivers are the Derwent and the Dove, which both join the Trent in the south. The Derwent, 106 kilometres long, rises on the moorland of Bleaklow. The Dove rises on Axe Edge Moor and forms the boundary with Staffordshire for most of its length. The older Carboniferous limestones and gritstones lie in the north, the softer Permo-Triassic mudstones and sandstones in the south.

A hand axe found near Hopton suggests that humans visited the area, probably briefly, some 200,000 years ago, and hunter-gatherers lived in limestone caves on the Nottinghamshire border between about 12,000 and 7,000 BCE. Neolithic settlers left chambered tombs for collective burial, mostly in central Derbyshire; those at Minninglow and Five Wells date to between 2500 and 2000 BCE. The henge monument of Arbor Low has been dated to 2500 BCE. Clear signs of agriculture and settlement appear only in the Bronze Age, with field clearance and hut circles on the Peak District moors and a settlement at Swarkestone.

The county's shape has shifted with local government reorganisation. Several Sheffield suburbs, among them Totley, Dore and Mosborough, were Derbyshire's until they passed to Sheffield between 1900 and 1933, and Mosborough in 1967. In 1974 Derbyshire gained part of the Longdendale valley and Tintwistle from Cheshire.

Derbyshire has about a million inhabitants, and Derby is the largest settlement, followed by Chesterfield. The county council sits at Matlock. The county is rich in lead, iron, coal and limestone; limestone quarrying, which supplied lime for building and steelmaking and later cement, remains a major industry. Three reservoirs in the north, Howden, Derwent and Ladybower, were built early in the 20th century to supply Sheffield, Derby and Leicester. Visitors come to Chatsworth House, Hardwick Hall, Haddon Hall, Bolsover Castle and the towns of Buxton, Bakewell and Matlock Bath.
derek-walcott: Derek Alton Walcott was born on 23 January 1930 in Castries, Saint Lucia, with a twin brother, the playwright Roderick Walcott. His family was of English, Dutch and African descent. His father, a civil servant and talented painter, died when the twins were one year old, and his mother, a teacher, often recited poetry at home. The family belonged to a minority Methodist community, overshadowed by the island's Catholic culture dating from French colonial rule.

As a young man he trained as a painter under Harold Simmons. At 14 he published his first poem in The Voice of St Lucia, and by 19 he had published 25 Poems (1948) and Epitaph for the Young (1949), printed with money from his mother. He then studied at the University College of the West Indies in Kingston, Jamaica.

Walcott moved to Trinidad in 1953 and in 1959 founded the Trinidad Theatre Workshop. His collection In a Green Night (1962) won international attention, and his play Dream on Monkey Mountain won an Obie Award in 1971. In 1972 he was appointed an Officer of the Order of the British Empire. He taught at Boston University for more than two decades, founding the Boston Playwrights' Theatre there in 1981, and retired in 2007.

He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1992, the second Caribbean writer to do so after Saint-John Perse. The Nobel committee described his work as a poetic oeuvre of great luminosity, sustained by a historical vision. In 2016 he was made one of the first knights of the Order of Saint Lucia.

Walcott wrote more than twenty plays, many concerned with the uncertain status of the West Indies after colonial rule. In his 1970 essay What the Twilight Says he described the region as a colonised space with few truly indigenous forms. He held that artists after colonialism and slavery had both freedom and the challenge to begin again. Methodism shaped his work from the start; he said he never separated poetry from prayer.

His epic poem Omeros (1990) loosely echoes Homer's Iliad. Its characters include the island fishermen Achille and Hector and the housemaid Helen, and it explores the beauty of the islands and the colonial burden. Many critics regard it as his major achievement. Walcott died at home in Saint Lucia on 17 March 2017, aged 87.
derg: The Derg, Amharic for committee or council, was officially the Provisional Military Administrative Council. It was a military junta that ruled Ethiopia, then including present-day Eritrea, from 1974 to 1987, when its members formally civilianised the administration, though they stayed in power until 1991. It arose after mutinies early in 1974, beginning with soldiers of the 4th Brigade at Nagelle, who were unhappy about the lack of food and water, and spread to the air force and the army's Second Division. The Derg was announced as the Coordinating Committee of the Armed Forces, Police and Territorial Army by junior and mid-level officers and police.

Each of 40 units was to send three representatives, none above the rank of major, since senior officers were deemed too compromised by their association with the regime. The Derg first assembled at the Fourth Division headquarters and elected Major Mengistu Haile Mariam as chairman. No new members were ever admitted.

In July 1974 the Derg obtained from Emperor Haile Selassie the power to arrest government officials at every level, and it imprisoned two former prime ministers and most of their cabinets. On 12 September 1974 it deposed and imprisoned the emperor, and on 15 September it renamed itself the Provisional Military Administrative Council. On 23 November it killed its chairman, General Aman Andom, with 60 officials of the former government. The monarchy was formally abolished in March 1975, and Haile Selassie died in August in mysterious circumstances.

On 4 March 1975 the Derg announced a land reform under the slogan Land to the Tiller, which nationalised all rural land, and it nationalised most industries. From 1976 to 1978 it conducted the Red Terror against separatists and rival Marxist-Leninist groups. Mengistu emerged as leader in 1977. Ethiopia became the Soviet bloc's closest ally in Africa. In 1987 Mengistu dissolved the Derg and established the People's Democratic Republic of Ethiopia under a Workers' Party.

The Derg's rule coincided with the famine of 1983 to 1985, in which around 1.2 million people died, mostly in the north. It also disestablished the Ethiopian Orthodox Church in 1974 and declared a policy of state atheism. In January 1991 the Ethiopian People's Revolutionary Democratic Front captured Gondar, Bahir Dar and Dessie, and on 21 May Mengistu left for Kenya and then Zimbabwe. The regime fell later that month.
derry: Derry lies on both banks of the River Foyle, close to the border with County Donegal, with which it has had a close link for many centuries. The original walled city stands on a hill on the west bank, where the river once branched and enclosed the hill as an island. Over the centuries the western branch dried up and became the low-lying district now called the Bogside. The name is an anglicisation of the Irish Daire or Doire, meaning oak-grove, and derives from the earliest reference, Daire Calgaich, the oak-grove of Calgach.

Saint Colmcille, a holy man from Tír Chonaill, the old name for almost all of modern County Donegal, is traditionally seen as the founder of the original settlement. Until 1610 the west bank belonged to Donegal. In that year the Crown transferred it to The Honourable The Irish Society and combined it with County Coleraine, part of County Antrim and a large part of County Tyrone to form County Londonderry. Planters organised by the London livery companies rebuilt the town with high walls against Irish insurgents who opposed the plantation, and in 1613 it was renamed Londonderry.

In 1649 the garrison, which supported the Parliament in London, was besieged by Scottish Presbyterian forces loyal to Charles I. It was relieved by an unlikely alliance of Roundhead troops under George Monck and the Irish Catholic general Owen Roe O'Neill. The city was rebuilt in the 18th century, many Georgian houses survive, and its first bridge over the Foyle was built in 1790. In the 18th and 19th centuries the port was an important point of embarkation for Irish emigrants to North America, and shirt-making, begun in 1831, became the main industry.

Derry is a cathedral city of 85,279 people at the 2021 census, the second largest in Northern Ireland after Belfast. It is the only city in Ireland whose walls survive completely intact, and they are the largest monument in state care in Northern Ireland. Its landmarks include St Columb's Cathedral, the first post-Reformation cathedral built for an Anglican church. In the late 1960s the city became a focal point of the civil rights movement in Northern Ireland, and the Troubles are widely regarded as having begun there with the Battle of the Bogside.
desi-bouterse: Desiré Delano Bouterse was born on 13 October 1945 in Domburg, in Suriname's Wanica District, into a multiracial family of Amerindian, African, Dutch, French and Chinese ancestry. He was raised in Paramaribo by an aunt. In 1968 he moved to the Netherlands, was conscripted into the Dutch armed forces and trained as a non-commissioned officer at the Koninklijke Militaire School in Weert. On 11 November 1975 he returned to Suriname, which had become independent from the Netherlands, wanting to help build its army, and in 1979 he became chairman of a new military workers' union, Bomika.

On 25 February 1980 Bouterse, Roy Horb and fourteen other sergeants, known as the Group of Sixteen, overthrew the government of Henck Arron in the Sergeants Coup. Bouterse became chairman of the National Military Council and the de facto ruler, and until 1988 he held power behind presidents he had installed. The population widely supported the takeover, which was officially aimed at corruption and unemployment. The regime imposed a curfew, censored the press and in 1985 banned political parties.

On 7 and 8 December 1982 fifteen prominent men who had criticised the dictatorship, among them lawyers, journalists and a union leader, were taken to Fort Zeelandia, then Bouterse's headquarters, where they were tortured and shot dead. These are the December murders. Bouterse accepted political responsibility as leader but denied direct involvement. He is also suspected of directing the Moiwana massacre of 1986 against a Maroon village in the Surinamese Interior War, fought against the Jungle Commando, led by his former bodyguard Ronnie Brunswijk. In 1999 a Dutch court sentenced him in absentia to eleven years for trafficking cocaine, which he always denied.

Bouterse founded the National Democratic Party in 1987. He led the country again from 1990 to 1991 and served as the eighth president of Suriname from 2010 to 2020. A trial for the December murders began in 2007, and in 2012 the National Assembly passed an amnesty act for him. The trial was forced to continue, and he was sentenced to twenty years in prison for the murders. He refused to report to prison and was a fugitive until his death on 23 December 2024. Some hold him responsible for human rights violations during his rule in the 1980s.
desiderius: Desiderius, also called Daufer, was born in Brescia around 720. He was a royal officer, the duke of Tuscia, and became king of the Lombards on the death of Aistulf in 756. Aistulf's predecessor Ratchis left his monastic retreat at Montecassino and tried to seize the kingdom, but Desiderius quickly put the revolt down with the support of Pope Stephen II. At his coronation he promised to restore many lost papal towns to the Holy See and even to enlarge the Papal State.

From 757 Desiderius suppressed resistance in the duchies of Spoleto and Benevento. When Liutprand, Duke of Benevento, challenged him and threatened to place himself under the protection of Pepin the Short, Desiderius obtained naval help from Byzantium, ended the revolt and gave the duchy to Liutprand's son Arechis. He also deposed Alboin of Spoleto and exercised the ducal powers there himself. In August 759 he made his son Adelchis associate king. Like his predecessors he pursued an expansionist policy against the papacy, and in 760 he did not follow through on a promise to Pepin's envoys to return captured cities.

After the death of Pope Paul I in 767, Desiderius seized a priest named Philip from the monastery of St Vitus on the Esquiline Hill in Rome on 31 July 768 and appointed him pope. Philip was not recognised and left the same day to return to his monastery. Charlemagne married Desiderius's daughter Desiderata in 770 and repudiated her in 771. In 773 Pope Hadrian I broke openly with the king and, when Desiderius moved against the papal cities, appealed to Charlemagne; because the Lombards had blocked the passage through the Alps, his embassy went by sea.

In the spring of 773 Charlemagne sent two Frankish armies against the Lombards. After an eight-month siege he captured Pavia and Desiderius himself, whom he exiled to the abbey of Corbie. Charlemagne took the further title rex Langobardorum, the first time a Germanic king adopted the title of a kingdom he had conquered, though he let the Lombards keep their laws. Desiderius was the last Lombard king and died around 786. In Brescia he founded the church of San Salvatore, which still stands as a monument of Lombard architecture. In his tragedy Adelchi, written in 1822, Alessandro Manzoni portrays him as a vain ruler who destroys his kingdom through ambition.
desmond-tutu: Desmond Mpilo Tutu was born on 7 October 1931 in Klerksdorp, Transvaal, to a Motswana mother and a father from the amaFengu branch of the Xhosa. His father was principal of a Methodist primary school. His parents could not afford medical school, and he trained as a teacher at Pretoria Bantu Normal College from 1951. After the Bantu Education Act of 1953 he and his wife left teaching. With Huddleston's support he chose to become an Anglican priest and entered St Peter's Theological College in Rosettenville, Johannesburg.

Tutu was ordained in 1961 and studied theology at King's College London from 1962. After returning in 1966 he taught at the Federal Theological Seminary in Alice, where he was the first black member of staff, and then directed the Theological Education Fund for Africa from 1972. In 1975 he became the first black dean of St Mary's Cathedral, Johannesburg, living in Soweto rather than the dean's residence in a white suburb, and then Bishop of Lesotho. From 1978 to 1985 he was general secretary of the South African Council of Churches.

He was the first black Bishop of Johannesburg, enthroned in February 1985, and called on the international community in his inaugural sermon to introduce economic sanctions unless apartheid was dismantled within 18 to 24 months.

In September 1986 he was enthroned as Archbishop of Cape Town, again the first black man in the post. After the 1994 election Nelson Mandela chose him to chair the Truth and Reconciliation Commission, and he retired as archbishop in 1996. Mandela awarded him the Order for Meritorious Service at a farewell ceremony in June 1996. He stressed non-violent protest and foreign economic pressure as ways to bring about universal suffrage, while warning the government that anger at apartheid would lead to racial violence. He was diagnosed with prostate cancer in January 1997.

Tutu died on 26 December 2021. Theologically he sought to fuse ideas from black theology with African theology. He was popular among South Africa's black majority and internationally praised for his activism, but many white South Africans considered him too radical, some anti-apartheid activists thought him too moderate, and Jewish groups accused him of making antisemitic statements. After apartheid he campaigned for gay rights and spoke on a wide range of subjects, and he retired from public life in 2010.
despotate-of-the-morea: The Despotate of the Morea, also called the Despotate of Mystras, was made out of territory taken from the Frankish Principality of Achaea. That principality had been organised from former Byzantine land after the Fourth Crusade of 1204. Its ruler William II Villehardouin lost the Battle of Pelagonia to the Byzantine Emperor Michael VIII Palaeologus and had to ransom himself by giving up most of the eastern Morea and his newly built strongholds.

This territory became the nucleus of the despotate. The Morea was the name of the Peloponnese in the medieval and early modern periods, and the territory was usually ruled by one or more sons or brothers of the reigning emperor, who held the title of despotes.

In 1349 the emperor John VI Kantakouzenos reorganised the territory as an appanage for his son, the despot Manuel Kantakouzenos, who for most of his rule kept peace with his Latin neighbours and secured a long period of prosperity. After Manuel's death in 1380 the rival Palaiologos dynasty took the Morea, and Theodore I Palaiologos became despot in 1383.

He ruled until 1407, recognised the suzerainty of the Ottoman Empire, and invited Albanians to settle, who developed into the Arvanite community. Later despots were sons of Manuel II Palaiologos: Theodore II, Constantine, Demetrios and Thomas. In 1430 the despotate expanded to the whole peninsula through dowry settlements and Constantine's conquest of Patras. Its capital, the fortified city of Mystras near ancient Sparta, became an important centre of the Palaiologan Renaissance.

In 1446 Sultan Murad II destroyed the Hexamilion wall at the Isthmus of Corinth. The despots Demetrios and Thomas Palaiologos, brothers of the last emperor, sent no aid when Mehmed II captured Constantinople in 1453. Their rule was unpopular and provoked an Albanian-Greek revolt, in which they invited Ottoman troops to help them. After they failed to pay their annual tribute, Mehmed came into the Morea in May 1460. Demetrios became a prisoner and Thomas fled, and by the end of the summer virtually all the cities held by the Greeks had submitted.

A few places held out. Monemvasia obtained Thomas's consent to place itself under the Pope's protection, the Mani Peninsula resisted under a coalition of local clans and later came under Venetian rule, and Graitzas Palaiologos held Salmeniko Castle until July 1461, when he and his garrison escaped to Venetian territory. This ended the last of the Byzantine Empire proper. After 1461 the only non-Ottoman territories in the Morea were Venetian: Modon, Koroni, Argos and Nafplion. Thomas Palaiologos and his son Andreas kept the title of despot in exile.
dessau: Dessau lies on a floodplain where the Mulde flows into the Elbe, and the setting brings yearly floods; the worst, in 2002, nearly covered the Waldersee district. The town is surrounded by numerous parks and palaces, which make it one of the greenest towns in Germany. Its railway from Berlin opened on 1 September 1840, and the Dessau-Bitterfeld line, opened on 17 August 1857 and electrified in 1911, was the first fully electrified long-distance railway in Germany.

Dessau was first mentioned in 1213. It became an important centre in 1570, when the Principality of Anhalt was founded with Dessau as the capital of a state within the Holy Roman Empire. In 1603 that state was split into four, later five, Anhalts, and Dessau became the capital of the small state of Anhalt-Dessau. Two of the noble lines died out in 1863, and the Duchy of Anhalt was united again. From 1918 to 1945 Dessau was the capital of the Free State of Anhalt.

The Bauhaus school moved to Dessau in 1925 after it was forced to close in Weimar, and Walter Gropius, Paul Klee and Wassily Kandinsky were among its lecturers there. The Nazis' control of the city council forced the closure of the Dessau Bauhaus in 1932. Allied air raids on 7 March 1945 almost completely destroyed the town, six weeks before American troops occupied it. It was rebuilt in concrete-slab architecture and became a major industrial centre of East Germany. In 2007 Dessau became part of the municipality of Dessau-Roßlau.

Dessau is a district of the independent city of Dessau-Roßlau in Saxony-Anhalt, and until 1 July 2007 it was an independent city. Several Bauhaus buildings form part of the World Heritage Site Bauhaus and its Sites in Weimar, Dessau and Bernau, among them Gropius's school building. Others include the Dessau-Törten Estate of 1926–1928. The Garden Kingdom of Dessau-Wörlitz, an 18th-century landscape garden in the English style, is also a World Heritage Site. The composer Kurt Weill was born in Dessau, as was the philosopher Moses Mendelssohn in 1729.
dessau-worlitz-garden-realm: The gardens have their roots in the seventeenth century, when Prince John George II of Anhalt-Dessau married the Dutch princess Henriette Catharina of Orange in 1659. She brought engineers and architects from the Low Countries, who laid out a town, a palace and a Baroque garden at Oranienbaum, and Dutch influence remained strong for decades.

Leopold III became Duke of Anhalt-Dessau in 1758. Five years later he and his friend the architect Friedrich Wilhelm von Erdmannsdorff made a Grand Tour of Europe. The ancient architecture of Italy, the English landscape gardens, among them Stourhead, and the ideals of the Enlightenment shaped their taste. Leopold began changing the countryside in 1765, and over the next forty years he adapted several parks and palaces, including Oranienbaum, Georgium, Mosigkau and Großkühnau.

Wörlitzer Park was laid out between 1769 and 1773 beside an anabranch of the Elbe. Leopold meant it to serve also as a school of architecture, gardening and agriculture, so large parts were open to the public from the start. Erdmannsdorff designed most of the buildings and Johann Friedrich Eyserbeck laid out the gardens. Wörlitz Palace, finished in 1773, was the first Neoclassical building in present-day Germany. The synagogue of 1790, a rotunda modelled on the Temple of Vesta at Tivoli, expressed Leopold's religious tolerance. The park also has an artificial volcano on an island, inspired by Leopold's visit to Naples and Vesuvius, and the Gothic House begun in 1774, modelled on Horace Walpole's villa at Strawberry Hill.

Other parts have their own character. Oranienbaum was rebuilt in a Chinese style in 1780, with a pagoda and a tea house. Luisium, built from 1774 to 1778, was a gift to Leopold's wife Louise, and Leopold died there on 9 August 1817 after a riding accident. Mosigkau, built from 1752 to 1757, is a Rococo palace that holds Flemish Baroque paintings.

The cultural landscape covers 142 square kilometres within the Middle Elbe Biosphere Reserve in Saxony-Anhalt. UNESCO designated it a World Heritage Site in 2000 for its landscape design and its witness to the ideals of the Enlightenment. The grounds were divided into four parts by a railway line and the A9 motorway. The Kulturstiftung Dessau-Wörlitz, which runs the park, has its seat in Großkühnau Castle.
desteapta-te-romane: The original text was written in the Romanian Cyrillic alphabet. The melody was originally a sentimental song called Din sânul maicii mele, composed by Anton Pann after hearing the poem. In 1848 Andrei Mureșanu wrote the poem Un răsunet and asked Gheorghe Ucenescu, a singer of the Șcheii Brașovului church, to find him a suitable melody. After Ucenescu sang him several lay melodies, Mureșanu chose Pann's song instead. It was first sung on the streets of the Șcheii Brașovului neighbourhood in Brașov in late June 1848, and it at once became the revolutionary anthem.

The song was sung in all the major Romanian conflicts that followed. It was heard at Romania's declaration of independence from the Ottoman Empire during the Russo-Turkish War of 1877 to 1878 and during the First World War, and it was broadcast heavily after the coup of 23 August 1944, when Romania turned against Nazi Germany and joined the Allies. It was also used on solemn occasions in the Moldavian Democratic Republic between 1917 and 1918, and it was the anthem of Moldova from 1991 to 1994, until Limba noastră replaced it.

After the Communist Party abolished the monarchy on 30 December 1947, this and other patriotic songs closely associated with the previous regime were outlawed. Nicolae Ceaușescu's government permitted the song to be played and sung in public but never gave it state recognition as the anthem of the Socialist Republic of Romania. Romania adopted it officially as the national anthem on 24 January 1990, after the revolution of December 1989, replacing the communist-era anthem Trei culori.

Its message is a call to action, a now-or-never urge for change like that of many anthems, which is why Nicolae Bălcescu called it the Romanian Marseillaise. The anthem has eleven stanzas, of which only the first, second, fourth and last are sung on official occasions under Romanian law, while the full version is sung on the National Holiday on 1 December. Short versions, as at sporting events, use only the first stanza and the first half of the second. National Anthem Day, on 29 July, is an annual observance in Romania.
detmold: Detmold is a city in North Rhine-Westphalia and today the administrative centre of the district of Lippe and of the Regierungsbezirk Detmold. About 5 kilometres to its south-west lies the Grotenburg hill, with a prehistoric circular rampart and the Hermann monument. The monument commemorates the Battle of the Teutoburg Forest of 9 CE, in which Germanic tribes led by Hermann, in Latin Arminius, defeated Roman legions under Publius Quinctilius Varus, though the battle may or may not have been fought near the present town.

Detmold was first mentioned as Theotmalli in 783, the year of a battle between the Saxons and Charlemagne's forces nearby, during the Saxon Wars. In 1263 Bernard III of Lippe fortified the settlement at the crossing of the trade route from Paderborn to Lemgo over the Werre with stone walls and gave it a municipal charter. Market rights granted in 1265 led to rapid economic growth. Its population was reported as 305 in 1305. Its defences were strengthened after severe damage in the conflict with Soest in 1447, and a fire in 1547 destroyed more than 70 houses.

In 1550 Detmold became the permanent residence of Count Simon III of Lippe. The counts became princes in 1789, and the town remained capital of the small Principality of Lippe until 1918, when all princely states in Germany were abolished. From 1919 to 1947 it was the capital of the Free State of Lippe. When Lippe was incorporated into the new state of North Rhine-Westphalia, the town became the seat of the Lippe district.

Street lighting with oil lanterns was introduced in 1809. By 1835 Detmold was the most populous town in Lippe, with over 4,000 residents, and it grew to 12,000 in 1900 and over 30,000 in 1950. In the administrative reform of 1970, 25 nearby villages were incorporated.

The Renaissance castle stands in the town park. Other sights include the Externsteine, the Hermannsdenkmal, the Lippisches Landesmuseum and the Detmold open-air museum. The city is known for its Music Academy and the Landestheater Detmold, and the Church of Lippe has its central administration there. Johannes Brahms lived in Detmold in the winters of 1857–60. The population is 74,438.
detroit: Detroit takes its name from the French word détroit, meaning strait, because the city stands on a narrow north–south passage of water linking Lake St. Clair with Lake Erie; the French called the river le détroit du Lac Érié.
