The basin was inhabited by Paleo-Indian hunter-gatherers as early as 11,000 years ago, followed by Woodland mound-building societies, and at European contact it was a borderland of Iroquoian and Anishinaabe nations. In the Ojibwe language the area is called Waawiiyaataanong, meaning where the river bends.

The first Europeans to explore the river were a French expedition led by Adrien Joliet in 1669, and in 1679 René-Robert Cavelier, Sieur de La Salle sailed Le Griffon into it. Antoine de la Mothe Cadillac and Alphonse de Tonty founded the fort in 1701. After the British took the settlement, Chief Pontiac failed to seize it in 1763, and the Royal Proclamation of 1763 set a buffer zone restricting European settlement south of the Great Lakes and west of the Appalachian Mountains.

The Great Fire of 1805 destroyed nearly all of the colonial buildings. The town was incorporated as a city in 1806, but the incorporation was repealed three years later, and it was reincorporated in 1815. During the War of 1812 it was captured at the Siege of Detroit and occupied by the British until 1813. After Michigan joined the Union in 1837, Detroit served as its first capital.

In 1913 Henry Ford's moving assembly line cut chassis assembly time by nearly 90 percent, and by 1920 the city's automakers were producing a million cars a year, roughly half of world production. The United Auto Workers was founded in Detroit in 1935. Decline began in the 1950s with industrial deconcentration and suburbanisation, and the population fell from a peak of 1.85 million in 1950 by more than 65 percent. In 2013 the city filed for bankruptcy, and it exited in 2014.

Detroit is the most populous city in Michigan and the seat of Wayne County, with 639,111 inhabitants at the 2020 census. It faces the Canadian city of Windsor across the river, and the Ambassador Bridge and the Detroit–Windsor tunnel connect them. General Motors, Ford and Chrysler, the three large car makers, are headquartered in the metropolitan area. The city gave rise to the music of Motown and techno, and its Art Deco buildings include the Guardian Building, the Penobscot Building and the Fisher Building. UNESCO named it a City of Design in 2015.
deutsche-mark: A mark had been the currency of Germany since 1873, when the gold-based Goldmark was introduced. It left the gold standard with the First World War, became the Papiermark through hyperinflation, and was replaced by the Rentenmark from 15 November 1923 and the Reichsmark in 1924. After the Second World War the occupying powers could not agree on a currency reform, and each printed its own occupation currency.

The Deutsche Mark was introduced on Sunday 20 June 1948 by Ludwig Erhard. Eleven experts managed by Edward A. Tenenbaum devised the reform, and Tenenbaum created the name, at first a temporary one. Each person received an allowance of DM 60. The reform replaced the old money at one new mark to ten old and wiped out 90 per cent of government and private debt as well as private savings.

One Deutsche Mark was divided into 100 pfennigs. The Bank deutscher Länder took responsibility for it in 1948 and the Deutsche Bundesbank in 1957. From 1950 the coins carried the inscription Bundesrepublik Deutschland, and a mint mark showed where each was struck. On 9 July 1959 it replaced the Saar franc in the Saarland. Four series of banknotes were issued; the fourth, introduced in 1990 against advances in forgery, showed German artists and scientists, chosen in equal numbers of men and women, and added a DM 200 note.

The currency was meant to protect western Germany from a second wave of hyperinflation and to stop barter and black-market trade. Although at first distributed only in the three western zones, it angered the Soviet authorities, who cut all road, rail and canal links between those zones and West Berlin, beginning the Berlin Blockade. The United States and Britain launched an airlift and distributed the new currency in West Berlin as well.

The mark earned a reputation as a strong store of value and became a source of national pride during the Wirtschaftswunder of the 1950s, although over its 53 years its purchasing power fell by more than 70 per cent. It was introduced in East Germany in July 1990, East German marks being exchanged at 1:1 for the first M 4,000 and 2:1 for larger amounts. The Council of the European Union fixed its irrevocable rate at DM 1.95583 to the euro, effective 1 January 1999.
deutschlandlied: The poem was written in 1841 by August Heinrich Hoffmann von Fallersleben while on holiday on Heligoland, then a British possession, and was first published with Haydn's music. Its setting was the German Confederation of 1815-1866, a federation of 35 monarchical states and four free cities, which the larger powers used to oppress liberal and national movements. Under Metternich's censorship, demands for a united Germany usually went with demands for freedom of the press.

The year after writing it Hoffmann lost his post as librarian and professor in Breslau because of this and other revolutionary works, and had to go into hiding until he was pardoned after the revolutions of 1848.

The first line, Deutschland, Deutschland über alles, was an appeal to the German monarchs to give a united Germany a higher priority than the independence of their small states. Later, especially in Nazi Germany, the words came to be heard as expressing German superiority over other countries. The first stanza names the Meuse, the Adige, the Neman and the Little Belt, though the song was not meant to mark the borders of a nation-state.

The second stanza toasts German women, loyalty, wine and song. In the third, the call for Einigkeit und Recht und Freiheit, unity and justice and freedom, expresses a wish for a united Germany ruled by law rather than by arbitrary monarchy.

The song became one of the most widely known patriotic songs of the German Empire, and was said to have been sung by student regiments at Langemarck in 1914. President Friedrich Ebert made it the official national anthem on 11 August 1922. During the Nazi era the first stanza was sung, followed by the Horst-Wessel-Lied.

In 1952 Chancellor Konrad Adenauer and President Theodor Heuss agreed that only the third stanza should be sung on official occasions, and in November 1991 President Richard von Weizsäcker and Chancellor Helmut Kohl declared it alone to be the anthem of reunified Germany. Singing the first stanza is now considered taboo, though it is not illegal.
devanagari: Devanagari belongs to the Brahmic family of scripts of India, Nepal, Tibet and Southeast Asia. It descends from the Brahmi script of the third century BCE, which evolved into the Nagari script, which in turn gave rise to Devanagari and Nandinagari. The name combines deva with nagari, an adjective from the Sanskrit nagara, 'town' or 'city', meaning 'urban'; the meaning of the prefix deva, 'heavenly' or 'god', remains unclear. The word Nagari for a script of northern India is attested by Al-Biruni in the eleventh century, while the form Devanagari is attested by the eighteenth century at the latest.

Nagari was in regular use by the seventh century CE and was fully developed by about the end of the first millennium. Evidence of its spread includes the mid-eighth-century Pattadakal pillar in Karnataka, which carries both Siddha Matrika script and an early Telugu-Kannada script, and the Kangra Jawalamukhi inscription in Himachal Pradesh, written in both Sharada and Devanagari. The eleventh-century Udayagiri inscriptions in Madhya Pradesh and an inscribed brick of 1217 now in the British Museum attest Sanskrit in Nagari script.

Devanagari is a left-to-right abugida with 48 primary characters, 14 vowels and 34 consonants. It has no letter case. It favours symmetrical, rounded shapes within squared outlines and is recognised by the horizontal line, the shirorekha, along the top of full letters. Its orthography reflects pronunciation, and its letters follow a phonetic order based on the manner and place of articulation, called the varnamala, 'garland of letters'.

Successive consonants without a vowel between them may join as conjuncts. Many consonants that have a vertical stroke lose it in such clusters, so that t-va is written tva. The virama marks the absence of a vowel. A subscript dot, the nukta, adds sounds from Persian, Arabic and English to Hindi, and further signs serve Marathi, Kashmiri and Sindhi. A single vertical bar, the danda, ends a sentence or half-verse and a double bar a full verse.

Devanagari has been used for over 120 languages, the most widespread being Hindi, and is one of the official scripts of India and Nepal. Marathi, Sanskrit, Pali, Nepali, Konkani, Maithili and Santali are among the languages that use it as a primary or secondary script. Religiously educated people in South Asia long used it to record and pass on information, alongside local scripts such as Modi, Kaithi and Mahajani that served administration and commerce.

Several methods romanise it. IAST is the academic standard for Sanskrit and the de facto standard of printed publications, while the Hunterian system is the national system of India. The Unicode Standard defines four blocks for it, and InScript is the keyboard layout standardised by the Government of India.
deventer: Deventer lies in the historical region of Salland, largely on the east bank of the River IJssel, with a small part on the west bank. The settlement was founded on a river dune, and the river, with the trade it carried, has shaped the city's history. The IJssel has also often overflowed its banks. From 1241 the city held the Katentol, a toll on shipping that it had received on long lease from the Elten stift and that brought in much money in the Middle Ages.

The place is mentioned in 9th-century sources from the Diocese of Utrecht, and a charter of 877 mentions seven farmsteads at the Deventer harbour. It was probably founded around 768 by the English missionary Lebuinus, who built a wooden church on the east bank. A Saxon expedition burned the church in January 772, which was the cause of Charlemagne's first punitive war against the Saxons. The Vikings looted and burned the village in 882; it was rebuilt at once and fortified with an earthen wall.

Between 1000 and 1500 Deventer grew into a flourishing trade city, thanks to a harbour that could take large ships, and it joined the Hanseatic League. Its trade in dried haddock and cod from Norway gave its citizens the nickname Deventer Stokvis. Geert Groote was born there and his Brethren of the Common Life were based there, influencing Thomas à Kempis and Erasmus. Deventer had printing presses as early as 1477. A Latin School existed from about 1300 and remained in service in changing forms until 1971; Erasmus attended it from 1475 to 1484.

From 1500 to 1800 less water flowed through the IJssel, which reduced the importance of the harbour, and the religious war of 1568 to 1648 brought economic decline. In the 19th century Deventer became an industrial town.

Deventer is one of the oldest cities in the Netherlands, with the country's oldest stone house, De Proosdij, whose earliest parts date from around 1130, and its oldest scientific library, the Athenaeum Library, founded in 1560. Its landmarks include the Gothic St Lebuin's Church, the Brink market square and the Waag of 1550, now the city museum. The railway bridge and harbour were bombed heavily in the Second World War, though the city centre was largely spared. The Deventer honey cake has been made locally for over 500 years.
devils-island: In the 16th and 17th centuries French convicts were sentenced to serve as galley slaves, which was virtually a death sentence. After the galleys of the Levant Fleet were decommissioned in 1666, prisoners were kept chained on hulks moored in harbours until the hulks rotted and sank. The French Navy complained of the cost and of the disruption to the shipyards, and after his coup in 1851 Emperor Napoleon III ordered the hulks closed and civil-law convicts sent overseas.

Algeria, Haiti, Cuba, the Dominican Republic and Texas were considered before the government chose French Guiana. France had repeatedly failed to colonise it, and about 75 per cent of the 12,000 colonists sent in 1763 died in their first year. In 1852 Napoleon called for volunteers from the hulks, and 3,000 convicts applied.

The penal colony of Cayenne included sites on the mainland at Kourou, Cayenne and St. Laurent, and three islands in the Salvation Islands. Île Royale received the general population, Saint-Joseph Island was the Reclusion where inmates were punished by solitary confinement in silence and darkness, and Devil's Island held political prisoners.

Convicts were either transportés, civil-law prisoners sentenced under doublage, which required them to work in the colony for a period equal to their sentence afterwards, or déportés, convicted of political crimes. A law of 30 May 1854 required those whose sentence exceeded eight years to remain in French Guiana for life. Among the inmates were 239 republicans who had opposed Napoleon III's coup.

More than 80,000 prisoners were sent to the system, and the vast majority never returned to France. Disease, mosquitoes and harsh treatment killed many, and the death rate was 75 per cent at its worst. Few escaped, since the only way out of the island prisons was by water. Alfred Dreyfus, unjustly convicted of treason, was sent to Devil's Island on 5 January 1895, and the Dreyfus affair publicised the horrors of the system.

In 1938 René Belbenoît's book Dry Guillotine aroused public outrage, and the French government announced plans to close the colony. The Second World War delayed this, but the prisons were closed one by one from 1946 until 1953, and the Devil's Island facility was the last. Henri Charrière's bestselling book Papillon of 1969 describes his escape from the island with a companion, though they were recaptured. Devil's Island is now closed to the public, but the two larger islands have restored prison buildings that serve as museums.
devon: Devon is a ceremonial county in South West England, bordered by the Bristol Channel to the north, Somerset and Dorset to the east, the English Channel to the south and Cornwall to the west. It straddles a peninsula and so, uniquely among English counties, has two separate coastlines. It contains Dartmoor and part of Exmoor, two upland moors that are the source of most of its rivers, including the Taw, Dart and Exe. The longest river, the Tamar, forms most of the border with Cornwall. The southeast coast is part of the Jurassic Coast World Heritage Site, and the county gives its name to the Devonian geologic period.

Human remains from 30 to 40,000 years ago have come from Kents Cavern in Torquay, and Dartmoor is thought to have been occupied by Mesolithic hunter-gatherers from about 6000 BCE. In the Iron Age and Roman periods the region belonged to the Dumnonii, a Celtic British people whose name is thought to mean deep valley dwellers, and from which the name Devon derives. The Romans held the area under military occupation for around 350 years. After the formal Roman withdrawal in 410 CE, one of the leading Dumnonii families attempted to create a dynasty and rule as kings of Dumnonia.

Saxon incursions from the east began around 600 CE, first as small bands settling along the coast of Lyme Bay and the southern estuaries. Devon became a frontier between the Britons and Anglo-Saxon Wessex, and Dumnonia was partly assimilated into the kingdom of Wessex. King Æthelstan set the western boundary with Cornwall at the Tamar in 936. William Camden, in his Britannia of 1607, described Devon as one part of an older, wider country that once included Cornwall.

The county town is Exeter. Plymouth, the largest settlement and a historic port, and the Torbay conurbation of Torquay, Paignton and Brixham are administratively separate. Many of the resorts on the coast grew rapidly with the arrival of the railways in the 19th century. Devon is known for its mariners, among them Sir Francis Drake, Sir Walter Raleigh and Robert Falcon Scott. The cream tea of scones, jam and clotted cream is thought to have originated in the county, though neighbouring counties also claim it.
devshirme: Devshirme, meaning collecting and usually translated as child levy or blood tax, was the Ottoman practice of forcibly recruiting soldiers and bureaucrats from among the children of their Balkan Christian subjects and raising them in the religion of Islam. It is first mentioned in written records in 1438 but probably started earlier.

It came out of the kul system of slavery that developed in the early centuries of the Ottoman Empire. Beginning with Murad I, the Ottomans felt a need to counteract the power of Turkic nobles by developing Christian vassal soldiers and converted kapıkulu as personal troops. The system created a faction of soldiers and officials loyal to the sultan, and slave administrators rose after troubles between Mehmed II and the Turkish grand vizier Çandarlı Halil Pasha the Younger, the first grand vizier to be executed.

Ottoman officials took male Christian children aged 7 to 20, every four to seven years according to the historian William Gervase Clarence-Smith, one for every forty households. The boys had to be unmarried and were ordered to cut all ties with their families. They were relocated to Istanbul, converted, circumcised and trained for the Janissary infantry corps or for palace duties. The most talented, the ichoghlani, were trained for the highest positions of the empire, and the others joined the military.

Orphans, only sons and Jews were exempt, as were the major cities and the children of local craftsmen. Muslims were not allowed into the system, with some exceptions, though some Muslim families smuggled their sons in. Some recruits were castrated and became eunuchs, and several of these became grand viziers, among them Hadım Ali Pasha and Sinan Borovinić. Skanderbeg, Sinan Pasha and Sokollu Mehmed Pasha were recruited through it.

Locals resented the levy. Parents begged and tried to buy their children out, married the boys at 12 or converted to Islam to escape it, and revolts, though rare, included one in Albania and Epirus in 1565. Many scholars consider the practice a violation of Islamic law, as David Nicolle does, while Halil İnalcık argues that the boys were not slaves once converted. The system produced many grand viziers, provincial governors and military commanders from the 15th to the 17th century.

It began to die out as Ottoman soldiers preferred to recruit their own sons. In 1594 Muslims were officially allowed to take the positions held by the devshirme, the recruitment of Christians effectively stopped by 1648, and the practice was abolished in the early part of the reign of Ahmet III (1703–1730).
dewas: Dewas lies on the level plains of the Malwa plateau, north-east of Indore, south-east of Ujjain and south-west of Shajapur. To the south the land rises gently to the Vindhya Range, the source of the Chambal and Kali Sindh rivers, and the main river at Dewas is the Kshipra. The name comes from the Devi Vashini hill in the city, known as Tekri, which has a temple of the deities Devi Tulja Bhawani, Chamunda Mata and Kalika Mata. The word is believed to join Dev, deity, and Vas, abode in Marathi, so that Dewas means abode of the gods. E. M. Forster, inspired by the area, wrote The Hill of Devi in 1953.

Dewas began as a sovereign Maratha territory in the first half of the 18th century, founded by the brothers Tukoji Rao, who headed the Senior branch, and Jivaji Rao, who headed the Junior, of the Pawar clan. Members of the clan served as early as the reign of Chhatrapati Shivaji Maharaj, and under Chhatrapati Shahu they fought in campaigns against the Nizams, the Mughals and the Portuguese on the western coast. In recognition of their loyalty the family received the hereditary titles Sena Sapt Sahasri, Commander of Seven Thousand, and Vishwas Rao, The Trustworthy.

In the British period the town was the capital of two princely states, Dewas Senior and Dewas Junior, both in the Malwa Agency of the Central India Agency and each entitled to a 15-gun salute. In 1901 the senior branch had an area of 446 square miles and a population of 62,312, and the junior branch 440 square miles and 54,904 people. Their courts were composed of Sardars, Mankaris, Istamuradars, Thakurs and Jagirdars. After India's independence in 1947 both Maharajas acceded to India and their states were integrated into Madhya Bharat, which became a state of India in 1950 and was merged into Madhya Pradesh in 1956.
Dewas is the administrative capital of Dewas district in Madhya Pradesh. It is an industrialised city and houses a government bank note press. Its population was 289,550 at the census of 2011.
dezful: Dezful lies at the foot of the Zagros Mountains, about 155 kilometres from Ahvaz, the provincial capital, and 650 kilometres from Tehran, on the main north-south highway to Ahvaz. The area around it has been home to civilizations for about 5,000 years. Its people speak Dezfuli, a dialect distinct to the city, and Shushtari, sometimes considered one of the most archaic dialects of the Iranian plateau. The name comes from Persian words for fortress and bridge; the original form was Dezhpul, changed after the Muslim conquest because Arabic lacks the sounds p and zh.

According to excavations by Walther Hinz, Awan, capital of the first dynasty of Elam, lay at Dezful. The name is believed to come from a Sasanian bridge over the Ab-e Dez built by Shapur II, beside which the Sasanians built a fortress. The area grew into the city, though the name was not commonly used until the 12th century. The stone foundation of the bridge is still visible, while its upper part was rebuilt in brick during the early Islamic, Saljuq and Qajar periods; in the 14th century Hamd-Allah Mostawfi described it as 520 paces long, with forty-two arches.

The Ranashi Dynasty was centred at Dezful until its fall in 1542/3 and was a vassal of the Safavid Empire from 1508 to 1514. A Mandaean community lived there for many centuries, and the Shia jurist Morteza Ansari was born there in 1781. When George Curzon visited in the late 19th century the principal industry was indigo, with 120 factories, and the city was known for fine reed pens.

Dezful is the capital of Dezful County in Khuzestan province, Iran, with a population of 264,709 in the 2016 census. Sugarcane has been grown in the region for more than a thousand years, and the Dezful reed pen has been made there for about three hundred years.
dhaka: Dhaka lies in central Bangladesh on the eastern bank of the Buriganga River, on the lower reaches of the Ganges Delta. The land is flat and close to sea level, and the city is bounded by the Buriganga, Turag, Dhaleshwari and Shitalakshya rivers, which leaves it susceptible to flooding in the monsoon seasons. The origin of the name is uncertain. It may come from the dhak tree, once common in the area, from the goddess Dhakeshwari, or from the dhak, a drum played at the inauguration of the Bengal capital in 1610.

Urban settlements in the area date to the first millennium. The region belonged to the ancient district of Bikrampur, ruled by the Sena dynasty, and under Islamic rule to the district of Sonargaon. Isa Khan and his son Musa Khan, who ruled from Sonargaon, headed a confederation of twelve chieftains that resisted Mughal expansion in eastern Bengal in the late 16th century. When the Ganges changed course, the earlier capital Gour lost its strategic importance, and Dhaka and Chittagong became the eastern frontiers of the Mughal Empire.

An early modern city developed from the 17th century as a provincial capital and commercial centre of the Mughal Empire. Dhaka was the capital of Mughal Bengal for 75 years, in two separate periods. It was the hub of the muslin trade and one of the most prosperous cities in the world, home to merchants from across Eurasia. The Mughals named it Jahangirnagar in honour of the emperor Jahangir and decorated it with gardens, tombs, mosques, palaces and forts. It was once called the Venice of the East.

Under British rule Dhaka gained electricity, railways, Western-style universities and a modern water supply, and became an administrative and educational centre as capital of the province of Eastern Bengal and Assam after 1905. In 1947 it became the administrative capital of East Pakistan, and the partition of India emptied the city of its Hindu population, which had come to form a majority during the previous century and dominated its economy. After the Liberation War of 1971 it became the capital of independent Bangladesh.

Dhaka is the capital and largest city of Bangladesh and the seat of its government. It has a heritage of about 2,000 buildings from the Mughal and British periods, and its most prominent landmark is the modernist Jatiya Sangsad Bhaban, designed by Louis Kahn. UNESCO has recognised the Bengali New Year parade, the Jamdani sari and rickshaw art as intangible cultural heritage.
dharmachakra: The Sanskrit noun dharma derives from the root dhṛ, meaning to hold or maintain, and means what is established or firm. Spoked-wheel symbols are among the most ancient in Indian history. A wheel symbol appears frequently on Indus Valley Civilisation artefacts, particularly on several seals, and is present in a sequence of ten signs on the Dholavira Signboard. Some historians associate such wheels with solar symbolism: in the Vedas the god Surya is linked to a solar disc, a chariot of one wheel, and a wheel is the main attribute of Vishnu.

In Buddhism the wheel represents the Buddha's teaching, the Buddha himself and the walking of the path to enlightenment. The Buddha is said to have set the wheel of dharma in motion in his first sermon, described in the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta. Buddhism took the image from the Indian idea of the ideal king, the chakravartin or wheel-turner, who possessed a perfect wheel. Siddhartha Gautama could have become such a king but became instead a wheel-turning sage.

Designs have 8, 12, 24 or more spokes. In the Indo-Tibetan tradition the eight-spoked wheel stands for the noble eightfold path, and the hub, rim and spokes for the three trainings of sila, prajña and samadhi. The Theravada exegete Buddhaghosa explains the turning of the wheel as wisdom, knowledge and insight. A wheel can also symbolise the cycle of rebirth, the wheel of samsara, which the Buddhist path reverses.

The earliest Indian monuments with dharmachakras are the Ashokan Pillars, such as the lion pillar at Sanchi. At early sites such as Bharhut and Sanchi the wheel was often a symbol of Gautama Buddha himself, paired with the triratna, umbrellas, gems and garlands. A pairing of wheel and deer recalls the Deer Park at Sarnath and appears on the clay seals of the vihāra at Nālandā.

The largest surviving group of free-standing stone dharmachakras comes from the Dvaravati culture of present-day Thailand, where Eng Jin Ooi and Peter Skilling count at least forty, about twelve of them inscribed. A wheel of this kind stood on an octagonal pillar set on a circular brick base. Their makers suggest that wheels on this scale were a devotional practice particular to Dvaravati. A 24-spoke Ashoka dharmachakra stands at the centre of the flag of India.
dhimmi: Dhimmi, 'protected person', refers to the state's obligation under sharia to protect the life, property and freedom of religion of non-Muslims in return for their loyalty and payment of the jizya tax. The status was first applied to Jews, Christians and Sabians, the People of the Book, and was later extended to Zoroastrians, Hindus, Jains and Buddhists; Muslim governments in the Indus basin readily gave it to the Hindus and Buddhists of India.

The Pact of Umar is traditionally held to be an agreement between the caliph Umar and the Christians of Jerusalem in the seventh century, but academic historians believe its present form was the work of later jurists who attributed it to Umar, and that much of it was borrowed from the Theodosian and Justinian codes.

Adult, free, healthy men paid the jizya; women, children, the elderly, slaves, the disabled and travellers were exempt. Dhimmis did not pay the zakat paid by Muslims but their own religious dues, and they did not bear arms or perform military service. Islamic law forbade the enslavement of free dhimmis. The communities kept their own leaders, courts and personal and religious laws, such as the Jewish Halakhic courts, and a qadi usually could not interfere unless the parties chose Islamic law.

Restrictions included bans on building new places of worship or repairing old ones without Muslim consent, on loud prayers and church bells, on teaching children the Quran and on seeking converts among Muslims. Dhimmis were made to wear distinctive dress and to avoid riding on saddles, and in Mamluk Egypt they could not ride even donkeys inside cities. Forced conversion was forbidden, but cases of it are well documented.

Historians judge the system differently. Marshall Hodgson describes an official policy that dhimmis should feel inferior and know their place. Bernard Lewis holds that the restrictions on Jews were social and symbolic rather than practical, and María Rosa Menocal argues that Jews under the caliphate were better off than in Christian Europe.

In the 19th century pressure from European powers and from Muslim reformers gradually relaxed the inequalities. The Ottoman Reform Edict of 18 February 1856, issued partly under pressure from France, Austria and the United Kingdom, proclaimed equality between Muslims and non-Muslims, abolished the jizya and allowed non-Muslims to join the army. The dhimma and the jizya are no longer imposed in countries with a Muslim majority.
dhofar: Dhofar lies in south-western Oman between the Arabian Sea and the Dhofar Mountains, a semi-circular range that runs into the sea at Ras Hamar and Mirbat. It has three distinct physical tracts: a cultivated coastal belt, Al Haffah, a desert plain about 60 km long, and the mountains. From mid-June to mid-September the south-west monsoon, known locally as Khareef, brings clouds that are trapped by the mountains, so that Dhofar is unique on the southern Arabian coast in having monsoon rainfall for about three months. The uplands rise to between 900 and 1,200 metres and slope away northwards towards the Empty Quarter. Frankincense grows wild in the dry northern wadis, where the dry air determines its quality.

A site at Aybut Al-Auwal has yielded stone tools of the Arabian Nubian Complex, dated by two luminescence estimates to about 106,000 years ago, and Bronze Age tomb complexes have been found at Hodor. Dhofar was a major exporter of frankincense in ancient times, some of it traded as far as China. Al-Baleed, near Salalah, was home to the Manjawi civilisation from the 12th to the 16th centuries. Marco Polo, writing about 1300, called Dufar a great and noble city whose people were Muslims, with a Count subject to the Sultan of Aden. Before Omani rule it was part of the sultanate of Kathiri, and was later controlled mostly by the Al-Hakli (Qara) tribes.

In 1876 Sayyid Fadhl bin Alawi, who had come from Mecca, made himself de facto ruler and claimed allegiance to the Ottomans, but local sheikhs expelled him in 1879. The Sultan of Muscat administered Dhofar as a separate holding, and in the 1917 Gazetteer of Arabia frankincense made up most of its trade. During the First World War it supplied much of the food and grain for the British Army in Mesopotamia. From 1963 the Omani Civil War was fought there between the Sultan's forces and the Dhofar Liberation Front and then the Popular Front for the Liberation of Oman and the Persian Gulf. The campaign was declared over in December 1975.

Dhofar is the largest of the eleven governorates of Oman by area, covering 99,300 square kilometres, and its capital and largest city is Salalah, which has an international airport and a major seaport. It has ten wilayats. The local Arabic dialect, Dhofari Arabic, differs from that of the rest of Oman, and many people speak Modern South Arabian languages such as Shehri, also called Jibbali, and Harsusi. The Al Kathiri are the largest tribe in Salalah and Dhofar. The region has long been known as a source of frankincense.
dholavira: Dholavira lies at Khadirbet in Bhachau Taluka of Kutch District, Gujarat, on the island of Khadir Bet in the Kutch Desert Wildlife Sanctuary, within the Great Rann of Kutch. It takes the name of a modern village 1 kilometre to the south, and it is known locally as Kotada timba. The site lies on the Tropic of Cancer, between two seasonal streams, the Mansar in the north and the Manhar in the south. Earthquakes have repeatedly struck it, among them a severe one around 2600 BCE.

A resident of the village, Shambhudan Gadhvi, found the site in the early 1960s and tried to draw official attention to it. J. P. Joshi of the Archaeological Survey of India recorded it in 1967 or 1968. The Survey has excavated it since 1990 under Ravindra Bisht, with 13 field seasons between 1990 and 2005. Bisht defined seven stages of occupation. Radiocarbon dates and comparison with Amri II-B pottery led to the first two being renamed the Pre-Harappan Dholaviran Culture, dated c. 3500 to 3200 BCE and c. 3200 to 2600 BCE. The city declined slowly after about 2100 BCE and was briefly abandoned before being reoccupied.

Finds include animal bones, gold, silver, terracotta ornaments, pottery and bronze vessels, and archaeologists believe the city was an important trading centre linking settlements in south Gujarat, Sindh and Punjab with western Asia. Excavation uncovered 225 seals and 60 clay impressions, most of them square stone stamps with an animal above which ran writing. The unicorn appears on 65 per cent of them. A bead-making industry produced about 12,000 beads of steatite, carnelian, agate, lapis lazuli and other materials, and the largest collection of stone bead-drilling tools known from an Indus site, between 1,500 and 1,600 pieces, came from here.

85 metres. Unlike Harappa and Mohenjo-daro it was built to a geometrical plan of three divisions, the citadel, the middle town and the lower town, each with its own defences, gateways and streets. The citadel, defended by double ramparts, was the most heavily fortified part. Beside it stood the bailey, where important officials lived.

Seven hemispherical mud-brick constructions, some shaped like a spoked wheel, were built over rock-cut chambers and held burial goods but, with one exception, no skeletons. Dholavira is one of the five largest Harappan sites. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, Dholavira: a Harappan City, on 27 July 2021.
di-xin: Di Xin was the younger of three sons of Di Yi. His elder brother Zi Qi had a mother of low birth, while Di Xin's mother was the principal consort, so he was made heir and took the throne after his father's death. He was born Zi Shou, and the Zhou called him Shou, King of Shang. Di Xin is his temple name, recorded in bronze inscriptions of his own time. The name King Zhou, in which zhou means a horse's crupper, was a derogatory title given after his death. Later texts describe him as tall, strong and quick-witted, able to fight beasts bare-handed.

Di Xin moved the Shang capital to Mo, later renamed Zhaoge, in modern Qi County in Henan. Bronze inscriptions record his wars with the Renfang, Linfang and Hufang, and a long campaign against the Renfang in the east, a Dongyi people, which Zhou accounts say wore the Shang down. Oracle bones show him performing the ancestral rituals of the Shang religion. Zhou writers noted with horror that he gave office to fugitives on merit and also appointed women, whom the Shang state held in high respect.

The Zhou portrayed him as a tyrant who drank, indulged his favourite Daji and tortured his subjects. The Book of Documents lists six charges against him, and Sima Qian adds the Lake of Wine and Forest of Meat and the death of his uncle Bi Gan, whose heart he is said to have had cut out. Doubts began early. In the Analects, Zigong says that the wickedness of Zhou was not as great as the name implies. The Southern Song scholar Luo Mi thought such stories were largely imitation, and historians of the Doubting Antiquity School noted that the accusations grew more numerous in later sources.

Around 1046 BCE King Wu of Zhou attacked at the Battle of Muye. The Li gui bronze is the only contemporary record of the battle. When defeat was clear, Di Xin is alleged to have put on his finest clothes and burned himself at the Deer Terrace Pavilion. Another text says that King Wu killed him with an axe. His son Wu Geng was left to rule part of the old Shang lands, but joined the Rebellion of the Three Guards, which the Duke of Zhou crushed within three years. Di Xin's brothers Zi Qi and Zi Yan later ruled the state of Song. Chinese tradition made him, with Jie of Xia, the model of the tyrant whose fall justifies a change of dynasty.
diadochi: When Alexander the Great died on 10 June 323 BCE he left an empire of many essentially independent territories, stretching from Macedon and the Greek city-states to Bactria and parts of India, and including Anatolia, the Levant, Egypt, Babylonia and most of the former Achaemenid Empire. His companion cavalry, the hetairoi, were officers without fixed rank whom he assigned where needed. At his death these men became the Diadochi, who knew where they had stood but not where they would stand, and without Alexander they had to make their own appointments.

The generals disputed rule between Alexander's half-brother Arrhidaeus and his unborn child with Roxana. A compromise made Arrhidaeus king as Philip III, to rule jointly with Roxana's child if it was a son, with Perdiccas as regent. At the Partition of Babylon Ptolemy received Egypt, Lysimachus Thrace, Antigonus Phrygia, Lycia and Pamphylia, and Eumenes of Cardia Cappadocia and Paphlagonia, while Antipater and Craterus were to rule Macedon and Greece. Greek cities rose in the Lamian War, which ended with the Battle of Crannon on 5 September 322 BCE.

War between the generals followed. Perdiccas was murdered by his own generals during an invasion of Egypt, and Antipater became regent. When he died in 319 BCE, passing over his son Cassander in favour of Polyperchon, civil war broke out. In 310 BCE Cassander secretly murdered Alexander IV and Roxana. At the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE Antigonus I Monophthalmus was killed fighting a coalition of Cassander, Lysimachus and Seleucus I Nicator, and the unified empire was finally broken up.

The Diadochi founded the Ptolemaic, Seleucid and Antigonid dynasties, which ruled for centuries in Egypt, the Levant, Asia Minor, Mesopotamia, Persia and Macedon. The Antigonid kingdom fell to the Roman Republic, a rump Seleucid kingdom in Syria was conquered by Pompey in 64 BCE, and Egypt was annexed to Rome in 30 BCE. The term is an ancient Greek word meaning successors; its Latin form entered modern history writing in the 19th century through Johann Gustav Droysen, who divided the age into the period of the Diadochi and that of the Epigoni, their sons.
diana-mythology: Diana was an ancient goddess common to all the Latin tribes, with independent origins in Italy. She was first a goddess of the wilderness and the hunt, and early Roman inscriptions celebrate her chiefly as a huntress. Her primary sanctuary was a woodland grove overlooking Lake Nemi, where she was worshipped as Diana Nemorensis, Diana of the Wood. Evidence suggests that worship there flourished from at least the 6th century BCE until the 2nd century CE. Legend said that Orestes and Iphigenia founded the sanctuary after fleeing from the Tauri.

Tradition says King Servius Tullius dedicated her temple on the Aventine Hill, outside the pomerium, in keeping with her being a goddess of all the Latins and not of the Romans alone. Worship probably spread into the city from about 550 BCE, as she became combined with the Greek Artemis, a process that culminated in her appearance beside Apollo at the first lectisternium in Rome in 399 BCE.

Early Roman gods were numina, powers without bodily form, and Diana probably had little mythology when Rome was founded. Under Greek influence she became the daughter of Jupiter and Latona, twin of Apollo and, usually, a virgin goddess. In Ovid's version of the story of Actaeon, the young hunter came upon her bathing in a grotto, and she turned him into a deer, so that his own dogs tore him apart.

She was also a goddess of the countryside, of crossroads, of the Moon and of childbirth. Her earliest epithet was Trivia, from the three-way crossroads she guarded, which also pointed the way to the underworld. As Diana Lucina she protected women in labour. At Nemi she was venerated from the late 6th century BCE as a triple goddess, Diana, Luna and Hecate. She was also a household goddess: Horace had an altar to her in his villa.

Sermons and other church documents show that Diana worship persisted in remote communities of post-Roman Europe, though many of the cults were probably local goddesses or nymphs that Christian writers called Diana. Gregory of Tours reported that the deacon Vulfilaic found an image of Diana on a hill at what is now Margut and destroyed it. James George Frazer reinterpreted the rites at Nemi in The Golden Bough, and Charles Godfrey Leland's Aradia made her Queen of the Witches. Diana is revered in modern neopagan religions, among them Roman neopaganism and Wicca.
diane-de-poitiers: Diane de Poitiers was born on 9 January 1500 at the Château de Saint-Vallier, to Jean de Poitiers and Jeanne de Batarnay. As a girl she was briefly in the retinue of Anne de Beaujeu and was educated in the principles of Renaissance humanism, including Greek and Latin, rhetoric, finance, law and architecture. On 29 March 1515, at fifteen, she married Louis de Brézé, seigneur d'Anet and Grand Seneschal of Normandy, who was 39 years her senior. They had two daughters, Françoise and Louise.

After Louis died in 1531 she wore black and white for the rest of her life, the permitted colours of mourning and the symbolic colours of the two sides of the moon, playing on her name. She kept her husband's offices and revenues, and her legal skill impressed Francis I, who allowed her to manage her inherited estates without a male guardian.

In 1526 the princes Francis and Henry were sent to Spain as hostages for their father, who had been captured at Pavia. Diane, a lady-in-waiting, gave Henry his farewell kiss, and at a tournament in 1531 he wore her colours. In 1533 Henry married Catherine de' Medici, to whom Diane was related as a second cousin, and it is generally believed that Diane became his mistress in 1534. She remained his lifelong companion for the next 25 years.

After Francis I died in 1547, Henry II banned Francis's mistress Anne de Pisseleu from court and confiscated her duchy of Étampes. Diane became Duchess of Valentinois in 1548 and Duchess of Étampes in 1553. Henry trusted her to write many of his official letters, which were signed jointly as HenriDiane, and she directed the education of his children until 1551. He entrusted her with the Crown Jewels and gave her the Château de Chenonceau. She was a major patron of French Renaissance architecture, commissioning Philibert de l'Orme to remodel the Château d'Anet and to build the arched bridge at Chenonceau in 1555.

In 1559 Henry was severely wounded in a jousting tournament, wearing Diane's favour rather than his wife's. Catherine took control, and Diane was not admitted to his deathbed or invited to his funeral. She was obliged to exchange Chenonceau for the Château de Chaumont and lived out her remaining years at Anet in comfortable obscurity. She died on 25 April 1566.

During the French Revolution her tomb was opened and her remains thrown into a mass grave. When French experts exhumed her remains in 2009 they found high levels of gold in her hair, and it has been suggested that the drinkable gold she reportedly took to preserve youth contributed to her death. She was reburied at Anet in May 2010.
die-drome: Die lies in the valley of the Drôme, surrounded by the Glandasse mountain, 2,041 metres high, a massive and steep rocky barrier that separates the area, the Diois, from the Vercors Plateau. It is a commune and a subprefecture of the Drôme department, and its territory is part of a regional natural park. It was a county in the High Middle Ages and was the see of a Catholic diocese, with its church serving as the cathedral.

Habitation in the Neolithic is confirmed by the excavations at Chanqueyras, and a large engraved standing stone and two small menhirs found near the wine cooperative are now in the museum. Late Bronze Age remains were found at La Roche de Marginal. A first settlement seems to have appeared at the beginning of the Roman era, on a small pass beside the Drôme, at the crossroads between the valley and the track to Trièves, and there is much evidence of extensive urbanisation in the 1st century.

At the beginning of the 2nd century Die gained monumental architecture and replaced Luc-en-Diois as the Roman provincial capital of the Celtic people of the northern Voconces. It received the formal status of a colony towards the end of the 2nd century or during the 3rd, and it became an important centre of worship of the goddess Cybele. When the empire showed signs of weakness, between 285 and 305, a wall just over a mile long was built around the town, enclosing 25 hectares and using fragments of funerary monuments. The town had two main gates, that of Saint-Pierre to the west, demolished in 1891, and that of Saint-Marcel to the east.

The first recorded bishop of the ancient diocese of Die was Nicaise in 325, the only Gallic church representative at the First Council of Nicaea. The diocese was merged with that of Valence in 1276, separated at the end of the 17th century and suppressed during the French Revolution.

Die has fewer than 5,000 inhabitants and is the economic and social centre of the Diois. It is best known for its sparkling wine, Clairette de Die, and the cooperative winery is the largest employer of the Diois. Its museum shows the Roman remains and the story of the Diois from prehistory, through its time as an episcopal city in the Middle Ages, to the devastation of the religious wars. Historic monuments stand within the Gallo-Roman walls.
die-zeit: Die Zeit, German for The Time, is a national weekly newspaper published in Hamburg. Its first edition appeared on 21 February 1946. The founding publishers were Gerd Bucerius, Lovis H. Lorenz, Richard Tüngel and Ewald Schmidt di Simoni, and Marion Gräfin Dönhoff joined as an editor in March 1946. The paper appeared under the lettering that Carl Otto Czeschka designed in 1946, inspired by The Times, which shows the British coat of arms between its two words. The paper's founding editorial, Unsere Aufgabe, set out the publishers' own view of its mission.

Dönhoff was publisher of Die Zeit from 1972 until her death in 2002, and in 1983 the former chancellor Helmut Schmidt joined her. Josef Joffe and Michael Naumann later joined them. Editors-in-chief have included Richard Tüngel, Josef Müller-Marein, Dönhoff herself from 1968 to 1972, and Theo Sommer from 1973 to 1992. The paper's first masthead carried a version of the Hamburg crest, but the Hamburg Senate objected that it was a misuse of a state emblem for commercial purposes, and on 27 June 1946 the crest was replaced by the key and crown of the coat of arms of Bremen, with the approval of Bremen's mayor Wilhelm Kaisen. That design is still used as the logo of the whole publishing group.

The Zeitmagazin first appeared as a supplement in 1970, ended in 1999 and was reintroduced on 24 May 2007. A redesign by Mario Garcia in January 1998 introduced the headline type Tiemann-Antiqua and body text in Garamond. The online edition, Zeit Online, merged with Tagesspiegel Online and zoomer.de in 2009 and has published some stories in English. Since March 2017 part of its content has been available only for payment.

The publishing house, Zeitverlag Gerd Bucerius, is owned by the Georg von Holtzbrinck Publishing Group and Dieter von Holtzbrinck Media. The paper appears on Thursdays and is printed in Mörfelden-Walldorf. It is divided into sections including Politik, Streit, Dossier, Geschichte, Wirtschaft, Wissen and Feuilleton. It is regarded as highbrow and as centrist and liberal or left-liberal in outlook, and it often publishes dossiers, essays and excerpts of lectures that look at a single topic from several viewpoints, often in long and detailed articles.

Its large Nordisch format is a trademark, often mocked in literature and cabaret, though in fact it is no bigger than that of a dozen other German newspapers. The circulation was 500,000 in 1993 and 504,072 in the second half of 2012, with an estimated readership of just over 2 million, which made it the most widely read German weekly.
diego-de-almagro: Diego de Almagro was born of humble origins, the illegitimate son of Juan de Montenegro and Elvira Gutiérrez, in the village of Almagro or in Malagón in Ciudad Real, and took his surname from the village. In Seville he served in the household of Luis Gonzalez de Polanco, who used his influence to secure him a passage to the New World after Almagro stabbed another servant.

He landed at Santa María la Antigua del Darién, in Panama, on 30 June 1514, with the expedition of Pedro Arias Dávila. There he received an encomienda and farmed, and on an expedition under Gaspar de Espinosa he became a close friend of Francisco Pizarro and Hernando de Luque. By 1524 the three had formed an association to conquer lands to the south. He lost an eye to an arrow at Punta Quemada.

After Pizarro's defeat of the Inca army under Atahualpa at the Battle of Cajamarca in 1532, Almagro joined him with more men and arms. In August 1534 he founded Santiago de Quito near Lake Colta, to forestall Sebastián de Belalcázar, and in December of that year Trujillo, which he named after Pizarro's birthplace.

Charles V divided the conquered lands between Nueva Castilla, for Pizarro, and Nueva Toledo, for Almagro. Almagro left Cuzco on 3 July 1535 with about 750 Spaniards, following the Inca trail and then crossing the Andes, where cold and hunger killed Spaniards and, above all slaves unused to the climate. He took possession of Chile in the Copiapó valley and explored as far as the Aconcagua. Almagro found neither gold nor cities, and his troops plundered local property and carried off captives as porters and slaves.

Almagro returned to Cuzco in 1537. On the night of 8 April 1537 his men seized the city and imprisoned Hernando and Gonzalo Pizarro, and on 12 July 1537 they defeated an army sent by Francisco Pizarro at the Battle of Abancay. Hernando was freed in return for control of Cuzco. In April 1538 the Almagristas were beaten at Las Salinas and Rodrigo Orgóñez was killed. Almagro fled to Cuzco but was captured, and his appeal to the king was ignored.

He was garrotted in his dungeon and beheaded on 8 July 1538. His son Diego de Almagro II, called El Mozo, was proclaimed governor of Peru by the conspirators who killed Pizarro on 26 June 1541. He was defeated at Chupas on 16 September 1542 and executed in Cuzco.
diego-rivera: Diego Rivera was born on 8 December 1886 in Guanajuato, the son of a well-to-do couple. He began drawing at three, and from the age of ten studied at the Academy of San Carlos in Mexico City. The governor of Veracruz sponsored his further study in Europe, where he arrived in 1907. He settled in Paris among the artists of Montparnasse, and Amedeo Modigliani painted his portrait in 1914. From 1913 to 1917 he embraced Cubism, and around 1917, inspired by Paul Cézanne, he turned to Post-Impressionism, with simple forms and large patches of vivid colour.

Rivera returned to Mexico in 1921 to join the government mural programme planned by José Vasconcelos, which included José Clemente Orozco, David Alfaro Siqueiros and Rufino Tamayo. His first significant mural, Creation, was painted in January 1922. That year he joined the Mexican Communist Party, and his later murals, in fresco only, treated Mexican society and the 1910 Revolution in large, simplified figures and bold colours with an evident Aztec influence. The series at the Secretariat of Public Education in Mexico City was begun in September 1922 and finished in 1928.

In 1929 he was expelled from the party because of suspected Trotskyite sympathies. In the United States he painted in San Francisco, and in 1931 the Museum of Modern Art in New York held a retrospective. From 1932 to 1933 he painted the twenty-seven frescoes of Detroit Industry, partly paid for by Edsel Ford. His mural Man at the Crossroads for Rockefeller Center was destroyed in 1933 after he refused to remove a portrait of Lenin, and he repainted it in 1934 in Mexico City.

Rivera was an atheist. His fresco A Dream of a Sunday Afternoon in the Alameda Park, painted in 1946, included a sign reading that God does not exist, and the work was not shown for nine years until he agreed to remove the inscription. It also gave the figure of La Calavera Catrina, created by José Guadalupe Posada, indigenous features. He married Frida Kahlo in 1929, divorced her in 1939 and remarried her in 1940. He died on 24 November 1957, and the government of Mexico has declared his works historic monuments.
diego-silang: Diego Silang y Andaya was born on 16 December 1730 in Aringay, then part of Pangasinan and now in La Union. His father was Pangasinense and his mother Ilocano. He was baptised on 7 January 1731 in Vigan, in the then undivided province of Ilocos, where as a boy he worked as a messenger for a local Castilian priest. Fluent in Spanish, he carried correspondence from the Ilocos to Manila, journeys on which he first saw the injustices of colonial rule.

Spain was allied with France in the Seven Years' War, and the British seizure of Manila in October 1762 inspired risings in the far north of Luzon. Silang at first wanted to replace Spanish functionaries in the Ilocos with native-born officials and offered to lead Ilocano forces on the Spanish side. The Spanish administrators instead transferred their powers to the Catholic Bishop of Nueva Segovia, who rejected the offer. The revolt drew on grievances over Spanish taxation and abuses and on Silang's belief that church and government in the Ilocos should be led by trained Ilocano officials.

Joaquín Martínez de Zúñiga, writing in 1805, gave a hostile account. He called Silang very quick and artful and said he persuaded the chiefs and many commoners, especially those of Vigan, that to keep the Catholic faith they must arm against the Spaniards and deliver them to the English. Armed men demanded that the alcalde give up his staff of government to the vicar-general; he did so and escaped from the province. The rebels then demanded of the bishop-elect, a Dominican named Ustariz, an exemption from the tribute, while Silang gathered troops for wider operations.

Silang was killed on 28 May 1763, aged 32, by a friend, a Spanish-Ilocano mestizo named Miguel Vicos, whom church authorities had paid and who was helped by Pedro Becbec. Gabriela Silang was forced to retreat to what is now Abra, led her troops towards Vigan and was driven back; she and her men were hanged on 20 September 1763, she last of all. The Philippine Navy has named two frigates after Diego Silang, one in service from 1976 to 1990 and one that entered service in 2025.
diego-velazquez: Velázquez was born in Seville, the first child of Juan Rodríguez de Silva, a notary, and Jerónima Velázquez, and was baptised on 6 June 1599. His paternal grandparents were Portuguese and had moved to Seville decades earlier. When offered knighthood in 1658 he claimed descent from the lesser nobility in order to qualify, though his grandparents may have been tradespeople. Raised in modest circumstances, he showed an early gift for art and was apprenticed to Francisco Pacheco, a learned teacher who encouraged his students' intellectual development. A contract of 17 September 1611 formalised a six-year apprenticeship.

By the early 1620s Velázquez had established his reputation in Seville. After the death of the court painter Rodrigo de Villandrando in December 1622, the Count-Duke of Olivares summoned him to court, and on 30 August 1623 Philip IV sat for him. The king was pleased, and Olivares commanded him to move to Madrid, his home for the rest of his life. He spent a year and a half in Italy from 1629 and returned in January 1631. For the Palacio del Buen Retiro he painted equestrian portraits of the royal family and The Surrender of Breda, his only surviving painting of contemporary history, in which the Spanish general stands before his Dutch counterpart as an equal.

He made a second journey to Italy in 1649, accompanied by his assistant Juan de Pareja, then a slave, and painted Pope Innocent X in Rome. He returned to Spain in 1651. In 1652 the king chose him as aposentador mayor, responsible for the court's quarters, an office that interfered with his painting. Las Meninas, completed in 1656, four years before his death, is regarded as his masterpiece.

He began in a precise tenebrist style and later developed a freer manner with bold brushwork. He used Caravaggio's realism and chiaroscuro only as a starting point, with a fluid handling of light and shade closer to Titian's. On his first trip to Italy he adopted canvases prepared with a light-gray ground, which gave greater luminosity and a cool, silvery range of colour. He painted directly from life. He is estimated to have produced between 110 and 120 known canvases, and no etchings or engravings.

His reputation languished in the 18th century, but by its end his importance was recognised, and in 1778 Goya made etchings after his paintings. In 1957 Pablo Picasso recreated Las Meninas in 44 variations.
diego-velazquez-de-cuellar: Little is known of Velázquez's early life. He was born in Cuéllar, in the Segovia region of Spain, around 1465, served for a time in the Spanish military in Naples and then lived in Seville. In September 1493 he was one of 1,500 men who sailed with Columbus on his second voyage, and he never returned to Spain. On Hispaniola he gained the regard of Bartholomew Columbus and became a trusted lieutenant of the governor Nicolás de Ovando. In July 1503 he put down a Taíno revolt at Jaragua and then founded Salvatierra de la Zabana and other towns. By 1511 he was one of the wealthiest men on the island.

King Ferdinand instructed Diego Columbus to conquer Cuba in the hope of gold and Native labour, and Velázquez was chosen to lead the expedition, which he had to finance himself. He sailed in January 1511 with four ships and three hundred men, among them Hernán Cortés and Pedro de Alvarado. A Taíno force led by Hatuey, formerly a chief from Hispaniola, resisted and was defeated after two months. According to Bartolomé de las Casas, Hatuey was captured and burned alive. Baracoa was settled by August 1511, and Pánfilo de Narváez became second in command.

In 1513 three expeditions went west; Narváez defeated a force of 2,500 Taínos under the chief Caguax, the last significant resistance. By 1515 Velázquez had founded Bayamo, Trinidad, Sancti Spiritus, Havana, Camagüey and Santiago de Cuba, which became the capital.

He rewarded relatives and associates with encomiendas, and by 1522 the encomenderos controlled almost 3,000 Indian labourers. From Cuba he sent Francisco Hernández de Córdoba to the Yucatán in 1517 and Juan de Grijalva in 1518. He then chose Cortés to lead a third expedition, but doubted him and tried to replace him. Cortés sailed in February 1519 with ten ships and about 500 men. When Velázquez sent Narváez against him in 1520 with about 1,000 men, Narváez was defeated and most of his force joined Cortés. Velázquez lost a large fortune, and Cuba was left depopulated.

Diego Colón sent Alonso Zuazo in January 1521 to replace Velázquez, but Velázquez was restored in July 1523. In 1522 Carlos I recognised Cortés as governor of New Spain. Velázquez died on 11 or 12 June 1524 and was buried under the altar steps of the new cathedral in Santiago. At his death he was said to be the richest Spaniard in the Americas. He had founded towns that remain important and made Cuba a centre of trade and a staging point for expeditions of conquest.
dieric-bouts: Dieric Bouts, also called Dirk Bouts in some museums and institutions, may have studied under Rogier van der Weyden, and his work was influenced by van der Weyden and by Jan van Eyck. He was married twice and had four children. His two daughters went to convents, and his two sons became painters who carried the Bouts workshop into the mid-16th century. The elder, Dieric the Younger, appears to have continued his father's style until his early death in 1491, and the younger, Aelbrecht, developed a style unmistakably his own.

Bouts' earliest work is the Triptych of the Virgin's Life in the Prado in Madrid, dated about 1445. In 1464 the Leuven Confraternity of the Holy Sacrament commissioned from him the Altarpiece of the Holy Sacrament for St Peter's Church. Its central panel, the Last Supper, shows Christ as a priest consecrating the Eucharistic host rather than focusing on the betrayal by Judas. It is the first Flemish panel painting of the subject, and its four servants, dressed in Flemish clothes, are most likely portraits of members of the confraternity.

After he became city painter of Leuven in 1468, Bouts received commissions for the Town Hall. The first was an altarpiece of the Last Judgment (1468–1470), of which two wings survive in Lille and a fragment of Christ in Stockholm. The second was the Justice Panels (1470–1475), which occupied him until his death in 1475. He finished one panel and began a second, both showing the life of the 11th-century Holy Roman Emperor Otto III; they are now in Brussels, and the other two panels planned were never completed.

Many of his authentic works are small devotional panels, usually of the Virgin and Child, such as the Davis Madonna in New York. His 1462 Portrait of a Man in the National Gallery in London is the first instance of a sitter in three-quarter view before a discernible background with a glimpse of landscape through a window.

Bouts was among the first northern painters to use a single vanishing point, as in his Last Supper, where the lines of the central room converge above Christ's head. The small side room has its own vanishing point, and neither falls on the horizon of the landscape seen through the windows. Only the Last Supper and the Justice Panels are definitely his; the Last Judgment panels and the triptych of the Martyrdom of St Erasmus are fairly secure attributions, and many others are disputed. A retrospective, Dieric Bouts, Creator of Images, was held at the museum of Leuven in 2023.
dies-irae: The Dies irae is a Latin sequence, a medieval poem with accentual stress, rhymed lines and a trochaic metre. It is attributed to Thomas of Celano, a Franciscan, or to Latino Malabranca Orsini, a lector at the Dominican studium at Santa Sabina in Rome. Some sources trace it much further back, to Gregory the Great, Bernard of Clairvaux or Bonaventure. The text is found, with slight differences, in a 13th-century Franciscan calendar missal in the national library at Naples. The manuscript must date from 1253 to 1255, since it lacks the name of Clare of Assisi, who was canonised in 1255.

The hymn appears to draw on the Vulgate text of the prophet Zephaniah, 1:15-16, a day of wrath and tribulation, and on images from the Book of Revelation, from Matthew's account of the sheep and goats and from the Jewish prayer Unetanneh Tokef.

The poem describes the Last Judgment. A trumpet summons souls before the throne of God, where the saved are delivered and the unsaved cast into eternal flames. The last two stanzas differ in structure from the rest. The penultimate, the Lacrimosa, has two rhyming couplets in place of rhyming triplets, and the final stanza, Pie Iesu, has assonance instead of rhyme, with catalectic lines. Some scholars therefore think they were added to suit the poem to liturgical use.

The Dies irae was for centuries the sequence of the Requiem Mass in the Roman Rite, and it appears in the Roman Missal of 1962. Its place in the Mass is evident in the great settings by Mozart and Verdi. The liturgical reforms of 1969 and 1970 removed it from funerals and other Masses for the dead, on the ground that it overemphasised judgment, fear and despair. It was kept in an edited form as a hymn in the Liturgy of the Hours on All Souls' Day and in the last week before Advent.

The first polyphonic settings that include it are by Engarandus Juvenis in 1490 and Antoine Brumel in 1516. The plainchant melody, in the Dorian mode, became one of the most quoted in music, after Berlioz used it in the Symphonie fantastique. Walter Scott quoted its first two stanzas in The Lay of the Last Minstrel, and Goethe used three in the Cathedral scene of Faust. William Josiah Irons made an English version in 1849.
diesel-engine: In 1878 Rudolf Diesel, then a student at the Polytechnikum in Munich, attended the lectures of Carl von Linde, who explained that steam engines convert just 6 to 10 percent of heat energy into work, whereas the Carnot cycle allows much more. According to Diesel this gave him the idea of a highly efficient engine working on that cycle. He was also shown a fire piston, a traditional fire starter based on rapid compression.

Diesel sought firms to build the engine and, with help from Moritz Schröter and Max Gutermuth, persuaded both Krupp in Essen and the Maschinenfabrik Augsburg. He obtained a patent on 23 February 1893, signed a contract with Krupp on 10 April, and on 24 April both firms agreed to build a single prototype at Augsburg. In the winter of 1893 and 1894 he redesigned the engine and added an air-blast injection system. After the engine ran for 88 revolutions in February 1894 the Maschinenfabrik Augsburg's stock rose by 30 percent. The engine still caused problems, and Krupp considered cancelling its contract before a third prototype was rushed together.

In a diesel engine only air, or air mixed with exhaust gas, is compressed in the cylinder. The compression raises its temperature enough to ignite atomised fuel injected at high pressure, so no spark plug is needed. Torque is controlled by changing the amount of fuel injected rather than by throttling the air, and the engine is also called a compression-ignition engine. Its fuel efficiency is better than most other combustion engines because of the high compression ratio and the lack of throttling, reaching up to 43 percent in passenger cars and 55 percent in large two-stroke marine engines. High-speed engines above 1,000 rpm power trucks, buses, tractors and cars, while slow-speed engines run below 300 rpm.

In 1893 Diesel suggested that the engine might power lorries, and the first diesel lorries came to market in 1924. The first diesel locomotives appeared in 1913, and diesel engines later replaced steam on all non-electrified railways. Nearly all modern diesel locomotives are diesel–electric, the engine driving a generator that powers electric traction motors. Large ships use slow two-stroke diesels, and submarines are usually diesel–electric.

Before the Second World War diesel engines also powered aircraft, including the airship Hindenburg. Diesels drive construction and farm machinery and stationary generators. In passenger cars they were long popular in bigger models and have been used in smaller cars in Europe since the 1980s.
digambara: Digambara, Sanskrit for sky-clad, names one of the two major schools of Jainism, the other being Svetambara, the white-clad. Digambaras hold that they are the original followers of Mahavira, who taught that nakedness symbolised complete detachment and spared a monk the distraction of acquiring and washing garments. In tradition the schools divided in the time of Chandragupta Maurya (c. 324-297 BCE). A twelve-year famine struck Magadha, and a group of monks led by Bhadrabahu, said to be the last who knew the complete original canon, migrated south to Karnataka and kept to strict asceticism, including nudity. Monks who stayed in the north under Sthulabhadra took to wearing white robes. Digambaras say the northern group kept beliefs and practices they consider heretical.

The oldest archaeological evidence for Digambaras is the Mangalam inscriptions, which record stone beds made for Digambara monks by workers of the Pandyan king Netunceliyan I, around 270 BCE. Statues of tirthankaras from Mathura dated to the second century CE or later are naked, and Svetambara iconography appears there only from the late fifth century.

Digambara monks own nothing. They are wandering mendicants who carry a community-owned picchi, a broom of fallen peacock feathers used to brush insects from their path or seat so as not to kill them. The tradition shares the Jain principles of aparigraha, non-attachment, ahimsa, non-violence, and anekantavada, the many-sidedness of reality. Digambaras maintain that women cannot attain nirvana, while Svetambaras hold that women, and eunuchs, can. The two schools have differed in dress, temples and iconography, attitudes to female monastics, legends and the texts they treat as important.

Digambara monastic lineages trace their descent to Mahavira, among them the Mula Sangha and the Kashtha Sangha. For most of the second millennium CE ascetic life centred on lineages of bhattarakas. In the seventeenth century a lay movement at Agra led to the division into Terapanthi and Bisapanthi sub-sects, and the Terapanthis, led by Pandit Todarmal and Banarasidas, rejected the bhattarakas' authority.

From about the middle of the first millennium CE the Western Ganga, Rashtrakuta and Chalukya dynasties of the Deccan and south India patronised Digambara teachers. Under the Rashtrakuta dynasty the scholar Jinasena advised King Amoghavarsha I (r. 814-878 CE), and he and his disciple Gunabhadra wrote the Mahapurana. Jain caves at Ellora, such as the Indra Sabha, contain Digambara images. Kundakunda, author of the Samayasara and Pravacanasara, is regarded as the tradition's most significant scholar-monk. Digambara communities live today across India, including Rajasthan, Maharashtra, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
dijon: Dijon lies in a plain drained by two small converging rivers, the Suzon, which crosses the town mostly underground from north to south, and the Ouche on its southern side. South of the town rises the côte, the hillside of vineyards that gives the department its name. The city is about 310 km south-east of Paris and has a climate that is oceanic with continental influence. The Canal de Bourgogne passes through the city and links the Yonne and the Seine in the north-west with the Saône to the south-east; these waterways were largely completed before the 19th century and were the main means of industrial transport until railways took over in the mid-19th century.

The earliest archaeological finds within the city limits date to the Neolithic period. Dijon later became a Roman settlement called Divio, which may mean sacred fountain, on the road from Lyon to Paris. Saint Benignus, the city's apocryphal patron saint, is said to have introduced Christianity to the area before being martyred.

The province was home to the Dukes of Burgundy from the early 11th until the late 15th century, and Dijon was a place of great wealth and power and one of the major European centres of art, learning and science, with Dijon Abbey playing an influential role. The Palace of the Dukes of Burgundy now houses the city hall and the Museum of Fine Arts. In 1513 Swiss and Imperial armies invaded Burgundy and besieged Dijon, which the governor, Louis II de la Trémoille, defended. After long negotiations he persuaded the besiegers to withdraw. The population, which had called on the Virgin Mary for help, saw this as a miracle and began to venerate Notre-Dame de Bon-Espoir, Our Lady of Good Hope.

Dijon was occupied by anti-Napoleonic coalitions in 1814, by the Prussian army in 1870–71, and by Nazi Germany from June 1940. It was liberated by the French Army and the Resistance on 11 September 1944. Henry Darcy built a system of purified water for its citizens a quarter-century before Paris had one.

Dijon is the prefecture of the Côte-d'Or department, with 161,830 inhabitants in the commune in 2023. Its historic centre keeps Capetian, Gothic and Renaissance buildings, half-timbered houses of the 12th to 15th centuries and roofs of glazed terracotta tiles in geometric patterns. The Well of Moses, a sculpture by Claus Sluter, is among its best-known works. In 2015 UNESCO registered the historic centre as part of the Climats, terroirs of Burgundy World Heritage site. Dijon mustard dates from 1856, when Jean Naigeon substituted verjuice for vinegar.
dili: Dili lies on the northern coast of the island of Timor, on a small area of flat land hemmed in by mountains, facing the Ombai Strait of the Savu Sea. The central mountain range of Timor runs to the south and reaches the coast to the west and east of the core city. The climate is a rather dry tropical savanna one, with a rainy season from November to April and a dry season from May to October.

Early records about Timor are sparse, and the archives of Dili were destroyed in 1779, 1890, 1975 and 1999. Dili became the chief port and economic hub of what is now Timor-Leste when it was designated the capital of Portuguese Timor in 1769.

When the Pacific War began in 1941, Australian and Dutch troops were sent to Dili despite Portuguese objections, and the Japanese invaded in response. The Japanese left the Portuguese governor nominally in place but took over the administration, and much of Dili was destroyed by the invasion and by later Allied bombing. An Australian official told the Portuguese governor of the Japanese surrender on 23 September 1945, and the city returned to Portuguese control.

In 1975 a civil war between Timorese political parties led to a declaration of independence and then an Indonesian invasion. Under Indonesian rule the city was developed, with landmarks such as the Immaculate Conception Cathedral and the Cristo Rei of Dili, and its population passed 100,000. Resistance met violent repression, and a massacre in Dili brought international pressure that led to an independence referendum. After the vote for independence violence broke out, and up to 70 per cent of the country's infrastructure was destroyed in 1999, including 68,000 homes in Dili. A period of United Nations rule followed, and in 2002 Dili became the capital of independent Timor-Leste.

Dili is the capital and largest city of Timor-Leste and its chief port, with an international airport inside the city limits. The language of the locality is Tetum. The 2022 census counted 324,269 people in the Dili Municipality. Most of the country's universities are in the city, and the Immaculate Conception Cathedral and Cristo Rei remain its landmarks.
dillenburg: Dillenburg lies on the eastern edge of the Westerwald range, in the narrow valley of the Dill, which flows from the border of Hesse and Westphalia to Wetzlar and empties into the Lahn. The Dietzhölze flows into the Dill in the town. It was formerly the seat of the old Dillkreis district, now part of the Lahn-Dill-Kreis, and it lies on the Orange Route, a German-Dutch holiday road that joins places associated with the House of Orange-Nassau.

Dillenburg is first mentioned in a document of 1254 and was the ancestral seat of the Orange branch of the House of Nassau. The first castle on the Schlossberg was of wood, so that no pictures of it exist, and it was destroyed in the Dernbacher Feud. William I of Orange-Nassau, who was born in Dillenburg, organised the Dutch resistance against Spain from exile between 1567 and 1572. The land was administered by the presidents of the House of Nassau-Dillenburg. In the Seven Years' War the stately home was destroyed in 1760, and a street, Wilhelmstraße, was built out of its remains.

In 1797 one of the earliest schools of forestry in Europe, founded a decade earlier at Hungen by Georg Ludwig Hartig, was moved to Dillenburg. It continued there until 1805, when Hartig lost his position as Inspector of Forests for the Prince of Orange-Nassau after Napoleon dissolved the principality.

In the 19th century the building of the Deutz–Gießen railway and the use of iron ore found on the Lahn, Dill and Sieg brought the Industrial Revolution to the region, with many mines, foundries and metalworking works. Branch lines were built from Dillenburg to places such as Gönnern and Ewersbach. In the Second World War the town was a target of Allied attacks because of its marshalling yard, and Niederscheld, now part of the town, was bombed because parts for the V-2 rocket were built at the Adolfshütte. Ore mining later became ever less profitable, and the last blast furnace, in Oberscheld, ceased operations.

The Wilhelmsturm, built between 1872 and 1875 on the Schlossberg, is the landmark of the town and houses the Orange-Nassau Museum. The casemates beneath the former castle, from the 16th century, are among the biggest defensive works in Europe, and parts of them have been excavated and may be toured. Other buildings include the Evangelical Town Church of 1491, the Dillturm of 1597 and the Untertor, or Lower Gate, of 1344, with alterations in 1594 and 1737. The town is twinned with Breda, Diest, Hereford and Orange. In November 2017 its name was officially extended to Oranienstadt Dillenburg, to recall its connection with the House of Orange-Nassau.
dillingen-an-der-donau: Dillingen an der Donau lies in Swabia in Bavaria, Germany, and is the administrative centre of the district of Dillingen. Besides the town proper, the municipality includes the villages of Donaualtheim, Fristingen, Hausen, Kicklingen, Schretzheim and Steinheim. Schretzheim is notable for an Alemannic cemetery of the 6th to 7th century, with 630 row graves.

The counts of Dillingen ruled from the 10th to the 13th century, and in 1258 the territory was turned over to the prince-bishops of Augsburg. After the Reformation they moved to the Catholic city of Dillingen and made it one of the centres of the Counter-Reformation. A university there was closed by Napoleon in 1804, its philosophical and theological faculties still existed in the 20th century, and in 1971 it became part of an academy for teacher training.

In 1800, during the War of the Second Coalition, French armies under Jean Victor Moreau fought Habsburg regulars and Württemberg contingents under Pál Kray, who had taken refuge in the fortress at Ulm. Moreau approached from the east and, after a small group captured a foothold on the northern bank of the Danube, moved against the fortress on both sides of the river. This culmination of the Danube Campaign of 1800 forced Kray to abandon Ulm and withdraw into eastern Bavaria.

Natives and residents include the painter Heinrich Vogtherr, the theologian Johann Michael Sailer, who taught there and became Bishop of Regensburg in 1829, and the priest and hydrotherapist Sebastian Kneipp, who began his theological studies in Dillingen in 1848.
