The town is twinned with Bondeno in Italy, Brand-Erbisdorf in Germany and Naas in Ireland.
dilmun: Dilmun was an East Semitic-speaking civilisation of Eastern Arabia, mentioned from the 3rd millennium BCE onwards. It lay in the Persian Gulf on a trade route between Mesopotamia and the Indus Valley Civilisation, close to the sea and to artesian springs, and it encompassed Bahrain, Kuwait and eastern Saudi Arabia. Its land was then fertile, thanks to wells that have since dried and to a much wetter climate. Its people wrote cuneiform in the Akkadian language, and its main deity was Inzak, whose spouse was Panipa. In Sumerian myth Dilmun is a paradisiacal land in the story of Enki and Ninhursag, and the place where the flood hero Ziusudra was taken by the gods to live forever.

Dilmun was an important trading centre from the late 4th millennium to 800 BCE. It first appears in Sumerian clay tablets of the late 3rd millennium BCE found in the temple of Inanna at Uruk, and an inscription of Ur-Nanshe of Lagash, around 2300 BCE, says that the ships of Dilmun brought him wood as tribute. Metals such as copper, wood, perfumes and pearls came from Dilmun to Ur, and timber, ivory, lapis lazuli and gold also reached Mesopotamia. Weights and measures at Dilmun were identical to those of the Indus and not to those of southern Mesopotamia.

From around 2050 BCE Dilmun seems to have been at its peak, with Qal'at al-Bahrain probably its capital and the largest royal burial mounds raised. A decline is visible from around 1720 BCE and a recovery from about 1650 BCE. From at least 1500 BCE Dilmun was probably ruled by the Mesopotamian Sealand dynasty and then by the Kassite dynasty of Babylon. Assyrian inscriptions of 1250 to 1050 BCE claim its tribute, and Babylonian records of 567 BCE place it under the king of Babylon. Its commercial power declined between 1000 and 800 BCE as piracy flourished. The name fell from use after Babylon collapsed in 538 BCE, and the area was later called Tylos in the Hellenistic period.

The Barbar Temple was the first part of Dilmun society to be rediscovered, by Geoffrey Bibby and Peter Glob from 1954. Dilmun is generally located in the Gulf region, though one archaeologist, Theresa Howard-Carter, proposed in 1987 an unidentified mound near the Shatt al-Arab between Qurnah and Basra, and some scholars think the name first denoted the eastern province of modern Saudi Arabia.
dima-hasao: From about 1500 the area was part of the Dimasa Kingdom, also called the Kachar kingdom, which had its capital at Maibang and Dimapur. In the colonial period Khaspur in the present Cachar district became its administrative centre, and an internal schism divided the old kingdom. The last Dimasa king, Govinda Chandra Hasnusa, assigned the hilly tract to Kashi Chandra, who soon declared independence and was murdered by the king.

Kashi Chandra's son Tularam Senapati kept up the struggle and, with British help, carved out his own territory; in 1829 David Scott, the British agent, recognised him as ruler of the hilly tract. After Tularam died in 1850, Angami raids and an incident at Semkhor village opened the way to British influence, and in 1852 the territory was annexed to the Nowgong district of British Assam.

The subdivision was abolished in 1866 and shared among three districts, and in 1880 the present area became a subdivision of Cachar with its headquarters first at Gunjung and from 1895 at Haflong. On 17 November 1951 the United Mikir and North Cachar Hills District was created, and on 2 February 1970 the North Cachar Hills became a district of their own. On 30 March 2010 it was renamed Dima Hasao, which means Dimasa Hills in the Dimasa language.

Dima Hasao covers 4,888 square kilometres, with Haflong as its headquarters, and is one of two autonomous hill districts of Assam. It has Sixth Schedule status under the Constitution of India and is administered by the Dima Hasao Autonomous Council, which controls almost every department except the police and law and order.

It has three subdivisions: Haflong, Maibang and Diyungbra. Its tribal population includes Dimasa Kachari, Zeme Naga, Hmar, Kuki, Karbi and Khasi people. At Maibang stands a rock-cut temple of the goddess Ranachandi, or Mahamaya, carved from a single block of black sandstone. Jatinga village is known for birds that appear to fall dead between September and November.
dimapur: Many historians explain the name as the city of the Dimasa people, from the Dimasa Kachari words di, water, ma, big, and pur, settlement. The Ahom chronicles, the Buranjis, sometimes call it Che-din-chi-pen, brick town, and European scholars also described it as the Brick City. The city is said to have been founded by the Kachari king Mahamanipha, who ruled from 1330 to 1370, and it remained the capital of the Kacharis until the Ahom ruler Suhungmung captured it.

Between 1406 and 1439 the Ming dynasty had political contacts with the Dimasa and neighbouring kingdoms. In 1406 the Ming made the Dimasa kingdom a tusi and set up a Pacification Superintendency, with Lawangpa as superintendent, and the chieftain sent horses and local products as tribute. The ruins in Dimapur include a brick wall nearly 2 miles long and two tanks about 300 yards square, which show a city of considerable size. In the early 19th century the Dimasa chiefs, with the help of Brahmins, claimed descent from Hidimba.

Dimapur is the largest city and municipality in Nagaland, near the border with Assam on the banks of the Dhansiri River, a tributary of the Brahmaputra. During the Second World War it was the centre of action between British India and Imperial Japan and an important logistics hub and staging post for the Allied offensive. Reinforcements came through it by rail and road after the Japanese reached Kohima, about 77 kilometres away, and an airfield supplied forces in Burma.

The city is the main gateway and commercial centre of Nagaland, and its railway station is the second busiest in north-east India. Its population is a mix of people from all over India, and it is known as Mini India. Christianity and Hinduism are its largest religions. The ruins of the Kachari Rajbari are a national heritage site, and the Dimapur Jain Temple was built in 1947.
dimitrie-cantemir: Dimitrie Cantemir was born in Silişteni, Moldavia, on 26 October 1673, the son of Constantin Cantemir and Ana Bantăș, a learned daughter of a local noble family. His surname is of Turkic or Tatar origin. In 1685 the Ottoman overlords named Constantin voivode of Moldavia. Although Constantin himself was illiterate, he educated his sons Dimitrie and Antioh thoroughly, and Dimitrie learned Greek and Latin as a child. Between 1687 and 1710 he spent most of his time in Constantinople as a hostage or envoy, learning Turkish, studying Ottoman history at the Patriarchate's Greek Academy and composing Ottoman music. When Constantin died in 1693 Dimitrie briefly succeeded him but was passed over within three weeks in favour of Constantin Duca.

Appointed voivode again in 1710, Cantemir believed that Ottoman Turkey was collapsing. By a secret agreement at Lutsk he placed Moldavia under Russian control and joined Peter the Great in his war against the Turks. The campaign ended in failure at Stănilești in July 1711, and the Cantemirs were forced into exile in Russia. Native voivodes of Moldavia were replaced by Greek phanariots. In 1712 Peter presented him with the Bogorodskoye District. Cantemir was made a Russian prince by Peter and a prince of the Holy Roman Empire by Charles VI, and lived on an estate at Dmitrovka near Oryol. He died there on 21 August 1723, the day he was awarded his German title, and in 1935 his remains were returned to Iași.

Cantemir was a polyglot, speaking and writing eleven languages, and wrote as philosopher, historian, composer, musicologist, linguist, ethnographer and geographer. In 1714 he became a member of the Royal Academy of Berlin. His History of the Growth and Decay of the Ottoman Empire circulated in manuscript for years, was printed in London in 1734 and remained the standard work on the Ottoman Empire until the middle of the 19th century; Edward Gibbon used it. Later scholarship contests many points because some of his sources were doubtful.

For the Berlin Academy he wrote the Descriptio Moldaviae in 1714, covering geography, ethnography and economy, and drew a manuscript map of Moldavia which was the first real map of the country. His Chronicle of the Antiquity of the Romano-Moldavo-Wallachians asserted the Latin origin of the Romanian language. A Hieroglyphic History of 1705 is considered the first Romanian novel. In music he composed about forty Ottoman pieces and preserved 350 traditional instrumental works in a notation of his own in Edvar-i Musiki.
dinant: Dinant lies in the Upper Meuse valley, in the Ardennes, where the river cuts deeply into the western Condroz plateau. Between the rock face and the river the original settlement had little room, and the town grew into a long, thin line along the river shore. The navigable river carried the raw materials of its brassware to the workshops and the finished goods away, and the limestone cliffs above supported a quarrying industry producing black marble and bluestone. Its name comes from the Celtic Divo-Nanto, meaning Sacred Valley.

The area was populated in Neolithic, Celtic and Roman times. Dinant is first mentioned as a settlement in the 7th century, when Perpète of Maastricht, Bishop of Tongeren, moved his main residence there and founded the church of Saint Vincent. In the 11th century the emperor Henry IV granted the Prince-Bishopric of Liège market and justice rights over the town, which became one of its 23 principal cities, the bonnes villes. The first stone bridge on the Meuse dates from the end of that century.

In 1466, during the Liège Wars, Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy, and his son Charles the Bold punished an uprising by casting 800 burghers into the Meuse and setting fire to the city. Late medieval Dinant and its rival Bouvignes specialised in dinanderie, objects cast and finished in a silvery brass alloy, among them aquamaniles, candlesticks and altar furniture, supplied through the Meuse valley and the Rhineland. After the Bishopric of Liège was ceded to France in 1795, the dinanderies fell out of fashion and the economy rested on leather tanning and playing cards.

On 15 August 1914 French and German troops fought for the town in the Battle of Dinant, and on 23 August Saxon troops of the German Army summarily executed 674 inhabitants, the largest massacre committed by the Germans in 1914. In 1940 Erwin Rommel's 7th Panzer Division took the town on 13 May after crossing the Meuse.

Dinant is a town of the province of Namur, in Wallonia, about 30 km south of the city of Namur. Its landmark is the Collegiate Church of Notre Dame, rebuilt in Gothic style after falling rock from the cliff partly destroyed the Romanesque church in 1227, with an onion-domed tower. Above it rises the Citadel, first built in the 11th century and rebuilt in 1821.
diocletian: Diocletian was born Diocles to a family of low status in the Roman province of Dalmatia, probably at or near Salona. The first forty years of his life are mostly obscure. He was an Illyrian soldier who served under Aurelian and Probus, and in 282 Emperor Carus made him commander of the Protectores domestici, the elite cavalry attached to the imperial household, which earned him a consulship in 283.

After Carus died in 283, his sons Numerian and Carinus became joint emperors. Numerian was found dead in a closed coach in Bithynia, and Eutropius and Aurelius Victor both describe the death as an assassination. The army proclaimed Diocles emperor under the name Diocletianus, and he defeated Carinus at the Battle of the Margus.

Diocletian judged that rule by one man was too dangerous, since Aurelian and Probus had been assassinated. In 286 he raised Maximian to the rank of Augustus to rule the West, while he governed the East. On 1 March 293 each appointed a junior colleague with the title Caesar: Constantius for Maximian and Galerius for Diocletian. This rule of four is known as the Tetrarchy. He campaigned against the Sarmatians and Carpi, built forts along the Danube, and in 299 made a favourable peace with Persia after Galerius had sacked Ctesiphon.

He separated and enlarged the civil and military services, reorganised the provinces and established new administrative centres at Nicomedia, Mediolanum, Sirmium and Treverorum, nearer the frontiers than Rome. He styled himself an autocrat, with an imposing court ceremony. He turned requisition into a tax based on heads and land, tied to a regular census. His Edict on Maximum Prices of 301, an attempt to curb inflation, was counterproductive and quickly ignored.

In 303 Diocletian ordered the persecution of Christians. According to Lactantius, he first believed that excluding Christians from the bureaucracy and army would be enough, while Galerius pushed for their extermination. It became the last, largest and bloodiest official persecution of Christianity in the empire, and it failed to eliminate it.

Weakened by illness, he left office on 1 May 305, the first Roman emperor to abdicate voluntarily. He retired to a fortified palace near Spalatum on the Dalmatian coast, which forms the historic core of Split. His tetrarchic system collapsed after his abdication, and civil wars followed until Constantine defeated Licinius in 324.
diodorus-siculus: Diodorus gives his birthplace in his own work as Agyrium in Sicily, now called Agira. Apart from his writings, antiquity provides almost nothing about his life. The only other notice is in the Chronicon of Jerome, which records under the year of Abraham 1968, equated with 49 BCE, that Diodorus of Sicily, a writer of Greek history, became illustrious. His English translator, Charles Henry Oldfather, remarked on a striking coincidence: one of only two known Greek inscriptions from Agyrium is the tombstone of a Diodorus, the son of Apollonius. The last work attributed to him is dated to 21 BCE.

His universal history, which he named Bibliotheca historica or Historical Library, was written between 60 and 30 BCE and ran to forty books. Books 1 to 5 and 11 to 20 survive; fragments of the lost books are preserved in Photius and in the Excerpts of Constantine Porphyrogenitus. The first section, books I to VI, treats the mythic history of non-Hellenic and Hellenic peoples up to the destruction of Troy and is geographical in plan. It describes ancient Egypt in book I, Mesopotamia, India, Scythia and Arabia in book II, North Africa in book III, and Greece and Europe in books IV to VI.

The second section, books VII to XVII, covers the world from the Trojan War to the death of Alexander the Great. The third, from book XVII to the end, runs from Alexander's successors to either 60 BCE or the beginning of Julius Caesar's Gallic Wars. Because the end is lost, it is unclear whether Diodorus reached the Gallic War, as he promised at the start, or stopped at 60 BCE, perhaps old and tired from his labours.

The title acknowledges that the work was assembled from many sources. The authors on whom he drew include Hecataeus of Abdera, Ctesias of Cnidus, Ephorus, Theopompus, Hieronymus of Cardia, Duris of Samos, Diyllus, Philistus, Timaeus, Polybius and Posidonius.
diogenes-the-cynic: Diogenes was born in Sinope, a Milesian colony on the Black Sea, the son of Hicesias, a money-changer. He and his father were accused of debasing the currency. Ancient sources disagree on who was responsible, and modern scholars are divided: some see the episode as a fiction symbolising his aim to revalue the currency, meaning to challenge conventional values, while others point to debased Sinopean coins as evidence of a historical core. It is unclear whether he was banished or fled. Plutarch notes that the hardships of exile made him a philosopher.

Diogenes advocated a shameless life lived according to nature rather than social convention. He lived by begging, sheltered in a large ceramic storage jar, and was said to wander the marketplace by day with a lit lamp, saying that he was looking for a man, that is, a wise man. Asked where he came from, he answered kosmopolitēs, a citizen of the world. Plato is said to have called him Socrates gone mad.

According to Diogenes Laertius, he wrote dialogues, letters and tragedies, none of which survive. The best-known anecdote has Alexander the Great, probably in 336 BCE at the Isthmus of Corinth, ask whether he wanted anything; Diogenes replied that Alexander should stand a little out of his sun, and Plutarch reports Alexander as saying that if he were not Alexander he would be Diogenes.

Ancient sources give several accounts of his death, among them self-asphyxiation, a raw octopus and an infected dog bite. A story that he died on the same night as Alexander is probably legend, and one modern scholar thinks he most plausibly died of old age, in or near Corinth. The Corinthians arranged his funeral and buried him outside the city walls. After his death Cynicism diverged: one branch, founded by Zeno of Citium, evolved into Stoicism, while another, beginning with Crates of Thebes, preserved his principles until Sallustius of Emesa in the 5th century CE. His attitude to the rich gave the word cynicism its modern sense.
diogo-cao: Little is known of the early life of Diogo Cão, who is also called Diogo Cam. According to tradition he was born in Vila Real, Portugal, around 1452, and his grandfather Gonçalo Cão had fought for Portuguese independence at the Battle of Aljubarrota. By 1480 he was sailing off the coast of Africa in the service of King João II, and there is a record that he returned to Portugal with captured Spanish ships.

The Treaty of Alcáçovas of 1480 confirmed Portugal's monopoly on trade and exploration along Africa's west coast. João II sent a fleet in 1481 to build the fortress of São Jorge da Mina on the Gold Coast and restarted the programme of exploration southward. Cão was chosen to lead the first voyage, in 1482.

Cão filled his ship with stone pillars, called padrões, surmounted by the cross of the Order of Christ and engraved with the Portuguese royal arms, to be erected at significant landmarks. He stopped at São Jorge da Mina to resupply, reached the mouth of the Congo River and marked it with a padrão on Shark Point. He sailed a short way up the river and began modest trade with the people of the Bakongo kingdom. Told that their king lived farther upriver, he sent four Christian native messengers to find him, and went on south along the coast of present-day Angola, raising a second padrão at Cabo de Santa Maria.

On his return to the Congo he found that his messengers had not come back, and he took four local men visiting his ship to Portugal. He reached Lisbon by 8 April 1484, where João II ennobled him and granted him an annuity and a coat of arms showing two padrões. On the second voyage, of 1484 to 1486, he carried the four men home and sailed about 170 kilometres up the Congo to the Yellala Falls, where an inscription records his passage. He set up two more padrões, at Cabo Negro and Cape Cross, the latter probably marking the end of his progress southward.

Information about his death is scanty and contradictory. A legend on Martin Behaim's globe reads hic moritur, here he dies, which seems to place his death on the African coast in 1486, but the historian João de Barros never mentions it. All four of his pillars have been found on their original sites. Those of the Kongo estuary, Cabo Negro and Cabo de Santa Maria are in the Museum of the Lisbon Geographical Society, and the Cape Cross pillar, long in Berlin, has been returned to Namibia. Fernando Pessoa's poem Padrão, in his book Mensagem, takes Cão as its subject.
diomedes: In myth Diomedes was the son of Tydeus and Deipyle. Tydeus, an Aetolian of royal blood and the son of Oeneus, king of Calydon, was exiled for killing relatives and found refuge at Argos, where King Adrastus gave him his daughter Deipyle in marriage. Tydeus died among the Seven against Thebes, and according to the Iliad Diomedes was then a small child. He later succeeded his maternal grandfather Adrastus as king of Argos.

According to Homer, Diomedes came to Troy with 80 ships, a contribution third only to those of Agamemnon (100) and Nestor (90), with Sthenelus, his charioteer and probably closest friend, and Euryalus fighting under him. He is the key fighter in the first third of the Iliad. He is the only human besides Heracles granted strength to fight immortals, and he wounded both Ares and Aphrodite in a single day, yet he retreated before Apollo, which some interpreters read as his keeping within mortal limits.

Diomedes was a companion of Odysseus, and both were favourites of Athena. After the seer Helenus revealed that Troy would not fall while the Palladium, an image of Athena, stood inside its walls, the two stole it, and Diomedes is generally regarded as the one who carried it to the ships. After Troy fell, Diomedes and Nestor decided to leave at once, and Diomedes reached Argos four days later, one of the few Achaean commanders to return safely.

Tradition says Diomedes went to Daunia in Apulia, where King Daunus gave him land and his daughter Euippe in return for help against the Messapians. He built Argyrippa, hosted Aeneas there and gave back the Palladium, as an oracle had told him to give it to a Trojan. The Greeks and Romans credited him with founding many towns in southern Italy, among them Arpi, Beneventum, Brundusium, Canusium, Venafrum, Ancona, Adria and Venusia.

Strabo lists four traditions of his end: he went home to Argos and died, he stayed at Urium, he disappeared on the island of Diomedea in the Adriatic, whose birds were said to be his companions, or he stayed among the Heneti and was mysteriously deified. Pindar says Athena made him immortal. Hero cults of Diomedes are attested in Cyprus, Metapontum and along the Adriatic coast. At Argos his shield was carried through the streets with the Palladium at the festival of Athena. In the Inferno Dante places him in the Eighth Circle of Hell, among the counsellors of fraud.
dionysia: The Dionysia consisted of two related festivals, the Rural Dionysia and the City Dionysia, held in different parts of the year. The rural festival was originally held at Eleutherae in Attica to celebrate the cultivation of vines, and took place in the winter month of Poseideon. Its central event was a procession in which phalloi were carried, accompanied by basket-carriers and bearers of loaves, water jars and goatskin bags of wine. Contests of dancing and singing followed, and in larger towns such as Piraeus and Eleusis there may have been dramatic performances. Aristophanes parodied the rural festival in The Acharnians, and his description is the earliest surviving account.

The City Dionysia was established under the tyranny of Peisistratus in the 6th century BCE. It was held probably from the 10th to the 16th of the month Elaphebolion, in March and April, and was run by the archon, who chose two assistants and ten curators. By tradition it began when Eleutherae joined Attica and brought a statue of Dionysus to Athens, where it was at first rejected; Dionysus then sent a plague, which ended when the Athenians accepted the cult. On the first day citizens, metics and delegates from colonies carried the statue to the Theatre of Dionysus.

The next day, at the proagon, playwrights announced the titles of their plays and judges were chosen by lot. Tradition holds that Thespis gave the first tragedy at the festival in 534 BCE. In the 5th century BCE three playwrights each presented three tragedies and a satyr play on successive days, and from 487 or 486 BCE comic poets also competed, each with one play. Most surviving Greek tragedies, including those of Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, were first performed in the Theatre of Dionysus. Winners received a wreath of ivy.

Tragic output continued through most of the 4th century BCE, and at least one older play was revived each year. New plays were written until the 2nd century BCE, when new works of comedy and tragedy appear to have ceased. Drama continued, but prizes went to wealthy producers and prominent actors rather than to the long-dead playwrights. Knowledge of the winners comes from damaged inscriptions, the Fasti, the Didascaliae and the Victors Lists. Modern followers of Hellenism celebrate the Dionysia as a holiday.
dionysius-i-of-syracuse: Dionysius was the son of Hermocrates, a prominent Syracusan general, and began his working life as a clerk in public office. His achievements in the war against Carthage that began in 409 BCE led to his election as supreme military commander in 406 BCE, and in the following year he seized total power.

He seized it with the help of mercenaries, initially 600 men and later 1,000, granted to him as a bodyguard after he faked an attack on his own life. Having consolidated his position he imposed them on the whole community, which signalled the end of democracy in Syracuse. He was married at the same time to Aristomache, who bore him a daughter, Arete, and to Doris of Locris, mother of his son Dionysius II.

Dionysius fought a war with Carthage from 397 to 392 BCE with mixed success. He failed to drive the Carthaginians out of Sicily, and at his death they still held at least a third of it. In southern Italy he led an expedition against the Italiote League in 387 BCE, joined by the Lucanians, devastated the lands of Thurii and Croton, and took Rhegium in 386 after a long siege, selling its inhabitants as slaves. Sparta did not condemn his autocracy and even helped establish it, and he allowed Sparta to conscript mercenaries and assisted it in the Corinthian War with mercenaries and ships.

Around 387 to 385 BCE he began an intensive colonisation of the Adriatic, to dominate the sea routes to the grain markets of the Po Delta, gain access to Epirus and the riches of Delphi. He made pacts with the Illyrians and the Senones, and founded or settled Ancona, Adria, Issa and Lissos. This gave him control of the routes that carried Po Valley grain to Greece.

Sources differ on his death in 367 BCE. According to some he drank himself to death after his tragedy The Ransom of Hector won a prize at the Lenaia festival in Athens. Cicero and Diodorus Siculus report natural causes shortly after the news of the victory. Others say his physicians gave him an overdose of a sleeping potion at the instigation of his son Dionysius the Younger, who succeeded him, and Justin claims a conspiracy of his own kin, though a modern historian finds no evidence for it.

The ancients regarded him as the worst kind of despot, cruel, suspicious and vindictive. He was one of the first Greek rulers given divine honours in his lifetime, and his innovations in military technique, such as siege engines, became standard under Alexander the Great and later generals.
dionysus: Dionysus is the god of wine-making, orchards, fruit, vegetation, fertility, festivity, ritual madness, religious ecstasy and theatre. Nineteenth-century scholars often regarded him as a foreign deity admitted late into the Greek pantheon, since his myths so often show a god who travels abroad and struggles for acceptance on his return. Later evidence has shown him to be among the earliest gods attested on the Greek mainland. His name, written di-wo-nu-so, appears on Linear B tablets from Mycenaean Pylos that link him with offerings of wine. His worship was firmly established by the seventh century BCE.

Wine was a religious focus of the cult and was regarded as the god's earthly incarnation. It could ease suffering, bring joy and inspire divine madness. His thyrsus, a fennel stalk sometimes wound with ivy, was both a wand and a weapon against those who opposed him. His procession was made up of female followers, the maenads, and of satyrs. In the Orphic tradition the first Dionysus was a son of Zeus and Persephone, dismembered by the Titans and reborn. In another account Zeus took the infant from the womb of Semele, a daughter of Cadmus, after she was killed by a thunderbolt, and so he is called the one with two mothers.

In myth he discovered the vine, was driven mad by Hera, and was cured by the goddess Cybele. He travelled through Asia and to India, and when Alexander the Great reached a city called Nysa near the Indus, the locals said that Dionysus had founded it.

The Rural Dionysia, held in the winter month of Poseideon, centred on a procession followed by dramatic performances and competitions. The Anthesteria, an Athenian festival at the beginning of spring, opened the wine vats and was believed to let the dead rise from the underworld. In Rome the cult was established around 200 BCE in the Aventine grove of Stimula, near the temple of Liber Pater, with whom Bacchus was identified. The Roman state treated independent festivals of Bacchus, the Bacchanalia, as subversive, and made their celebration a capital offence except in forms it approved and supervised. The festivals' sacred dramas were the initial driving force behind the development of theatre in Western culture.
dipendra-of-nepal: Dipendra Bir Bikram Shah Dev was born on 27 June 1971 at the Narayanhiti Royal Palace, the eldest child of Birendra, then Crown Prince of Nepal, and Princess Aishwarya. He was educated at Kanti Ishwori High School in Kathmandu and Budhanilkantha School, then at Eton College in the United Kingdom and Tri Chandra College, and later joined the Nepalese Military Academy at Kharipati. He studied geography at Tribhuvan University for a master's degree and was a doctoral student there, and he received further military training and pilot training.

He was interested in social services and sports, became a karateka while studying in the United Kingdom and received a black belt at around the age of 20. He was a patron of the National Sports Council and the Nepal Scouts, and he wrote articles for Nepalese periodicals, often on nationhood and nationality.

On 1 June 2001 Dipendra opened fire at a party in a house on the grounds of the Narayanhiti Royal Palace. According to the official inquiry's findings he shot and killed his father King Birendra, his mother Queen Aishwarya, his younger brother Prince Nirajan, his younger sister Princess Shruti, his uncle Prince Dhirendra, his aunts Princess Shanti and Princess Sharada, his cousin Princess Jayanti and his uncle-in-law Kumar Khadga Bikram Shah, before shooting himself in the head. Because his father was dead he succeeded as king while in a coma. He died on 4 June 2001, after three days as king, and his uncle Gyanendra succeeded him.

His motives remain unknown. A leading theory holds that he wished to marry Devyani Rana, whom he had met in England, and that his parents objected and told him he would have to give up his right to succeed to do so. Other theories hold that he was unhappy with the shift from absolute to constitutional monarchy after the 1990 People's Movement.
diponegoro: Diponegoro was born on 11 November 1785 in Yogyakarta. In his youth the VOC was dissolved, the British invaded Java and Dutch rule returned. He advised his father during the British period and helped British forces so far that Stamford Raffles offered him the sultan's title, which he declined. When his father died in 1814, the Dutch supported his younger half-brother Hamengkubuwono IV, although the late sultan had urged that Diponegoro succeed him.

A devout Muslim who lived in seclusion, Diponegoro was alarmed by the laxity in religious observance at his half-brother's court and by its pro-Dutch policy. Famine and plague spread in 1821. After Hamengkubuwono IV died in 1822 in mysterious circumstances, leaving an infant heir, Diponegoro was passed over again, though he believed he had been promised the succession.

Dutch rule was unpopular with farmers because of rising taxes and failed harvests, and with nobles who had lost the right to lease land. Many believed Diponegoro to be the Ratu Adil, the just ruler foretold in the Pralembang Jayabaya, and the eruption of Mount Merapi in 1822 and a cholera epidemic in 1824 suggested that a cataclysm was near. The Java War began in 1825. Diponegoro's guerrilla tactics, ambushes and denial of supplies inflicted heavy losses on the Dutch at first. General De Kock then adopted a strategy of fortified camps and mobile forces, and from 1829 Diponegoro lost the initiative.
His forces also attacked the Chinese minority in Java, for example at Ngawi and along the Bengawan Solo, and the relationship between the Chinese and the Javanese was never the same afterwards.

In March 1830 Diponegoro was invited to negotiate at Magelang under a flag of truce and was taken prisoner on 28 March. He saw this as a betrayal, while the Dutch said he had surrendered, and the painters Raden Saleh and Nicolaas Pieneman later depicted the scene in opposite ways. He was taken to Manado in 1830 and moved to Fort Rotterdam in Makassar in July 1833. His wife and some followers went with him. There he wrote his autobiography, the Babad Diponegoro.

Diponegoro died in Makassar on 8 January 1855, aged 69, and was buried in Kampung Melayu on land the Dutch donated; his tomb is visited by pilgrims today. Indonesians remember his struggle as an inspiration for the National Revolution, and in 1973 he was made a National Hero of Indonesia. An army regional command, a university in Semarang and warships are named for him. In March 2020 King Willem-Alexander of the Netherlands gave a kris identified as Diponegoro's to Indonesia, although there is doubt whether it is the original.
dirham: The word dirham ultimately comes from drachma, the Greek coin. The Greek-speaking Byzantine Empire lay partly in the Levant and traded with Arabia, and the coin circulated there in pre-Islamic times and afterward. Near the end of the 7th century it became an Islamic currency, bearing the name of the sovereign and a religious verse. The Arabs introduced their own coins. The Ottoman dirham was based on the Sasanian drachm, written drahm in Middle Persian, which was itself based on the Greek dram or drachma.

The dirham, also spelled dirhem or drahm, is a unit of currency and of mass, and it was historically a silver coin. As a unit of mass it was used across North Africa, the Middle East and Persia, with varying values. The Islamic dirham was 8 daniq, and ten dirhams were equal to seven mithqal, or 2.975 grams of silver. In the late Ottoman Empire the standard dirham was 3.207 grams, and 400 dirhems made one oka. In Egypt in 1895 it was equivalent to 47.661 troy grains, or 3.088 grams.

The Islamic dirham was struck in many Mediterranean countries, including Al-Andalus, and the Byzantine Empire struck a related silver coin, the miliaresion. Between the 10th and 12th centuries it could be used as currency in Europe, notably in areas with Viking connections such as Viking York and Dublin.

Jewish law mentions the dirham as a unit of weight, for example for the silver pledged in marriage contracts and for the quantity of flour from which a portion of dough must be separated. Maimonides, in his commentary on the Mishnah, used the Egyptian dirham to estimate that quantity, and later rabbis gave differing weights for it, from about 3.0 to 3.36 grams. The name dirham remains the name of the currencies of Morocco, the United Arab Emirates and Armenia.
diriyah: The ruins of old Diriyah lie on either side of the narrow valley known as Wadi Hanifa. Built almost entirely of mud brick, they are divided into three districts, Ghussaibah, Al-Mulaybeed and Turaif, set on hills overlooking the valley. Turaif is the highest. Part of the city wall, also of mud brick, still stands along the edges of the wadi with some high observation towers. The modern town stands lower, at the foot of the hill, and north of it in the valley lie gardens, palm groves and small farms.

According to the chroniclers of Nejd, the city was founded in 1446-47 by Mani' Al-Muraydi, an ancestor of the Saudi royal family. He and his clan came from the area of Al-Qatif in eastern Arabia at the invitation of Ibn Dir', then ruler of a group of settlements that now make up Riyadh, and the settlement was named after him. It first occupied Ghusaybah and Al-Mulaybeed, and Turaif was settled later. By the 18th century Diriyah was a well-known town in Nejd.

Muhammad ibn Saud emerged from a struggle within the ruling family, the Al Miqrin, and became emir. In 1744 he took in the religious scholar Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab, and he agreed to implement his views. The First Saudi State was born, with its capital at Diriyah. Within decades Ibn Saud and his descendants subjugated all of Nejd and the eastern and western regions of Arabia. Their conquest of Mecca and Medina drew the anger of the Ottoman Empire and led to the Ottoman-Saudi War of 1811 to 1818.

In 1818 an Egyptian army under Ibrahim Pasha entered Diriyah after a siege of about six months, destroyed the houses and cut down every tree in the palm groves. The Egyptians were estimated to have lost 10,000 men and the Saudi forces 1,800. When the Saudis revived their fortunes in 1824 and again in 1902, they made their capital at Riyadh. The area was resettled in the late 20th century, and a new town founded in the late 1970s is now the seat of its own governorate.

Among the historic structures are Salwa Palace, the largest on the site, which rises four storeys and was probably finished by Saud ibn Abdul Aziz, imam from 1803 to 1814; the Saad bin Saud Palace; and the mosque of Imam Muhammad bin Saud, where Imam Abd al-Aziz bin Muhammad was assassinated while leading prayer in November 1803. At-Turaif District was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2010.
dirty-war: In 1955 the Argentine military removed Juan Perón from the presidency in the Revolución Libertadora, and Peronism was then proscribed. Resistance came from workplaces and trade unions, and over the following decade leftist guerrilla groups arose, among them the Uturuncos and the People's Guerrilla Army. Perón died on 1 July 1974 and was succeeded by his vice-president and third wife, Isabel Perón. Paramilitary groups, mostly the Triple A death squad run by José López Rega, carried out hundreds of killings in these years. The exact start of the repression is debated: some date it to 1969, others to the Trelew massacre of 1972, the Triple A in 1973 or Isabel Perón's decrees of 1975 against the guerrillas. The military overthrew her on 24 March 1976.

The military junta used the name Dirty War, claiming that a war with different methods was needed to keep social order and eradicate subversives. Human rights groups have rejected the term because it implies a civil war and a justification for the killings. At the 1985 trial the prosecutor Julio Strassera called it a euphemism. The targets were guerrillas and sympathisers, but also students, trade unionists, writers, journalists and artists. Estimates of those killed or disappeared run from 13,000 to 30,000, many of them impossible to document.

Victims were held incommunicado in clandestine detention centres, at least 340 by later findings, and tortured. About 3,000 deaths are estimated at the Navy Engineering School alone. Some prisoners were drugged and thrown alive from aircraft over the Río de la Plata in what became known as death flights, one of which was organised by the navy captain Adolfo Scilingo. Children born in the camps or taken with their parents were given to other families; the Grandmothers of the Plaza de Mayo had records of 172 at the time of the national inquiry. The Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo held their first vigil in 1977.

Economic collapse, public discontent and the Falklands War ended the junta. After the 1983 elections President Raúl Alfonsín set up the National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons, led by the writer Ernesto Sábato, which documented the disappearance of nearly 9,000 people by name. In 1985 the nine members of the juntas were tried, and Jorge Rafael Videla was sentenced to life imprisonment. Nearly 300 people were prosecuted.

Laws that had granted pardons were repealed by Congress in 2003 and declared unconstitutional by the Supreme Court in 2005, and prosecutions resumed in 2006. In that year 24 March was made a public holiday, the Day of Remembrance for Truth and Justice.
dissolution-of-czechoslovakia: Czechoslovakia was created with the end of Austria-Hungary after the First World War. In 1918, at a meeting in Pittsburgh, Tomáš Garrigue Masaryk and other Czech and Slovak representatives signed the Pittsburgh Agreement, which promised a common state of two equal nations, Slovaks and Czechs. The Czechoslovak Constitution of 1920, however, specified a single Czechoslovak nation. Political tension followed between Czechoslovakists and those seeking greater autonomy for the Slovaks. In March 1939, under pressure from Adolf Hitler, the First Slovak Republic was created as a German satellite state, and after the war the two parts were reunited in the Third Czechoslovak Republic. In 1969 the Czech Socialist Republic and the Slovak Socialist Republic became constituent states of the federation.

After the Velvet Revolution of 1989 ended communist rule, many Czechs and Slovaks wanted to keep a federal state. By 1991 the Czech Republic's GDP per capita was some 20 per cent higher than Slovakia's, and transfer payments from the Czech budget to Slovakia stopped in January 1991. Czech parties had little presence in Slovakia and the reverse. The government demanded continued control from Prague, while Slovaks asked for decentralisation, and leading Slovak parties, notably the Slovak National Party, advocated looser complete independence and sovereignty.

Historians debate whether the dissolution was inevitable, pointing to differences between the two nations dating from Austria-Hungary and to the 1968 constitution with its minority veto, or the result of events between 1989 and 1992. The partition took effect at the end of 1992, and, unlike the breakup of Yugoslavia, it brought no violence. No referendum was held, and the decision was unpopular at the time.

The national territory was divided along the existing internal borders, with disputes over a few places settled by negotiation, compensation and a treaty. Most federal assets, including army equipment and rail and air infrastructure, were divided in a ratio of two to one, the approximate ratio of the Czech and Slovak populations. The two states first kept the Czechoslovak koruna, but adopted separate currencies in February 1993. Each republic kept its own symbols, the Czech lion and the Slovak double cross. Neither state claimed to be the sole successor, Czechoslovakia's membership in the United Nations ended, and both were admitted as new states on 19 January 1993.

A customs union remained until both countries joined the European Union on 1 May 2004. On the dissolution all Czechoslovak citizens became citizens of the Czech Republic or Slovakia according to criteria such as residence and birthplace. Soon afterwards polls showed many people on both sides had opposed the split.
dissolution-of-the-soviet-union: Mikhail Gorbachev was elected General Secretary on 11 March 1985, just over four hours after the death of Konstantin Chernenko. He meant to revive a stagnating economy and came to see that this required reforming political and social structures. His glasnost allowed nationalist movements and ethnic disputes to be expressed and to grow into dominant political forces. Commentators also point to chronic economic stagnation and the burden of the arms race with the United States.

In 1989 limited competitive elections were held for a new Congress of People's Deputies, and the revolutions of 1989 in the Warsaw Pact countries increased pressure for republican autonomy. Estonia was the first republic to declare state sovereignty, on 16 November 1988, and Lithuania the first to declare independence, in March 1990. In 1990 all fifteen republics held competitive elections, and the Communist Party lost them in five.

On 17 March 1991 a Union-wide referendum was held in which 77.85 per cent of voters endorsed keeping a reformed Soviet Union; the Baltic republics, Armenia, Georgia and Moldova boycotted it. In August 1991 communist hardliners tried to overthrow Gorbachev. The coup failed, but the turmoil weakened the central government, and many republics declared independence in the following days and months.

On 8 December the leaders of the Russian, Byelorussian and Ukrainian republics signed the Belovezha Accords, declared that the Soviet Union no longer existed and set up the Commonwealth of Independent States. Kazakhstan was the last republic to declare independence, on 16 December. Gorbachev resigned on 25 December and passed his powers, including control of the nuclear launch codes, to Boris Yeltsin, and the Soviet flag was lowered from the Kremlin. On 26 December the Soviet of the Republics formally dissolved the Soviet Union.

The dissolution marked the culmination of the revolutions of 1989 and the end of the Cold War. Russia became the recognised successor state and continued the Soviet seat at the United Nations. Several successor states kept close links with Russia through the Commonwealth, while the Baltic states moved towards the West. The end of Soviet aid brought crisis to Cuba and North Korea, and disputes over territory and minorities led to conflicts in some successor states.
divine-comedy: Dante Alighieri belonged to the Guelphs, who in general favoured the papacy over the Holy Roman Emperor. Florence's Guelphs split around 1300 into the White Guelphs and the Black Guelphs, and the White Guelphs later supported greater imperial power in Italy. Dante was among the White Guelphs exiled in 1302 after troops under Charles of Valois entered the city at the request of Pope Boniface VIII, who supported the Black Guelphs. The exile lasted the rest of his life and shows throughout the poem, from prophecies of his banishment to the damnation of some of his opponents.

The work was originally titled Comedìa. Dante used the word because poems in the ancient world were classed as high (tragedy) or low (comedy), and low poems had happy endings and everyday language. The adjective Divina first appears in Giovanni Boccaccio's Trattatello in laude di Dante, written between 1351 and 1355.

The poem has 14,233 lines in three cantiche, Inferno, Purgatorio and Paradiso, each of 33 cantos, and an introductory canto brings the total to 100. Its verse form is terza rima, in tercets of eleven-syllable lines. The story is told in the first person and runs from the night before Good Friday to the Wednesday after Easter in the spring of 1300. Virgil guides Dante through Hell and most of Purgatory, Beatrice from the end of Purgatorio, and Bernard of Clairvaux through the last cantos.

Hell has nine circles, Mount Purgatory nine rings crowned by the Garden of Eden, and Heaven nine celestial spheres beneath the Empyrean. Each punishment in Hell is a contrapasso, a symbolic instance of poetic justice: in Canto XX the fortune-tellers must walk with their heads turned backwards. Allegorically the poem represents the soul's journey towards God.

According to the Italian Dante Society, no manuscript in Dante's own hand survives, although some 800 copies from the 14th and 15th centuries are listed. Giovanni da Serravalle made the first complete translation, into Latin prose, in 1416, and Enrique de Villena completed a Castilian prose version in 1428. The first printed edition appeared at Foligno on 11 April 1472, in 300 copies, of which fourteen survive.

The poem was recognised as a masterpiece in the centuries after it was written, largely fell into obscurity during the Enlightenment, and was rediscovered in the English-speaking world by William Blake and the Romantic writers of the 19th century. Erich Auerbach held that it inaugurated literary realism in modern fiction. In 1919 Miguel Asín Palacios argued that Dante drew on the Islamic tradition of Muhammad's night journey to heaven, but Francesco Gabrieli and other scholars have not found the claim convincing.
division-of-korea: Korea had been a nominal protectorate of Japan after the Russo-Japanese War ended in 1905 and was formally annexed in 1910, when Emperor Gojong was deposed. Nationalist and radical groups struggled for independence but never united in one movement, and the Korean Provisional Government in exile in the Republic of China gained wide recognition only with the Second World War.

At the Cairo Conference in November 1943 Franklin D. Roosevelt, Winston Churchill and Chiang Kai-shek declared that Korea would in due course become free and independent. Roosevelt raised a trusteeship with Joseph Stalin at Tehran and Yalta, and Stalin did not object but wanted it short. The Soviet Union declared war on Japan on 8 August 1945 and advanced quickly into the north, which made the United States anxious that it would occupy the whole peninsula.

On 10 August 1945 two young officers, Dean Rusk and Charles Bonesteel, were told to define an American zone at very short notice. No experts on Korea were consulted. Rusk later said that had he known Korean history he would almost surely have chosen a different line. Soviet troops entered Pyongyang on 24 August and found a committee under the nationalist Cho Man-sik, and the Soviet administration allowed local People's Committees to function. Koreans there enjoyed more autonomy than people in Soviet-controlled Eastern Europe, though Soviet soldiers also looted and were accused of rape.

The Moscow Conference of December 1945 agreed a trusteeship of up to five years, which Koreans opposed. A US-Soviet Joint Commission met in 1946 and 1947 and failed. Crossing the parallel without a permit became illegal in May 1946, and Lyuh Woon-hyung, the last senior politician committed to left-right dialogue, was assassinated on 19 July 1947. After the matter went to the United Nations, elections were held in the south only, over the objection of the commission's chairman, K. P. S. Menon. Strikes followed, and a rising on Jeju island was put down at a cost of 25,000 to 30,000 lives.

The Republic of Korea was proclaimed on 15 August 1948, and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea followed on 9 September. Each claimed the whole peninsula, and armed skirmishes along the border continued until North Korean forces invaded the South on 25 June 1950. A UN force led by the United States intervened.

The North overran 90 per cent of the south before a counter-attack drove it back, and UN troops then crossed the parallel in October despite warnings from the People's Republic of China. The war lasted until 1953, ended in stalemate and left the peninsula divided by the Korean Demilitarized Zone. Both regimes regarded the division, after more than a millennium of unity, as controversial and temporary.
divrigi: Divriği lies on a gentle slope on the south bank of the Çaltısuyu river, a tributary of the Karasu, which flows into the Euphrates. It is the district capital of Divriği District in Sivas Province and has about eleven thousand people. Large iron mines lie nearby, and the Hittites may already have mined and used the ore of the area.

In the 9th century the town was known as Abrik. It was founded around 850 by Karbeas, the leader of the Paulicians, an Armenian sect regarded by its opponents as heretical, and the Paulicians fortified it and made it the capital of their state, with the support of Arabs and the emir of Malatya. Later called Tephrike in Greek, it was recaptured by the Byzantine Empire during the reign of Emperor Basil I. It was temporarily renamed Leontokome, after Emperor Leo VI, and made into a thema.

In the early eleventh century the town was part of the territory given to the Armenian king Seneqerim-Hovhannes of Vaspurakan in exchange for his own lands. After the Battle of Manzikert it came under the Sultanate of Rûm, and the Mengüjeks built the Great Mosque and hospital. The traveller Evliya Çelebi recorded that the town's people included Greeks and Turkomans as well as Armenians and Kurds.

The Great Mosque and Hospital of Divriği, of the 13th century, stand on UNESCO's World Heritage List for the carving and architecture of both buildings. A medieval castle, mostly of the thirteenth century, crowns a steep hill above the town. The railway arrived in 1937, and iron ore from the nearby mines is still exported by it. Most of the district's villages are inhabited by Alevis.
divrigi-great-mosque-and-hospital: Divriği was founded in the 9th century under Byzantine rule. After the defeat of the Byzantines at Manzikert in 1071 Turkish tribes occupied it, and in the 12th century the Mengujekid dynasty controlled it and nearby Erzincan. The dynasty later divided into two branches, one ruling from Divriği and the other from Erzincan, and it was related by marriage to the Seljuks of Konya. The Mengujekid rulers were patrons of arts, science and literature, which may explain why exceptional artists were present, and itinerant artisans moving from patron to patron probably gave rise to the eclectic architecture.

The complex stands in the upper town, below the citadel. The mosque adjoins the hospital, with which it shares its southern qibla wall, and a mausoleum is attached to the hospital. The north portal of the mosque gives the date 626 AH (1228–1229) and names its patron as Ahmadshāh ibn Sulaymān, a ruler of the Divriği branch. The inscription on the hospital portal calls it a dār al-shifā' (house of healing) and ascribes its foundation to Tūrān Malik. The chief architect, Khurramshāh ibn Mughīth al-Khilātī, came from Ahlat.

The mosque's north portal is marked by the density of its high-relief carving. Inside, stone piers support stone vaults, and the central bay was probably open to the sky. A wooden minbar of 1243 signed by Ibrahīm ibn Ahmad al-Tiflīsī survives. The hospital portal, on the west, is less dense and in places seems unfinished; rooms and iwans surround a covered courtyard with a pool, and one room served as a dynastic tomb chamber.

Inscriptions record several major restorations between the 15th and 19th centuries, and more followed in the 20th. The carving and eclectic architecture place the complex among the most important works of architecture in Anatolia, and it was inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List in 1985.
diyala-river: The Diyala is a tributary of the Tigris, 445 kilometres long. It rises near Hamadan in the Zagros Mountains of Iran and descends through the mountains, forming the border between Iran and Iraq for some 32 kilometres. It flows southwest of the Hamrin Mountains and enters the Tigris below Baghdad. The upper reaches cannot be navigated because of narrow defiles, but the valley is an important trade route between Iran and Iraq. In the early Islamic period its lower course formed part of the Nahrawan Canal, and Diyala Governorate in Iraq is named after it. In Kurdish the river is called Sirwan, said to mean roaring sea or shouting river.

The valley flourished from the Jemdet Nasr and Early Dynastic periods to the Akkadian period. At Eshnunna (Tell Asmar) twelve statues of the Early Dynastic period were found in the Tell Asmar Hoard. A brightly coloured pottery known as Scarlet Ware, painted with haematite and with pictorial scenes, developed around 2800 BCE along the river. It was traded to Susa and was also popular in Luristan, because the valley carried one of the main routes between southern Mesopotamia and the Iranian plateau. Eshnunna became especially prominent in the Larsa period.

In 693 BCE the Assyrians and the Elamites fought the Battle of Diyala River. Herodotus calls the river the Gyndes and says that Cyrus the Great dispersed it into 360 channels as a punishment after a sacred white horse perished in it. In March 1917 the British Empire defeated the Ottoman Empire at the confluence with the Tigris, which led to the fall of Baghdad.

The University of Chicago Oriental Institute excavated the lower Diyala basin from 1930 to 1937 and the University of Pennsylvania in 1938 and 1939, at Tell Agrab, Tell Asmar, Ishchali (ancient Neribtum) and Khafaje (ancient Tutub). Henri Frankfort and others led the work, which covered the period from the late Uruk to the end of the Old Babylonian period. Of some 12,000 objects, most stayed unpublished, and the Diyala Database Project, begun in 1992, has been publishing them. The Hamrin Dam Salvage Project excavated further sites from 1977 to 1981. Dams now control the river, among them Darbandikhan and Hemrin in Iraq.
diyarbakir: Diyarbakır stands on a high plateau on the banks of the Tigris, where the historic fortress rises, and is the administrative centre of Diyarbakır Province in southeastern Turkey. It is considered one of the oldest continually inhabited cities in the world, with settlement since c. 8,000 BCE. In antiquity it was Amida. After the Muslim conquests of the 7th century it became Diyar Bakr, the abode of the tribe of Bakr, a portion of which had been ordered to settle in the lands near the city. In Turkish it was also called Kara Âmid, Black Amid, after its black basalt walls.

The first major civilisation in the region was the Hurrian kingdom of the Mitanni. Nearly every polity that controlled Upper Mesopotamia later ruled the city, among them the Arameans, Assyrians, Achaemenid Persians, Seleucids and Parthians. The Roman Republic gained control in 66 BCE, and in 359 Shapur II of Persia captured Amida after a siege of 73 days. Syriac Christianity took hold between the 1st and 4th centuries, and the Byzantine emperor Theodosius II made Amida capital of Mesopotamia Prima. The walls were built in antiquity and restored and extended by the emperor Constantius II in 349.

Amida fell in 639 to the armies of the Rashidun Caliphate, and the Great Mosque was built afterwards in the city's centre. The city belonged to the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates, and forces loyal to the caliph al-Mu'tadid recovered it in 899. It then fell under the Hamdanid dynasty, the Buyid dynasty and the Marwanids. The Ottomans conquered it in 1514 under Sultan Selim I, and the Safavid governor was evicted and killed in the Battle of Chaldiran that followed. The Armenian Catholic diocese had some 5,000 members in 1903 but lost most of its population in the Armenian genocide of 1915, when its last bishop was killed with some 600 of his flock.

Diyarbakır is the largest Kurdish-majority city in Turkey. Its walls form a circle of about 5.5 kilometres around the old city, with four gates and 82 watch-towers. The Diyarbakır Fortress and Hevsel Gardens Cultural Landscape was named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015. The Great Mosque, built by the Seljuk sultan Malik Shah in the 11th century, is one of the oldest in Turkey and is built in alternating bands of black basalt and white limestone.
djemal-pasha: Ahmed Djemal was born on 6 May 1872 in Mytilene on Lesbos, the son of Mehmed Nesib Bey, a military pharmacist. He graduated from the Kuleli Military High School in 1890 and from the staff college in Istanbul in 1893. Posted to the II Army Corps in 1896 and later to the Salonica frontier, he came to sympathise with the Committee of Union and Progress, a secret reformist party, and joined it in 1898. After the Young Turk Revolution of 1908 he sat on its central committee. He governed the Adana Vilayet from 1909 to 1911, where he helped Armenian victims of the Adana massacres and was praised by Christian missionaries as a competent administrator, and he served in the Balkan Wars.

Djemal became Minister of the Ottoman Navy in February 1914 and, with Talaat and Enver, one of the Three Pashas who effectively ruled the empire during the First World War. He had first favoured an alliance with France. In October 1914 he authorised the Black Sea strike that brought Russia, Britain and France into war against the empire. In 1915 he was given full military and civil powers in Syria. His two attacks on the Suez Canal failed, and wartime hardship and natural disasters turned the population against Ottoman rule.

Between 1915 and 1916 he had 34 Syrian and Lebanese politicians and nationalists executed, among them the men hanged in Damascus and Beirut on 6 May 1916. Arabs called him as-Saffah, the Butcher. Some people in Aleppo praised him for a water pipeline that saved the city from drought in 1917. Historians contest his role in the Armenian genocide: he favoured forced assimilation and conversion, and his policies allowed some Armenians to survive. Wolfgang Gust says he preserved perhaps 150,000 lives while helping to kill another 150,000.

After the empire's defeat in October 1918 Djemal fled with other leaders of the Committee to Germany and Switzerland, and a military court sentenced him to death in absentia. In 1920 he went to Central Asia as a military adviser to the Afghan army. He was assassinated in Tiflis on 21 July 1922 by members of the Armenian Revolutionary Federation, as part of Operation Nemesis, a plan to kill the surviving chief perpetrators of the Armenian genocide. He was buried at Erzurum. In Syria and Lebanon 6 May is Martyrs' Day, a national holiday marking the executions of 1916, and the squares where they took place were renamed Martyrs' Square.
djenne: Djenné sits on the floodplain between the Niger and Bani rivers at the southern end of the Inland Niger Delta, in central Mali. The annual flood begins in July and reaches its maximum in October, and the town then becomes an island reached by causeways. Some 2.5 kilometres to the south-east lies the archaeological site of Djenné-Djeno, one of the earliest and most important urban sites in West Africa, first settled around 200 BCE according to excavations by Susan and Roderick McIntosh. The present town was first settled after 1000 CE.

Djenné-Djeno developed into a large walled urban complex between 300 and 850 CE. After 1100 its population declined, and by 1400 it was abandoned, for reasons that are unknown. Djenné itself survived as a centre of regional trade. Between the 15th and 17th centuries much of the trans-Saharan trade in salt, gold and slaves passing through Timbuktu went through it, and both towns were centres of Islamic scholarship. Seventeenth-century chronicles give conflicting accounts of its relation to the Mali Empire. Sonni Ali conquered it in 1471 after a siege of about six months, and under the Songhai it had about 40,000 people.

A Moroccan army defeated the Songhai at Tondibi in 1591, and the Mali Empire's attempt to fill the void was beaten outside Djenné's walls in 1599. The town formed part of the Segou kingdom from 1670 to 1818 and the Massina Empire from 1818 to 1861. René Caillié, in 1828, was the first European to visit it. French forces occupied it in April 1893 and made Mopti the regional capital, so that Djenné's importance declined.

Djenné is a town and urban commune of the Mopti Region. It is noted for its Sudanese-style architecture, in which nearly all buildings, among them the Great Mosque, are of sun-baked earthen bricks coated with plaster, and the adobe needs replastering at least every other year. The town is a centre of Islamic scholarship, with Quranic schools that draw students from outside the region. In 1988 UNESCO named the Old Towns of Djenné, comprising four archaeological sites, a World Heritage Site.
djerba: Djerba covers 514 square kilometres in the Gulf of Gabès and is administratively part of the Medenine Governorate. In the time of the ancient Greeks it was known as Lytos or Meninx, and it is speculated to have been the island of the lotus-eaters where Odysseus was stranded. The city of Girba, which gave the island its name, was a suffragan bishopric of the Roman province of Tripolitania.

Archaeological and genetic evidence show that the ancestors of the Berbers have lived in the region for more than 20,000 years. The island was settled by the Phoenicians, who came from Tyre and Sidon, in the 12th century BCE according to the account followed here. They spread the pottery industry and the making of purple dye, and are thought to have introduced olive trees. Prosperity continued under the Romans, and the Vandals under King Gaiseric conquered the island after reaching the Maghreb in 429 CE.

Djerba was taken by Arab forces in 665, during the invasion of Tunisia in which the Ibadi sect prevailed. It was sometimes subordinate to the Aghlabids and sometimes to the Rustamids but always semi-independent, until the Fatimid Caliphate controlled the area from 909 to 972. Normans held it from 1135 to 1159, when the Almohad Caliphate drove out their garrison. The Ottomans entered part of Ifriqiya in 1574, and the island suffered under French colonial rule from 1881 until independence in 1956.

Djerba is the largest island of North Africa. According to oral history its Jewish minority has lived there continuously for more than 2,500 years, since the destruction of the Temple of Jerusalem, and the first physical evidence known to historians, from the 11th century, comes from the Cairo Geniza. The El Ghriba synagogue has been in use for over 2,000 years. The wetland of Djerba Bin El Ouedian, a habitat for migratory birds, was listed as a Ramsar site in 2007, and in 2023 the island was designated a World Heritage Site.
djoser: Djoser, also read Zoser, was a pharaoh of the Third Dynasty and is often counted as the founder of the Old Kingdom. In contemporary inscriptions he is known by his Horus name Netjerikhet, meaning divine of body. He was the son of King Khasekhemwy and Queen Nimaathap, though whether he directly succeeded Khasekhemwy has been uncertain. The Egyptologist Toby Wilkinson argues from burial seals in Khasekhemwy's tomb at Abydos that Djoser was his direct successor and the founder of the dynasty.

Manetho gives him a reign of twenty-nine years and the Turin King List nineteen. Wilkinson's reconstruction of the Royal Annals gives twenty-eight complete or partial years. Djoser sent expeditions to the Sinai Peninsula, where the local inhabitants were subdued and turquoise and copper were mined. The painted limestone statue of Djoser found at Saqqara in 1924 to 1925 is the oldest known life-sized Egyptian statue.

His main monument is the step pyramid at Saqqara, the earliest colossal stone building in ancient Egypt. It began as a nearly square mastaba, and five smaller steps were piled on top. It was once 62 metres high, with a base of about 125 by 109 metres, covered in polished white limestone. Beneath it lies a maze of corridors and chambers, with a burial chamber at the bottom of a shaft 28 metres deep, sealed by a plug stone of 3.5 tons. More than 40,000 stone vessels were found in the galleries.

Imhotep, Djoser's head of the royal shipyard and overseer of all stone works, directed the construction. Manetho credits Tosorthros with discovering how to build with hewn stone, which modern scholars think he meant to ascribe to Imhotep, later deified by Greeks and Romans as Aesculapius.

The date of his death is uncertain, and his relationship to his successor Sekhemkhet is not known. The Famine Stela, probably made in the Ptolemaic period but claiming to date from his reign, tells how Djoser rebuilt the temple of Khnum at Elephantine and so ended a seven-year famine. Some regard it as a legend. A papyrus of the 2nd century CE from Tebtunis preserves a long demotic story about Djoser and Imhotep. The Egyptian historian al-Nuwayri, who lived from 1279 to 1333, described him as a wise ruler and said the Copts held a feast in his honour called the vine festival.
dmitri-shostakovich: Dmitri Dmitriyevich Shostakovich was born on 25 September 1906 (12 September in the old style) in Saint Petersburg, the second of three children of Dmitri Boleslavovich Shostakovich and Sofiya Vasilievna Kokoulina. His paternal grandfather, Bolesław Szostakowicz, was of Polish and Lithuanian descent and had taken part in the January Uprising of 1863-1864; he was exiled to Narym in 1866 and later became a banker in Irkutsk. Shostakovich pursued a dual career as pianist and composer, and in 1927 he was among the Soviet contestants in the first International Chopin Piano Competition in Warsaw. He became internationally known after the premiere of his First Symphony in 1926.

His relationship with the Soviet government was complex. His opera Lady Macbeth of the Mtsensk District, first performed in 1934, was at first a success. On 26 January 1936 Joseph Stalin attended a performance with Vyacheslav Molotov, Andrei Zhdanov and Anastas Mikoyan and left without speaking to anyone; the work was later condemned, which put the composer's career at risk. After the German invasion of 1941 he stayed at first in Leningrad, was refused for military service because of poor eyesight, and served as a volunteer in the Conservatory's firefighter brigade.

In 1948 he and other composers, including Sergei Prokofiev and Aram Khachaturian, were denounced for formalism under the Zhdanov decree. Most of his works were banned and his family lost privileges. The censure was rescinded in 1956. In 1960 he joined the Communist Party, which was required for the chairmanship of the RSFSR Union of Composers; his son recalled that this reduced him to tears, and he later told his wife that he had been blackmailed.

His output is dominated by fifteen symphonies and fifteen string quartets. His music is broadly tonal, with sharp contrasts, elements of the grotesque and ambivalent tonality, and shows the influence of Gustav Mahler. He often quoted himself, as with the theme of Katerina's aria from Lady Macbeth in his Eighth and Fourteenth String Quartets. His song cycle From Jewish Folk Poetry was not approved in 1949 and could not be performed until after Stalin's death. Whether he used music as covert dissent is disputed. Solomon Volkov's 1979 book Testimony, which claimed to be his memoirs, alleged coded anti-government messages. Shostakovich died on 9 August 1975 in Moscow and was buried in Novodevichy Cemetery.
dmitrov: Dmitrov lies 65 kilometres north of Moscow, on the Yakhroma River and the Moscow Canal, at an altitude of 179 metres. It is the administrative centre of Dmitrovsky District in Moscow Oblast and one of the oldest urban areas in the oblast. Its name means Dmitri's, and it is explained by the fact that the patron saint of Vsevolod, the son of Yury Dolgoruky born where the town was founded, was Saint Demetrius.

Yury Dolgoruky founded the town in 1154. In the 13th century the settlement marked the point where the borders of the Grand Duchy of Moscow, Tver and Pereslavl-Zalessky met. It belonged to the princes of Galich-Mersky, who lived far to the north, until 1364, when it was incorporated into the Grand Duchy of Moscow. Dmitry Donskoy and his grandson Vasily II each granted Dmitrov as an appanage to a younger son, so that it became the capital of a tiny principality. It received town rights in 1374.

The reign of Ivan III's son Yury Ivanovich, from 1503 to 1533, began the golden age of the town. During it the black-domed Assumption Cathedral in the kremlin and a smaller monastery cathedral of Sts. Boris and Gleb were built. The town then passed to Yury's brother Andrey of Staritsa. In 1569 it was seized from Vladimir of Staritsa and added to the Oprichnina, and it declined afterward. It suffered further damage in the Time of Troubles, when the Poles ransacked it.

The Grande Armée briefly occupied Dmitrov in 1812. The anarchist prince Peter Kropotkin spent his last years there after the Russian Revolution. Soviet archaeologists excavated the local kremlin in the 1930s. In November 1941 German troops occupied the town and crossed the Moscow-Volga Canal from there.

Dmitrov had a population of 65,574 at the 2021 census. It is a railway junction, on the branch from Moscow's Savyolovsky terminal to Savyolovo and the branch to Alexandrov, and a cargo port on the Moscow Canal. The kremlin's Assumption Cathedral stands as a reminder of the town's golden age.
dmitry-donskoy: Dmitry Ivanovich was born in Moscow on 12 October 1350, the eldest son of Ivan II of Moscow and his second wife, Alexandra Velyaminova, daughter of Vasily Velyaminov, the tysyatsky (military commander) of Moscow. Ivan died on 13 November 1359, when Dmitry was nine. Real power then rested with his father's advisers, led by Velyaminov, while Metropolitan Alexius supervised the boy's education and wielded significant influence in the government.

In 1360, amid political turmoil in the Golden Horde, the khan Nawruz Beg gave the Grand Principality of Vladimir to Dmitry Konstantinovich of Suzdal. In 1362 Dmitry Ivanovich received a patent (yarlyk) from the rival khan Murad and, with the Moscow boyars and his cousin Vladimir Andreyevich of Serpukhov, drove his rival from Vladimir. In January 1366 he married the rival's youngest daughter, Eudoxia, which secured peace between the two principalities.

After taking the throne of Tver in 1366, Mikhail Aleksandrovich challenged Moscow with Lithuanian support. A Lithuanian army came to his aid, but the new stone walls of Moscow withstood the siege. Dmitry invaded Tver again in 1370, and the Lithuanian grand duke Algirdas, finding him well prepared, proposed a truce and withdrew. Mikhail received a patent from Mamai in 1371 but could not enforce it. A treaty negotiated by Alexius had Algirdas recognise the grand principality as Dmitry's patrimony. On 1 September 1375 Mikhail acknowledged Dmitry as his elder brother.

From 1374 Dmitry refused to pay tribute to Mamai. In 1378 his forces defeated a Mongol army at the Battle of Vozha River. In 1380 Mamai himself led a large force against Moscow. Sergius of Radonezh blessed Dmitry before the Battle of Kulikovo, and the battle opened with a single combat in which the Russian champion Alexander Peresvet and Temir-Murza of the Horde killed each other. Dmitry won, and from the battle took his name Donskoy, 'of the Don'. Tokhtamysh then deposed Mamai and overran Moscow in 1382; Dmitry pledged loyalty to him and was reinstated as grand prince of Vladimir.

Dmitry died in Moscow on 19 May 1389. He was the first grand prince to bequeath his titles to his son, Vasily I of Moscow, without consulting the khan. He had at least twelve children with Eudoxia. In Russian historiography he is regarded as a national hero and a central figure of medieval Russia. The Russian Orthodox Church canonised him as a saint on 6 June 1988, with his feast day on 19 May.
dmitry-pozharsky: Dmitry Mikhaylovich Pozharsky was born in Klin County, north of Moscow. As in many Russian noble families, he bore a baptismal name, Kuzma, used only in religious contexts, and the public name Dmitry. He descended from a branch of the Rurik dynasty that ruled Starodub-on-the-Klyazma, near Suzdal. The family estate burned down in the 15th century, and the family took the name Pozharsky from the Russian word pozhar, meaning conflagration. His mother, Maria Feodorovna Pozharskaya, came from the Beklemishev family.

His early career is not documented until the Time of Troubles, when he took part in the Zemsky Sobor that elected Boris Godunov tsar. He fought in the Polish-Muscovite War from 1605, routed the Cossacks of Ivan Bolotnikov at the Pekhorka River and commanded the defence of Zaraysk in 1610. He was wounded on 19 March 1611 while defending his house at Lubyanka Square in the Moscow uprising.

In autumn 1611 a delegation offered him command of the Second Volunteer Army at Nizhny Novgorod. He agreed on condition that Kuzma Minin, a representative of the city's merchants, assist him. The army spent half a year at Yaroslavl, and on 18 August 1612 it encamped near Moscow. Pozharsky fought the relief force of Hetman Chodkiewicz for four days, while Prince Dmitry Trubetskoy captured the provisions meant for the Poles in the Kremlin. Famine followed, and the garrison surrendered in October on a promise of safe passage. Most of the Poles were nonetheless slaughtered, Trubetskoy's Cossacks attacking and robbing the prisoners.

Pozharsky and Trubetskoy headed the government for half a year until a new tsar was elected, and Pozharsky was made a boyar. The system of mestnichestvo kept him from supreme command in later campaigns. He managed several state offices, governed Novgorod in 1628–30 and built churches, among them the Kazan Cathedral beside Red Square. He married twice and had three sons, and his line died out with his grandson in 1685. Mikhail I gave him the title Saviour of the Fatherland, and a bronze Monument to Minin and Pozharsky was erected on Red Square during the Napoleonic Wars.
dnieper: The Dnieper, also called the Dnipro or Dnepr, rises in the sedge bogs of the Valdai Hills near Smolensk in central Russia, at an elevation of 220 m. It is about 2,200 km long and drains a basin of 504,000 square kilometres. Of its length, 485 km are in Russia, 700 km in Belarus and 1,095 km in Ukraine, and for 115 km it forms the border between Belarus and Ukraine. It is the longest river of Ukraine and of Belarus. The Dnieper meets the Southern Bug in the Dnieper-Bug estuary, where the city of Kherson stands. Almost 2,000 km are navigable, as far as Dorogobuzh.

Herodotus called the river Borysthenes, a name derived from a Scythian form meaning either yellow place or place of beavers, and a later name was Danapris. In antiquity it was part of the Amber Road trade routes. The modern names all come from Old East Slavic Dŭněprŭ, whose origin is disputed. One derivation is from a Sarmatian or Scythian name meaning farther river or deep river, the latter because the river has few fords.

The Dnieper Rapids lay on the trade route from the Varangians to the Greeks, which the Kyiv Chronicle mentions. The route was probably established in the late 8th and early 9th centuries and gained importance from the 10th until the early 11th century. The middle course had nine major rapids and 30 to 40 smaller ones, and the Varangians had to portage their ships round seven of them while guarding against Pecheneg nomads. During the Ruin of the later 17th century the area was contested between the Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth and the Russian Empire, and the river came to divide what is now Ukraine into right-bank and left-bank areas.

In the Soviet period the river was harnessed for hydroelectric power. The first plant, the Dnieper Hydroelectric Station near Zaporizhzhia, was built between 1927 and 1932, and it flooded the rapids. It was destroyed in World War II and rebuilt between 1944 and 1950. Its output was 558 MW at first and 750 MW after the rebuilding, supplying 3.5 billion kWh of electricity a year.

Six sets of dams and hydroelectric stations stand between the mouth of the Pripyat and Kakhovka, and the reservoirs have large ship locks that allow vessels access as far as the port of Kyiv. The Dnieper-Bug Canal links the river to other waterways in Europe. The Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant lies beside the mouth of the Pripyat, a tributary of the Dnieper. The Dnieper is one of the national symbols of Ukraine and is named in its national anthem.
dniester: The Dniester rises in Ukraine near the city of Turka, close to the border with Poland, and flows toward the Black Sea. Part of its course marks the border of Ukraine and Moldova. It then runs through Moldova for 398 kilometres, and later forms a further stretch of the Moldova-Ukraine border before it crosses Ukraine to the sea, where its estuary forms the Dniester Liman.
