Along the lower half of the river the western bank is high and hilly and the eastern one low and flat. The river is regarded as the de facto end of the Eurasian Steppe.

In the Neolithic the river lay at the centre of the Cucuteni-Trypillian culture, which flourished in this area from roughly 5300 to 2600 BCE and left thousands of archaeological sites. Its settlements held up to 15,000 inhabitants, among the first large farming communities in the world. The Greeks called the river Tyras, from a Scythian word meaning rapid. Herodotus said that it rose in a large lake, Ptolemy placed its sources in the Carpathian Mountains, and Strabo wrote that they were unknown. It formed part of the boundary between Dacia and Sarmatia.

The river formed the northeastern border of the Bulgarian Empire in the 7th to 10th centuries. According to Constantine VII, the Varangians used boats on the Dniester and Dnieper on their trade route from the Varangians to the Greeks. From the 14th century to 1812 part of the river was the eastern boundary of the Principality of Moldavia. Between the World Wars it formed part of the boundary between Romania and the Soviet Union. After Moldova declared its independence in 1991, the area east of the river that had been part of the Moldavian SSR declared itself the Pridnestrovian Moldavian Republic, or Transnistria, with its capital at Tiraspol.

The river is known in Ukrainian as Dnister, in Romanian as Nistru and in Russian as Dnestr. Its most important tributaries are the Răut and the Bîc. Moldova marks Dniester Day on the last Sunday of May.
do-aklin: Do-Aklin is also called Gangnihessou, Ganye Hessou or Dogbari. Very little is known about him, and most of it belongs to folklore. According to oral tradition, the Aja were led to Allada by King Agassu from the city of Tado. Agassu was the son of a Tado princess and a leopard, or in some versions a brave Yoruba hunter. When he tried to take over Tado he was defeated, and he moved with his followers to found Allada.

Around 1600, three brothers in the lineage of Agassu, or two in some versions, fought over the succession to the throne. It was decided that each would settle a new territory. The agreement was reached at Houégbo: Teagbanlin would found a state at what is now Porto-Novo, another son would take control in Allada, and Do-Aklin would settle on the Abomey plateau to the north.

Do-Aklin is said to have brought significant gifts for the local population and so to have been allowed to live among them. The mixing of the local people with the Aja from Allada is said to have created the Fon. His symbol was a bird, a drum and a club, and his motto was that he was the biggest bird and the sonorous drum, whom nobody can prevent. Many versions consider him the first king of Dahomey, although the kingdom was founded after his death. His son, or in some versions his grandson, Dakodonu built the palace and founded the kingdom around 1640 by defeating a local chieftain.

The anthropologist J. Cameron Monroe holds that the lineage connection to the royal house of Allada is probably a later creation, used by Dahomey to legitimise its conquest of Allada, since in the legend its kings were also rightful successors to the Allada throne. He reads the supposed brotherhood of the founders of Dahomey and Porto-Novo in the same way, as a reflection of the rivalry between the two states.
dobrica-cosic: Dobrica Ćosić was born Dobrosav Ćosić on 29 December 1921 in the village of Velika Drenova near Trstenik, Serbia. He attended a vocational agriculture school in Valjevo and joined the communist youth organisation in Negotin in 1939. In 1941 he joined the communist Partisans, and after the liberation of Belgrade in October 1944 he held communist leadership positions, including work in the Serbian republican Agitation and Propaganda commission. His first novel, Daleko je sunce (The Sun is Far Away), appeared in 1951, was a success and launched his literary career; by then he had stopped working professionally for the Communist Party.

In 1956 he was in Budapest for a meeting of literary magazine editors when the Hungarian revolt began, and he returned to Belgrade on 31 October on a plane carrying Yugoslav Red Cross aid. He wrote a detailed report that some think shaped the official Yugoslav view of the revolt. In late 1956 Tito and Edvard Kardelj chose him for the committee that drew up a new party programme, completed in 1958. In 1961 he joined Tito on a 72-day voyage on the yacht Galeb to eight non-aligned African countries.

Between 1961 and 1962 he argued with the Slovenian intellectual Dušan Pirjevec over autonomy, nationalism and centralism, favouring a stronger federal authority; Tito supported his arguments, yet measures after 1962 followed Pirjevec's position. As Yugoslavia decentralised after 1963, Ćosić became convinced that the Serbian population was imperilled. In May 1968 he condemned the nationalities policy in a speech to the Central Committee of the Serbian League of Communists, objecting especially to greater autonomy for Kosovo and Vojvodina, and thereafter acted as a dissident. He was nominated for the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1975.

After Tito's death Ćosić helped lead a movement for equality for Serbia within the Yugoslav federation. He was a member of the Serbian Academy of Sciences and Arts and endorsed Slobodan Milošević's leadership in 1989. In 1992 he became the first president of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, formed by Serbia and Montenegro, and held the office until 1993. Liberal Serbs saw him as one of the key figures behind the Greater Serbia project. He later turned against Milošević and was removed from his post for that reason, and in 2000 he publicly joined the anti-Milošević organisation Otpor!. His books have been translated into 30 languages, and he twice won the NIN award for literature. He died in Belgrade on 18 May 2014, aged 92.
dobruja: Dobruja lies between the lower Danube and the Black Sea in Southeastern Europe. It includes the Danube Delta, a marshy region in its northeastern corner, the Romanian coast and the northernmost part of the Bulgarian coast. Apart from the delta, the land is hilly, with an average altitude of about 200 to 300 metres; its highest point is the Țuțuiatu peak in the Măcin Mountains, at 467 metres. Most scholars derive the name from the Turkish form of the name of a 14th-century ruler, Dobrotitsa, in the way the Turks named other lands after early rulers.

The region has been inhabited since the Palaeolithic, and its Neolithic cultures include the Hamangia culture, named after a village on the coast. Greek colonists from Miletus founded Histria in 657 or 656 BCE, and Callatis, Tomis and other colonies followed on the coast. Rome extended its influence over the region from 28 or 29 BCE, when the Getic ruler Rholes helped the proconsul Marcus Licinius Crassus against the Bastarnae.

In the following centuries Dobruja passed between Byzantine and Bulgarian rule. Sviatoslav I of Kiev occupied it in 968, and the Byzantines under John I Tzimisces took it back in 971. The Bulgarian Empire regained it in 1187, and the Tatars first invaded in 1241. In the 14th century a local ruler, Balik, was followed by his son Dobrotitsa. Mircea the Elder of Wallachia took control in 1388 or 1389, and the Ottomans annexed the region in 1420, holding it until the late 19th century. Russia occupied it several times during the Russo-Turkish wars, and the invasion of 1829 depopulated many villages and towns.

After the war of 1878 the northern part went to Romania, in exchange for Southern Bessarabia, and the southern part to Bulgaria, reduced by the Treaty of Berlin. Romania took Southern Dobruja in 1913 after the Second Balkan War and kept it after the First World War under the Treaty of Neuilly of 1919. In September 1940 the Treaty of Craiova returned it to Bulgaria, with a population exchange in which Romanians left the south and Bulgarians the north. The Paris Peace Treaties of 1947 reaffirmed that border.

Dobruja is divided between Romania and Bulgaria and covers about 23,100 square kilometres, with some 1.2 million people, roughly three quarters of them in the Romanian part. Northern Dobruja forms the counties of Constanța and Tulcea, with the cities of Constanța, Tulcea, Medgidia and Mangalia. Southern Dobruja belongs to the provinces of Dobrich and Silistra, whose main towns bear those names. In Romania, 14 November is observed as Dobruja Day.
dodecanese: The Dodecanese are a group of 15 larger and about 150 smaller islands in the south-eastern Aegean Sea, off the coast of Anatolia, of which 26 are inhabited. They mark the eastern limit of the Sea of Crete and belong to the wider Southern Sporades. Rhodes has been the dominant island since antiquity, and Kos and Patmos are historically the most important of the others. The name means the Twelve Islands. In the Byzantine period it referred to twelve Cyclades islands around Delos, and it passed to the present group under Ottoman rule, when twelve islands kept privileges in taxation and self-government. The name was firmly established by 1920.

The islands were inhabited from prehistoric times and ruled by Mycenaean Greeks from about 1400 BCE until the Dorians arrived about 1100 BCE. In the 6th century BCE the Dorians founded Lindos, Kameiros and Ialyssos on Rhodes, which with Kos and the mainland cities of Knidos and Halicarnassos formed the Dorian Hexapolis. The three cities of Rhodes united in 408 BCE and built a new capital. The Colossus of Rhodes was built in 304 BCE. Persia took the islands about 499 BCE, Mausolus of Caria conquered them in 357 BCE and Alexander the Great's Macedonia followed. Cassius sacked them in 42 BCE.

The islands stayed Byzantine for nearly a thousand years, and the Knights Hospitaller strengthened Rhodes in 1309. Their fortifications repelled the Sultan of Egypt in 1444 and Mehmed II in 1480, but Suleiman took Rhodes in 1522. Under Ottoman rule the islands paid a special tax in return for autonomy and prospered. Kasos was destroyed by the Egyptians in 1824 after playing a prominent part in the Greek War of Independence.

Italy occupied the islands, except Kastellorizo, in 1912 during the Italian-Turkish war, and formally annexed them under the Treaty of Lausanne as the Possedimenti Italiani dell'Egeo. Ikaria joined Greece in 1912, and Kastellorizo came under Italian rule in 1921. Italian rule brought hospitals and aqueducts, and a form of Aegean citizenship exempted the islanders from the population exchange between Greece and Turkey. The islands joined Greece in 1947.

The islands are overwhelmingly Greek-speaking. A Turkish Muslim minority lives on Rhodes and Kos. Most have a hot-summer Mediterranean climate, and south-east Rhodes records the highest mean annual sunshine in Greece. Hundreds of Byzantine churches survive.
dodoma: Dodoma lies in the centre of Tanzania, 453 kilometres west of Dar es Salaam and 441 kilometres south of Arusha. Its name means it has sunk in the Gogo language. The city has an area of 2,669 square kilometres, of which 625 square kilometres is urbanised. It has a semi-arid climate with warm to hot temperatures all year, about 610 millimetres of rain a year and a wet season between December and April. The indigenous ethnic groups are the Gogo, Rangi and Sandawe.

Dodoma began as a small market town called Idodomya. The modern town was founded in 1907 by German colonists during the building of the central railway. Its layout followed the colonial planning of the time, with a European quarter segregated from a native village.

In 1967 the government invited the Canadian firm Project Planning Associates to draw up a master plan for Dar es Salaam, which was growing rapidly, and the plan was cancelled in 1972. After a nationwide referendum the government announced that the capital would move to a more central place. The move was meant to bring social and economic gains to the central region and to divert development from a single coastal city, which was seen as contrary to socialist unity. The rural environment of the region was seen as the heartland of ujamaa, and so as right for a ujamaa capital that could learn from neighbouring villages.

The winning plan, by Project Planning Associates, envisaged a city of 400,000 people by 2000 and 1.3 million by 2020. It was intended to be the first non-monumental capital, unlike Abuja, Yamoussoukro, Brasília or Washington, D.C., with curving forms rather than grids, buses before cars, and the garden city model. It was meant to be the chief village in a nation of villages. Dodoma became the official capital in 1996. Much of the design was never carried out, and government offices and embassies resisted moving, so many remained in Dar es Salaam, which stayed the commercial capital.

Dodoma is the capital of Tanzania and the seat of its parliament. The Central Railway Line, begun under German rule, runs through the city to Dar es Salaam, a distance of 465 kilometres. In 2022 the city had 765,179 people. The University of Dodoma and St John's University of Tanzania both opened in 2007.
dodona: Dodona lay in a remote region of Epirus away from the main Greek city-states, yet it was considered second only to Delphi in prestige. Aristotle placed Hellas around Dodona and the river Achelous and said that its inhabitants, the Selloi, had once been called Graikoi and were now Hellenes. Some scholars therefore trace the words Hellenes and Hellas to this district. The oracle was first controlled by the Thesprotians and then by the Molossians, and Strabo names Mount Tomaros as the mountain at whose foot the temple stood.

Offerings of the fourteenth and thirteenth centuries BCE show that cult activity already existed in the Late Bronze Age, and evidence for the cult of Zeus dates from about the same time. Homer, in the Iliad, has Achilles pray to Zeus of Dodona, and mentions priests called Selloi who slept on the ground with unwashed feet. Some scholars hold that the oracle was originally that of a Mother Goddess, later called Dione, who shared it with Zeus.

Priestesses appear by the time of Herodotus, who gives the story of two black doves from Egyptian Thebes, one of which settled in an oak at Dodona and spoke in a human voice. Over 4,200 oracular tablets have been found, dating from the mid-sixth to the early second century BCE, all in Greek and naming more than 1,200 people, almost all Greeks.

About 290 BCE King Pyrrhus made Dodona the religious capital of his realm, rebuilding the Temple of Zeus, adding a festival with games, music and drama in a theatre, and building a wall round the oracle and the holy tree. The Aetolians looted and burned the sanctuary in 219 BCE, and Philip V of Macedon rebuilt it. In 167 BCE the Romans under Aemilius Paulus destroyed the Molossian cities, possibly including Dodona. Emperor Julian consulted the oracle in 362 CE. Pilgrims still came until 391 or 392 CE, when Emperor Theodosius closed the pagan temples and cut down the ancient oak. A bishop of Dodona attended the First Council of Ephesus in 431.

Dodona never eclipsed Delphi but its fame spread beyond Greece. In the Argonautica of Apollonius of Rhodes the ship Argo could prophesy because it contained an oak timber from Dodona. Ancient writers disagreed about the oracle's origins: Strabo, citing Ephorus, said the Pelasgi founded it, and reported a story that it was moved from Thessaly. According to a recent interpretation, the sound of the oracle came from bronze objects hung from the oak branches and rung by the wind like a chime.
doha: Doha stands on the Persian Gulf coast in the central-east of Qatar, at an elevation of about 10 metres, north of Al Wakrah and south of Al Khor and Lusail. Its name comes from the Arabic dohat, meaning roundness, a reference to the rounded bays along the coast. The climate is hot desert, with long, extremely hot summers, short mild winters and very little rain, mostly between October and March. Land reclamation off the coast has added 400 hectares of land and 30 kilometres of coastline.

Doha began in the 1820s as an offshoot of the older settlement of Al Bidda. The earliest documented mention of Al Bidda dates from 1681, in an account by the Carmelite Convent, and in 1765 the German explorer Carsten Niebuhr mapped it as Guttur. In January 1823 the British political resident John MacLeod visited Al Bidda to meet Buhur bin Jubrun, chief of the Al-Buainain tribe and the initial founder of Doha, and noted that it was the only substantial trading port on the peninsula. Written records often conflated the two settlements because they lay so close together.

The Al Thani family migrated to Doha from Fuwayrit shortly after Bin Tarif's death in 1847 and in the following years took control of the town, at various times switching allegiance between the Al Khalifa of Bahrain and the Saudis. Pearling became central to the economy, and the population grew to about 12,000 in the first half of the 20th century. In 1907 the city accommodated 350 pearling boats with crews of 6,300 men. That year the pearl market collapsed, and the aftermath led to the country's first custom house in Doha.

Qatar ratified its first constitution in April 1970 and became independent in 1971, when Doha was declared the capital. The University of Qatar opened in 1973 and the Qatar National Museum in 1975. In the 1970s the old neighbourhoods were razed and their inhabitants moved to new suburbs such as Al Rayyan, Madinat Khalifa and Al Gharafa.

Doha is the capital, largest city and main financial hub of Qatar, and over 80% of the country's population live in the city or its suburbs. Its population is overwhelmingly composed of expatriates, with Qatari citizens a minority, and most residents are Muslim. The metropolitan area includes Education City, devoted to research and education, and Doha Sports City, which includes Khalifa International Stadium. The city hosted the 2006 Asian Games and the 2022 FIFA World Cup.
dol-de-bretagne: Dol-de-Bretagne is a commune in the Ille-et-Vilaine département in Brittany, 6 km from the English Channel coast and 22 km south-east of Saint-Malo. Records cite it mostly by its Breton name, Dol, a term for a low and fertile place in the flood plain of a waterway, like the Welsh dôl, 'meadow'.

The Welsh Saint Teilo is recorded at Dol in 549, where he joined Samson of Dol, and the fruit groves they planted are still known as the groves of Teilo and Samson. Dol figured prominently in the formation of the Duchy of Brittany. Nominoe, the ruler of Brittany, tried to establish a metropolitan archbishop for the Breton church to give it autonomy and to secure his independence from the Carolingian Empire; Rome took centuries to recognise the Archbishop of Dol. After the duchy was formed in 939, the archbishop often wielded great political power and was once regent to a young duke.

In 1064 William, Duke of Normandy, led an expedition against Brittany in which Harold Godwinson took an active part, and scene 18 of the Bayeux Tapestry shows the capture of the castle at Dol. William, by then King of England, besieged the town again in 1076 without success after the king of France broke the siege. Henry II of England took it in 1164. In June 1173 Hugh de Kevelioc, 5th Earl of Chester, captured it in the Revolt of 1173–1174, and Henry retook it the same year with an army of 20,000 mercenaries. Guy of Thouars took the town in 1204.

Dol is reputed to be the origin of the royal House of Stewart, and a plaque there commemorates this. The Stewart monarchs descend from Alan the Seneschal of the Bishop of Dol, whose descendants came to Britain at the request of Henry I. Walter Fitzalan became the first Steward of Scotland under David I, and Malcolm IV made the office hereditary in his family. In the fourteenth century Walter Stewart married Marjorie Bruce, daughter of Robert I of Scotland, and their son became King Robert II.

Dol Cathedral is a significant building in an eclectic mix of styles, and the town has other heritage sites, among them a 12th-century house. Dol is also one of the settings of a lai by Marie de France, Le Fresne, in which Gurun, lord of Dol, is a main character.
dome-of-the-rock: The Dome of the Rock stands at the centre of the Temple Mount, the site of Solomon's Temple and the Second Jewish Temple, which Herod the Great greatly expanded in the 1st century BCE and the Romans destroyed in 70 CE. In 638 the Arab armies of Umar ibn al-Khattab conquered Byzantine Jerusalem; he was advised by Ka'b al-Ahbar, a rabbi who had converted to Islam, that the site was that of the former Jewish Temples.

The Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik ordered the shrine built during the Second Fitna, in 691 to 692. It was raised over the Foundation Stone, from which Muslims believe the Night Journey of Muhammad began. Its octagonal plan and mosaics were patterned on nearby Byzantine churches and palaces. Its inscriptions are the earliest to proclaim Islam and Muhammad, and the interior frieze concerns the nature of Isa (Jesus) rather than the Night Journey.

The plan is octagonal. A dome about 20 metres across, on a raised drum, stands on 16 supports inside an octagonal arcade of 24 piers and columns; the two rings form an inner ambulatory around the rock, with a second between the inner and outer octagon. Each outer wall is about 60 metres wide and 36 metres high, with four entrances, one for each cardinal direction. The columns and capitals were reused from older ancient buildings. Early descriptions mention the golden look of the dome, and the interior is decorated with mosaic, faience and marble, much of it added centuries after completion.

The dome collapsed in 1015 and was rebuilt in 1022 to 1023 under the Fatimid al-Zahir. The Crusaders, who took Jerusalem in 1099, gave the shrine to the Augustinians, who made it a church, and the Knights Templar, who took it for the Temple of Solomon, called it the Templum Domini and used its image on their seals; it became the model for their round churches in Europe. Saladin recaptured Jerusalem on 2 October 1187, removed the marble the Crusaders had laid over the rock and replaced the cross on the dome with a crescent.

Suleiman had the Umayyad mosaics on the exterior replaced by Ottoman tiles, a work dated by inscriptions to 1545 to 1552 and later. Major restoration followed under Jordanian rule from 1959 to 1964 and again in the 1990s, when the dome was gilded. UNESCO designates the monument a World Heritage Site.
domesday-book: The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says that after a large meeting and deep consultation with his council the king sent his men into every shire in 1085 to find out how many hides of land there were, what land and stock the king himself held, and what each archbishop, bishop, abbot, earl and landholder had and what it was worth. Most shires were visited by royal officers who held a public inquiry, probably in the shire court, attended by representatives of every township and of the local lords. The return for each hundred was sworn by twelve local jurors, half English and half Norman.

The survey's main purpose was to record the fiscal rights of the king: the land tax called the geld, miscellaneous dues and the income of the crown lands. After the Norman Conquest and the confiscation of landed estates, William needed to show that the Crown's rights had not suffered, and historians believe he wanted a definitive reference point on property holdings in case of disputes. Organising the returns by feudal tenure also showed him each baron's under-tenants, whom he wished to bind by oath to himself.

The work consists of two independent books. Little Domesday covers Norfolk, Suffolk and Essex and is more detailed, since it records the livestock on lords' home farms; Great Domesday covers most of the rest of England and parts of Wales bordering English counties, abbreviated and rearranged by a single scribe. Northumberland, Durham and most of Cumberland and Westmorland are omitted, as they did not pay the geld, which framed the book. Space was left for London and Winchester but never filled.

Entries are grouped in chapters by tenant-in-chief, each listing the manors he held from the king: bishops, abbots, barons from Normandy, Brittany and Flanders, serjeants and English thegns. Each county opens with the king's lands. A manor's entry gives its assessment, arable land, plough teams, meadow, woodland, mills and fisheries, its peasants by class, and its annual value at the time of Edward the Confessor's death, when the new owners received it and at the survey. The book names 13,418 places and tallies 268,984 heads of household, and lists 5,624 mills and 28,000 slaves.

The name Domesday, in use from the 12th century, was explained by Richard FitzNeal, writing around 1179, by comparison with the Last Judgment: from its decisions there was no appeal. The volumes were kept in the royal treasury at Winchester and later moved with it to Westminster, and are now held at the National Archives at Kew. They were printed in full in 1783. The geographer H. C. Darby called it probably the most striking statistical document in the history of Europe, while noting omissions, ambiguities and clerks' errors in the use of Roman numerals.
domestication: Domestication is a multi-generational mutualistic relationship in which one species, such as humans or leafcutter ants, takes over control and care of another, such as sheep or fungi, to obtain a steady supply of resources. The word comes from the Latin domesticus, belonging to the house, and it is not the taming of an individual animal.

The term stayed loosely defined until the American archaeologist Melinda A. Zeder defined it in the 21st century as a long-term relationship in which humans control and care for another organism to gain a predictable supply of a resource, with mutual benefits. She noted that it is not synonymous with agriculture, which depends on domesticated organisms but does not follow automatically from domestication.

The process is gradual, geographically diffuse and based on trial and error. In animals it changes genes for behaviour, making them less aggressive; in plants it changes genes for form, such as larger seeds and cereal heads that no longer shatter. Domestication syndrome is the set of traits that distinguish domesticated species from their wild ancestors.

The first animals domesticated were terrestrial vertebrates. Dogs diverged from wolves and developed a commensal relationship with Upper Paleolithic or Mesolithic humans at least 15,000 years ago, in the Late Pleistocene. Goats, sheep and cows were domesticated around 11,000 years ago, the horse around 5,500 years ago in central Asia as a riding animal, and the chicken in East Asia at least 3,250 years ago. The silkworm and the western honey bee were domesticated over 5,000 years ago for silk and honey.

Plant domestication began around 13,000 to 11,000 years ago with wheat and barley in the Middle East, alongside lentil, pea, chickpea and flax. From around 10,000 years ago Indigenous peoples in the Americas began to cultivate peanuts, squash, maize, potatoes, cotton and cassava. Rice was first domesticated in China some 9,000 years ago, and sorghum in Africa. Agriculture developed in some 13 centres, each with different crops and animals.

Scholars differ widely on its effects on society. Anarcho-primitivism holds that it destroyed hunter-gatherer harmony with nature and brought social hierarchy, possibly by violence or enslavement. David Nibert holds that it involved violence against animals and damage to the environment. Other species also domesticate: ambrosia beetles, leafcutter ants and fungus-growing termites have each independently domesticated fungi on which they feed.
dominate: The term was proposed in the 19th century by the German scholar Theodor Mommsen, who set it against the Principate established by Augustus in 27 BCE. In his view the Principate was a system in which imperial authority was embedded within Roman Republican institutions. The later period, beginning with Diocletian about 284 CE, marked a break in the constitutional basis of the empire, which moved from one legitimised by a republican senate and people to one in which the emperor became the state. The historian Jochen Bleicken credits Mommsen with introducing both concepts to divide the history of the Roman Empire into periods.

Mommsen's lectures, published after his death, described the Dominate of Diocletian and Constantine as sharply different from the Principate. He saw an oriental ruler as its model, an empire divided where it had been united, a new capital, and a reformed administration. The army became a mobile force in which foreigners, above all Germans, served, a finance administration developed, and Constantine reintroduced a universal gold coin, the solidus.

Titles mattered to him. The word dominus, first used of slave-owners, became a title for the emperor as well as for a god, and it appeared on coins under Aurelian combined with deus. Diocletian introduced genuflection in the ceremony of adoration, where earlier emperors had been greeted with a handshake or a kiss. Mommsen noted that the idea of a god on earth could not be reconciled with Christianity, so the god was abandoned, but the lord remained.

Since the start of the 20th century scholars have increasingly rejected the idea of a rupture around Diocletian's time. They accept that significant changes occurred but do not see them as altering the emperor's legal position or the basic structure of Roman government. Mommsen's view was criticised for overemphasising law, and Ronald Syme's work, with its stress on networks of people, challenged it. In 1978 Bleicken argued that the division into Principate and Dominate rested on no genuine constitutional change and that both terms were ill suited to strict periodisation, and that Mommsen's view reflected reactions to absolutism in post-Napoleonic Europe. The Oxford Classical Dictionary now regards the term as nearly obsolete.
domingo-faustino-sarmiento: Sarmiento was born on 15 February 1811 at Carrascal, a poor suburb of San Juan. His mother sold her weaving to build a house, and of the fifteen children of the marriage only Domingo reached adulthood. In the civil wars that followed the election of Bernardino Rivadavia in 1826 he sided with the centralising Unitarians against the rural Federalists, and in 1831 he fled to Chile, where he wrote political commentary and taught. After returning to San Juan in 1836 he founded the journal El Zonda, which a punitive tax forced to close in 1840. He belonged to the Generation of 1837, reformers who advocated republicanism, free trade and freedom of speech.

Between 1843 and 1850 he was frequently in exile. In Chile he wrote Facundo, published in instalments in El Progreso in 1845, which attacked the governor of Buenos Aires, Juan Manuel de Rosas, and contrasted European civilisation with the barbarism of the gaucho and the caudillo. He returned to Buenos Aires in 1855 and was elected president, against the manoeuvres of Bartolomé Mitre, serving from 1868 to 1874.

His government carried out the first national census in 1869, which counted 1,836,490 inhabitants, of whom 71 per cent were illiterate. The Subsidies Law of 1871 funded new schools, and primary schools rose to 1,816, with pupils increasing from 30,000 to 110,000. About 75 teachers, mostly women, were brought from the United States. Immigration rose, with 280,000 arrivals, the railway network grew from 573 to 1,331 kilometres, and about 5,000 km of telegraph lines were laid. The Paraguayan War ended in March 1870.

After his term Sarmiento served as senator and briefly as interior minister, and in 1882 helped pass the law making schools free, mandatory and separate from religion. He died of a heart attack in Asunción on 11 September 1888, aged 77, and was buried in Buenos Aires. Miguel de Unamuno considered him among the finest writers of Castilian prose. He admired the liberty of the United States but warned that liberty could turn into anarchy and civil war.
dominican-order: The order grew out of a medieval ideal in which men of God were no longer expected to stay behind the walls of a cloister but travelled among the people, taking the apostles of the early Church as their example. Two orders of mendicant friars came from it: the Friars Minor, led by Francis of Assisi, and the Friars Preachers, led by the Castilian priest Dominic de Guzmán.

In 1203 he accompanied Diego de Acebo, Bishop of Osma, on a diplomatic mission to Denmark. The south of France was then a stronghold of the Cathars, whom the Church considered heretical. In 1206 Dominic established several women he had reconciled to the faith in a convent at Prouille, near Toulouse, which became the foundation of the Dominican nuns and later his headquarters for missionary work.

Dominic set up a religious community in Toulouse in 1214 and in 1215 gave it an institutional form with the approval of Bishop Foulques of Toulouse. It followed the Rule of Saint Augustine, which made its members canons regular rather than monks, able to carry out ministry and common life while living in individual poverty. Its founding documents name two purposes, preaching and the salvation of souls. Pope Honorius III approved the order by the bull Religiosam vitam on 22 December 1216.

The Pax Mongolica of the 13th and 14th centuries allowed missionaries to travel east. Dominican friars were preaching on the Volga steppes by 1225, and in 1240 Pope Gregory IX sent others to Persia and Armenia. Jordanus Catala de Severac went first to Persia and in 1321 to India, and recorded his observations in a book translated as Wonders of the East. Later, Gaspar da Cruz worked across the Portuguese empire in Asia and in 1569 or 1570 published the first European book devoted wholly to China.

The order's highest authority is the General Chapter, made up of the Chapter of Provincials, the heads of the provinces, and the Chapter of Definitors, who represent each province. This arrangement is unique in the Catholic Church. New legislation takes effect only after three successive meetings approve it.

Friars include ordained priests and non-ordained cooperator brothers. Their life rests on four pillars: prayer, study, community and preaching, and a long period of study precedes the solemn vow. Alongside the friars stand the cloistered nuns, active sisters, whose congregations are largely a product of the 19th century, priestly fraternities, lay Dominicans and associates. Dominican friars numbered 6,058 in 2013 and 5,369 in 2024.
dominican-republic: The country occupies the eastern part of Hispaniola, with the Atlantic Ocean to the north and the Caribbean Sea to the south, and shares a border of 376 km with Haiti. It is the second-largest country in the Antilles by area, after Cuba. The Cordillera Central is the highest range in the West Indies and holds the four highest peaks in the Caribbean, among them Pico Duarte at 3,098 metres. The capital and largest city, Santo Domingo, lies on the southern coast.

The Arawakan-speaking ancestors of the Taíno reached Hispaniola by around 600 CE, and by 1492 the island was divided into five Taíno chiefdoms. Christopher Columbus landed on 5 December 1492 and claimed the island for the Crown of Castile. In 1496 his brother Bartholomew built Santo Domingo, the first permanent European settlement in the Americas. Taíno chiefs such as Anacaona, Caonabo and Enriquillo resisted the conquest, but their numbers fell drastically from smallpox, measles and other diseases, and enslaved people from Africa were imported in their place. The last record of pure Taínos dates from 1864, though Taíno ancestry survived through intermixing.

By the Treaty of Ryswick in 1697, Spain ceded the western third of the island to France. A group of Dominicans declared independence from Spain in November 1821 but were annexed by Haiti in February 1822. Independence came in 1844 after the Dominican War of Independence, and the Spanish were permanently ousted in the Restoration War of 1863–1865. The United States occupied the country from 1916 to 1924. Rafael Trujillo ruled from 1930 until his assassination in 1961, and Joaquín Balaguer held office in 1966–1978 and 1986–1996.

The Dominican Republic is a representative democracy with an elected president and a bicameral Congress. Its culture has a European basis influenced by African and Taíno elements. Santo Domingo's Colonial Zone is a World Heritage Site and holds the first cathedral, palace, monastery and fortress built in the Americas. The name Dominican comes from Saint Dominic.
dominion: The word dominion means that which is mastered or ruled. The British used it of their colonies and territorial possessions from the 16th century, and it was sometimes applied to Wales from 1535 to around 1800. It was conferred as an official title on the Colony of Virginia about 1660 and on the Dominion of New England in 1686. The later status followed the mid-19th-century achievement of full responsible government in British colonies, whose legislatures could then make laws in all matters except foreign affairs, defence and international trade.

At the London Conference of 1866 Samuel Leonard Tilley proposed the name One Dominion under the Name of Canada for the confederation of the Province of Canada, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, taking it from Psalm 72, verse eight. The British North America Act 1867 began the use of the title Dominion of Canada, though it gave no extra autonomy.

The Imperial Conference of 1907 introduced the idea of the Dominions as self-governing countries, referring to Canada and Australia in this way. In 1919 the self-governing Dominions signed the Treaty of Versailles independently of the British government and became individual members of the League of Nations. The Balfour Declaration of 1926 gave Australia, Canada, the Irish Free State, New Zealand, Newfoundland and South Africa the status of autonomous communities within the British Empire, equal in status and not subordinate to one another, though united by a common allegiance to the Crown.

The Statute of Westminster of December 1931 confirmed their full legislative independence. At the request of Australia and New Zealand it applied to them only when their parliaments confirmed it, in 1942 and 1947. Newfoundland suspended its self-government in 1934 after an economic collapse and joined Canada in 1949.

After the Second World War the empire became the Commonwealth of Nations. India and Pakistan became dominions in 1947 and Ceylon in 1948. At the Commonwealth Prime Ministers' Conference of 1949, when India intended to become a republic, the term Commonwealth country replaced dominion so that realms and republics could both be full members. By 1952 the United Kingdom no longer used the term for member nations, though it stayed in loose use for around thirty more years, mostly for smaller realms where the monarch remained head of state.
domitian: Domitian was born in Rome on 24 October 51 as the youngest son of Vespasian and Flavia Domitilla Major. He had an older sister, Domitilla the Younger, and an older brother, Titus. The Flavians had risen from relative obscurity to prominence in four generations, gaining wealth and status under the Julio-Claudian emperors. Domitian spent much of his youth in the shadow of Titus, who won military renown in the First Jewish-Roman War, while their father and brother were away commanding armies in Germania and Judaea.

After Vespasian became emperor in 69, Domitian received honours but no responsibilities. In 70 he persuaded Domitia Longina, daughter of the general Gnaeus Domitius Corbulo, to leave her husband and marry him. For about ten years his role stayed largely ceremonial.

After the death of Titus, Domitian was declared emperor by the Praetorian Guard. His reign of fifteen years was the longest since that of Tiberius. He dropped the republican facade kept by his father and brother, moved the centre of government to the imperial court and drastically curtailed the powers of the Senate. According to Pliny the Younger, he believed the empire should be governed as a divine monarchy. He took the office of perpetual censor to control public and private morals.

He revalued the Roman coinage, raising the silver purity of the denarius from 90% to 98%. A financial crisis in 85 forced it down to 93.5%, still above the levels of Vespasian and Titus. Around fifty structures were built, restored or completed in Rome, among them the Stadium of Domitian, the Odeon of Domitian and the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus on the Capitoline Hill, and the Flavian Palace on the Palatine Hill.

His campaigns were mostly defensive. He developed the Limes Germanicus, a network of roads, forts and watchtowers along the Rhine, and founded the Legio I Minervia in 82. On 1 January 89 Lucius Antonius Saturninus, governor of Germania Superior, rose in revolt with two legions and the Chatti; the rising stayed within his province and was put down.

Domitian was assassinated on 18 September 96 in a plot by court officials. Suetonius gives the main role to the chamberlain Parthenius; the blow was struck by Parthenius' freedman Maximus and Stephanus, a steward of Domitian's niece Flavia Domitilla. The Senate proclaimed Nerva emperor the same day, and condemned Domitian's memory to oblivion.

Most surviving accounts come from senatorial or aristocratic writers such as Tacitus, Pliny the Younger and Suetonius, who wrote after his death. Only the poets Martial and Statius, who praised him extravagantly, wrote during his reign. Since the 20th century, historians such as Brian W. Jones have described him as a ruthless but efficient autocrat whose policies laid foundations for the peaceful second century.
domodossola: Domodossola lies at the foot of the Alps, in the Toce plain at the crossroads of the Bognanco, Divedro, Antigorio, Vigezzo and Isorno valleys. It stands at the confluence of the Bogna and Toce rivers, 272 metres above sea level, and is the main centre of the Ossola. Much of its municipal territory is mountainous, and the ski resort of Domobianca lies within it, on the slopes of the Moncucco.

The area has been inhabited since prehistoric times. Known as Oscella, the town was the chief town of the Lepontii when the Romans conquered the region in 12 BCE, and a Roman road linking Mediolanum to Lake Maggiore passed through it. Afterwards it belonged to the Ostrogothic Kingdom, whose king Theodoric the Great fortified the nearby Mattarella hill. In the sixth century the Lombards sacked and burned it, and the Franks later drove them out. It then became a fief of the bishop-count of Novara, who built a castle there. A collegiate church of the eleventh century gave it the name Domus Oxile, which gradually became its modern name.

In 1381, after Swiss raids and the conflict between Guelphs and Ghibellines, the town swore fealty to Gian Galeazzo Visconti, Lord of Milan, in exchange for military protection. After the Italian Wars it came briefly under the French, then for nearly two centuries under the Spaniards and in 1706 under the Austrians. The Treaty of Worms of 1743 gave it to the Kingdom of Sardinia, and in 1818 King Victor Emmanuel I made it the capital of the new Province of Ossola. The opening of the Simplon Tunnel in 1906 put it again on a major international route. Industry and hydroelectric plants brought growth, and the population almost doubled between 1881 and 1921.

On 10 September 1944 Italian Resistance forces liberated Domodossola, which became the capital of the Republic of Ossola, one of the largest partisan republics in German-occupied northern Italy. German and Fascist forces crushed the republic on 23 October 1944, and many inhabitants fled to Switzerland to escape reprisals. In 1945 the city flag was awarded the Gold Medal of Military Valor.

Domodossola is a city and comune in the Province of Verbano-Cusio-Ossola in Piedmont, northern Italy. It is the main railway hub in northern Piedmont and an international stopping point between Milan and Brig in Switzerland through the Simplon Pass. Its best-known landmark is the Sacro Monte Calvario, a pilgrimage site and UNESCO World Heritage Site, on the same hill as the remains of the medieval castle of Mattarella. Its name is widely known in Italy from the spelling alphabet, in which D stands for Domodossola.
don-quixote: In July 1604 Miguel de Cervantes sold the rights to El ingenioso hidalgo don Quixote de la Mancha, later called Part I, to the publisher and bookseller Francisco de Robles for an unknown sum. The licence to publish was granted in September, printing finished in December, and the book came out on 16 January 1605. It was an immediate success. Most of the 400 copies of the first edition went to the New World, and although most were lost in a shipwreck near Havana, about 70 reached Lima and were sent on to Cuzco. For Cervantes and his readers it was a single volume, and the mention of further adventures to be told was conventional rather than a plan for a sequel.

The hero is an hidalgo of nearly 50 from an unspecified place in La Mancha, Alonso Quixano, who lives frugally with his niece and housekeeper. His obsession with chivalric romances leads him to become a knight errant. He dons an old suit of armour, renames himself Don Quixote, names his old workhorse Rocinante and chooses as his lady love Aldonza Lorenzo, whom he renames Dulcinea del Toboso. Cervantes writes that the rest of the book was translated from an Arabic text by the Moorish historian Cide Hamete Benengeli. Don Quixote does not see the world as it is, while his squire, the farm labourer Sancho Panza, brings an earthy wit to his lofty rhetoric.

Part One also holds stories told by figures the two men meet, the longest being The Ill-Advised Curiosity, about the Florentine nobleman Anselmo, who talks his friend Lothario into testing his wife's fidelity. Part Two appeared ten years later and is an early example of metafiction, since its characters have read the first part. The names play on words: Rocinante is a reversal, Dulcinea alludes to illusion, and quixote is a term for the armour that protects the thighs.

Cervantes had probably written no further than Chapter 59 of Part Two by late July 1614. In about September a spurious Part Two by a certain Alonso Fernández de Avellaneda was published at Tarragona. Its author, never identified with any consensus, insulted Cervantes in the prologue, and Cervantes answered in the later chapters of his own Part Two. Within seven years of Part One the book had been translated into French, German, Italian and English. It influenced Alexandre Dumas's The Three Musketeers and Edmond Rostand's Cyrano de Bergerac, and inspired works by Pablo Picasso and Richard Strauss. It gave English the word quixotic and the phrase tilting at windmills, meaning attacking imaginary enemies.
don-river: The Don is the fifth-longest river in Europe. It rises in the town of Novomoskovsk, 60 kilometres south-east of Tula, and flows 1,870 kilometres to the Sea of Azov. Its upper half meanders gently south, while the lower half makes a great eastern curve past Voronezh before the final stretch, an estuary, runs west-south-west. Its basin lies between the Dnieper basin to the west, the lower Volga basin to the east and the Oka basin to the north. The main tributary is the Seversky Donets, and the main city on the river is Rostov-on-Don.

The name derives from the Avestan and Rigveda word dānu. According to the Kurgan hypothesis, the Volga-Don region was the homeland of the Proto-Indo-Europeans around 4,000 BCE. In antiquity some Greek geographers viewed the river as the border between Europe and Asia. The Greeks called it the Tanaïs, which was also the name of a city on it, situated in the Maeotian marshes; they also called it Iazartes, and Pliny gives its Scythian name as Silys. A Greek source traditionally, though not certainly, attributed to Plutarch placed the Amazons of Greek mythology on the Don. Byzantine traders used the river, and it has been a major trading route ever since.

In the early Middle Ages the Khazar Khaganate controlled much of the lower Don and built the limestone fortress of Sarkel on its left bank to defend a vital portage between the Don and the Volga. After the Mongol conquests most of the basin passed to the Golden Horde, which set up the trade outpost of Azak in the estuary, an area speculated to be the source of the Black Death in the mid-14th century. The Don Cossacks, who settled the valley in the 16th and 17th centuries, took their name from the river. Its middle and upper reaches were not mapped accurately before the Tsardom of Russia gradually conquered the area in the 16th century.

The Volga-Don Canal, 101 kilometres long, links the Don with the Volga where the two rivers come within about 100 kilometres of each other, and the Tsimlyansk Dam raises the Don's level there, forming the Tsimlyansk Reservoir. Below it, three dam-and-ship-lock complexes maintain depth for 130 kilometres. The Kochetovsky Lock was built in 1914–19 and doubled in 2004–08. The region is the setting of Mikhail Sholokhov's novel And Quiet Flows the Don.
donald-ii-of-scotland: Domnall mac Causantín, anglicised as Donald II, was the son of Constantine I, Causantín mac Cináeda. The Prophecy of Berchán gives him the epithet Dásachtach, the Madman. He came to the throne on the death or deposition of his cousin Giric, whose date is not certainly known but is usually placed in 889. Giric had killed Donald's uncle Àed mac Cináeda, who reigned from 877 to 879.

The Chronicle of the Kings of Alba says Donald held the kingdom for eleven years, from 889 to 900, and that the Northmen wasted Pictland in his reign. It reports a battle at Innisibsolian in which the Scots defeated the Danes, so that he is thought to have fought the Vikings in the north continuously.

The Annals of Ulster and the Chronicon Scotorum date his death to 900 and call him king of Alba rather than king of the Picts. This change of title is seen as a step towards the kingdom of the Scots, but historians do not generally credit it to Donald. The consensus is that the key changes occurred in the reign of Constantine II, though the reign of Giric has also been proposed.

The Chronicle says he was killed at Opidum Fother, modern Dunnottar, by the Gentiles. It has been suggested that the attack on Dunnottar was no small raid but linked to the ravaging of Scotland attributed to Harald Fairhair in the Heimskringla. The Prophecy of Berchán places his death at Dunnottar but seems to blame Gaels rather than Norsemen, and other sources report that he died at Forres. He was buried on Iona. His cousin Constantine II succeeded him, and Donald's son Malcolm later became king as Malcolm I.
donatello: Donato di Niccolò di Betto Bardi was born in Florence, probably in 1386, judging from his own tax declaration of July 1427, in which he claimed to be 41. His father, Niccolò di Betto Bardi, was a wool-stretcher and a member of the wool workers' guild. Donatello's first appearance in the records is in January 1401, when, aged about 15, he was accused in Pistoia of hitting a German with a stick. He appears to have befriended, and perhaps worked with, the goldsmith Filippo Brunelleschi, some ten years older. All accounts describe him as amiable and well liked but poor at the business side of his career, accepting more commissions than he could handle, and he enjoyed steady Medici patronage.

By early 1408 Donatello had the commission for a life-size prophet for Florence Cathedral, to pair with one by Nanni di Banco; it was not placed as intended and appears to be lost. He also made statues for the niches of Orsanmichele, and developed stiacciato, a very shallow relief, with Saint George Freeing the Princess as an early milestone. Around 1425 he formed a partnership with the architect Michelozzo, which lasted nine years and ended partly because of Donatello's delays on an exterior pulpit for Prato Cathedral. In the 1430s and 1440s he made many dancing children, putti and spiritelli.

His bronze David, now in the Bargello, is his best-known work: the first known free-standing nude statue since antiquity, conceived fully in the round at nearly life size. It was probably commissioned by Cosimo de' Medici between 1434 and 1440. In 1443 he was called to Padua by the heirs of the condottiere Gattamelata, whose equestrian monument, cast mostly in 1447 or 1448 and finished in 1450, was installed in 1453. His ten years there are thought to have stimulated Padua's later table bronzes. He worked in Siena between 1457 and 1461, though ageing.

Donatello remained in Florence after returning from Siena and died in 1466, on 13 December. In his last years, with assistants, he made the reliefs that now form two pulpits in San Lorenzo, assembled in that form only in the following century. His influence can be seen in all Florentine sculpture of the 15th century and well beyond, and most of his major church works remain in place, with the main museum collection in the Bargello. Giorgio Vasari, writing around a century after the events, recognised his stature but made clear errors, placing his birth in 1403.
donation-of-constantine: In many manuscripts, including the oldest, the document is titled Constitutum domini Constantini imperatoris. It was included in the 9th-century Pseudo-Isidorean decretals. Its origin is debated. One suggestion is that an early draft was made shortly after the middle of the 8th century to assist Pope Stephen II in his negotiations with Pepin the Short, who in 754 received the pope's anointing as king; the lands Pepin then gave the pope became the Papal States.

Another view holds that it was a move in Roman church politics to raise the Lateran against the rising Vatican, perhaps composed by a Greek monk in a Roman monastery. The German medievalist Johannes Fried distinguishes the Donation from a shorter, earlier forgery, the Constitutum Constantini, of which he thinks it a later expansion.

The text is dated 30 March without a year, and names as Constantine's co-consul in his fourth term (315) a Gallicanus who held the office in 317. It has Constantine profess Christianity and grant Pope Sylvester I imperial insignia and privileges and the Lateran Palace. Rome, the rest of Italy and the western provinces are made over to the papacy. Sylvester is also given supremacy over the four principal sees of Alexandria, Antioch, Jerusalem and Constantinople.

It rests on the 5th-century Acts of Sylvester, in which the pope rescues the Romans from a dragon and cures the emperor's leprosy through baptism. Because it implied that Sylvester held imperial rank before Constantinople was inaugurated in 330, it also served to reduce the authority of Constantinople.

The earliest known allusion may be a letter of 778 in which Pope Hadrian I urged Charlemagne to follow Constantine's example. Pope Leo IX was the first pope to invoke the decree directly, in 1054, in a letter to Patriarch Michael I Cerularius of Constantinople, citing much of it in the belief that it was genuine. In the 11th and 12th centuries it was often cited in the investiture conflicts. Dante regretted the evil born from the donation.

Doubt had been raised since 1001, when Otto III's chancery denied its authenticity. In the mid-15th century Nicholas of Cusa and Reginald Pecocke concluded independently that it was a forgery. Lorenzo Valla argued from philology that its language could not belong to the 4th century and could most likely be dated to the 8th. Valla's treatise was taken up by Protestant writers such as Ulrich von Hutten and Martin Luther. Caesar Baronius admitted the forgery in his Annales Ecclesiastici, published from 1588 to 1607, after which it was almost universally accepted as such.
donatism: Donatism was a schism from the Catholic Church in the Archdiocese of Carthage, rooted in the Christian community of Roman Africa. During the Diocletianic Persecutions the governor was satisfied when Christians handed over their scriptures as a token repudiation of faith, and critics called those who did so traditores. The Donatists were rigorists: the church must be a church of saints, and sacraments given by traditores were invalid. In 311 Caecilian was consecrated bishop of Carthage by Felix of Aptungi, an alleged traditor. His opponents consecrated Majorinus, who was succeeded by Donatus Magnus, after whom the movement is named.

Constantine gave money to Caecilian for churches damaged in the persecution and nothing to the Donatists, which worsened the dispute. A commission appointed by Pope Miltiades condemned the Donatists in 313, and the Council of Arles in 314 ruled against them again. In 317 Constantine issued an edict threatening death to anyone disturbing the imperial peace and another calling for confiscation of Donatist church property, but by 321 he asked the bishops for moderation. The movement spread mainly among the indigenous Berber population and blended Christianity with local customs. The Circumcellions, as opponents called them, were roving groups who regarded martyrdom as the supreme virtue and sometimes used violence.

Augustine of Hippo campaigned against Donatism as bishop. He taught that a sacrament is valid whatever the character of the priest, and he justified force against the Donatists, though he rejected the death penalty. In 409 a decree condemned them as heretics and ordered them to surrender their churches. Donatism survived the Vandal conquest and the Byzantine reconquest, and it is unknown how long it lasted. In the Middle Ages and the Reformation the charge of Donatism was made against reformers such as John Wycliffe and Jan Hus, who held that the moral failings of priests invalidated their offices.
donato-bramante: Bramante was born Donato di Pascuccio d'Antonio and is also known as Bramante Lazzari. He was born at Fermignano near Urbino, where in 1467 Luciano Laurana was adding an arcaded courtyard and other Renaissance features to Federico da Montefeltro's ducal palace. He knew the painters Melozzo da Forlì and Piero della Francesca, who were interested in perspective. His architecture has eclipsed his painting.

Around 1474 Bramante moved to Milan, a city with a deep Gothic tradition, and built several churches in the new antique style. From 1476 Duke Ludovico Sforza made him virtually his court architect. His commissions culminated in the trompe-l'œil choir of Santa Maria presso San Satiro, built in 1482 to 1486. Space was limited, so he made a theatrical apse in bas-relief that combines perspective with Roman details. He also built the tribune of Santa Maria delle Grazie in 1492 to 1499 and the cloisters of Sant'Ambrogio in 1497 to 1498, and worked on Pavia Cathedral, setting the design and creating the crypt and part of the apse.

In 1499 the French army drove out his Sforza patron, and Bramante went to Rome, where Cardinal Riario already knew him. Cardinal Della Rovere, soon to be Pope Julius II, took notice of him. He designed the cloister of Santa Maria della Pace in 1500 to 1504 and in 1502 the Tempietto of San Pietro in Montorio, built over the spot where Peter was martyred. Though small, it has the strict proportions and symmetry of classical buildings, with slender Doric columns and a dome, and it marked the beginning of the High Renaissance in Rome.

In November 1503 Julius II engaged him for the complete rebuilding of St Peter's Basilica, the grandest architectural commission in 16th-century Europe. The cornerstone of the first great pier of the crossing was laid on 17 April 1506. Bramante planned a centralised Greek cross, which symbolised sublime perfection for him and his generation, with four chapels filling the corners between equal transepts, each capped with a smaller dome around the great dome. The plan was more Romano-Byzantine in form than the church built, and it was fundamentally altered when the nave was extended after his death. Michelangelo later executed a design based on it.

He also planned the Cortile del Belvedere, a vast courtyard linking the buildings of the Vatican, and designed the Palazzo Caprini. Very few of his drawings survive, though some by his assistants do. He wrote about architecture and composed eighty sonnets. He died on 11 April 1514.
donaueschingen: Donaueschingen lies in the Baar basin in the southern Black Forest, in the Schwarzwald-Baar district of Baden-Württemberg. It stands about 13 kilometres south of Villingen-Schwenningen, 24 kilometres west of Tuttlingen and about 30 kilometres north of the Swiss town of Schaffhausen. The town takes its name from the Danube, German Donau, which begins at the confluence here of the Brigach and the Breg, its two source tributaries. An enclosed karst spring in the park of Donaueschingen Palace, the source of the Donaubach, is also known as the source of the Danube. The heights of the municipal area fall from 1,020 metres in the Black Forest to about 660 metres on the Baar plateau and rise again above 900 metres at the Swabian Alb.

The place is first recorded as Esginga in 889, and the modern form of its name is first attested in 1292. In 1283 Rudolph von Habsburg granted the principality of Baar and Donaueschingen to Heinrich von Fürstenberg, a grant that carried the right to brew beer, which is the origin of the Fürstenberg Brewery. In 1488 possession passed to the Count of Fürstenberg-Baar, and from the 18th century the town was the residence of the princes of Fürstenberg, who lived in Schloss Donaueschingen.

In 1806 it came under the rule of the Grand Duchy of Baden and received township in 1810. A large part of the town was destroyed by fire in 1908. It has a tradition as a military garrison: the French military had barracks there from 1945 to 2014, and until the early 1990s the United States Air Force ran a contingency hospital, which was most used in 1989, when it housed refugees leaving East Germany for the West. The Fürstenberg princes were nominally mediatised and deposed as absolute rulers, but they kept much property, including the palace and its gardens. They owned an important manuscript of the Nibelungenlied, Manuscript C, until they sold it in 2001.

The town had 21,750 people in 2015 and is a regional rail hub where four lines join, including the Schwarzwaldbahn and the Höllentalbahn to Freiburg. The long-distance Danube Cycle Trail starts there. The Donaueschingen Festival for contemporary music, founded in 1921 and one of the world's oldest festivals for new music, takes place every October, and guest composers have included Paul Hindemith, Arnold Schoenberg, Pierre Boulez, John Cage and György Ligeti. The Fürstenberg Library holds early copies of five of Mozart's operas, an important source for reviving historically informed performance of 18th-century opera.
donbas: The Donbas lies in south-eastern Ukraine between the middle and lower Donets river in the north and the Azov Upland and Lowland in the south, across the border from Russia. The core area, about 23,000 square kilometres, corresponds roughly to the Donets Ridge, where coal seams reach the surface and which is known as the Old Donbas. Coal elsewhere lies at depths of 500 to 600 metres or more, in areas that became producing regions only after the Second World War.

Nomadic peoples including the Scythians, Alans, Huns, Pechenegs, Kipchaks, Tatars and Nogais lived on this steppe for centuries. It was largely unpopulated until the second half of the 17th century, when Don Cossacks founded the first permanent settlements. The first town, Solanoye (now Soledar), was founded in 1676 for rock-salt working. The area, called the Wild Fields, lay under the Cossack Hetmanate and the Crimean Khanate until the Russian Empire conquered the one and annexed the other in the mid to late 18th century.

Coal was discovered in 1721 and exploited on a large scale from the mid to late 19th century, when the name Donbas came into use. Early steel mills were set up at Luhansk in 1795, near Yenakiieve in 1859 to 1864 and at Lysychansk in 1866 to 1870. The Welsh businessman John Hughes founded Yuzivka, later Donetsk, in 1869 and built a steel mill and collieries. Landless peasants came in large numbers to find work, and poor conditions led to strikes, including a wave in 1905.

The region was incorporated into the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic in 1919. Coal output fell sharply between 1913 and 1920, and pre-war levels returned by 1928 to 1929. Under German occupation in 1941 to 1943, 279,000 civilians were killed in what is now Donetsk Oblast and 45,649 in Luhansk Oblast, and production of 1940 was restored only in 1949. After independence in 1991 industry declined sharply. In 2014 unrest in the region grew into a war that has continued within the wider Russo-Ukrainian war.

The Donbas is usually taken to mean Donetsk Oblast and Luhansk Oblast. Donetsk is considered its unofficial capital, and other large cities include Mariupol, Luhansk, Makiivka, Horlivka, Kramatorsk, Sloviansk, Alchevsk, Sievierodonetsk and Lysychansk. At the census of 2001 the population of the Ukrainian part was about 58 percent ethnic Ukrainian and 38 percent ethnic Russian. The region remains defined by coal, iron and steel.
dongmyeong-of-goguryeo: The records of Dongmyeong are often regarded as partly mythological, and how far they are historical is debated. Much of his story is taken from an earlier one about the founder of Buyeo, which the Goguryeo monarchy appropriated in the 4th century CE to raise its own standing. The best-known versions are in the Samguk sagi and the Samguk yusa. Chumong, his personal name, was a Buyeo word for an excellent archer, and Dongmyeong, Brilliant Saintly King of the East, is a posthumous name.

In the story, Lady Yuhwa, daughter of Habaek, bore a large egg that animals refused to harm, and a boy hatched from it. He was a master of archery by seven. Daeso, eldest son of Geumwa, king of Eastern Buyeo, feared him, and Yuhwa told him to leave. Pursued, he reached the Eomsa River and, declaring himself a son of the Heavenly God and grandson of Habaek, made fish and turtles form a bridge.

He gathered followers, reached Jolbon Stream and founded Goguryeo, taking the surname Ko at the age of 21. In the first year of his reign he struck the Mohe, who surrendered. He defeated Song Yang, king of Biryu, in an archery contest, and Song Yang submitted in June of 36 BCE and was made Marquis of Damul. Later campaigns subdued the State of Haengin and the Northern Okjeo. In 19 BCE his son Yuri arrived from Buyeo and was named crown prince.

A variant noted by the compilers of the Samguk sagi says that Biryu and Onjo were sons of Soseono by an earlier husband, and that Dongmyeong married her. When Yuri became crown prince, Biryu left with Onjo and Soseono to found a kingdom of his own.

According to the Gwanggaeto Stele, Dongmyeong rode a dragon into Heaven at 39, and only his whip was buried at Yongsan. The Confucian Kim Pusik read this as a metaphor and wrote that he died and was buried there. Goguryeo worshipped him as an ancestral deity, and Balhae and Goryeo succeeded the kingdom. The Hoengseong Ko clan of Korea and the Koma clan of Japan consider him their founder. Other records, among them the tombstone of Go Ja, suggest that Goguryeo was older than the Samguk sagi's chronology allows.
dorchester-dorset: Dorchester stands on gently sloping ground beside the south bank of the River Frome, about 7 miles (11 km) north of Weymouth, south of the Dorset Downs and north of the South Dorset Ridgeway. Growth to the north and north-east is limited by the river's floodplain and watermeadows. The chalk hills of the ridgeway carry over five hundred ancient monuments, including barrows, stone circles and hillforts, and many finds from the area are displayed in the Dorset Museum in the town.

The earliest settlements lay about 2 miles (3.2 km) south-west of the modern centre near Maiden Castle, a large Iron Age hill fort that was one of the most powerful settlements in pre-Roman Britain; different tribes lived there from about 4000 BCE. The Romans defeated the local tribes by about 70 CE and set up a garrison from which grew the town they called Durnovaria. It is recorded in the 4th-century Antonine Itinerary and became a market centre, a road junction and staging post, and one of the twin capitals of the Durotriges.

Around 790 the first recorded Viking raid of the period came ashore on the Isle of Portland. Beaduheard, the king's reeve in Dorchester, rode out with a few men, took the newcomers for merchants and was killed with his companions. By 864 the area was held by Saxons who called themselves Dorsaetas, and the town's name passed through Dornwaraceaster to Dorchester.

Fires struck the town in 1613, 1622, 1725 and 1775; the first destroyed 300 houses and two churches, All Saints and Holy Trinity. After the Monmouth Rebellion the town was the site of the Bloody Assizes, presided over by Judge Jeffreys. In 1833 the Tolpuddle Martyrs founded the Friendly Society of Agricultural Labourers; because members swore an oath, they were arrested and tried in the Shire Hall, with cells beneath the courtroom.

Dorchester is the county town of Dorset, with a weekly market, a hospital, schools and a college serving the surrounding area. It has 293 listed structures, among them the Church of St George, with a late 11th-century south door, the Church of St Peter, mostly of 1420 to 1421, Shire Hall, Max Gate and the Roman town house. Thomas Hardy lived at Max Gate and made Dorchester the model for Casterbridge in The Mayor of Casterbridge.
dordogne: Dordogne is a large rural department in the Nouvelle-Aquitaine region, roughly half-way between the Loire Valley and the Pyrenees. It is named after the river Dordogne and corresponds roughly to the ancient county of Périgord. It is the third largest department of metropolitan France and the largest landlocked one. Four Périgords are distinguished: Périgord Vert, around Nontron; Périgord Blanc, around the prefecture Périgueux; Périgord Pourpre, around Bergerac, a wine region; and Périgord Noir, around Sarlat, which overlooks the valleys of the Vézère and the Dordogne.

The county of Périgord dates back to the time when ancient Celtic Gaulish tribes lived in the area. The name is explained by the Gaulish word Petrocore, meaning four tribes. The Petrocores took part in the resistance against the Roman occupation of Gaul. Gallo-Roman remains include the ruined tower and arena at Périgueux, formerly Vesone, and villa remains at Montcaret. After the province of Guienne passed to the English Crown following the remarriage of Eleanor of Aquitaine in 1152, Périgord came under English suzerainty, and it oscillated between France and England for more than three hundred years until the end of the Hundred Years' War in 1453.

In the late 15th and early 16th centuries the nobility erected most of more than 1,200 châteaux, manors and country houses. In the second half of the 16th century the violence of the Wars of Religion reached a peak partly focused on Périgord, and Bergerac was one of the most powerful Huguenot strongholds. Dordogne is one of the original 83 departments created on 4 March 1790 during the French Revolution, formed from the former province of Périgord.

The prefecture is Périgueux. The population peaked at 505,789 in 1851 and declined to 373,000 by 1975, before rising again to about 417,000 by 2023. The department has more than 1,500 castles, among them Beynac, Biron and Hautefort, along with bastides and abbeys. Writers associated with the region include Michel de Montaigne and Étienne de La Boétie. The caves of Lascaux are closed to the public, and a replica, Lascaux II, is open to visitors.
dordrecht: The municipality covers the whole of Dordrecht Island, bordered by the rivers Oude Maas, Beneden Merwede, Nieuwe Merwede, Hollands Diep and Dordtsche Kil. The city formed along the Thure river in the midst of peat marshes, in the Rhine-Meuse-Scheldt delta. The name appears as Thuredriht around 1120 and seems to mean a thoroughfare: a canal or river through which ships were pulled by rope from one river to another. An older explanation from the Latin trajectum, a ford, was rejected in 1996. English once called it Dort or Dordt, and its inhabitants call it Dordt.

A remark of about 1120 records that Count Dirk IV of Holland had been murdered in 1049 near Thuredrech, which refers to the place. In 1572, four years into the Dutch Revolt, representatives of all the cities of Holland except Amsterdam, together with the Watergeuzen under William II de la Marck, met in Dordrecht in a secret First Assembly of the Free States. The meeting was a rebellious act, since only King Philip II or his stadtholder, then the Duke of Alba, could call the States of Holland.

From 13 November 1618 to 9 May 1619 the Synod of Dordrecht met to settle the dispute between the central tenets of Calvinism and the school of thought of Jacobus Arminius, whose followers, the Remonstrants, had set out their dissent in the Five Articles of Remonstrance of 1610. They were opposed by the Contra-Remonstrants, or Gomarists, led by the theologian Franciscus Gomarus.

Merchants of Dordrecht helped found sugar plantations in the West Indies, which led at the end of the 17th century to a sugar refining industry; the city had 16 refineries in the 18th century, against 120 in Amsterdam and 40 in Rotterdam. Its economic importance nonetheless began to wane in that century. From 1780 to 1787 it was a home of the Patriots, who sought to remove the hereditary stadtholder, until it capitulated to Prussian troops on 18 September 1787.
The opening of the Voorne Canal in 1829 and of the Nieuwe Waterweg in 1883 ended Dordrecht's role as a first-rate sea harbour; by 1910 Rotterdam sent about 200 times as much cargo up the Rhine.

Dordrecht is the fifth-largest city of South Holland, with about 123,000 inhabitants in 2025, and the most important city of the Drechtsteden. Its medieval centre has over 950 monuments, seven historic churches and six museums. The Grote Kerk, built between 1285 and 1470, has a 65-metre tower with a carillon of 67 bells. The Nieuwkerk of 1175 is the city's oldest building, and the Augustinian monastery Het Hof, built in 1275, was the meeting place of the First Assembly of the Free States.
dorians: The Dorians were one of the four major groups into which the Greeks of the Classical period divided themselves, with the Aeolians, Achaeans and Ionians. The earliest literary mention is in the Odyssey, which already places Dorians on Crete. Accounts of their origin vary. One theory, widely believed in antiquity, held that they came from the mountains of northern Greece, such as Macedonia and Epirus. Herodotus presents the events later called the Dorian invasion as transfers of population from Thessaly, and Pausanias has Dorians from Oeta led by Hyllus, a son of Heracles, who built ships at Naupactus to cross the Gulf of Corinth.

Modern scholarship treats the Dorian invasion as a concept meant to explain the replacement of East Greek (Ionian) speech in the Peloponnese by West Greek (Doric) speech in official circles. Its objectives have not been met, though investigation has ruled out speculative hypotheses. Most scholars doubt that it was the main cause of the collapse of Mycenaean civilisation, and the source of the West Greek speakers remains unattested by solid evidence.

Most Dorians settled in the Peloponnese, but they also held Crete, Rhodes, Sicily and parts of southern Italy. In Asia Minor the Dorian Hexapolis comprised Halicarnassus and Cnidus, Kos, and Lindos, Kameiros and Ialyssos on Rhodes. Colonies from Corinth, Megara and the Dorian islands lay along the southern coast of Sicily from Syracuse to Selinus, and Taras was a Spartan colony. In the fifth century BCE Dorians and Ionians were the two most politically important Greek peoples, and Thucydides saw the Peloponnesian War in part as Ionians fighting Dorians. Scholars dispute how far fifth-century Greeks identified themselves in this way, and Thucydides shows that alignment was not always ethnic.

Dorian communities varied from the trade centre of Corinth to the military state of Sparta, yet all Greeks knew which places were Dorian. Dorians were distinguished by the Doric dialect, which kept the long a that became eta in Attic-Ionic, and by a calendar built on festivals, notably the Hyacinthia and the Carneia. Doric colonies kept it. Dorian women are said to have had more freedom and economic power than other Greek women, with Spartan women the freest. The Doric order of architecture, the Dorian mode in music, said by classical writers to be martial, and a prominent cult of Helios are associated with Dorian societies. Tsakonian, a descendant of Doric, is still spoken on the southern Argolid coast.
dormition-cathedral-moscow: Excavations in 1968 indicated that the site was a medieval burial ground, which supports the view that a wooden church stood there in the 12th century. In the 14th century Metropolitan Peter persuaded Ivan I, known as Ivan Kalita, to build a cathedral to the Theotokos in Moscow like the Cathedral of the Dormition in Vladimir. Work began on 4 August 1326 and the limestone church was consecrated on 4 August 1327.

By the late 15th century it was dilapidated, and in 1472 the Moscow architects Kryvtsov and Myshkin began a new building. In May 1474, as it neared completion, it collapsed in an earthquake. Ivan III then invited Aristotele Fioravanti, an architect and engineer from Bologna, to design a cathedral from scratch.

Fioravanti travelled to Vladimir to study Russian methods of building, and the cathedral there was again taken as a model. The foundation was laid in 1475 and Metropolitan Geronty consecrated the church in 1479. It has six pillars, five apses and five domes, which symbolise Jesus Christ and the Four Evangelists, and is built of white-stone blocks on a raised limestone foundation. Fioravanti did not use the cantilever vaults usual in Russian architecture but introduced groin vaults and transverse arches, and for the upper parts he used larger specially made bricks that reduced weight.

Four of the six interior columns are slender Corinthian columns, which give the interior its light and spacious effect. The design proved popular and became a template for many other Russian churches.

The interior is dominated by frescoes. The iconostasis dates from 1547, with its two highest tiers added in 1626 and 1653 or 1654. Tsars added to it important icons taken from conquered cities, among them an icon of Saint George from the 12th century brought from Veliky Novgorod in 1561. The Theotokos of Vladimir was kept here from 1395 to 1919 and is now in the Tretyakov Gallery.

The cathedral is regarded as the mother church of Muscovite Russia. Ivan the Terrible was crowned here in 1547 as the first Russian Tsar, and monarchs were crowned here until 1896. Metropolitans and patriarchs were installed here, and most are buried in it. Fires in 1518, 1547, 1682 and 1737, looting by Polish-Lithuanian forces in 1612 and French occupation, when it was used as a stable, damaged it. After the 1917 revolution the Bolshevik government closed the Kremlin churches and made the cathedral a museum, and the last Easter service was held in 1918. It was returned to the Russian Orthodox Church in 1991 and is part of the Moscow Kremlin Museums.
