dornbirn: Dornbirn stands 437 metres above sea level in the Alpine Rhine Valley, at the foot of the Karren mountain, which belongs to the Bregenz Forest chain at the edge of the Eastern Alps. It lies near the borders of Switzerland, Germany and Liechtenstein, and the river Dornbirner Ach runs through it on its way to Lake Constance. It is the largest city in Vorarlberg, the westernmost Austrian state, and the tenth largest in Austria. It is the administrative centre of a district that also includes Hohenems and Lustenau. Its territory once consisted of four quarters, Markt, Hatlerdorf, Oberdorf and Haselstauden, and by the 20th century two more were formed in the west, Rohrbach and Schoren.

The earliest evidence of human presence in the area dates from the Mesolithic. The name derives from torrin puirron, the settlement of Torro, an Alemannic farmer, and has nothing to do with pears, though the fruit appears on the town emblem. The name is first mentioned in 895 in a document from St Gallen.

Dornbirn became part of the Habsburg Monarchy in 1380. In 1793 it was raised to a market community, and it received municipal status only in 1901. The mountain village of Ebnit was annexed in 1932, and in 1969 Dornbirn became the seat of the new district administration. On 10 August 1881 Emperor Franz Joseph I inaugurated the first telephone service in the Habsburg empire there. The town long ranked as a major centre of the textile industry, which declined seriously from the 1980s. The Mohrenbrauerei, Vorarlberg's oldest operating brewery, was founded in 1834.

The City Museum Dornbirn covers local history, early photography, crafts, agriculture and the textile industry, and Inatura is an interactive natural history museum. Dornbirn is an important commercial and shopping centre and a junction of regional bus lines and of the railway between western and eastern Austria. The Vorarlberg University of Applied Sciences, founded in 1989 as a school of technology, was recognised as a university in 1999.
dorset: Dorset is a ceremonial county of South West England with an area of 2,653 square kilometres. It is bordered by Somerset, Wiltshire, Hampshire and Devon, and by the English Channel to the south. Its landscape combines chalk downs, steep limestone ridges and low-lying clay valleys, and the north of the county contains part of Cranborne Chase. The highest point is Lewesdon Hill, 279 metres, in the south-west. The coastline, with Lulworth Cove, the Isle of Portland, Chesil Beach and Durdle Door, is largely part of the Jurassic Coast World Heritage Site because of its geological and palaeontological importance.

The first visitors were Mesolithic hunters from around 8000 BCE. Neolithic settlers arrived around 3000 BCE and made the Dorset Cursus, a monument 10.5 kilometres long. From 2800 BCE Bronze Age farmers cleared woodland and raised round barrows on the chalk hills. In the Iron Age the Durotriges built a series of hill forts, most notably Maiden Castle, one of the largest in Europe. The Romans arrived in 43 CE; the Legio II Augusta under Vespasian captured Maiden Castle, and the Roman settlement of Durnovaria, now Dorchester, was founded nearby. Bokerley Dyke, built by the post-Roman inhabitants, delayed the Saxon advance for almost 150 years.

The name comes from Dorchester: the Saxons called the town Dornwaraceaster, and Dornsæte meant the people of the area. The county developed in the 7th century. The first recorded Viking raid on the British Isles took place in Dorset in 789, and the Black Death entered England at Melcombe Regis in 1348. Dorset's monasteries, among them Shaftesbury, Cerne and Milton, were sold off in the dissolution of 1536-1541 with little resistance.

In the English Civil War the Royalists held the whole county except Poole and Lyme Regis in 1642, but the Parliamentarians had almost reversed this within three years. In 1645 about 2,000 Clubmen, vigilantes weary of the war's depredations, offered battle to Fairfax's army at Hambledon Hill and were routed. Corfe Castle, the last Royalist stronghold, fell in 1646. The Duke of Monmouth's rebellion began when he landed at Lyme Regis in 1685; at the Bloody Assizes in Dorchester Judge Jeffreys heard 312 cases, with 74 accused executed, 175 sentenced to transportation and nine whipped.

In 2021 the ceremonial county had about 779,775 residents. It is largely rural, with many small villages and no cities; the main urban area is a south-eastern conurbation of Bournemouth, Poole and Christchurch, which historically belonged to Hampshire in the case of Bournemouth and Christchurch. Dorchester is the county town. Agriculture was once the principal industry but has declined in favour of tourism. The county has more than 1,500 scheduled monuments and no cathedral.
dositej-obradovic: Dositej Obradović was born Dimitrije Obradović, probably in 1739, in the Banat village of Čakovo in the Habsburg monarchy, now Ciacova in Romania. He grew up bilingual in Serbian and Romanian and learned classical Greek, Latin, modern Greek, German, English, French, Russian and Italian. On 17 February 1757 he became a monk in the Serbian Orthodox monastery of Hopovo in Syrmia and took the name Dositej. He translated many European classics into Serbian, including Aesop's Fables, and on 2 November 1760 left the monastery for Hilandar on Mount Athos.

From 1761 he studied Latin in Zagreb and then taught in Serbian schools in Dalmatia, among them Kninsko Polje, Golubić near Knin and Plavno. He was ordained a priest by Vasilije Petrović. He studied Greek on Corfu and in 1782 enrolled at the University of Halle to study philosophy. In 1783 he moved to Leipzig, where he published his first work and studied under Johann Eberhard, a disciple of Christian Wolf. In 1785 he presented his Leipzig books to the British Museum Library in London, the first modern Serbian books it acquired.

More than a third of his life was spent in Austria, where he was influenced by Joseph II and the German Enlightenment. He was also an Anglophile who saw England as the land of spiritual freedom, and his forty years of travel took him across Europe and Asia Minor. During the First Serbian Uprising of 1804 he was in Italy, where he published the poem Vostani Serbije in honour of Karađorđe Petrović and the insurgents. In 1807 he moved to Belgrade at Karađorđe's invitation and became Serbia's first minister of education.

In Belgrade he founded the Velika škola, the first higher education institution in Serbia, which later developed into a university. He helped introduce the literature of western European countries to the Serbs and, with Vuk Karadžić, whom he influenced, is recognised as a father of modern Serbian literature. Because the Serbian population often suffered famine, he also introduced potato cultivation. He died in Belgrade in 1811 and was buried in the Cathedral of Saint Archangel Michael after a large funeral procession.
dost-mohammad-khan: Dost Mohammad Khan was a Pashtun of the Mohammadzai branch of the Barakzai tribe, born in Kandahar in the Durrani Empire. His father, Payandah Khan, chief of the Barakzai, was killed in 1800 by King Zaman Shah Durrani, and his mother belonged to the Qizilbash. He was the eleventh son and spoke Pashto, Persian, Punjabi and Turkish.

His elder brother Fateh Khan helped install Mahmud Shah Durrani in 1800 and restore him in 1809, but Mahmud Shah had him assassinated in 1818. The Barakzai brothers then stripped Mahmud Shah of everything but Herat and divided his lands, and Dost Mohammad received Ghazni, to which he added Kabul, the richest of the Afghan provinces.

Early in his rule the Afghans lost the Peshawar valley to the Sikh army of Ranjit Singh at the Battle of Nowshera in 1823. Ranjit Singh used the dethroned Sadozai prince Shah Shujah Durrani against him, and in 1834 Dost Mohammad defeated Shah Shujah under the walls of Kandahar. In 1837 his son Akbar Khan defeated the Sikhs at the Battle of Jamrud, where the Sikh general Hari Singh Nalwa was killed.

He welcomed the British envoy Alexander Burnes to Kabul in 1837, but Lord Auckland would not accept his advances, and when he renewed relations with Russia the British set troops in motion in 1838. Shah Shuja was restored in Kabul on 7 August 1839 and Dost Mohammad was exiled to Mussoorie in November 1840.

He was restored after Shah Shuja was murdered in April 1842, and, convinced that war with the British would damage Afghanistan, he sought an alliance with them. He subdued the Hazarajat and Bamian in 1843 and put down a Kohistani rebellion in 1846. His son Mohammad Akram Khan invaded Balkh in 1849, and the province was annexed.

On 30 March 1855 Dost Mohammad signed an offensive and defensive alliance with the British, and in 1857 he joined them against Persia. He took no part in the Indian Rebellion of 1857. In 1862 the ruler of Herat captured Farah, which gave him a pretext to attack. Herat fell on 27 May 1863 after a long siege, and he died on 9 June, after forty years in the politics of South and Central Asia.

His son Sher Ali Khan succeeded him, and he was buried at the Gazurgah in Herat. He ruled for 36 years. He had united Kabul, Kandahar and Herat in one state, as few of his predecessors had done, and state revenue rose from about 500,000 rupees at the start of his rule to 7 million by his death.
douai: Douai lies on the river Scarpe, about 40 kilometres from Lille and 25 kilometres from Arras, and is a sub-prefecture of the Nord department. Its site probably corresponds to a 4th-century Roman fortress, Duacum. From the 10th century it was a fiefdom of the counts of Flanders. In English the town was historically spelled Douay or Doway.

The town grew into a flourishing textile market centre in the Middle Ages. Flanders passed to the Dukes of Burgundy and in 1477 to the Habsburg dynasty. Louis XIV's troops took Douai in 1667, and the Treaty of Aix-la-Chapelle of 1668 ceded it to France. During successive sieges from 1710 to 1712 the British Army almost completely destroyed it.

The University of Douai was founded under the patronage of the Spanish king while the town belonged to the Spanish Netherlands. From the 1560s until the French Revolution it was a centre for educating English Catholics escaping persecution in England. The English College, founded by William Allen, stood beside Irish and Scots Colleges and Benedictine, Franciscan and Jesuit houses. About 60 Jesuits went to England in the 1570s and around 500 by 1603, among them Edmund Campion and Robert Persons.

In 1609 the English College published a translation of the Old Testament which, with the New Testament published at Rheims 27 years earlier, formed the Douay–Rheims Bible, used almost exclusively by Anglophone Roman Catholics for more than 300 years. The Benedictine priory of St Gregory the Great was founded at Douai by Saint John Roberts in 1605 and was expelled in 1793, settling at Downside Abbey in 1814. A second English Benedictine house took over its buildings in 1818 and returned to England in 1903 as Douai Abbey. The airfield at La Brayelle hosted the world's first aeronautical meeting in 1909.

The Gothic belfry, begun in 1380 on the site of an earlier tower, is 80 metres high and holds a carillon of 62 bells. It was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2005 as part of the Belfries of Belgium and France. The Porte de Valenciennes gate dates from 1453, and the collegiate church of St Peter is 112 metres long. Chemical and metal engineering are the main industries, and a Renault assembly plant has stood nearby since 1970.
douala: Douala lies on the Atlantic coast of Cameroon, on the banks of the Wouri River, approximately 210 kilometres west of Yaoundé. The two sides of the estuary are linked by the Bonaberi Bridge. The climate is tropical, with warm and humid conditions through the year and heavy rain. The city is divided into seven districts, among them Akwa, the business district, and Bonanjo, the administrative district. The names of districts refer to Duala lineages; the prefix bona means descendant of.

The first Europeans to visit the area were the Portuguese, in about 1472. They called the estuary of the Wouri the Rio dos Camarões, the Shrimp River. By 1650 a town had been formed by immigrants, said to have come from Congo, who spoke the Duala language. In the 18th century it was a centre of the transatlantic slave trade. In 1826 Douala appeared to consist of four villages: Deido, Akwa, Njo and Hickory-town, today Bonaberi, across the river.

The town came under German rule in 1884 and became the capital of the territory, called Kamerun, until the capital was moved to Buéa in 1902. A first urban plan of 1896 provided for a hospital, the governor's residence and port buildings. After the First World War, in 1919, France received a mandate to administer Douala. From 1940 to 1946 it was the capital of Cameroon. Cameroon became independent in 1960 with its capital at Yaoundé, and Douala became the major economic city. Between May and December 1991 it was at the centre of the civil disobedience campaign known as the ghost town operation, in which economic activity shut down to force the government to allow multi-party politics.

Douala is the largest city of Cameroon, its economic capital and the capital of the Littoral Region, and its port has long been the largest in Central Africa. It handles most of the country's exports, such as oil, cocoa, coffee and timber. French and English are official languages, and Duala, which gives the city its name, is its lingua franca. The Cathedral of Saints Peter and Paul was built between 1925 and 1930, and the mausoleum of the Kings Akwa in 1935.
dougga: Dougga lies 4.6 kilometres south-south-west of the modern town of Téboursouk, on a plateau with a clear view of the surrounding plains in the Oued Khalled. The site offers a high degree of natural protection, which helps to explain its early occupation. The ridge of the Fossa Regia, a ditch and boundary made by the Romans after the destruction of Carthage, lies to the east and marks the place as a point of contact between the Punic and Berber worlds. The archaeological site covers 75 hectares and, lying in the countryside, has been protected from modern urban encroachment.

The city appears to have been founded in the 6th century BCE. Some historians identify it with Tocae, which a lieutenant of Agathocles of Syracuse captured at the end of the 4th century BCE and which Diodorus of Sicily called a city of beautiful grandeur. An inscription proving a sanctuary to the dead Numidian king Massinissa has been dated to 139 BCE, in the reign of Micipsa. The Romans granted Dougga the status of an indigenous city, a civitas, after their conquest. From 205 CE the city and its community fused into a municipality, bearing the title liberum, and it was later made a Roman colony.

Most of the visible remains date from the 2nd and 3rd centuries. The Capitol was completed in 166 or 167, a circus 393 metres long was built in 225, and there is evidence for more than twenty temples, a number owed to the philanthropy of wealthy families. The bishopric of Thugga survived through the Arian Vandal Kingdom and the Orthodox Byzantine Empire and ended with the Muslim conquest of the Maghreb. The site was never completely abandoned: a small village of the descendants of its inhabitants remained for a long time. The first Western visitors to leave eyewitness accounts arrived in the 17th century.

UNESCO qualified Dougga as a World Heritage Site in 1997, describing it as the best-preserved Roman small town in North Africa. Among its best-known monuments are the Mausoleum of Ateban, one of the very rare examples of royal Numidian architecture, the Capitol, the Roman theatre, and the temples of Saturn and of Juno Caelestis. The bilingual inscription from the mausoleum, which gives the same text in Punic and in Berber, was taken by the British consul Read and is held by the British Museum. Many works of art from the site, among them a portrait of Lucius Verus, are in the Bardo National Museum in Tunis.
douglas-hyde: Hyde was born on 17 January 1860 at Longford House in Castlerea, County Roscommon. His father was a Church of Ireland rector, and Hyde grew up at Kilmactranny in Sligo and then at Frenchpark in Roscommon, taught at home by his father and aunt. As a boy he was fascinated by the Irish spoken by older people nearby, above all the gamekeeper Séamus Hart. He rejected family pressure to become a clergyman and studied at Trinity College Dublin, where he became fluent in French, Latin, German, Greek and Hebrew and graduated in 1884.

In November 1892 Hyde wrote a manifesto, The necessity for de-anglicising the Irish nation, arguing that Ireland should follow its own traditions in language, literature and dress. In 1893 he helped found the Gaelic League, which promoted Irish culture, music, dance and language. Pádraig Pearse, Éamon de Valera, Michael Collins and Ernest Blythe all became politicised through it. Uncomfortable with the growing politicisation of the movement, he resigned its presidency in 1915. He was elected to the Seanad in 1925 and became Professor of Irish at University College Dublin.

In 1938 he was chosen after inter-party negotiations as the first President of Ireland, elected unopposed. Both main parties admired him, wanted to honour his work for the Irish language, and saw a non-Catholic president as an answer to the claim that the state was confessional. He was inaugurated on 26 June 1938 and recited the declaration of office in Irish. He kept to a quiet reading of the office and suffered a severe stroke in April 1940.

Hyde left office on 25 June 1945 and did not seek a second term. He lived his last four years in a house on the grounds of Áras an Uachtaráin and died on 12 July 1949, aged 89. At his state funeral at St Patrick's Cathedral in Dublin, a Church of Ireland service, all but one Catholic member of the cabinet waited outside, because of the rules of the Catholic Church then in force. He was buried at Frenchpark.
douglas-isle-of-man: Douglas stands on the east coast of the Isle of Man, on a sweeping bay at the mouth of the River Douglas, which forms the city's harbour and main commercial port. The name, in Manx Doolish, is generally agreed to come from a Proto-Celtic word meaning deep river, from the river nearby. Onchan to the north-east forms a conurbation with Douglas.

Little archaeological evidence survives, though a bronze weapon and the Ballaquayle Viking treasure hoard, both found in the 1890s, hint at the site's early importance. The Chronicle of the Kings of Man and the Isles mentions Douglas in 1190, when monks of St Mary's Abbey at Rushen stayed there, and in 1313, when Robert the Bruce spent a night at the monastery of Duglas. In 1511 only thirteen households lived in the settlement, and most property was rented as chambers by non-residents, which suggests it began as a non-urban port linked to the herring fishery and trade.

In 1681 Thomas Denton described Douglas as the main place of resort on the island. Merchants' houses, warehouses and quays were built to handle the running trade, as smuggling was known, and after the Revestment Act of 1765 the town gained from transatlantic trade, helped by links with Liverpool. Its population rose from about 800 in 1710 to nearly 2,500 in 1784.

From around 1870 Douglas became a leading holiday resort. Visitors rose from 60,000 a year in 1870 to 182,000 in 1884. The first town council was elected in 1860 and tackled sewage and unsanitary housing, and the old streets were cleared in schemes between the 1870s and 1920s. In the 1860s the High Courts and then, in 1869, Tynwald moved to Douglas from Castletown, the ancient capital.

Douglas had 26,677 inhabitants in 2021, nearly a third of the island's population, and received city status by letters patent in 2024. It is the island's main centre for business, finance and shipping, and the Isle of Man TT motorcycle races start and finish there. The Tower of Refuge, built in 1832 on Conister Rock for shipwrecked sailors at the instigation of Sir William Hillary, founder of the RNLI, stands in the bay.
douglas-macarthur: Douglas MacArthur was born on 26 January 1880 at Little Rock Barracks in Arkansas, the youngest of three sons of Arthur MacArthur Jr., an army captain who received the Medal of Honor for the Battle of Missionary Ridge, and Mary Pinkney Hardy MacArthur. He graduated first in his class from the United States Military Academy in 1903 and joined the 3rd Engineer Battalion, which sailed for the Philippines that October. In 1914 he conducted a reconnaissance during the American occupation of Veracruz for which he was nominated for the Medal of Honor.

In the First World War he joined the 42nd Division, became a brigadier general on 26 June 1918 at 38,. He was Superintendent of West Point from 1919, became the army's youngest major general at 45 in 1925, and was sworn in as Chief of Staff on 21 November 1930. When the Philippines gained semi-independent status in 1935, President Manuel Quezon asked him to supervise the creation of a Philippine Army, and he became a field marshal of it.

S. Army Forces in the Far East. Much of his air force was destroyed in December 1941, and he escaped to Australia in March 1942, where on 18 April he was made Supreme Commander of the Southwest Pacific Area. In October 1944 he led the campaign that liberated the Philippines.

As Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers in Japan he worked through the Japanese government and the Emperor Hirohito, and the Allies shielded the emperor from war responsibility. His headquarters drafted a constitution in 1946, which took effect on 3 May 1947. It made the emperor a figure acting on ministerial advice, renounced war in Article 9 and enfranchised women. In the Korean War he led the United Nations Command from 1950, and after China entered the war he was removed by President Harry S. Truman in April 1951. On 19 April he gave a farewell address to Congress.

MacArthur died at Walter Reed Army Medical Center on 5 April 1964, aged 84. An estimated 150,000 people filed past his body as it lay in state at the Capitol. His legacy is contested. Walter R. Borneman wrote that a public stunned by Pearl Harbor needed a hero and embraced him. He is one of only five people to hold the rank of General of the Army.
douro: The Douro, called Duero in Spanish and Durius in Latin, is the largest river of the Iberian Peninsula by discharge and the third longest after the Tagus and the Ebro. Its basin covers about 97,290 square kilometres. It rises at the Pico de Urbión and runs west across the northern Meseta Central of Castile and León. Its largest tributary, the Esla, carries more water than the Douro itself at their confluence. In Spain the river crosses five provinces, Soria, Burgos, Valladolid, Zamora and Salamanca, in semi-arid plains of wheat, sheep and vineyards.

For 112 kilometres it forms part of the border between Spain and Portugal, in narrow canyons. This stretch was a historical barrier to invasions and created a cultural and linguistic divide. In Portugal the tributaries are small and fast-flowing, and the river reaches the Atlantic between Porto and Vila Nova de Gaia.

In Roman times the river was personified as the god Durius. The origin of its name is uncertain: it may have been a Celtic name or may come from a pre-Indo-European root for water, and the idea that it means golden is a folk etymology. According to Claudio Sánchez-Albornoz, part of the drainage basin was depopulated in the 8th century by a deliberate act of Alfonso I of Asturias to defend his kingdom.

Port wine from the vineyards of the Portuguese valley was long carried downriver in flat-bottomed boats called rabelos and stored in cellars at Vila Nova de Gaia, opposite Porto. The Douro railway line was completed in 1887. Dams with locks were built along the river in the 1960s and 1970s, allowing river traffic into the upper regions.

Fifteen dams regulate the river and generate hydroelectric power, and the last five, in Portugal, allow navigation through locks. The wine region around Pinhão and São João da Pesqueira is considered the centre of port production, and the Douro vinhateiro is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, as are the historic centre of Porto and the Côa Valley Paleolithic Art site, near Foz Côa.
dover-new-hampshire: Dover lies in Strafford County, New Hampshire. It is drained by the Cochecho and Bellamy rivers, both flowing into the tidal Piscataqua River, which forms its eastern boundary and the border with Maine. The Cochecho, a name meaning the rapid foaming water in the Abenaki language, drops 34 feet at Cochecho Falls, which gave water power for sawmills and later textile mills. The city is named for Dover in Kent, England. Because it was an early settlement in Abenaki lands, settlers built fortified log houses called garrisons, which gave Dover the nickname the Garrison City.

In 1623 the brothers William and Edward Hilton, fishmongers sent from London by the Laconia Company, settled at Pomeroy Cove on Dover Point, which made Dover the oldest permanent settlement in New Hampshire. In 1633 a group of English Puritans bought the plantation and renamed it Bristol; the name Dover was used from 1637. When the group's benefactors lost interest, the settlers formed their own government, signing the Combination of the People of Dover in 1640, and voted to join Massachusetts.

On 7 September 1676 Major Richard Waldron tricked about 400 Native Americans into a mock battle near Cochecho Falls and had them captured; half were sent to Massachusetts, seven or eight were hanged and others were sold into slavery. On 28 June 1689 Dover suffered a devastating attack in revenge, the first of King William's War, in which fifty-two colonists, a quarter of the population, were captured or killed. Raids continued for half a century. In 1828 about half of the 800 women at the Cocheco Manufacturing Company walked out in what is described as the first women's strike in the United States. Dover became a city in 1855.

Dover is the county seat of Strafford County, with a population of 32,741 at the 2020 census. Its former mills at Cocheco Falls now house offices, a restaurant and housing, and the Children's Museum of New Hampshire occupies a former mill building.
draa-river: The Draa, also spelled Dra or Drâa, is Morocco's longest river, at 1,100 kilometres. It is formed by the confluence of the Dadès River and the Imini River, flows from the High Atlas south-eastward to Tagounite, and from there mostly westward to the Atlantic, somewhat north of Tan-Tan. Most of the year the part below Tagounite is dry. The El Mansour Eddahabi dam, built in 1971, serves Ouarzazate and regulates the flow. In the first half of the 20th century the lowest course marked the boundary between the French protectorate of Morocco and the area under Spanish rule.

Humans have lived in the valley since at least the Lower Paleolithic, as shown by Oldowan and Acheulean tools near Tamegroute. Neolithic rock art shows hunting scenes and domesticated cattle, and the earliest may date to the 3rd millennium BCE. The river was known to the ancient Romans. During the reign of the Wattasid Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Muhammad, Askia Ishaq I of the Songhai Empire sent Tuareg raiders into the valley to avenge a diplomatic insult, after Morocco had demanded the cession of the Taghaza salt mine.

The upper valley, about 200 kilometres long, consists of six stretches of oases and palm groves, from the Mezguita oasis in the north to Mhamid el Ghuzlan in the south, with towns including Agdz, Zagora and Tagounite. Its villages are mostly fortified ksour, and the southern stretch alone has 55 of them. Two languages are spoken, a local Colloquial Arabic and the Berber language Shilha. The valley also holds the Fezouata formations, Lower Ordovician deposits whose fossils include organisms previously thought to have died out after the mid-Cambrian.
drakensberg: The Drakensberg is the eastern portion of the Great Escarpment, which encloses the central southern African plateau. It stretches for more than 1,000 kilometres from the Eastern Cape northwards, forming successively the borders between Lesotho and the Eastern Cape, between Lesotho and KwaZulu-Natal, between KwaZulu-Natal and the Free State and between KwaZulu-Natal and Mpumalanga. In Mpumalanga it includes the Blyde River Canyon, the Three Rondavels and God's Window, and it continues into Limpopo, where parts are called the Wolkberg and Strydpoort mountains. Its highest peak is Thabana Ntlenyana at 3,482 metres, and other peaks include Mafadi, Njesuthi, Champagne Castle and Giant's Castle.

The Afrikaans name Drakensberge comes from the earliest Dutch settlers' Drakensbergen, Dragons' Mountains. The Zulu name uKhahlamba and the Sotho name Maloti mean barrier of up-pointed spears. Who first gave the Dutch name, and why, is unknown. The escarpment is formed of steep rift valley walls raised around a bulge of continental crust during the breakup of Gondwana. Its rocks vary along its length: ancient quartzite in the north, Karoo sedimentary rocks in the middle and a thick layer of basalt, erupted 180 million years ago, in the borders of Lesotho and the Eastern Cape.

The caves in the Clarens sandstone along the border of KwaZulu-Natal and Lesotho hold paintings by the San. This part of the range has between 35,000 and 40,000 works of San rock art, described as the largest collection of such painting in the world. About 20,000 individual paintings have been recorded at 500 caves and overhangs between Royal Natal National Park and Bushman's Nek. They are hard to date, but anthropological evidence, including many hunting implements, shows that San people lived in the Drakensberg at least 40,000 years ago and possibly more than 100,000 years ago.

The high slopes have the Tugela Falls, with a total drop of 947 metres, and are the source of the Orange River, southern Africa's longest river, and the Tugela. The rivers supply water to the industrial provinces of Mpumalanga and Gauteng. The uKhahlamba Drakensberg Park was listed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in 2000. Towns around the range include Ladysmith, Newcastle, Dundee and Ulundi, the former Zulu capital, and all of Lesotho, whose capital is Maseru, lies within it.
draupadi: Draupadi appears in the Mahabharata, a Sanskrit epic revised over many centuries, whose oldest surviving parts probably date to about 400 BCE. Her name means daughter of Drupada, and she is also called Krishna, Panchali and Yajnaseni. The epic describes her as born fully grown from a fire sacrifice held by King Drupada of Panchala, who wanted a son strong enough to kill Drona. She is called learned, and Yudhishthira praises her as a skilled speaker. Drupada arranged a contest for her hand in which suitors had to string a great bow and pierce the eye of a golden fish by its reflection.

In the epic Draupadi becomes the common wife of the five Pandava brothers: Yudhishthira, Bhima, Arjuna, Nakula and Sahadeva. Polyandry was rare in Hindu society, and the epic gives previous lives and divine sanction to explain it. At the game of dice in the Kuru court, Yudhishthira loses his kingdom and his own freedom and then stakes her. She is dragged into the assembly, and when Dushasana tries to disrobe her, her garment extends endlessly. Dhritarashtra grants her two boons, which free the Pandavas.

She accompanies them through thirteen years of exile, the last spent disguised as a maid to Queen Sudeshna of Matsya. When Duryodhana refuses to return the kingdom, she presses for war. The Kurukshetra War kills her father, her brothers and her five sons, and afterwards she is empress of the Kuru kingdom for thirty-six years.

In the epic's conclusion she joins the Pandavas on their final journey toward heaven and is the first to fall. In parts of India she is worshipped as a goddess, Draupadi Amman, with over 400 temples in southern India and among Tamil communities abroad, where fire walking is a prominent ritual. She is named among the panchakanya, five women whose names are believed to dispel sin when recited. A Pali Jataka tale presents her marriage as a cautionary example, and a Digambara Jain text rejects the polyandry and says she married only Arjuna.
drava: The Drava is a river in southern Central Europe, 710 kilometres long, or 724 kilometres if its Sextner Bach source is added. It drains about 40,154 square kilometres, with a mean discharge of between 500 and 670 cubic metres per second depending on the season. In antiquity it was called Dravus or Draus in Latin, and medieval forms include Dravis, Drauva and Trah. The name is pre-Roman and pre-Celtic, probably of Indo-European origin from a root meaning flow, and gives its name to dravite, a kind of tourmaline. Herodotus mentions a river called the Carpis flowing north into the Danube, which has been supposed to be the Drava.

The river rises near the market town of Innichen in the Puster Valley of South Tyrol, Italy, and flows east into East Tyrol and Carinthia in Austria. At Lienz it receives the Isel, which is almost three times larger at that point. It passes Villach, the site of the ancient city of Teurnia and Spittal an der Drau, and enters Slovenia at Dravograd, where it runs for 142 kilometres through Maribor and Ptuj to the Croatian border at Ormož. It then turns south-east past Varaždin, and after taking the Mur forms most of the border between Croatia and Hungary. It is navigable for about 90 kilometres in Croatia, passes Osijek and flows through the Kopački Rit wetland into the Danube.

Besides the Isel and the Mur, its main tributaries include the Gurk, Möll, Lieser, Gail and Bednja. There are 22 hydroelectric power plants on it, and it is one of the most exploited rivers in the world for hydropower, though the region has exceptional biodiversity.
draza-mihailovic: Dragoljub Mihailović was born on 27 April 1893 in Ivanjica, in the Kingdom of Serbia, the son of a court clerk. Orphaned at seven, he was raised by an uncle in Belgrade and joined the Serbian Military Academy in October 1910. He fought in the Balkan Wars of 1912-1913, winning the Silver Medal of Valor, served in the First World War, including the Serbian Army's retreat through Albania in 1915, and received decorations on the Salonika front. He rose to colonel in 1935 and served as military attaché in Sofia and later in Prague.

After the German invasion of April 1941 Mihailović crossed the Drina into German-occupied Serbia with about 80 men and in May set up at Ravna Gora, calling his force the Command of Chetnik Detachments of the Yugoslav Army. He aimed to unite Serb bands and build an organisation able to take power once the Axis withdrew, rather than to confront the occupiers directly, fearing German reprisals against civilians and a Partisan takeover. By late 1941 his forces and Tito's Partisans were in open conflict, and by September he was losing men to the Partisans. On 11 January 1942 the government-in-exile named him Minister of the Army, Navy and Air Forces, and in June he became chief of staff of the Supreme Command.

Chetnik ideology included a Greater Serbia, and Chetnik forces carried out massacres and used terror to drive out non-Serbs, partly in response to Ustaše violence. Many Chetnik groups collaborated with the Axis, and British officers reported his reluctance to attack the occupiers. Operation Halyard, in 1944, rescued hundreds of downed Allied airmen with his help. Britain, however, shifted its support to Tito, and on 29 August 1944 King Peter dissolved Mihailović's command and on 12 September called on all to join Tito's army.

The Yugoslav authorities captured Mihailović on 13 March 1946, by one account by luring him onto a supposed British evacuation aircraft, by another through betrayal by Nikola Kalabić. His trial opened on 10 June, and the Allied airmen he had rescued were not allowed to testify. He was convicted of high treason and war crimes and shot in Belgrade on 17 July 1946. In his final statement he said, "I wanted much; I began much; but the gale of the world carried away me and my work."

Historians still disagree about his responsibility for collaboration and massacres. Jozo Tomasevich and Pavlowitch stress his failure to grow into his responsibilities and his limited control over local commanders. In May 2015 the High Court in Belgrade rehabilitated him, ruling that the communist trial had been politically and ideologically motivated; the request had drawn protests in Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia and Serbia.
drenthe: Drenthe lies in the north-east of the Netherlands and borders Overijssel to the south, Friesland to the west, Groningen to the north and the German state of Lower Saxony to the east. It has several heathlands and no significant rivers or lakes, and about 72 per cent of its land is used for agriculture.

People have lived in the region since prehistory, and artefacts from about 150,000 years ago are among the oldest found in the Netherlands. Until the Bronze Age it was one of the most densely populated parts of the country. The hunebedden, megalithic tombs built around 3500 BCE, are its most visible evidence: 53 of the 54 in the Netherlands stand in Drenthe, mostly in the north-east. Most Bronze Age objects found in the Netherlands also come from Drenthe, among them large bronze buckets made in eastern France or Switzerland for mixing wine with water, which suggest that it was a trading centre.

A document of 820 names the district as Pago Treanth. In 1024 to 1025 Emperor Henry II gave the county of Drenthe to Bishop Adalbold II of Utrecht, and the region's subjugation into the Holy Roman Empire culminated in the Drenther Crusade launched by the Papacy around 1228 to 1232. After long being subject to the diocese of Utrecht it passed to Emperor Charles V, who made it part of the Habsburg Netherlands.

When the Republic of the Seven United Provinces was declared in 1581, Drenthe joined it as the County of Drenthe. Because it was so poor it was exempt from federal taxes, and as a result it was denied representation in the States General and never gained full provincial status. The Batavian Republic granted it provincial status on 1 January 1796. Shortly before the Second World War the Dutch government built a camp near Hooghalen to intern German Jewish refugees. The German occupiers used it as a transit camp, Westerbork, from which Dutch Jews, Sinti, Roma and others were sent to camps in Germany and occupied Poland; Anne Frank was deported on the last train to leave it, on 3 September 1944.

The capital is Assen, and Emmen is the other large town. The province has about 502,000 inhabitants and the lowest population density in the European Netherlands. Over half its people speak the Drents dialect of Low Saxon, which the Dutch government recognises as a regional language.
dresden: Dresden lies on both banks of the Elbe, mostly in the Dresden Basin, with the eastern Ore Mountains to the south and the Elbe Sandstone Mountains to the east. Because the river receives water from the Ore Mountains, flood protection matters: large areas are kept free of buildings as a flood plain. The original parts of the city lie in the boroughs of Altstadt, the Old Town, and Neustadt, the New Town, and historic outskirts such as Friedrichstadt and Albertstadt, built in the 18th and 19th centuries, are named after Saxon sovereigns.

Dresden developed as a German trading settlement on the south bank of the Elbe, established by the Margrave of Meissen, Dietrich, who chose it as his interim residence in 1206, the year of the first documentary evidence. A stone bridge built in 1220 linked it with a Sorbian settlement on the northern bank, later called Altendresden. Under the electors Frederick Augustus I (1694–1733) and Frederick August II (1733–1763), who also ruled as kings of Poland in a personal union from 1697 to 1763, Dresden became a major centre of court culture. The Zwinger, the Japanese Palace, the Hofkirche and the Frauenkirche date from their reigns, and the Green Vault and the Porcelain Collection were founded.

In 1806 Dresden became capital of the Kingdom of Saxony established by Napoleon, who won the Battle of Dresden there on 27 August 1813. The population passed 100,000 in 1852 and peaked at 649,252 in 1933. The American and British bombing towards the end of the Second World War killed approximately 25,000 people, most of them civilians, and destroyed large parts of the city centre. Dresden then belonged to East Germany, and after reunification in 1990 it became capital of the re-established Free State of Saxony.

Dresden is the capital of Saxony and its second most populous city after Leipzig. The Frauenkirche, destroyed in the war, stood as a ruin for fifty years as a memorial before it was rebuilt between 1994 and 2005. The Dresden State Art Collections go back to the collections of the Saxon electors in the 16th century. Carl Maria von Weber and Richard Wagner had works first performed in the city, and Coventry, also heavily bombed, became its twin city in 1959.
dresden-frauenkirche: The Frauenkirche, the Church of Our Lady, is the third church on its site in Dresden. The first, a Romanesque church of the 11th century, stood outside the city walls and was the seat of an archpriest in the diocese of Meissen until the Reformation, when it became Protestant. A larger Baroque Lutheran church replaced it, built by the citizens between 1726 and 1743. The foundation stone, laid on 26 August 1726, enclosed a copy of the Augsburg Confession.

It was meant as a sign that the citizens would remain Protestant after their ruler, the elector Frederick August I, converted to Catholicism to become King of Poland. He supported the building, which reassured the people of Saxony that he would not impose his faith on them.

The architect was George Bähr, Dresden's city architect, who did not live to see it finished. His design placed the altar, pulpit and baptismal font in the centre, in view of the whole congregation, in keeping with Protestant worship.

Its most distinctive feature was a high dome, 67 metres tall and called the Stone Bell, a 12,000-ton sandstone structure resting on eight slender supports. Witnesses in 1760 said that over a hundred cannonballs fired by Prussian forces in the Seven Years' War bounced off it. Gottfried Silbermann built an organ for the church in 1736, and Johann Sebastian Bach gave a recital on it on 1 December. The dome shaped the skyline painted by Bernardo Bellotto and Johan Christian Dahl. In 1849 the church stood at the heart of the May Uprising.

The Allied bombing of Dresden began on 13 February 1945. The church withstood two days and nights, long enough for 300 people sheltering in the crypt to be evacuated, but the heat reached about 1,000 °C, the pillars gave way and the dome collapsed at 10 a.m. on 15 February. For 45 years the ruins stayed as a heap of stone. Residents had numbered fragments for later use, and in 1966 the remains were declared a memorial against war. From 1982 they became a place of peaceful protest.

After German reunification a citizens' initiative led by the musician Ludwig Güttler began a campaign to rebuild. The Dresden City Council decided in February 1992 to proceed, using Bähr's plans, and the foundation stone was laid in 1994. Of the original stones, about 3,800 were reused. The cost was 180 million euros. The exterior was finished in 2004 and the church was reconsecrated on 30 October 2005. It is seen as a symbol of reconciliation. A new gilded cross made in London by the silversmith Alan Smith, whose father had flown in the bombing, crowns the dome.
dreyfus-affair: In 1894 the Third Republic was twenty-four years old and its ministries were short-lived. The annexation of Alsace and Moselle fed an extreme nationalism, and antisemitism had grown virulent since the publication of Jewish France by Édouard Drumont in 1886. In September 1894 a housekeeper placed in the German Embassy in Paris by the Military Intelligence Service found a torn-up note, later called the bordereau, addressed to the German military attaché Maximilian von Schwartzkoppen, offering confidential French military documents. The Minister of War, General Auguste Mercier, ordered an investigation that restricted the search to artillery officers on the General Staff, and Major du Paty de Clam found Captain Alfred Dreyfus the probable author.

Dreyfus was arrested on 13 October 1894. On 22 December seven judges unanimously convicted him of collusion with a foreign power, and he was degraded and sent to Devil's Island. His brother Mathieu worked for years to win a retrial. In March 1896 Lieutenant Colonel Georges Picquart found the petit bleu, an unsent telegram addressed to Major Ferdinand Walsin Esterhazy. Picquart's superiors ignored him and sent him to Tunisia, and in January 1898 a court martial acquitted Esterhazy.

On 13 January 1898 Émile Zola published J'Accuse...! in L'Aurore. He was tried for defamation, and antisemitic riots broke out in cities across France. Dreyfus returned to France in 1899 and was tried at Rennes, where on 9 September the court convicted him again, by five votes to two, with extenuating circumstances, and sentenced him to ten years. President Émile Loubet pardoned him on 19 September 1899.

The pardon did not declare Dreyfus innocent, and his rehabilitation was completed only in 1906, when passions had cooled. Reinstated in the army as a major, he served throughout the First World War and ended his service as a lieutenant colonel. He died in 1935.

The affair split France between the Dreyfusards, among them Anatole France, Georges Clemenceau and Sarah Bernhardt, and the anti-Dreyfusards, who were mostly pro-army and Catholic. Most historians hold that the conflict served the republican order, strengthening parliamentary democracy and defeating monarchist and reactionary forces. It also spread antisemitism through all strata of society. The journalist Theodor Herzl, who was present at Dreyfus's degradation in 1895, is often seen as moved by the affair toward Zionism, though some scholars think he exaggerated its influence.
drina: The Drina is the longest tributary of the Sava and the longest karst river of the Dinaric Alps, and it belongs to the Danube drainage basin. It rises where the Tara and the Piva meet, between Šćepan Polje in Montenegro and Hum in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Measured from the source of the Tara, its longer headwater, it is 487 kilometres long. It is a fast, cold river with green water, running through limestone gorges, among them the Međeđa gorge, where it is only 12 metres wide at Tijesno. Near its mouth it spreads across the largest flood plain in former Yugoslavia, and it once entered the Sava near Šabac, 30 kilometres east of the present mouth.

The name comes from the Roman name Drinus, which derives from Greek and ultimately from a native name of Illyrian origin. Boats were long the main traffic on the river. In the second half of the 17th century the Ottoman traveller Evliya Çelebi wrote that people in the valley hollowed oak trunks into dugout canoes, with thousands of them at Zvornik sailing to Belgrade. In the 19th century loggers floated rafts of trunks down the Tara and the Drina to the sawmill at Foča.

Excavations from 2012 to 2015 at Orlovine near Mali Zvornik showed that stone ramparts above the river belonged to a large Byzantine city dating from the time of Justinian I, a bishop's seat with one of the largest Byzantine churches in Serbia. In September 1914 the river was the scene of the Battle of Cer and the Battle of Drina between Serbian and Austro-Hungarian armies.

The river forms much of the border between Bosnia and Herzegovina and Serbia. Its main towns include Foča, Goražde, Višegrad, Zvornik, Bajina Bašta and Loznica, and three hydroelectric stations dam it. The Mehmed Paša Sokolović Bridge at Višegrad, designed by the court architect Mimar Sinan, has been on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 2007. Ivo Andrić's 1945 novel Na Drini ćuprija (The Bridge on the Drina) is set around it, and Stanislav Binički's march honouring the Battle of Cer is known as the March on the Drina.
drobeta-turnu-severin: Drobeta-Turnu Severin lies on the northern bank of the Danube, close to the Iron Gates, in Mehedinți County in Oltenia. Drobeta is the name of the ancient Dacian and Roman towns at the site, first mentioned by Ptolemy of Alexandria in the 2nd century CE. Turnu means tower, after a tower built on the north bank by the Byzantines, and Severin is variously traced to Septimius Severus, to an Old Church Slavonic word for north, or to Severinus of Noricum, patron saint of the medieval colony.

Trajan's Bridge was built here in three years, between 103 and 105 CE, by Apollodorus of Damascus for the invasion of Dacia. It was considered one of the most daring works of the Roman world, with twenty arches between stone piers. Drobeta became the third urban centre of Dacia, after Sarmizegetusa and Apullum. Hadrian made it a municipium in 121, and in 193 Septimius Severus raised it to a colony, giving its residents equal rights with Roman citizens. By the middle of the 3rd century it had almost 40,000 inhabitants. The Huns destroyed it in the 5th century and Justinian I rebuilt it.

In the Middle Ages the Hungarian crown organised the Banate of Severin; its first Ban, Luca, is mentioned in 1233, and a new castle, Severin, rose over the ruins of Drobeta. The fortress was the most important strategic redoubt on the Danube, and the Wallachian rulers Litovoi and Basarab I died there. In 1524 a devastating attack by the Turks led by Suleiman left only one tower standing, which gave the town its name, the Tower of Severinus. It remained under Ottoman rule until 1829.

After the Treaty of Adrianople in 1829 the city was rebuilt from 1836, and the harbour was built in 1858. Severin became the county capital in 1841 and a city in 1851. By 1900 it had railway workshops and a shipyard that by 1914 was the largest in the country. In 1972 the name Drobeta was added to the city's name, during Nicolae Ceaușescu's rule. The remains of Trajan's Bridge, the bridgehead fort, the Roman baths and the amphitheatre are visible.
drogheda: Drogheda, from the Irish Droichead Átha, 'bridge at the ford', is the last bridging point on the River Boyne before it enters the Irish Sea, about 43 km north of Dublin. The hinterland holds many archaeological monuments from the Neolithic onwards, the passage tombs of Newgrange, Knowth and Dowth being the best known, and the density of prehistoric and early Christian sites shows a landscape settled for millennia. According to the historian John Bradley, however, neither documents nor excavation show any settlement at the town itself before the Normans came.

Drogheda began as two separately administered towns on either side of the Boyne: Drogheda-in-Meath, in the Lordship and Liberty of Meath, and Drogheda-in-Oriel, in what was then called Uriel, now County Louth. The division followed the twelfth-century boundary between two Irish kingdoms colonised by different Norman interests. The motte-and-bailey castle now known as Millmount Fort was probably built by the Norman Lord of Meath, Hugh de Lacy, before 1186. The earliest known town charter was granted to Drogheda-in-Meath by Walter de Lacy in 1194. In 1412 the two towns were united and became a county corporate.

In the medieval period Drogheda was an important walled town in the English Pale and often hosted the Irish Parliament, including the one that passed Poynings' Law, the legislation that subordinated the Irish Parliament's lawmaking to the king and his English Council. On Valentine's Day 1468 the Earl of Desmond and his two young sons were executed there on the orders of the Earl of Worcester, the Lord Deputy.

The town was besieged twice during the Irish Confederate Wars. In September 1649, in the second siege, Oliver Cromwell's army breached the walls from the south and took the town, and the Royalist defenders were massacred. Cromwell wrote that the officers were 'knocked on the head', every tenth soldier was killed and the rest were shipped to Barbados. The Battle of the Boyne was fought in 1690 about 6 km to the west, at Oldbridge.

Drogheda is a port town in County Louth, with its southern fringes in County Meath. Newgrange, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, lies 8 km to the west. Landmarks include Millmount Fort, now a museum, the barbican of St Laurence's Gate from the 1300s, the Tholsel of 1770, and St Peter's Church, which houses the preserved head of Saint Oliver Plunkett, executed in London in 1681. The Boyne Viaduct and Mellifont Abbey lie nearby.
druid: The word druid comes through French and Latin from the Gaulish druides, and most scholars derive it from a Proto-Celtic compound read as oak-knower or as a priest with strong insight. Classical authors placed druids only in Gaul and Britain. The earliest notices, of the 4th and 3rd centuries BCE, treat them as barbarian philosophers akin to the Persian magi. Because the druids committed nothing of their teaching to writing and cannot be securely identified in the archaeological record, nearly everything known about them comes from outside observers, much of it descended from the lost ethnography of Posidonius.

Diodorus and Strabo, drawing on Posidonius, describe druids arbitrating public and private disputes and even halting armies drawn up for battle. According to Caesar they had a single head who held office for life, and their pupils might remain in instruction for up to twenty years, memorising a great body of verse. The doctrine most often remarked on was the immortality of the soul.

Caesar and the Posidonian authors agree that no sacrifice took place without a druid. Diodorus and Strabo describe divination from a human victim, and Caesar reports victims burned inside a huge wickerwork image. Scholars weigh these reports differently: some note that the barbarity had propaganda value for Rome, while Bruce Lincoln holds that they go back to Greek sources older than any such motive. Excavations in pre-Roman Gaul show animal and human sacrifice, though the priests who officiated are nowhere named.

Augustus forbade the druidic religion to Roman citizens, a decree of the Senate under Tiberius was directed against druids, diviners and physicians, and Suetonius says Claudius abolished their religion. In Ireland, which Rome never reached, medieval literature preserves many druids, but these accounts are generally read as literary constructs of Christian authors.

From the 16th century druids became a screen for reinterpretation. John Aubrey attributed Stonehenge and Avebury to them, though the monuments are millennia older than the Iron Age Celts. In 1792 Edward Williams, known as Iolo Morganwg, invented the Gorsedd Beirdd Ynys Prydain, whose ritual survives in the National Eisteddfod. The Order of Bards, Ovates and Druids was founded in 1964, but modern Druidry has no genuine continuity with the ancient priesthood.
druze: The Druze call themselves al-Muwaḥḥidūn, meaning the monotheists. Their faith developed from the Ismaili branch of Shiʿa Islam, but they do not identify as Muslims. The creation of the faith in 1017-1018 is dominated by three men. Hamza ibn Ali ibn Ahmad, an Ismaili mystic from Khorasan, arrived in Fatimid Egypt in 1014 or 1016 and began to preach a unitarian doctrine. The Fatimid caliph al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah became central to it, and in 1018 the preacher ad-Darazī proclaimed him the incarnation of God. The Druze regard ad-Darazī as a heretic, and their name probably comes from his, perhaps applied by opponents.

The most widely accepted theory of the community's descent holds that the Druze come from twelve Arab tribes that migrated to Syria before and during the early Islamic period. After the Ottoman conquest of Syria in 1516 the Ma'an family were acknowledged as feudal lords of southern Lebanon, and Druze villages prospered. The Shihab family succeeded them as leaders in 1697. Feuds between the Qaysite and Yemenite factions, which grouped Druze and Christians alike, ended in the battle of Ain Dara in 1711, after which many Yemenite Druze migrated to the Hauran. Relations between Druze and Maronite Christians broke down from 1840 and led to the civil war of 1860.

In May 1909 the Druze of the Hauran rose against Ottoman authority, led by the al-Atrash family, in a dispute over taxes and conscription. General Sami Pasha al-Farouqi suppressed the revolt; about 2,000 Druze were killed and their leaders executed in 1910.

The Druze number between 800,000 and a million, mostly in Lebanon, Syria and Israel. Arabic is their primary language, and their central text is the Epistles of Wisdom. Core tenets are the unity of God, reincarnation and the eternity of the soul. Most religious practice is kept secret, and the community does not accept converts.

There is no clergy. A few initiates, the ʿuqqāl, hold the faith's secrets, while other members are called juhhāl. Prayer houses are called khalwa, and the Druze avoid iconography, using five colours as a religious symbol. They follow seven moral precepts, the first being truthfulness in speech.
du-gamla-du-fria: Dybeck published the traditional text of the ballad in Folk-lore I and the melody in 1845 in his Runa, where he also published his new text, Sång till Norden. His original lyrics consist of two verses, written in the spirit of Scandinavianism then popular. They refer to the Nordic region but not to Sweden itself, and patriotic sentiment is notably absent from them. Dybeck first wrote the opening as Du gamla, du friska, meaning you ancient, you healthy, and changed it to Du gamla, du fria in the late 1850s. In 1900 a priest who had known him told the opera singer Carl Fredrik Lundqvist of the change, and printings of the friska version then ceased.

The song is the de facto national anthem of Sweden. Like the anthems of Finland and the United Kingdom, it is not defined in the Basic Laws nor recognised by other legislation, unlike the flag and the coat of arms. It is used all the same at official events such as state visits and the Opening of the Riksdag, at sporting events and at the Nobel Prize Award Ceremony. Sweden also has a royal anthem, Kungssången.

After it began to act as a national anthem, various people wrote extra verses to make it more Swedish, among them Lundqvist, Frans Österblom and Louise Ahlén. None is accepted as part of the anthem or normally sung.

The song was regarded as the national anthem from the late 19th century and became predominant in 1893, when King Oscar II stood in acknowledgement of it at a dinner at Lund University. Many still regarded it as unsuitable as an anthem, and a contest of 1899 produced Sverige by Verner von Heidenstam but no new anthem. In 1938 Sveriges Radio began to play it at the close of its daily programming, and by the end of the 1930s its status was effectively established.
A motion to give it legal recognition in 1986 did not pass. In 2000 a Riksdag committee concluded that, since it had already become the national anthem in fact, formal recognition was unnecessary.
du-yuesheng: Du was born on 22 August 1888 in Gaoqiao, and his family moved to Shanghai the next year. By the age of nine he had lost his immediate family: his mother died in childbirth, his sister was sold into slavery, his father died and his stepmother vanished. He returned to Shanghai in 1902, worked at a fruit stall in the French Concession until he was dismissed for theft, and became a bodyguard in a brothel, and joined the Green Gang at 16. A friend introduced him to Huang Jinrong, the highest-ranking Chinese detective in the French Concession Police, for whom he became an enforcer in gambling and opium.

His rise came after Huang's arrest in 1924 for beating the son of Lu Yongxiang, the tuchun then ruling Shanghai: Du's diplomacy and money freed his mentor, and Du, Huang and Zhang Xiaolin became sworn brothers, known as the Three Tycoons of Shanghai. In April 1927 the three formed with Chiang Kai-shek the Chinese Progress Association. On the night of 11 April Du's lieutenant Wan Molin killed the labour leader Wang Shouhua at Du's house, and gang members wearing armbands marked Labor attacked workers and left-wing activists. Chiang rewarded him with the rank of major general and advisory posts.

From 1928 he moved into finance, founding the Zhonghui Bank and becoming a director of the Bank of China and the Bank of Communications. In 1931 he opened a temple to his ancestors; within months its private wings housed a heroin factory. When war with Japan broke out in 1937 he refused to cooperate with the Japanese, unlike Zhang Xiaolin, and went to Hong Kong, while Green Gang men working with Chiang's intelligence chief Dai Li smuggled weapons and goods to the Nationalist forces.

After the war he returned to Shanghai and founded the newspaper Shang Pao. He hoped to become mayor but gave way under pressure from Chiang, and in 1948 his son Du Weiping was sentenced to six months in an anti-corruption campaign led by Chiang Ching-kuo. In April 1949 he moved to Hong Kong, declining approaches from both the Kuomintang and the Communists. His health failed through asthma, and he died on 16 August 1951. He was buried in Xizhi in Taiwan, where the authorities raised a statue of him, though some doubt that the tomb holds his body.
dublin: Dublin lies at the mouth of the River Liffey in east-central Ireland, and its urban area covers about 345 square kilometres. The Dublin Mountains, a low sub-range of the Wicklow Mountains, border it on the south, with flat farmland to the north and west. The Liffey divides the city into the Northside and the Southside, and the city itself was founded where the River Poddle met the Liffey. The Grand Canal on the southside and the Royal Canal on the northside ring the inner city on their way from the west, both connecting with the River Shannon.

The name comes from the Middle Irish Du(i)blind, literally Blackpool, from dubh, meaning black, and linn, meaning pool. It referred to a dark tidal pool on the site of the castle gardens behind Dublin Castle, where the Poddle entered the Liffey. Old Norse Dyflin, Welsh Dulyn and Breton Dulenn all preserve the Middle Irish pronunciation.

Fish traps found during construction of the Convention Centre indicate human habitation 6,000 years ago, and others near St. James's Gate show Mesolithic activity. Ptolemy's map of about 140 CE gives what may be the earliest reference to a settlement nearby, calling it Eblana polis. A Christian ecclesiastical settlement known as Duibhlinn preceded the Viking settlement of about 841, Dyflin, which took its name from it; an excavation in Temple Bar has also found evidence of Anglo-Saxons there before 841. A Gaelic settlement, Áth Cliath, 'ford of hurdles', stood further up the river. The Irish government recognised 988 as the year of the city's first settlement, and Dublin marked its official millennium in 1988.

As the Kingdom of Dublin grew, the city became Ireland's principal settlement by the 12th century, following the Anglo-Norman invasion. It expanded rapidly from the 17th century and, after the Acts of Union in 1800, was briefly the second-largest city in the British Empire and sixth largest in Western Europe. Trinity College was established by Royal Charter in 1592 under Elizabeth I, and Guinness has been brewed at the St. James's Gate Brewery since 1759. After independence in 1922 Dublin became the capital of the Irish Free State, renamed Ireland in 1937.

Dublin is the capital and largest city of Ireland and its economic centre. The historic centre lies between the two canals, with O'Connell Street as its main thoroughfare and Grafton Street and Henry Street as the main shopping streets. The University of Dublin, the oldest university in Ireland, has Trinity College as its sole constituent college; the college was closed to Roman Catholics until 1793. Dublin City Council is led by a Lord Mayor, elected for a yearly term, who lives in the Mansion House.
dublin-castle: The castle was founded as a major defensive work by Meiler Fitzhenry on the orders of King John in 1204, some years after the Norman invasion of 1169. John commanded a castle with strong walls and good ditches for the defence of the city, the administration of justice and the protection of the king's treasure.

It stood on the highest point of central Dublin, beside the dark pool, the Dubh Linn that gave the city its name, where the River Poddle met the then much wider Liffey. Largely complete by 1230, it followed the Norman courtyard plan: a central square with no keep, tall walls and a circular tower at each corner. The Record Tower, from about 1228-1230, is the only part of the original fortification still standing.

The castle was the seat of English, and later British, government in Ireland under the Lordship of Ireland, the Kingdom of Ireland and the United Kingdom. It was the residence of the Lord Lieutenant or viceroy, housed the Chief Secretary for Ireland, served as a garrison and later for intelligence services, and at times held parliament and law courts. The Court of Castle Chamber sat there from about 1570. It was also a prison: Red Hugh O'Donnell and Art and Henry O'Neill escaped in January 1592, and Joseph Holt, a participant in the 1798 Rising, was held in the Bermingham Tower before transportation in 1799.

A fire in 1684 caused severe damage, and rebuilding turned the medieval fortress into a Georgian palace, with the State Apartments built in the 1740s. In 1907 the Irish Crown Jewels were stolen from the castle and never recovered. During the Easter Rising of 1916 twenty-five Irish Citizen Army members seized its entrance and guard room. In the Anglo-Irish War it was the centre of the British effort against separatism, and on the night of Bloody Sunday in 1920 three Irish Republican Army members were tortured and killed there.

After the Anglo-Irish Treaty of December 1921 the complex was ceremonially handed over to the Provisional Government led by Michael Collins. For about a decade it housed courts in place of the Four Courts, damaged in the Civil War. Douglas Hyde was inaugurated there as the first President of Ireland in 1938, and later presidents have been inaugurated in St Patrick's Hall. Elizabeth II was received there in 2011.

Visitors have not always praised the building: the Earl of Arran called it in the seventeenth century the worst castle in the worst situation in Christendom, and John Cornforth called it a piece of English make-do and mend. Today it holds the State Apartments, a museum, the Chester Beatty Library, the Garda Museum and the Revenue Museum, and is managed by the Office of Public Works.
dubrovnik: Dubrovnik is a city in southern Dalmatia, Croatia, on the Adriatic Sea, a seaport and the centre of Dubrovnik-Neretva County. Its population was 41,562 in 2021. UNESCO inscribed the Old City of Dubrovnik as a World Heritage Site in 1979, recognising its medieval architecture and fortifications. The two names, Dubrovnik and Ragusa, co-existed for centuries. Ragusa, recorded since at least the 10th century, was the official name of the Republic of Ragusa until 1808, while Dubrovnik, first recorded in the Charter of Ban Kulin in 1189, was in widespread use by the late 16th or early 17th century and is usually explained from a Slavic word for oak wood.

The area was inhabited in ancient times by the Illyrian tribe of the Pleraei. According to Constantine Porphyrogenitus, writing around 950, Ragusa was founded in the 7th century by refugees from Epidaurum, a Roman city about 15 kilometres to the south destroyed by Slavs fighting with the Avars. After the fall of the Ostrogothic kingdom the town came under Byzantine protection. In the 12th and 13th centuries it grew into an oligarchic republic and was under the sovereignty of Venice from 1205 to 1358. A fire destroyed most of the city on 16 August 1296, and a new urban plan followed. By the Peace Treaty of Zadar in 1358 it gained relative independence as a vassal of the Kingdom of Hungary.

Between the 14th and 19th centuries Dubrovnik ruled itself as a free state, prosperous from maritime trade, with its highest development in the 15th and 16th centuries, when it was noted for wealth and skilled diplomacy and was a cradle of Croatian literature. Latin was the official language until 1472, although most of the population spoke Croatian. An earthquake in 1667 almost destroyed the whole city. French forces occupied the republic on 27 May 1806, and in 1808 Marshal Marmont abolished it and joined its territory to the Napoleonic Kingdom of Italy.

After 1815 Dubrovnik belonged to the Kingdom of Dalmatia within the Habsburg Empire. In 1918 it became part of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, later Yugoslavia. During World War II it was in the Independent State of Croatia, and afterwards in the Socialist Republic of Croatia within Yugoslavia. In 1991, in the Croatian War of Independence, the Yugoslav People's Army besieged the city and shelled it, causing significant damage. After repair and restoration it became one of the best-known tourist destinations of the Mediterranean, often called the Queen of the Adriatic.
duccio: Duccio was born and died in Siena and worked mostly in the surrounding region of Tuscany. Much about his life and family is uncertain, though he is better documented than other Italian painters of his time. Archives record the debts he ran up and the fines he incurred, and some records say he was married with seven children. Gaps of years in the Sienese records have led scholars to speculate that he may have travelled to Paris, Assisi and Rome. Where he studied is debated: many believe he trained under Cimabue, while others think he learned from a Byzantine master in Constantinople.

Little is known of his painting before 1278, when, at the age of 23, he is recorded as having painted twelve account book cases. Only about thirteen of his works survive, and only two can be firmly dated, both major public commissions. The Rucellai Madonna, now in the Uffizi, was commissioned in April 1285 by the Compagnia del Laudesi di Maria Vergine for a chapel in Santa Maria Novella in Florence. The Maestà was commissioned for the high altar of Siena Cathedral in 1308, and Duccio completed it by June 1311.

Duccio's known works are on wooden panels, painted in egg tempera with gold leaf. His style resembles Byzantine art in its gold backgrounds and familiar religious scenes, but he began to soften its sharp lines. He used modelling of light and dark to reveal the figures beneath heavy drapery, so that hands, faces and feet became rounder and more three-dimensional. He was also one of the first painters to set figures in architectural settings, and he gave his figures a tenderness toward one another that makes Christ and the Virgin read as child and mother.

He had many followers, some of them anonymous masters known only through stylistic analysis. Simone Martini, from about 1305, and Pietro Lorenzetti, from about 1310, painted works with affinities to his, though each soon developed an independent style, and Ambrogio Lorenzetti is also named among those he influenced.
duchy-of-prussia: As Protestantism spread among the laity of the Teutonic Order's Prussian state, dissent grew against its Catholic rule. Albert, the Grand Master, a member of a cadet branch of the House of Hohenzollern, lacked the military resources to assert the Order's authority after losing a war against Poland, and his bishop, Georg von Polenz, had converted to Lutheranism in 1523. Martin Luther encouraged him to turn the Order's territory into a secular principality under his own rule.

On 10 April 1525 Albert resigned his office, became a Protestant and was granted the title Duke of Prussia by his uncle, King Sigismund I of Poland, in the Prussian Homage at Kraków, in a deal partly brokered by Luther. On 10 December 1525 the Prussian estates established the Lutheran Church by a Church Order. The Order was left with but 55 knights in Prussia.

The duchy had German, Polish (mainly in Masuria) and Lithuanian-speaking (mainly in Lithuania Minor) populations, and the capital remained Königsberg. Albert was formally a vassal of the Polish crown, but he kept self-government, his own army, his own currency, a provincial assembly and substantial autonomy in foreign affairs.

In 1544 Albert founded the Albertina University in Königsberg, which trained Lutheran pastors and theologians, and in 1560 Sigismund II Augustus of Poland gave it the rights and autonomy of Kraków University. Because services were held in native languages, exiled Lithuanian Protestant pastors were appointed professors, which made the Albertina a centre of Lithuanian language and literature.

Albert died in 1568 and his teenage son Albert Frederick inherited the duchy. In 1569 at Lublin the king also enfeoffed Joachim II of Brandenburg and his descendants as co-heirs. George William was invested with the duchy in 1623, which confirmed the personal union known as Brandenburg-Prussia.

During the Second Northern War Charles X Gustav of Sweden invaded and by the Treaty of Königsberg of January 1656 made the duchy a Swedish fief. When the war turned against him he made Frederick William, the Great Elector, full sovereign by the Treaty of Labiau. The Treaties of Wehlau and Bromberg in 1657 confirmed this, with John II Casimir of Poland recognising his full sovereignty. The burghers of Königsberg rejected the change, but in 1662 Frederick William entered the city with troops and forced it to swear allegiance.

Full sovereignty made it possible to raise the duchy to a kingdom in 1701, when Frederick III of Brandenburg became King in Prussia. After the First Partition of Poland in 1772, the former Ducal Prussia was reorganised as the Province of East Prussia.
dugout-canoe: A dugout is made from a log of suitable size, from which enough wood is removed to leave the vessel light and buoyant but still strong enough to carry its crew and cargo. The shape is fashioned to reduce drag, with sharp ends at bow and stern. The bark is stripped first. Before metal tools the log was hollowed out with controlled fires, and the burnt wood was removed with an adze. Another method was to chop parallel notches across the interior and split out the wood between them.

Some makers steamed the sides of the hollow log until pliable and bent them outwards to widen the beam and flatten the bottom. For rougher ocean water a dugout can be fitted with one or two outriggers, smaller logs mounted parallel to the hull on long poles.

Dugouts are the oldest boat type archaeologists have found, which probably reflects that massive timbers survive better than other materials such as bark. The Pesse canoe, found in the Netherlands, is believed to be the world's oldest boat and is carbon dated to between 8040 BCE and 7510 BCE. The Dufuna canoe from Nigeria, about 8,000 years old, is the oldest boat found in Africa, and a dugout of similar age from Kuahuqiao in Zhejiang, China, is the earliest found in Asia.

In Denmark, linden-wood dugouts found at Egådalen north of Aarhus are dated to 5210–4910 BCE and are the oldest known boats in Northern Europe. Linden was widely used in ancient Europe because the trees were abundant, grew tall, carved easily and were lighter than other forest trees.

In sub-Saharan Africa dugouts are commonplace from the Limpopo basin to West Africa and have been used for transport, fishing and hunting, once including the dangerous hunting of hippopotamus. Along the river system linking the Niger, Benue, Gambia and Senegal rivers and Lake Chad they carried people and goods along trade routes. A Nok terracotta of the first millennium BCE shows two paddlers with goods in a dugout.

In the Pacific Northwest cedar canoes over 18 metres long are made for everyday and ceremonial use. In the north-eastern woodlands the mishoon was burned out over several days. Pacific island canoes are very large and fitted with outriggers, and the Māori waka carried 40 to 80 warriors. According to Byzantine sources the Slavs built monoxyla, each holding 40 to 70 warriors, which the Rus used in attacks on Constantinople in the 9th and 10th centuries.
duncan-i-of-scotland: Duncan, in Gaelic Donnchad mac Crinain, was nicknamed An t-Ilgarach, the Diseased or the Sick. His ancestry is not certain, but modern texts make him the son of Crínán, hereditary lay abbot of Dunkeld, and Bethóc, a daughter of King Malcolm II. Earlier histories that follow John of Fordun supposed that he had ruled Strathclyde as an appanage between 1018 and 1034, an idea modern historians discount, though the Oxford Dictionary of National Biography supports it. Unlike the aged king of Shakespeare's Macbeth, the historical Duncan appears to have been a young man.

Malcolm II died on 25 November 1034 and Duncan succeeded him without apparent opposition. He may have been Malcolm's acknowledged successor, or tánaiste. The early part of his reign seems to have been uneventful, perhaps because of his youth. Macbeth is recorded as his dux, a word that meant a war leader, and since the dukes of Francia had replaced the Carolingian kings of the Franks half a century earlier, and England's Godwin of Wessex was also called dux, Macbeth may have been the power behind the throne.

In 1039 Duncan led a large Scottish army south to besiege Durham, and the expedition ended in disaster, though he survived. The following year he led an army north into Moray, Macbeth's domain, apparently on a punitive expedition. He was killed in action at the battle of Bothnagowan, now Pitgaveny near Elgin, by the men of Moray under Macbeth, probably on 14 August 1040.

Duncan is thought to have been buried at Elgin and later moved to the island of Iona. A variant of the Chronicle of the Kings of Alba gives his wife the Gaelic name Suthen, while John of Fordun, writing in the 14th century, made her a kinswoman of Siward, Earl of Northumbria, who would help restore her son Malcolm to the throne. Duncan had at least two sons.

Malcolm III, also called Máel Coluim mac Donnchada, was king from 1058 to 1093, after he assassinated and usurped Lulach, Macbeth's stepson. The second son, Donald III, or Domnall Bán, was king afterwards. Máel Muire, Earl of Atholl, is a possible third son, though this is uncertain. Duncan is the historical basis of the King Duncan of Shakespeare's Macbeth, written in 1606, in which he is killed in his sleep by Macbeth.
dungan-people: Dungan is a term used in territories of the former Soviet Union for Muslims of Hui origin; Turkic-speaking peoples in Xinjiang also sometimes call Hui Muslims Dungans. In Central Asia the Dungans call themselves Hui. The name is of obscure origin. One theory derives it from the Turkic word doñan, one who turns, comparable to the Chinese hui, and another from Donggan, Eastern Gansu, the region many Dungans trace their ancestry to, though the character gan differs. Central Asian Turkic and Tajik speakers have used it for Chinese-speaking Muslims for several centuries, and English and German writers used it from the 1830s.

The Dungans of the former Soviet republics descend from Hui who fled China after the Hui Minorities' War, also called the Dungan Rebellion, of the nineteenth century.
