According to Rimsky-Korsakoff, three groups crossed the Tian Shan into the Russian Empire in the severe winter of 1877-1878. About 1,000 people from Turpan, led by Ma Daren, reached Osh. A second group from Didaozhou in Gansu, led by the ahong Ma Yusuf, settled in the spring of 1878 at Yrdyk near Karakol; they numbered 1,130. A third, from Shaanxi, led by the rebel Bai Yanhu, settled at Karakunuz, now Masanchi, and numbered 3,314.

Under the Treaty of Saint Petersburg of 1881, which required Russian withdrawal from the Upper Ili basin, the Hui and Uyghur people of the Kulja area could move to the Russian side; Russian statistics record 4,682 Hui who did so between 1881 and 1883, settling at Sokuluk and in southeastern Kazakhstan and northern Kyrgyzstan. Some Dungans served in the Red Army in the Second World War. In February 2020 a conflict between ethnic Kazakhs and Dungans at Korday in Kazakhstan left ten dead according to official Kazakh sources, and about 600 people fled to Kyrgyzstan.

The Dungan language, which Dungans call the Hui language, is close to the Zhongyuan dialect of Mandarin spoken in southern Gansu and western Guanzhong in Shaanxi. It is tonal, preserves archaic Qing-era vocabulary, has loanwords from Russian, Arabic, Persian and Turkic, and is uniquely written in the Cyrillic script. More than two-thirds of Dungans also speak Russian.

Dungans keep elements of Chinese culture in cuisine and dress, and they practised foot binding until 1948, when the Soviet government banned it. Traditional marriage practices with matchmakers remain widespread. The Shaanxi Dungans hold more closely to Chinese customs than the Gansu Dungans. They have been counted in censuses as separate from Chinese, with 36,900 in Kazakhstan in 1999 and 58,409 in Kyrgyzstan in 2009. The nineteenth-century explorer Henry Lansdell noted that they abstained from spirits and opium and worked in farming, gardening and trade.
dunhuang: Dunhuang lies in an oasis in the far northwest of Gansu, with Crescent Lake and the Singing Sand Dunes nearby. It commands the western entrance to the Hexi Corridor, which leads to the north Chinese plains and the ancient capitals of Chang'an and Luoyang, and it stands where the southern Silk Road meets the road from India via Lhasa to Mongolia and southern Siberia. Its name is usually taken to mean Blazing Beacon, after the watchtowers lit to warn of raiding nomads, though scholars have proposed several other derivations.

By the 3rd century BCE the area was dominated by the Xiongnu, and it came under Chinese rule after Emperor Wu defeated them in 121 BCE. Dunhuang became one of four frontier garrison towns, and the Great Wall was extended to it. By the 2nd century CE the town had more than 76,000 people and served as a supply base for caravans crossing the desert. The first Buddhist caves of the area were cut in 353. Under the Sui and Tang it was a main stop on the routes between China and the rest of the world, and Sogdian merchants founded large colonies there.

After the An Lushan Rebellion weakened the Tang, the Tibetan Empire occupied the city until the local general Zhang Yichao expelled the Tibetans in 848. From 848 to about 1036 the city, under the Guiyi Circuit, was a multicultural entrepôt with one of the largest Sogdian communities in China. The Tanguts of Western Xia captured it in 1036, and the Mongols took it in 1227. Under the Ming it declined as trade moved to the southern sea routes. The present town was founded in 1725, east of the ruined old city.

Dunhuang is a county-level city in the prefecture-level city of Jiuquan. The Mogao Caves, 25 kilometres southeast of the city, hold 735 caves noted for Buddhist murals and statues and for the hoard of manuscripts found sealed in one cave. Other sites include the Yumen Pass, built in 111 BCE, the Yang Pass and the White Horse Pagoda. The manuscripts and artefacts from Dunhuang have been digitised by the International Dunhuang Project.
dunkirk: Dunkirk lies on the North Sea, 10 kilometres from the Belgian border, in the department of Nord. Its name derives from West Flemish dun, dune, and kerke, church, and so means church in the dunes. French Flemish, the local variety of Dutch, was commonly spoken there until the middle of the 20th century.

A fishing village arose in the late 10th century in a flooded coastal area held by the Counts of Flanders. About 960 Count Baldwin III had a wall built to protect it from Viking raids, and monks of Bergues Abbey drained the surrounding wetlands. The name is first mentioned in a tithe privilege of 27 May 1067. From 1384 it passed with Flanders to the Burgundian dukes and later to the Habsburg Netherlands. It was briefly held by Dutch rebels from 1577, and after Spanish forces retook it in 1583 it became a base for privateers known as the Dunkirkers. It changed hands between Spain, France and England until Charles II of England sold it to France on 17 October 1662 for £320,000.

In the First World War the city was bombarded from 1915, including by the German gun Lange Max in 1917, and its population fell from 39,000 in 1914 to 7,000 in the autumn of 1917. In 1940 more than 400,000 Allied soldiers were trapped around the port. Churchill ordered every available ship and boat to collect them, and 338,226 men, among them 123,000 French soldiers, were evacuated in Operation Dynamo. German forces held Dunkirk as a fortress until its commander surrendered on 9 May 1945.

Dunkirk is a port city with a commune population of about 86,000, and its harbour is the third largest in France. Its economy rests on steel, food processing, oil refining, shipbuilding and chemicals. Two of its belfries belong to the group of belfries of Belgium and France inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2005.
durance: The Durance has its source on the northern slope of the Sommet des Anges, above Montgenèvre, in the south-western Alps. It flows through Briançon, Embrun, Sisteron, Manosque and Cavaillon, receives the Verdon as its largest tributary, and joins the Rhône south of Avignon. The name is documented as Druentia in the 1st century CE and probably means the flowing one, from a Proto-Indo-European root meaning to run. The river keeps its name rather than the Clarée or the Guisane, which are longer where they join it, because the Durance valley is an old and important trade route, whereas the valleys of those two are effectively dead ends.

From antiquity until the 19th century the river was known for the difficulty of crossing it: its wide bed, strong current, changes of course after floods and inconstant flow hindered fords, and the only durable ones were at Mirabeau and Pertuis. In pre-Roman times it was the border between Celto-Ligurian peoples such as the Cavares and the Salyes. In the 12th century a flood swept away the town of Rama, and the flood of 1843 carried off several newly built suspension bridges. In the Middle Ages the county of Forcalquier stretched along the river, and the monks of Boscodon Abbey were given the privilege of floating timber down it in 1191.

The first known irrigation canal, the Canal Saint-Julien, was dug in 1171. The Adam de Craponne canal, 50 kilometres long, was dug in nine months in 1554. From 1839 to 1854 the engineer Franz Mayor de Montricher built the Marseille Canal, 80 kilometres long, to supply the city with drinking water, and it allowed the Marseille area to develop quickly. Freight on the river ended in the 20th century under competition from road and rail; there were ten raftmen left in 1896 and one in 1908.

A law of 1955 defined the Durance-Verdon project for producing electricity, supplying irrigation and drinking water and limiting floods. Over forty years it required 23 dams and water extraction points and the supply of 33 hydroelectric power stations. Most of the flow was diverted into canals downstream from Serre-Ponçon, whose lake is also a tourist attraction. The river and its valley are a protected Natura 2000 area. The Palais Longchamp in Marseille, built between 1862 and 1869, has a monument celebrating the arrival of the Durance's water, and the writer Jean Giono used the river in his imagined Provence.
durand-line: The Durand Line was established towards the end of the Great Game, the rivalry between the British and Russian empires, and made Afghanistan a buffer zone between their interests. Earlier, in the First Anglo-Afghan War, British-led Indian forces invaded in 1839 and were defeated in 1842. After the Second Anglo-Afghan War, which began in 1878, the Treaty of Gandamak of 1880 had Afghanistan cede control of various frontier areas to British India. In 1893 the government of India sent Mortimer Durand to Kabul to sign an agreement with Emir Abdur Rahman Khan fixing the limits of their spheres of influence and improving diplomatic relations and trade.

The single-page agreement, dated 12 November 1893, has seven short articles, among them a commitment not to interfere beyond the line. It created the Wakhan Corridor as a buffer between the British and Russian empires and gave Nuristan, then known as Kafiristan, and parts of Chitral to Afghanistan, while Afghanistan gave up claims to Waziristan and Chageh. It also permitted arms imports from British India and raised the subsidy paid to Afghanistan from 1.2 to 1.8 million rupees.

A joint survey began in 1894 and covered some 1,300 kilometres of the border. Three boundary commissions worked on it: the Asmar commission along Chitral, the Afghan-Waziristan commission and the Baluch-Afghan commission. At Nashagam on 9 April 1895 Nasrat and Bashgal were ceded to Afghanistan, and the Baluchistan section was completed on 13 May 1896. In 1896 the stretch from the Kabul River to China was declared demarcated by its continuous watershed ridge. The section near the Khyber Pass was demarcated after the Third Anglo-Afghan War, and the treaties of 1919 and 1921 confirmed the Indo-Afghan frontier. A short adjustment was made at Arundu in 1933 and 1934.

Pakistan inherited the line in 1947. On 26 July 1949 a loya jirga in Afghanistan declared that Afghanistan recognised neither the line nor any similar line and that all earlier agreements were void. In 1950 the British government held that Pakistan was in international law the inheritor of the rights and duties of the old Government of India and that the Durand Line was the international frontier. In 1956 the SEATO council likewise recognised that the sovereignty of Pakistan extended up to the line.

The line runs largely through mountains, south of the Hindu Kush, with its eastern end in the Karakoram and its western part in the lower, sparse Registan Desert. The Kunar, Kabul, Kurram and Gomal rivers cross it, and the Khyber Pass is the main land connection between Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent. Twelve Afghan provinces lie along the border, and in Pakistan it adjoins Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, Balochistan and Gilgit-Baltistan.
durango-city: The city stands at about 1,890 metres above sea level in the Valley of Guadiana, on the northwestern edge of the Central Mexican Highlands. Since the prehistoric period the area was a conduit for influences from north and south, between Aridoamerica and Mesoamerica. The first inhabitants were a people called the Nahoas, nomads who came from the north about 2,000 years ago. By the Post Classic period the area was inhabited by the Zacatecans and the Tepehuanos, who had migrated from the north-west.

Durango was founded on 8 July 1563 by the Spanish explorer Francisco de Ibarra, who named it after his hometown of Durango in the Spanish province of Biscay; the name is of Basque origin. He also named the surrounding area Nueva Vizcaya. The site was chosen for its proximity to the Cerro del Mercado, which was believed to contain large amounts of silver, though an important iron deposit was found in the end. Under Spanish rule the city was the capital of the province of Nueva Vizcaya in New Spain, which consisted mostly of what became the Mexican states of Durango and Chihuahua.

In 1826 the official name became Victoria de Durango, in honour of Guadalupe Victoria, the first president of Mexico and a native of the state. The diocese of Durango was erected in 1620 and became an archdiocese in 1891.

Victoria de Durango is the capital and largest city of the state of Durango. Its historic centre holds the largest concentration of historic monuments in northern Mexico, many in colonial and Baroque styles, and centres on the cathedral and the Plaza de Armas. The Cathedral Basilica became the cathedral in 1621, burned in 1634 and was rebuilt in the middle of the 18th century at the height of the city's mining prosperity. A mining tunnel that also served as a secret passage runs beneath it and is now a museum. The city's patron saint is Saint George, whose feast day is 23 April.
durban: Durban lies on the Natal Bay of the Indian Ocean, on the east coast of South Africa. North of the harbour and city centre is the mouth of the Umgeni River, and the flat city centre rises to the hills of the Berea on the west, while the Bluff runs along the coast to the south. The Zulu name, eThekwini, comes from itheku, meaning bay or lagoon. The city has a humid subtropical climate with hot, wet summers and mild, dry winters. Its natural harbour is one of the few between Port Elizabeth and Maputo, and it became a busy port of call for ship repairs after the port opened in the 1840s.

Archaeological evidence from the Drakensberg suggests that hunter-gatherers lived in the area from about 100,000 years ago, until agro-pastoralists from the north gradually absorbed them. Vasco da Gama sailed along the coast at Christmas 1497 and named it Natal, Portuguese for Christmas. In 1686 survivors of the wrecked Dutch East India Company ship Stavenisse were taken in by the Abambo people, a group of the Hlubi.

In 1823 James Saunders King and Lieutenant Francis George Farewell, former Royal Navy officers, sheltered from a storm in the Bay of Natal. In 1824 Farewell, with the trading company J. R. Thompson and Co. and with Henry Francis Fynn, set up a trading station at the bay and opened trade with Shaka, the Zulu king, who granted them land around it. The settlement was named after Sir Benjamin D'Urban in 1835 and became a borough in 1854. The Natal Railway Company opened South Africa's first operating steam railway, between the Point and the town, in 1860, and in the same year indentured labourers from British India began to arrive.

The Voortrekkers founded the Natalia Republic in 1839, with Pietermaritzburg as its capital. To keep Port Natal, Governor George Thomas Napier sent a force under Captain Thomas Charlton Smith, which built a fortified camp in May 1842. After its attack on a camp at Congella failed, the Voortrekkers besieged it. The trader Dick King and his servant Ndongeni rode to Grahamstown in 14 days to fetch reinforcements, and the siege was lifted. Britain annexed the republic in 1843. Natal became a province of the Union of South Africa in 1910, and Durban received city status in 1935.

Durban is the third most populous city in South Africa and the largest in KwaZulu-Natal, and its harbour is the busiest port in sub-Saharan Africa. It is the seat of the eThekwini Metropolitan Municipality, formed in 1999. Its people include large Zulu, Indian, White and Coloured communities, and the Indian community has influenced its cuisine, culture and religion. Its architecture runs from Victorian to contemporary, with Art Deco on many buildings.
durga: Durga's name means the impassable or unassailable one and is related to durg, a fortress. Words of this root occur in the Vedic literature, but the Vedic texts lack the legends later told of her. Asko Parpola reads a cylindrical seal from Kalibangan as showing a Durga-like goddess of war associated with the tiger, which would take her image back to the Indus Valley civilisation. In 1916 the historian Ramaprasad Chanda proposed that she developed from a mountain goddess worshipped by the dwellers of the Himalaya and the Vindhyas. Inscriptions of the 6th century CE already mention her victory over Mahishasura, and the Devi Mahatmya, composed between about 400 and 600 CE according to scholars, presents her as a well-established demon-slaying goddess.

In the Devi Mahatmya and the Devi Bhagavata Purana, the central texts of Shaktism, Durga is the embodiment of creation, preservation and destruction and is identified with Brahman, the ultimate reality. She is best known as Mahishasura-mardini, the slayer of the half-buffalo demon Mahishasura, who had won from Brahma the boon that only a woman could kill him. The gods gave form to their combined energy as a many-armed warrior woman, the Himalayas gave her a lion, and she killed the demon with her trident when he took buffalo form.

She is shown riding a lion or tiger with between eight and eighteen hands, each holding a weapon given by a male god, yet her face is calm. Shakta Hindus read the weapons as symbols of self-discipline, prayer and devotion. In Bengal she is a mother, of Ganesha, Kartikeya, Lakshmi and Sarasvati, although she is generally regarded as independent and not the consort of any god.

Her worship is most prominent in the east and north-east of the subcontinent. Durga Puja, held in the month of Ashvina, usually in September or October, is a major festival in Bengal, Odisha, Assam, Jharkhand and Bihar; clay images are worshipped for nine days and then immersed in water. Manuscripts of the 14th century give rules for it, and royalty and wealthy families sponsored public celebrations from at least the 16th century. In Nepal the festival is Dashain.

Images of her slaying the buffalo demon have been found at Buddhist sites in Afghanistan, Indonesia and north-eastern India, and in Indonesia at least 135 statues of Durga, dating from the 6th century onwards, have been found. Bankim Chandra Chatterjee's song Vande Mataram drew on her image as mother goddess.
durham-castle: Construction of the castle, of the motte and bailey design favoured by the Normans, began in 1072 under William the Conqueror, six years after the Norman Conquest and soon after the Normans first came to the North. The work was supervised by Waltheof, Earl of Northumbria, until he rebelled against William and was executed in 1076. Stone was cut from the cliffs below the walls and moved up with winches. The bishop of Durham, Walcher at the time, was appointed by the king to exercise royal authority on his behalf, with the castle as his seat, and after he bought the Earldom of Northumbria he began a line of prince-bishops.

The prince-bishops were entitled to raise an army, levy taxes and mint their own coinage, which gave them virtual autonomy as a defence against Scottish incursions and internal rebellions. Walcher built the castle as both a bishops' palace and a stronghold, with inner and outer baileys and a keep, and in May 1080 rebels from Northumbria besieged it for four days and killed him. In 1177 King Henry II seized the castle after a disagreement with Bishop Pudsey. Bishop Thomas Hatfield rebuilt the keep in the 1300s, and Bishop Antony Bek created the Great Hall in the early 14th century, now 14 metres high and over 30 metres long.

The Norman Chapel is the oldest accessible part of the castle, dated to 1075 or shortly after 1080. Its architecture is Anglian in character, possibly because forced Anglian labour was used. In the 15th century its windows were almost blocked by the expanded keep, and it fell into disuse until 1841. In the Second World War it served as a Royal Air Force command and observation post and it was re-consecrated in the 1950s. Tunstall's Chapel was built in the 16th century.

The bishops lost their temporal powers under the Durham (County Palatine) Act 1836. Auckland Castle had become the bishops' residence in 1832, and Bishop William Van Mildert donated Durham Castle to the University of Durham. University College moved in during 1837, after Bishop Edward Maltby had completed renovations. Since 1986 the castle and Durham Cathedral have been a World Heritage Site together, and seventeen elements of the castle are listed at Grade I. The castle is home to over 100 students and can be visited only on guided tours.
durham-university: Between around 1286 and 1291 the Benedictine monks of Durham established a hall at the University of Oxford. In 1381 it received an endowment from Thomas Hatfield, Bishop of Durham, and became Durham College, which was surrendered to the Crown in 1545 after the Reformation. Attempts to form a university in the city itself were made under King Henry VIII and under Oliver Cromwell, who issued letters patent in 1657 for a college. A proposal to let it confer degrees met opposition from Oxford and Cambridge, and the scheme was abandoned at the restoration of the monarchy in 1660.

The university came into being through the Durham University Act 1832, passed at the instigation of Archdeacon Charles Thorp with the support of the bishop of Durham, William van Mildert, and given royal assent by King William IV on 4 July 1832. It opened on 28 October 1833 and received a royal charter on 1 June 1837. Degrees were at first open only to members of the Church of England. Early accommodation was in the Archdeacon's Inn, now Cosin's Hall, and in 1837 the university was granted the use of Durham Castle, formerly the bishop's palace.

In the early twentieth century the Newcastle division, made up of Armstrong College and the Durham University College of Medicine, grew to outnumber the Durham colleges. A reform of 1909 made the university federal, with its seat fixed in Durham. From 1959 new colleges were founded on the Elvet Hill site, beginning with Grey College, named after the second Earl Grey, prime minister when the university was founded.

Durham is a collegiate university: academic departments provide research and teaching, while 17 colleges are responsible for domestic arrangements and welfare. Graduates have long used the Latin post-nominal letters Dunelm, from Dunelmensis, meaning of Durham. The estate includes 83 listed buildings, from the 11th-century Durham Castle to the 1960s students' union, and the university manages the Durham World Heritage Site with Durham Cathedral. Its library, founded in January 1833 with a gift of 160 volumes from Bishop van Mildert, includes Bishop Cosin's Library, founded in 1669.
durrani-empire: Ahmad Khan, of the Sadozai lineage of the Abdali tribe, was the son of Muhammad Zaman Khan, who had served as governor of Herat, and a commander under Nader Shah. After Nader Shah's death in June 1747 a loya jirga, or grand council, met near Kandahar for nine days. The two chief contestants were Hajji Jamal Khan of the Mohammadzai and Ahmad Khan. A holy man, Mohammad Sabir Khan, spoke for Ahmad Khan, reputedly placed sheaves of wheat or barley in his turban and crowned him with the title Durr-i-Durran, Pearl of the Pearls, from which the tribe took the name Durrani.

Ahmad Shah took Qalati Ghilji and Ghazni from the Ghilji and Kabul and Peshawar from the Mughal governor Nasir Khan. In 1749 the Mughal emperor Ahmad Shah Bahadur ceded Sindh and the Punjab to save his capital, and Ahmad Shah then took Mashhad from Shahrukh Afshar and subdued the peoples north of the Hindu Kush. He sacked Delhi in 1757. In 1762 his forces killed thousands of Sikhs in the Punjab, in what Sikhs call the Vaḍḍā Ghallūghārā, and destroyed the Golden Temple at Amritsar, yet the Sikhs rebuilt it and he never subdued them. He died east of Kandahar in 1772.

His son Timur Shah Durrani took the throne in November 1772 and made Kabul the capital. Timur's sons fought one another: Zaman Shah, who succeeded in 1793, was blinded and replaced by Mahmud Shah in 1801, and Shuja Shah ruled from 1803 to 1809. On 7 June 1809 Shuja signed with the British East India Company the first Afghan pact with a European power. By 1818 the Sadozai rulers held little more than Kabul and the land within 160 kilometres of it. Kashmir was lost to the Sikh Empire at the Battle of Shopian in 1819, and Ayub Shah was deposed in 1823.

The army was based on cavalry armed with flintlocks, who made hit-and-run attacks. Its core was 10,000 mounted ghulams, or slave-soldiers, carrying blunderbusses; a third of them were Qizilbash who had served Nader Shah. The bulk of the army was irregular Afghan tribal cavalry armed with lance and broadsword, and infantry played a very small part. Ahmad Shah balanced tribal alliances and hostilities, a balance his successors upset when they tried to rule without the other Durrani chiefs. The Barakzai under Dost Muhammad Khan later displaced the dynasty at Kabul, and the empire is regarded as the foundation of the modern Afghan state.
durres: Durrës lies on the Bay of Durrës, on a flat alluvial plain between the mouths of the Erzen and the Ishëm rivers, on the Adriatic coast of Albania. The municipality stretches from the mouth of the Ishëm at the Cape of Rodon, across the Bay of Lalzi, to the Shkëmbi i Kavajës in the south, and the climate is a hot-summer Mediterranean one.

The area was inhabited from the Eneolithic, and from protohistoric times by Illyrian peoples. Greek colonists from Corinth and Corcyra founded the city in 627 BCE, on the coast of the Taulantii, an Illyrian tribe. A flourishing commercial centre emerged, and the construction of a Doric-style treasury at Olympia by the citizens of Epidamnos about the 6th century BCE suggests that it was among the richest cities of the Greek world. After the Illyrian Wars the Roman Republic made Dyrrachium its sole name.

The city became part of the Roman Empire and then of the Byzantine Empire, and the Via Egnatia began there and ran east across the Balkans to Constantinople. Its bishopric was created around 58 and became an archbishopric in 449. The Byzantine walls were built in the sixth century, after the Visigoth invasion of 481. In the late 10th century it passed to Samuel of Bulgaria; around 1005 his governor, Ashot Taronites, fled to Constantinople and offered the city to Emperor Basil II, and it returned to Byzantine rule.

The Ottomans ruled from 1501 until 1912 and renamed it Dırac. The city did not prosper in the first two centuries and became a den of piracy; its significance for the Ottomans lay in its castle and its salt deposits. After Ismail Qemali raised the Albanian flag on 26 November 1912, Serbia occupied the city three days later. It became Albania's second national capital, after Vlorë, on 7 March 1914 under Prince Wilhelm, and remained so until 11 February 1920, when the Congress of Lushnjë made Tirana the capital.

Durrës is the second most populous city of Albania, with roughly 2,500 years of recorded history. Its port is one of the largest on the Adriatic, with daily ferries to Bari in Italy. The Amphitheatre of Durrës, once seating 20,000, is the largest amphitheatre in the Balkans and is on Albania's tentative list for World Heritage status. The Durrës Archaeological Museum holds the mosaic known as The Beauty of Durrës.
dushanbe: Dushanbe lies in the Hisar Valley, at 750 to 930 metres above sea level, at the confluence of the Varzob and the Kofarnihon rivers. The Hisar range, which reaches up to 4,000 metres, bounds it on the north and east, and the Babatag, Aktau, Rangontau and Karatau mountains bound it on the south, so that it is an intermontane basin. The climate has hot summers and chilly winters, and the surrounding mountains shield the city from the extremely cold air of Siberia. Before the 1960s most of the city stood on the left bank of the Varzob, but construction later carried it across.

In the Stone Age Mousterian tool-users lived in the Hisar Valley. The Hisar, Bishkent and Vakhsh cultures, whose stone tools were found within modern Dushanbe at the confluence of the Varzob and Luchob, are thought to have inhabited it in the second millennium BCE, keeping cattle, farming and weaving. The area was later settled by the Achaemenid Empire, Greco-Bactria, the Kushan Empire and the Hephthalites, and in the Middle Ages by settlements such as Hulbuk, with its palace. Islam was introduced in the eighth century.

The town first appears in the historical record in 1676, in a letter from the Balkh khan Subhonquli Bahodur to Tsar Fyodor III, although the Balkh historian Mahmud ibn Wali mentioned the area in the 1630s. It was called Kasabai Dushanbe, the town of Monday, after a large bazaar held each Monday. Its place between caravan routes to Karategin and the Alay Valley, and to Afghanistan through the Anzob Pass, helped the market grow. It then had a population of about 7,000 to 8,000. From the 17th to the early 20th century it was controlled at times by the Beg of Hisor, by Balkh and finally by Bukhara, before the Russian Empire conquered it.

The Bolsheviks captured Dushanbe in 1922, and in 1924 it became the capital of the Tajik Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic, which began its rapid growth. When the Tajik SSR separated from the Uzbek SSR in 1929, its capital was renamed Stalinabad on 19 October 1929, incorporating the nearby districts of Shohmansur, Mavlono and Sari Osiyo. The old name returned in late 1961 as a result of de-Stalinization. During the middle of the 20th century the city had a majority Russian and Eastern European population. Dushanbe became the capital of an independent Tajikistan on 9 September 1991, and the Tajik Civil War of the 1990s checked its growth.

Dushanbe is the capital and largest city of Tajikistan and holds most of the country's major hospitals. Its sights include the Tajikistan National Museum, the National Museum of Antiquities, Rudaki Avenue and the National Library. Its electricity is mainly hydroelectric, from the Nurek Dam, and its trolleybus system dates from 1955.
dusseldorf: Düsseldorf lies at the centre of the Lower Rhine basin, where the Düssel flows into the Rhine, and most of the city is on the east bank. It lies in the middle of the Rhine-Ruhr metropolitan region. Its name comes from the small river Düssel, with the suffix dorf, meaning village, so that the literal meaning is village on the Düssel. It reflects the original character of the settlement as a fishing and farming community on the riverbanks.

In the 7th and 8th centuries the odd farming or fishing settlement stood where the Düssel meets the Rhine, and the city grew from such settlements. In 1186 Düsseldorf came under the rule of the County of Berg, a state of the Holy Roman Empire. In 1263 the Count of Berg granted ferry rights to its inhabitants, and it gained city rights in 1288 after the Battle of Worringen.

In the Late Middle Ages and Renaissance it grew into a regional political and cultural centre under the Dukes of Berg and later as the capital of the United Duchies of Jülich-Cleves-Berg. In the 17th and 18th centuries it became known for its court culture and early art academy. During the Napoleonic era it was briefly part of the Grand Duchy of Berg. After the Congress of Vienna in 1815 the Rhineland, including Düsseldorf, was incorporated into the Kingdom of Prussia. The city lost its status as a capital but became the seat of a regional governor and it industrialised rapidly in the 19th century; its population passed 100,000 in 1882.

In the Second World War Düsseldorf was the location of a Nazi prison with forced labour subcamps and of five subcamps of the Buchenwald concentration camp, and the city's Rabbi, who had fled to the Netherlands, died in Auschwitz in 1943. The city entered the British occupation zone on 21 June 1945, and in 1946 it became the capital of the new state of North Rhine-Westphalia. Its population peaked at just over 705,000 in 1962.

Düsseldorf is the capital of North Rhine-Westphalia and, with 619,444 inhabitants in 2025, the second-largest city in the state after Cologne. It is an international business and financial centre, known for its fashion and trade fairs, and it has the largest Japanese community in Germany. The Kunstakademie Düsseldorf, its academy of arts, counts Joseph Beuys, Emanuel Leutze, August Macke and Gerhard Richter among its members.
dutch-east-india-company: After the Dutch Revolt began, the Portuguese used an international syndicate operating from Hamburg, which cut Dutch merchants out of the Asian trade, while their system could not raise its supply of pepper to meet demand. In 1580 the Portuguese crown had been united with the Spanish crown, with which the Dutch Republic was at war, so the Portuguese Empire became a fitting target. Dutch merchants such as Jan Huyghen van Linschoten and Cornelis de Houtman gained firsthand knowledge of the secret Portuguese routes.

The English formed a monopoly company in 1600, and in 1602 the States General followed, founding the United East India Company on 20 March by amalgamating existing companies, with a 21-year monopoly on Asian trade. Any citizen of the Dutch Republic could buy shares, which were traded in open-air markets, one of which became the Amsterdam Stock Exchange.

The charter let the company build forts, keep armies, make treaties and strike its own coins. For a time it monopolised nutmeg, mace and cloves and sold them at 14 to 17 times the price it paid in Indonesia, while as sole buyer it forced down the prices paid to producers in the Spice Islands. Jan Pieterszoon Coen, governor-general from 1619, stormed Jayakarta on 30 May 1619 and founded Batavia as headquarters. In the 1620s almost the entire native population of the Banda Islands was driven away, starved or killed so that Dutch plantations could grow nutmeg.

After 1730 the company declined, squeezed out of Persia, Suratte, the Malabar Coast and Bengal, while corruption and private trading by its staff spread. It paid dividends averaging about 18% for almost 200 years, but went bankrupt and was formally dissolved in 1799, and the government of the Batavian Republic took over its possessions and debt.

The headquarters were in Amsterdam, with a board of directors known as the Heeren XVII. At its height the company had 25,000 employees in Asia and 11,000 en route, recruited across north-west Europe and from local Asian labour markets. Posts included Batavia, the Cape Colony from 1652 and Dejima in Japan from 1641. Between 1602 and 1795 about one million seamen and craftsmen left Holland, and only about 340,000 returned. Twenty-five million pages of its records survive and were added to UNESCO's Memory of the World register in 2003.
dutch-empire: The Dutch rebel provinces declared independence from the Spanish Empire with the Act of Abjuration of 1581. In 1580 Philip II brought Portugal into the Iberian Union with Spain, which closed all Portuguese markets to the United Provinces, and in 1595 the Dutch set sail to acquire Asian goods for themselves. By 1600 Dutch traders had penetrated the Asian spice trade but lacked capital, and in 1602 the States General merged several enterprises into the semi-state-owned Dutch East India Company, the VOC, which was granted a monopoly over Asian trade. The Dutch West India Company followed in 1621 for the Atlantic, the Americas and the west coast of Africa.

Dutch activities abroad were at first commercial ventures that controlled shipping routes through strategically placed outposts rather than large territories. By the mid-17th century the two companies exercised quasi-governmental powers to negotiate treaties, wage war and administer territory. The conquest of the Banda Islands from 1609 to 1621, also called the Banda genocide, followed a collapse in negotiations over the Dutch nutmeg monopoly; under Jan Pieterszoon Coen massacres, deportations, starvation and disease left the islands severely depopulated. The West India Company took Pernambuco from Portugal in 1630 and by 1650 controlled the sugar and slave trades. The Cape of Good Hope was founded in 1652 as a victualling station.

Wars with England between 1652 and 1784 cost many settlements, and the rise of the British East India Company weakened Dutch influence. After the French invasion of 1795 made the Batavian Republic, Britain occupied Dutch colonies in Asia, South Africa and the Caribbean. After the Japanese occupation of 1942 to 1945 the Dutch East Indies became Indonesia, and Suriname became independent in 1975.

Aruba, Curaçao and Sint Maarten remain autonomous constituent countries of the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Names of Dutch origin survive in New York, among them Brooklyn, Harlem and Staten Island, and the Dutch Fort Zeelandia still stands in Paramaribo. Between 1800 and 1950 Dutch engineers built roads, railways and irrigation systems in Indonesia, which became the material base of the colonial and later Indonesian state. Dutch is the official language of Suriname, Aruba, Bonaire and Curaçao, and Indonesian inherited many words from Dutch.
dutch-golden-age: In 1568 the Seven Provinces that later signed the Union of Utrecht rebelled against Philip II of Spain, beginning the Eighty Years' War. Antwerp, then arguably the most important port in the world, fell to Spain on 17 August 1585 after a siege, and the division between the Northern and Southern Netherlands was established. Under the terms of the surrender, Protestants unwilling to reconvert were given four years to leave. More Protestants moved north between 1585 and 1630 than Catholics moved south, and many settled in Amsterdam, which became one of the most important ports and commercial centres in the world by 1630. The Peace of Westphalia in 1648 brought the Dutch Republic formal recognition of its independence.

The Dutch East India Company (VOC), founded in 1602, was among the first multinational corporations, financed by shares that established the Amsterdam Stock Exchange. It received a Dutch monopoly on Asian trade, which it kept for two centuries, and became the largest commercial enterprise of the 17th-century world. The Bank of Amsterdam was established in 1609. The Republic's position between the Bay of Biscay and the Baltic let its ships carry goods between the two, and the Dutch share of European shipping was well over half during most of the period. From 1640 the VOC held a monopoly on trade with Japan through Dejima, and until 1854 the Dutch were Japan's sole window to the Western world.

The prosperity came with violence. In 1621 Jan Pieterszoon Coen had almost all the inhabitants of the Banda Islands massacred, and about 1.7 million people were enslaved by Dutch slavers between the 17th and 19th centuries. Calvinism was the state religion, though bitter controversy between strict Calvinists and Remonstrants was settled in favour of the former at the Synod of Dort in 1618–19.

The Republic attracted scientists and thinkers from across Europe. The University of Leiden, founded in 1575, became a gathering place for intellectuals, and René Descartes, Jan Amos Comenius and Pierre Bayle all lived and published there. Wealthy merchants rather than nobles were the patrons of art. Dutch painting led in developing still life, landscape and genre painting, canals were dug and merchants built houses along them, and the book trade flourished, with the House of Elzevir producing reliable pocket editions of classical Latin texts. Conflicts with neighbouring powers and declining economic influence ended the period, usually dated to the Rampjaar of 1672. Since 2019 the Amsterdam Museum has stopped using the phrase Golden Age, saying it hides the colonial past and slavery.
dutch-republic: Until the 16th century the Low Countries consisted of duchies, counties and prince-bishoprics, almost all under the supremacy of the Holy Roman Empire. Seven provinces of the Spanish Netherlands revolted against Spanish rule, formed a mutual alliance in 1579 in the Union of Utrecht and declared their independence in 1581 in the Act of Abjuration. In 1588, when the States General could not agree on a new monarch, they confederated.

Each province kept a high degree of independence from the federal assembly, the States General. Each was led by a stadtholder, an office nominally open to anyone but usually given to a member of the House of Orange. Under the Peace of Westphalia in 1648 the republic gained about 20 percent more territory, governed directly by the States General as Generality Lands.

With only around 1.5 million inhabitants, the republic controlled a worldwide network of trade routes through the Dutch East India Company and the Dutch West India Company. Amsterdam became the hub of world trade, and by the mid-1660s had about 200,000 people. Refugees helped the economy, among them Portuguese and Spanish Jews, Protestants from Antwerp, French Huguenots and English Dissenters. Nearly half of Amsterdam's residents in the 17th and 18th centuries were first-generation immigrants.

After the death of William II in 1650 the regents allowed no new stadtholder in Holland for 22 years, and Johan de Witt became the dominant figure. The republic fought three naval wars against England between 1652 and 1674. In the Disaster Year of 1672 England, France, Münster and Cologne attacked it, Johan de Witt and his brother Cornelis were lynched and William III was appointed stadtholder.

After William III died in 1702 the office stood vacant in Holland, Zeeland and Utrecht until William IV was appointed in 1747. In this Second Stadtholderless Period the republic lost its great-power status and its primacy in world trade. Unrest in the 1780s was suppressed by a Prussian invasion supporting the stadtholder. Defeated by France, the republic ended in the Batavian Revolution of 1795, when the stadtholder was expelled.

The republic was a predecessor of the present-day Netherlands and its first independent nation state. It was more tolerant of different religions and ideas than contemporary states. Painters such as Rembrandt and Johannes Vermeer and scientists such as Hugo Grotius, Christiaan Huygens and Antonie van Leeuwenhoek worked under it, and the 17th century became known as the Dutch Golden Age.
dutch-west-india-company: When the Dutch East India Company (VOC) was founded in 1602, some Amsterdam traders objected to its monopoly and looked for other routes to Asia. Trade with the Caribbean was hampered by Spain, which refused to make peace if a West India Company were established, and during the Twelve Years' Truce the Dutch sailed to South America under foreign flags. After the truce expired in April 1621, the company was founded. Among its promoters were Reynier Pauw, Willem Usselincx and Jessé de Forest. On 3 June 1621 the States-General granted it a charter giving a 24-year monopoly on trade and colonisation in West Africa and on the American coast between Newfoundland and the Straits of Magellan.

Like the VOC, the company had five chambers, in Amsterdam, Rotterdam, Hoorn, Middelburg and Groningen, and a board of 19 members, the Heeren XIX. Funding was arranged only in 1623, when the States General and the VOC pledged one million guilders, and the capital of 2.8 million florins was smaller than the VOC's original 6.5 million. Investors came slowly, in part because shareholders had no control over the directors' policy, and the company offered foreign investors equal standing. Unlike the VOC it had no right to deploy military troops, and in 1623 it had 15 ships trading along the West African coast and Brazil.

After a plan to seize the Portuguese colonies failed, privateering became a major aim, and Piet Hein's capture of the Spanish silver fleet was its most spectacular success. The Dutch held Portuguese territory in north-eastern Brazil from 1624 to 1654, with Mauritsstad, present-day Recife, as the capital of New Holland, before being driven out. In North America the company allowed investors to found patroonships in New Netherland from 1629, of which Rensselaerswyck was the most successful, and Manhattan with Fort Amsterdam served as the first capital. It also held posts on the Gold Coast, the Slave Coast and briefly Loango-Angola. Fur and sugar were the main trade goods in the Americas, while African posts traded enslaved people, gold, copper and ivory.

In 1662 the company obtained asiento subcontracts with the Spanish Crown to deliver 24,000 enslaved Africans, and it made Curaçao a centre of the Atlantic slave trade. It could not repay its debts and was dissolved in 1674, but a second West India Company was chartered the same year with the same area and fewer directors. Sint Eustatius became its most profitable asset, and from 1738 it outsourced the slave trade to private enterprise. After the Fourth Anglo-Dutch War of 1780–1784 the British took Sint Eustatius, Berbice, Essequibo, Demerara and some forts on the Gold Coast. In 1791 it was decided not to renew the charter, and the territories passed to the States General.
dwight-d-eisenhower: Eisenhower was born David Dwight Eisenhower in Denison, Texas, on 14 October 1890, the third of seven sons of Ida Stover and David Jacob Eisenhower. His mother soon reversed his forenames to avoid two Davids in the family. All the boys were nicknamed Ike, and by the Second World War only Dwight still was. He graduated from West Point in 1915. In the First World War his request for an overseas assignment was denied, and he commanded a unit that trained tank crews at Camp Colt, his first command; he never saw combat.

He was promoted to brigadier general on 3 October 1941. In November 1942 he was appointed commander of the Allied forces in the North African theatre, in the campaign designated Operation Torch. In December 1943 President Roosevelt decided that he, not Marshall, would be Supreme Allied Commander in Europe, and he planned and carried out the Normandy assault of June 1944, Operation Overlord. After the German surrender he was military governor of the American-occupied zone of Germany, and he ordered camera crews to document the Nazi concentration camps for the Nuremberg Trials. He then served as Army Chief of Staff, president of Columbia University from 1948, and first supreme commander of NATO.

He entered the 1952 presidential race as a Republican, in part to block Senator Robert A. Taft, who opposed NATO, and won that election and the 1956 election, 457 to 73 in the electoral vote, against Adlai Stevenson II. As president he gave the Atoms for Peace speech to the United Nations on 8 December 1953, and in 1956 he signed the bill authorising the Interstate Highway System. After the Soviet launch of Sputnik he led the American response, which included NASA. Alaska and Hawaii were admitted as states in 1959. He died on 28 March 1969, aged 78.

His New Look policy relied on nuclear deterrence, building a stockpile of nuclear weapons and delivery systems to deter threats and save money by cutting expensive Army combat units. In his first State of the Union address in February 1953 he said he would use the authority of the presidency to end segregation in the District of Columbia and the Armed Forces, and when the services resisted he used government control of military spending to force the change. In his farewell address he warned of the dangers of massive military spending, which he called the military–industrial complex.
dynamite: Alfred Nobel's father, Immanuel Nobel, was an industrialist, engineer and inventor who built bridges and buildings in Stockholm. His construction work led him to look for ways of blasting rock that were more effective than black powder. At 17 Alfred was sent abroad for two years and in France studied under the chemist Théophile-Jules Pelouze, who cautioned him against using nitroglycerin as a commercial explosive because it was so sensitive to shock. Nobel invented the detonator, or blasting cap, which allowed a controlled explosion to be set off from a distance, and in 1863 he made his first successful detonation of pure nitroglycerin. On 3 September 1864 his brother Emil and several others were killed in an explosion at the factory at Heleneborg.

Despite the blasting cap, nitroglycerin was too unstable for commercial use. Nobel tried to combine it with a substance that would make it safe to handle without lessening its force. Mixtures with cement, coal and sawdust failed, but diatomaceous earth, which is fossilised algae, stabilised it. He obtained patents in England on 7 May 1867 and in Sweden on 19 October 1867. Dynamite is usually sold as cardboard cylinders about 200 mm long and 32 mm across, and is rated by its weight strength, the share of nitroglycerin it contains, usually from 20 to 60 per cent. It weeps nitroglycerin over time.

Dynamite rapidly gained wide use as a safer alternative to black powder and nitroglycerin. Nobel controlled his patents tightly and shut down unlicensed makers, though a few American businessmen avoided the patent by using other absorbents such as resin. In the United States it was first made by the Giant Powder Company of San Francisco. For several decades from the 1940s the largest producer in the world was the Union of South Africa, where De Beers established a factory at Somerset West in 1902 to supply the gold mines of the Witwatersrand.

Dynamite has never been popular in warfare, because it degenerates quickly under severe conditions and can be set off by fire or a stray bullet. The German armed forces adopted TNT as a shell filling in 1902.
dzungaria: Dzungaria, also called Northern Xinjiang or Beijiang, is the northern half of Xinjiang and covers about 777,000 square kilometres. The Altai Mountains bound it on the north and the Tian Shan on the south, and it borders Kazakhstan on the west and Mongolia on the east. Before the mid-18th century the name could cover a wider area, coterminous with the Oirat-led Dzungar Khanate. Its core is the triangular Dzungarian Basin, with the Gurbantünggüt Desert at its centre. The western corner of the basin is the Dzungarian Gate, a historically important gateway between Dzungaria and the Kazakh Steppe, and the northern corner is the valley of the upper Irtysh River.

The first inhabitants were Indo-European-speaking peoples such as the Tocharians in prehistory and the Jushi Kingdom in the first millennium BCE. The Han dynasty sent an explorer west along the northernmost Silk Road trackway, and in the latter half of the sixth century the Göktürk leader Istämi received Dzungaria as an inheritance from his father. Over the centuries the region was ruled or controlled, wholly or in part, by the Xiongnu, the Tang dynasty, the Mongol Empire and the Yuan dynasty, among others.

Travellers going west from China went either north of the Tian Shan through Dzungaria or south of it through the Tarim Basin. Trade usually took the south side and migrations the north, because the Tarim leads to the Ferghana Valley and Iran, while Dzungaria leads only to the open steppe.

The region takes its name from the Dzungar people, from the Mongolian zűn gar, meaning left hand, since the western Mongols, the Oirats, stood on the left when the Mongol Empire divided. Dzungar power reached its height in the second half of the 17th century, when Galdan Boshugtu Khan repeatedly intervened in the affairs of the Kazakhs, and its widest limit included Kashgar, Yarkand and Khotan. The Qing Empire destroyed the khanate about 1757–1759. At the time of the Qing conquest Dzungaria was inhabited chiefly by nomadic, steppe-dwelling Tibetan-Buddhist Dzungars. After what is called the Dzungar genocide the Qing repopulated the area with Han and Hui people, and in 1884 they unified Dzungaria and the Tarim Basin into one province, Xinjiang.

The main cities are Ürümqi, Yining and Karamay. Wheat, barley, oats and sugar beets are grown, irrigated with melted snow from the mountains, and cattle, sheep and horses are raised. The region has deposits of coal, gold and iron as well as large oil fields. The name has largely disappeared from the map, but survives in the Dzungarian Alatau and in the Djungarian hamster.
